For people under 60, they tended to level off after 8,000–10,000 steps. Another analysis combining multiple studies found benefits starting at about 3,867 steps/day. Thereafter, each additional 1,000 steps/day was associated with about a 15% lower risk of death. By exercise time: a combined analysis of multiple follow-up studies (observational, with no assignment to groups) found that people who did 1–2 times the guideline’s minimum amount of exercise had about a 31% lower risk of death than people who did none (HR 0.69). That amount is 7.5–15 MET·h/week, roughly equivalent to 150–300 minutes/week of brisk walking. People who did not reach the minimum still had about a 20% lower risk (HR 0.80). Those who did 3–5 times the minimum had about a 39% lower risk (HR 0.61), the largest reduction. Doing more did not lower it further, but showed no harm either (above 10 times the minimum, HR 0.69). Another pooled study measured activity with accelerometers: the quarter of people with the most moderate-to-vigorous activity had about a 48% lower risk of death than the quarter with the least (HR 0.52). An accelerometer is a device worn on the body to measure activity directly. This pooled study included 8 studies and 36,383 people, with an average age of 62.6 years and a median follow-up of only 5.8 years. The paper’s authors recalculated the results after excluding people who died in the first two years, and the results were essentially unchanged. But they also said bias caused by people moving less because they were ill might remain.
entries.sources: Paluch AE et al. (2022). Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9>; Banach M et al. (2023). The association between daily step count and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: a meta-analysis. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. <https://doi.org/10.1093/eurjpc/zwad229>; Arem H et al. (2015). Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship. JAMA Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2015.0533>; Ekelund U et al. (2019). Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis. BMJ. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l4570>
entries.notes: Step counts and exercise duration describe the same thing, just counted differently; meeting the target for either one is enough. The increase from 4,000 steps to 7,000 steps offers the best return; there is no need to insist on reaching 10,000 steps. Note that these types of studies are merely observational follow-ups: among the group that walks the least and moves the least, there is a mix of people who were already sick and unable to walk. They moved less because their health was failing, rather than dying early because they moved less. Consequently, the calculated differences are often inflated. For the few studies that directly measured activity levels using devices, the follow-up periods were short and the participants were older. Therefore, "risk reduced to 0.52 times" may be an overstatement—this is the book's inference. Nevertheless, the trend that more movement is better remains clear.

entries.title: Have blood lipids checked regularly in adulthood: once every 2 to 5 years before age 40, and annually starting at age 40; if you have hypertension or hyperlipidemia, take medications regularly as prescribed by a doctor, and do not stop on your own
entries.cost: Centrally procured antihypertensive drugs and statins cost a few yuan to several tens of yuan per month. Taking them once a day takes very little time. The difficulty lies in having to keep taking them continuously and not stopping just because you feel fine. A blood lipid test requires drawing one tube of blood. Those aged 65 and older have one free health checkup per year, which includes blood lipids; see Section 6, Item 18 (General Health Checkup Package).
entries.summary: For every 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure (the upper number), the probability of death drops by about 13%, and stroke drops by about 27%. When statins lower LDL cholesterol by 1 unit, the probability of death drops by about 10%. People who take their medication on time have a 30% to 45% lower probability of death compared to those who frequently miss doses. Have blood lipids checked once every 2 to 5 years before age 40, and annually starting at age 40.
entries.benefit: Pooling multiple randomized controlled trials: for every 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure, all-cause mortality risk is about 13% lower (RR 0.87). Systolic blood pressure is the high pressure reading. Major cardiovascular events are about 20% lower (RR 0.80). Stroke is about 27% lower (RR 0.73). Heart failure is about 28% lower (RR 0.72). Taking statins lowers low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL). For every 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL, mortality risk is about 10% lower (RR 0.90). With this same reduction, major vascular events are about 22% lower (RR 0.78). In addition, pooling multiple observational follow-up studies that only record without randomized grouping: individuals who take their medication as prescribed at ≥80% have a lower risk of death than those who frequently miss doses. For statins, this is about 45% lower (RR 0.55). For antihypertensives, this is about 29% lower (RR 0.71). Regarding how often to check blood lipids, according to the recommendations of the Healthy China Initiative: individuals under age 40 with normal blood lipids should be tested once every 2 to 5 years. Those aged 40 and older should be tested at least once a year. Individuals at high risk for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases should be tested once every 6 months. The 2023 edition of the Chinese Guidelines for Lipid Management maintains the same wording for before and after age 40, while revising the recommendation for high-risk individuals to testing based on individual clinical needs.
entries.sources: Ettehad D et al. (2016). Blood pressure lowering for prevention of cardiovascular disease and death: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)01225-8>; Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) Collaboration (2010). Efficacy and safety of more intensive lowering of LDL cholesterol: a meta-analysis of data from 170 000 participants in 26 randomised trials. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61350-5>; Chowdhury R et al. (2013). Adherence to cardiovascular therapy: a meta-analysis of prevalence and clinical consequences. European Heart Journal. <https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/eht295>; Healthy China Action Promotion Committee (2019). Healthy China Action (2019–2030), (11) Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease Prevention and Control Action (reprinted by Hunan Provincial Health Commission). <https://wjw.hunan.gov.cn/wjw/ztzl/knowledge/tzggzcfg/202003/t20200303_11359594.html>; Joint Committee on the Chinese Guidelines for Lipid Management (2023). Chinese Guidelines for Lipid Management (2023). Chinese Journal of Cardiology, 51(3), 221-255. <https://doi.org/10.3760/cma.j.cn112148-20230119-00038>; Li JJ et al. (2023). 2023 Chinese guideline for lipid management. Frontiers in Pharmacology, 14, 1190934 (English version of the preceding guideline; Chinese original unavailable, relevant content verified against the English version). <https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2023.1190934>
entries.notes: Only people for whom a doctor determines medication is necessary should follow this; healthy people do not need to take it. How often to test blood lipids is an official recommendation; no clinical trials have compared how many years between screenings is optimal. If a family member is diagnosed with familial hypercholesterolemia (an inherited disorder with naturally exceptionally high cholesterol), their first- and second-degree relatives should all undergo lipid testing. If parents have total cholesterol ≥6.2 mmol/L, their children should also be tested. If first- or second-degree relatives include males before age 55 or females before age 65 who suffered a myocardial infarction, stroke, or sudden cardiac death, their children should also be tested. The figures for "adherence to medication" come from observational follow-up studies; people who can stick to medication are inherently more self-disciplined, which tends to overstate the benefits. The figures from the preceding two sets of randomized controlled trials are more reliable. This section does not list blood sugar control as a separate item: the evidence for the benefit of lowering blood sugar further on all-cause mortality is not as consistent as that for blood pressure and blood lipids. For individuals with hypertension or diabetes, annual kidney testing is covered in Section 16, Item 13 (Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio).

entries.title: Sleep around 7 hours each night, and maintain a fixed sleep schedule
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Requires setting aside time to sleep; for most people, this means replacing phone scrolling time with sleep. The difficulty lies in locking down fixed bedtime and wake-up times.
entries.summary: For people who consistently get less than 7 hours of sleep, the probability of dying over the same follow-up period is about 10% higher. The more irregular the sleep schedule, the higher the risk. Compared to those with the most irregular routines, others have a 20% to nearly 50% lower risk. Whether a sleep schedule is regular predicts mortality risk better than sleep duration.
entries.benefit: Pooling 16 observational follow-up studies (recording only, no randomized grouping), covering 1.38 million people and 113,000 deaths: short sleepers had an approximately 12% higher mortality risk (RR 1.12). Long sleepers had an approximately 30% higher risk (RR 1.30). Another pooled analysis categorized participants by sleep duration: the 7-hour category had the lowest risk. For durations under 7 hours, each 1-hour decrease was associated with an approximately 6% higher risk (RR 1.06). For durations over 7 hours, each 1-hour increase was associated with an approximately 13% higher risk (RR 1.13). The UK Biobank has wrist accelerometer records from about 61,000 people (recording only, no randomized grouping), categorizing participants into five tiers based on sleep regularity. Compared to the least regular tier, the four more regular tiers had a 20%–48% lower mortality risk. Sleep regularity predicts mortality better than sleep duration. Another UK Biobank study measured sleep timing using wrist accelerometers in 51,562 people, during which 3,853 incident cardiovascular disease cases occurred. Social jetlag refers to the difference in sleep midpoints between workdays and weekends. Individuals with social jetlag of 2 hours or more had an approximately 30% higher risk of cardiovascular disease (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.11–1.54). This association also held true among people with normal sleep durations.
entries.sources: Cappuccio FP et al. (2010). Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. <https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/33.5.585>; Yin J et al. (2017). Relationship of Sleep Duration With All-Cause Mortality and Cardiovascular Events: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies. JAHA. <https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.117.005947>; Windred DP et al. (2024). Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study. Sleep. <https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsad253>; Kumar N, Krishnamurthy S (2026). Social jet lag is associated with incident cardiovascular disease independent of sleep duration and cardiac genetic risk. Journal of Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1111/joim.70133>
entries.notes: What needs to be corrected are sleeping too little and having an irregular schedule; there is no need to deliberately compress sleep duration. The higher risk observed in long sleepers is mostly reverse causation: depression, chronic illnesses, and sleep apnea cause people to sleep more. Furthermore, the point regarding sleep regularity is currently supported by two observational follow-up studies, both of which only recorded data without randomized grouping, representing Grade B evidence on their own. For how to make up for lost sleep after staying up late, see Item 38 of this section (Catch Up on Sleep the Next Evening After Staying Up Late). For how to treat chronic insomnia, see Section 3, Item 26 (Try Cognitive Behavioral Therapy First for Chronic Insomnia).

entries.title: Regularly play racket sports such as tennis, badminton, and table tennis
entries.cost: Venue fees cost several tens of yuan per session. Around 2 hours per week. The difficulty lies in coordinating both players and venues, as well as maintaining weekly attendance.
entries.summary: People who regularly play tennis, badminton, and table tennis have an approximately 50% lower probability of dying over the same follow-up period compared to non-players, with cardiovascular mortality about 56% lower. Swimmers have about a 28% lower risk. Running and soccer showed no statistically significant differences in this dataset.
entries.benefit: A UK observational follow-up study of 80,300 people compared individuals who participated in specific sports against those who did not. Those who played racket sports had an approximately 47% lower mortality risk (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.40–0.69, confidence interval). Cardiovascular mortality was about 56% lower (0.44, 0.24–0.83). Racket sports refer to tennis, badminton, and table tennis. For swimmers, these two numbers were 0.72 and 0.59, respectively; for aerobics, 0.73 and 0.64; for cycling, 0.85. Running and soccer showed no statistically significant differences.
entries.sources: Oja P, Kelly P, Pedisic Z, et al. (2017). Associations of specific types of sports and exercise with all-cause and cardiovascular-disease mortality: a cohort study of 80 306 British adults. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(10), 812-817. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096822>
entries.notes: Controversial. These studies are observational follow-ups only. People who play racket sports may naturally be healthier and engage in more social interaction. The lack of an observable difference in the running cohort also suggests that what is at play may be "what kind of people choose what kind of sport." Do not assume running is useless because of this entry; this section includes other entries calculated by total physical activity volume.

entries.title: Accumulate fragmented vigorous activities, such as climbing stairs and brisk walking while commuting, up to four or five minutes daily
entries.cost: Free, and requires no extra workout time to be carved out. The difficulty lies in remembering to take the stairs and walk faster rather than choosing convenience.
entries.summary: For people who do not exercise at all, having three 1-to-2-minute bursts of vigorous activity daily is associated with an approximately 40% lower probability of dying over the same follow-up period compared to those with none at all, and nearly half the risk of cardiovascular death. Vigorous activity refers to activities such as climbing stairs and walking briskly while commuting.
entries.benefit: A UK Biobank study examined 25,200 non-exercisers who did not engage in structured workouts. Over an average follow-up of 6.9 years, 852 deaths occurred. Some individuals engaged in three bouts of fragmented vigorous physical activity per day, lasting 1–2 minutes each. Compared to those with none at all, their risks of all-cause mortality and cancer mortality were 38%–40% lower. Cardiovascular mortality risk was 48%–49% lower. For those accumulating 4.4 minutes of such activity daily, all-cause and cancer mortality risks were 26%–30% lower, and cardiovascular mortality risk was 32%–34% lower.
entries.sources: Stamatakis E, Ahmadi MN, Gill JMR, et al. (2022). Association of wearable device-measured vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity with mortality. Nature Medicine, 28, 2521-2529. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-022-02100-x>
entries.notes: Controversial. This study directly measured physical activity using wearable devices, which is more reliable than asking participants to recall via questionnaires. However, it remains an observational follow-up without randomized grouping, and the follow-up lasted only 6.9 years. The study subjects were individuals who do not exercise at all; this item does not apply to those who already exercise regularly.

entries.title: Perform 30–60 minutes of strength training per week
entries.cost: Bodyweight squats and push-ups cost nothing. Train 1–2 times per week, 20–30 minutes per session. The difficulty lies in scheduling it into your weekly routine.
entries.summary: People who do 30–60 minutes of strength training per week have a 10% to 20% lower probability of dying over the same follow-up period compared to those who do not train. Training more does not yield better results. Combining strength and aerobic exercise produces the best outcomes.
entries.benefit: Pooling multiple observational follow-up studies (recording only, no randomized grouping): people who engage in strength training have a 10%–17% lower mortality risk than those who do not. More is not necessarily better; the reduction is largest at around 30–60 minutes per week, around 10%–20%, with additional training conferring no further benefit. People who do both strength and aerobic training have an even lower mortality risk than those who do neither.
entries.sources: Momma H et al. (2022). Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies. British Journal of Sports Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105061>
entries.notes: These types of studies are observational follow-ups only, and activity volume was self-reported by participants. The evidence behind "overtraining actually leads to worse outcomes" is very weak; there is no need to restrict training volume because of it. Strength training also offers older adults benefits such as fall prevention and muscle preservation, which are detailed in Section 1. For individuals with knee pain due to degeneration, training the thigh muscles is more effective than arthroscopic surgery; see Section 6, Item 33 (Arthroscopic Debridement).

entries.title: Avoid prolonged continuous sitting; stand up and move around at intervals
entries.cost: Free, and standing up a few times takes very little time. The difficulty lies in losing track of time once seated, making it necessary to set a reminder.
entries.summary: Those who sit the longest have 2.6 times the probability of dying over the same follow-up period compared to those who sit the least. Sitting continuously for extended stretches carries an additional separate risk. However, achieving 60–75 minutes of moderate-intensity activity daily largely offsets the excess risk brought on by prolonged sitting.
entries.benefit: A U.S. follow-up study observed people without assigning them to groups and measured their activity with accelerometers. It divided them into four groups by total time spent sitting each day. The group that sat the most had 2.63 times the risk of death of the group that sat the least (HR 2.63). Dividing people into four groups by how long they sat at a stretch, the group with the longest uninterrupted sitting periods had 1.96 times the risk of the group with the shortest (HR 1.96). So total time sitting and the length of each uninterrupted sitting period were each independently associated with risk. Another pooled analysis combined studies of more than a million people; these studies observed people without assigning them to groups. People who sat for more than 8 hours a day and did almost no exercise had 1.59 times the risk of death of another group (HR 1.59). That comparison group sat for less than 4 hours a day and was the most active. About 60–75 minutes of moderate-intensity activity a day could offset the additional risk from prolonged sitting. Even among those who sat for more than 8 hours a day, the most active group had an HR of only 1.04, with no statistically discernible difference.
entries.sources: Diaz KM et al. (2017). Patterns of Sedentary Behavior and Mortality in U.S. Middle-Aged and Older Adults: A National Cohort Study. Annals of Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.7326/M17-0212>; Ekelund U et al. (2016). Does physical activity attenuate, or even eliminate, the detrimental association of sitting time with mortality? A harmonised meta-analysis of data from more than 1 million men and women. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30370-1>
entries.notes: The reliable conclusion is that how much you move matters more than how long you sit; with enough exercise, the risk associated with prolonged sitting largely disappears. Bear in mind that these studies only followed and recorded people. Many of those who sat the most were already ill, so the “risk as high as 2.63 times” figure clearly includes people who sat more because they became ill first. Also, in the same pooled analysis, the risk associated with watching more than 3 hours of television a day was present at every activity level; in the most active group, that threshold merely shifted to 5 hours.

entries.title: Eat less processed meat (ham, bacon, sausages, and luncheon meat)
entries.cost: It costs nothing and may even save money, and it takes no extra time. The hard part is eating less of something you enjoy.
entries.summary: People who ate the most ham, bacon, and sausages had about a 20% higher probability of dying during the same period than those who ate the least. Each additional daily serving of processed meat was also associated with a probability about 20% higher.
entries.benefit: Pooling several follow-up studies (which observed people without assigning them to groups), the group that ate the most processed meat had about a 23% higher risk of death than the group that ate the least (RR 1.23). For red meat overall, the risk was about 29% higher (RR 1.29). For unprocessed red meat, it was about 10% higher (RR 1.10), but this result showed no statistically discernible difference. Another pooled analysis calculated risk by the amount eaten each day. Each additional daily serving of processed meat was associated with about a 23% higher risk of death (RR 1.23). Each additional daily serving of red meat was associated with a risk about 10% higher (RR 1.10).
entries.sources: Larsson SC, Orsini N (2014). Red meat and processed meat consumption and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis. American Journal of Epidemiology. <https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwt261>; Schwingshackl L et al. (2017). Food groups and risk of all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. <https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.117.153148>; Johnston BC et al. (2019). Unprocessed Red Meat and Processed Meat Consumption: Dietary Guideline Recommendations From the NutriRECS Consortium. Annals of Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.7326/M19-1621> (the opposing NutriRECS guideline)
entries.notes: Controversy. The NutriRECS guideline used a widely accepted method for rating evidence (GRADE) and rated these studies as “not very reliable.” It made only a very weak recommendation: keep eating as you do now. The two sides disagree about whether the evidence is strong enough, not about the direction of the association. No study says processed meat is beneficial. Unprocessed red meat has a small association, with no statistically discernible difference. Processed meat is what you should limit.

entries.title: Drink less alcohol or none at all
entries.cost: It costs nothing, saves money, and takes no extra time. The hard part is a little awkwardness when declining a drink in a social setting.
entries.summary: Once weekly consumption exceeds 100 g of pure alcohol, the more people drink, the earlier they die. 100 g of pure alcohol is about 2.5 L of beer. At age 40, people drinking 100–200 g a week live about half a year less; those drinking 200–350 g live one to two years less; and those drinking more than 350 g live four to five years less. For overall health, the best amount is none.
entries.benefit: A pooled analysis of 83 prospective follow-up studies, which observed people without assigning them to groups, included 600,000 current drinkers. The lowest risk of death was at no more than 100 g of pure alcohol per week. That is about 2.5 L of 5% beer or 300 mL of Chinese baijiu at 40% alcohol. At age 40, people drinking 100–200 g a week had a life expectancy about 6 months shorter. Those drinking 200–350 g a week had a life expectancy 1–2 years shorter. Those drinking more than 350 g had a life expectancy 4–5 years shorter. The original paper reported these three figures in years of life. The Global Burden of Disease study GBD 2016 combined various kinds of health loss and found that the lowest-risk level of drinking was 0 drinks per week. Another pooled analysis corrected for biases in study design. Compared with people who had never drunk in their lives, those drinking 1.3–24 g a day had about a 7% lower risk of death (RR 0.93). But this result showed no statistically discernible difference. The risk was about 19% higher for those drinking 45–64 g a day (RR 1.19) and about 35% higher for those drinking 65 g or more a day (RR 1.35).
entries.sources: Wood AM et al. (2018). Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)30134-X>; GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators (2018). Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories, 1990–2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31310-2>; Zhao J et al. (2023). Association Between Daily Alcohol Intake and Risk of All-Cause Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses. JAMA Network Open. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.6185>; Di Castelnuovo A et al. (2006). Alcohol dosing and total mortality in men and women: an updated meta-analysis of 34 prospective studies. Archives of Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1001/archinte.166.22.2437> (opposing view)
entries.notes: Controversy. The case for “a little drinking is beneficial” comes from a pooled analysis of 34 long-term follow-up studies. It reported that people who drank small amounts had an all-cause mortality rate up to 17%–18% lower. The amounts it gave were no more than 4 drinks a day for men and 2 for women. Within those limits, people who drank more actually had lower mortality. The opposing view is that the “nondrinker” group included people who had quit drinking because of illness and people whose health was already poor. A pooled analysis specifically accounted for these confounding factors; afterward, the apparent protective effect disappeared. The Global Burden of Disease study also found 0 to be safest. A cautious reading is: drinking a little does not noticeably shorten life, while drinking a lot does. There is no basis for “starting to drink for your health.” For how to drink less, see item 21 of this section (count your drinks first, then talk to a doctor). People who drink every day must not abruptly quit on their own; see item 20 of this section (do not abruptly quit on your own).

entries.title: If you drink every day and your hands shake or your heart races when you stop, do not abruptly quit on your own
entries.cost: One appointment with a psychiatrist or addiction medicine specialist costs a few to several dozen yuan. Severe cases require a few days in hospital.
entries.summary: People who drink heavily every day can develop withdrawal symptoms if they suddenly stop. Mild symptoms include shaking hands, sweating, a racing heart, and inability to sleep. Severe cases can involve seizures or delirium tremens, a potentially life-threatening emergency. Norway followed more than 30,000 people; among those who had experienced delirium tremens, 8% died each subsequent year. If you want to quit, go to a hospital first and explain clearly how much you drink each day.
entries.benefit: A 2026 clinical review states that people who have drunk heavily for a long time can develop withdrawal syndrome after suddenly stopping or substantially reducing alcohol intake. Symptoms include tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, anxiety, insomnia, perceptual disturbances, seizures, and delirium tremens. In general medical care, it is “common and potentially life-threatening.” A Norwegian nationwide registry cohort included 36,287 people diagnosed with alcohol dependence, alcohol withdrawal, or delirium tremens between 2009 and 2015: the annual mortality rate was 8.0% in the delirium tremens group, 5.0% in the alcohol withdrawal group, and 3.6% in the alcohol dependence group. The delirium tremens group had a standardized mortality ratio of 9.8 (95% CI 8.9–10.7; this is the confidence range), meaning that their risk of death was about 9.8 times that of the general population of the same age.
entries.sources: Caputo F, Lungaro L, Costanzini A, De Giorgio R, Addolorato G (2026). Alcohol withdrawal syndrome in hospitalized patients: a practical review. European Journal of Internal Medicine, 107103. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejim.2026.107103>；Bramness JG, Heiberg IH, Høye A, Rossow I (2023). Mortality and alcohol-related morbidity in patients with delirium tremens, alcohol withdrawal state or alcohol dependence in Norway: A register-based prospective cohort study. Addiction, 118(12), 2352–2359. <https://doi.org/10.1111/add.16297>
entries.notes: How to judge for yourself: if you drink almost every day, if going one day without alcohol makes your hands shake, leaves you sweating, makes your heart race, or prevents you from sleeping, or if you need a drink in the morning to feel comfortable, meeting any one of these conditions means you should not abruptly stop on your own. Standard hospital care uses benzodiazepines to get you through those days, while also giving thiamine (vitamin B1). This is rated B because the Norwegian cohort describes “what happened afterward to people who had experienced delirium tremens,” not “what happens when people abruptly quit on their own”; the link between the two is an inference. This is not advice to keep drinking. It is advice to stop in a different way: go to a hospital for help quitting. For how much drinking per week counts as too much, see item 19 of this section (drink less alcohol or none at all). For how to drink less, see item 21 of this section (count your drinks first, then talk to a doctor).

entries.title: If you want to drink less, first count how much you drink in a week, then talk to a doctor for a few minutes
entries.cost: It costs nothing. To count your drinks, just make a daily note. Asking about it during an outpatient visit costs nothing extra.
entries.summary: When a doctor spends a few minutes reviewing how much you drink, explaining the risks, and helping you set a goal, people drink an average of 20 g less pure alcohol per week a year later, roughly half a liter of beer. Talking for longer brings no additional benefit. For people who can no longer stop drinking, two medications have been shown to work in studies abroad: for about every 12 people treated, one additional person avoids returning to a pattern of drinking too much whenever they drink.
entries.benefit: Pooling 34 randomized trials with 15,197 people, those who received a brief intervention drank 20 g less pure alcohol per week after one year than those who received only minimal intervention or none (95% CI: 12 to 28 g less; this is the confidence range; moderate-quality evidence). The participants in these studies drank an average of 244 g per week at baseline. A brief intervention means advice or lifestyle counseling delivered in no more than 5 sessions totaling less than 60 minutes; talking longer brought no additional benefit. For medications: pooling 122 randomized trials with 22,803 people, acamprosate helped one additional person avoid returning to any drinking for every 12 people treated (95% CI 8 to 26); oral naltrexone at 50 mg a day helped one additional person avoid returning to heavy drinking for every 12 people treated (8 to 26).
entries.sources: Kaner EF, Beyer FR, Muirhead C, et al. (2018). Effectiveness of brief alcohol interventions in primary care populations. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2, CD004148. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD004148.pub4>；Jonas DE, Amick HR, Feltner C, et al. (2014). Pharmacotherapy for adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA, 311(18), 1889–1900. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2014.3628>
entries.notes: The size of the benefit is rated “small” because both bodies of evidence measured how much people drank, not mortality. Under this book’s rules, an effect measured only by a surrogate endpoint is rated “small.” Most of the medication trials were conducted abroad, most participants met the diagnostic criteria for alcohol dependence, and the trials also provided psychosocial intervention. The figures represent “the additional benefit on top of that.” For these two medications in China, whether they are approved for this use and can be prescribed depends on the doctor and the medicine’s package insert. Do not buy them online on your own. If you already have withdrawal symptoms, see item 20 of this section (do not abruptly quit on your own).

entries.title: Eat a small handful of nuts every day
entries.cost: Eating 28 g a day costs about two to three hundred yuan a year. You can eat them whenever convenient; it takes no extra time.
entries.summary: People who regularly ate nuts had about a 20% lower probability of dying during the same period than those who ate none. A difference was visible even at once a week: about 10% lower. The difference was clearest at a handful every day.
entries.benefit: Two U.S. follow-up studies covered 119,000 people and more than 3 million person-years. Person-years means the number of people multiplied by the number of years each was followed. Compared with people who ate no nuts: those who ate nuts less than once a week had about a 7% lower risk of death (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.90–0.96; this is the confidence range). Those who ate nuts once a week had about an 11% lower risk (0.89, 0.86–0.93). Those who ate nuts 2–4 times a week had about a 13% lower risk (0.87, 0.83–0.90). Those who ate nuts 5–6 times a week had about a 15% lower risk (0.85, 0.79–0.91). Those who ate nuts 7 or more times a week had about a 20% lower risk (0.80, 0.73–0.86).
entries.sources: Bao Y, Han J, Hu FB, et al. (2013). Association of nut consumption with total and cause-specific mortality. New England Journal of Medicine, 369(21), 2001-2011. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307352>
entries.notes: Buy plain, unsalted nuts. Nuts are fairly high in calories, so do not eat them without limit as a snack. Bear in mind that these studies only followed groups of people over time. People who eat nuts tend to have healthier lifestyles overall, so the figures should be taken with a grain of salt.

entries.title: Replace some red meat with fish and poultry
entries.cost: It costs nothing and takes no extra time. You are choosing a different kind of meat, not buying more. The hard part is changing your taste preferences a little.
entries.summary: Eating two additional servings of processed or red meat each week was associated with about a 3% higher probability of dying during the same period. For the same number of servings of fish or poultry, no increase was discernible. The effect of switching meat is relatively small among the measures in this section: make the switch when convenient, without making a big issue of it.
entries.benefit: A pooled analysis combined six U.S. follow-up studies involving nearly 30,000 people. Eating two additional servings of processed meat per week was associated with about a 3% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 1.02–1.05; confidence range). Eating two additional servings of unprocessed red meat per week was also associated with a risk about 3% higher (1.03, 1.01–1.05). For the same pattern of eating poultry, the figure was 0.99 (0.97–1.02); for fish, it was 0.99 (0.97–1.01). Neither of the latter two showed a statistically discernible difference.
entries.sources: Zhong VW, Van Horn L, Greenland P, et al. (2020). Associations of Processed Meat, Unprocessed Red Meat, Poultry, or Fish Intake With Incident Cardiovascular Disease and All-Cause Mortality. JAMA Internal Medicine, 180(4), 503-512. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.6969>
entries.notes: The difference from two servings a week is very small; do not expect to live years longer just by switching meats. If you are spending the same amount on meat, you can choose fish and poultry first.

entries.title: Replace some refined rice and white flour products with whole grains
entries.cost: Brown rice, oats, and whole-wheat flour products cost a little more than refined rice and white flour products, but take no extra time. The hard part is gradually getting used to the taste and texture.
entries.summary: People who ate an additional 90 g of whole grains each day had about a 17% lower probability of dying during the same period. 90 g is about three servings. The risk continued to fall up to around 200 g a day.
entries.benefit: A pooled analysis of several follow-up studies (which observed people without assigning them to groups) found that each additional 90 g of whole grains per day was associated with about a 17% lower risk of death (RR 0.83). 90 g is about 3 servings. This benefit continued up to 210–225 g per day. In another pooled analysis, each additional serving per day was associated with a risk about 8% lower (RR 0.92).
entries.sources: Aune D et al. (2016). Whole grain consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all cause and cause specific mortality: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. BMJ. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i2716>; Schwingshackl L et al. (2017). Food groups and risk of all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. <https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.117.153148>
entries.notes: You do not need to replace all your grains with whole grains. Replacing half already puts you in the range where the benefits are most pronounced. Bear in mind that these studies only followed and recorded people’s habits; people who eat whole grains may have been healthier to begin with, so the figures may overstate the benefit. Results also varied widely between studies (I² 83%; the higher this number, the less consistent the studies’ findings).

entries.title: Drink tea at least three times a week
entries.cost: A few dozen to a few hundred yuan a year. Brewing a cup takes a few minutes and hardly any time overall.
entries.summary: People who regularly drink tea had about a 15% lower probability of dying during the same period. From age 50, they lived an average of 1.26 years longer and spent 1.41 more years free of cardiovascular disease.
entries.benefit: A Chinese study of 100,900 people (China-PAR) followed half of them for at least 7.3 years. People who regularly drank tea had about a 15% lower risk of death (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.79–0.90; this is the confidence interval). Starting at age 50, regular tea drinkers had 1.41 more years free of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and a life expectancy 1.26 years longer.
entries.sources: Wang X, Liu F, Li J, et al. (2020). Tea consumption and the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: The China-PAR project. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 27(18), 1956-1963. <https://doi.org/10.1177/2047487319894685>; mycotoxins in tea: Cui P et al. (2020). Quantitative analysis and dietary risk assessment of aflatoxins in Chinese post-fermented dark tea. Food and Chemical Toxicology. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fct.2020.111830>; Zhou H et al. (2022). Mycotoxins in Tea (Camellia sinensis (L.) Kuntze): Contamination and Dietary Exposure Profiling in the Chinese Population. Toxins. <https://doi.org/10.3390/toxins14070452>; green tea extract and liver injury: Hu J et al. (2018). The safety of green tea and green tea extract consumption in adults - Results of a systematic review. Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yrtph.2018.03.019>
entries.notes: The point of debate is that these studies only followed and recorded people’s habits, and among Chinese men, tea drinkers are more likely to smoke and drink alcohol. The authors adjusted for some of these effects, but could not remove them completely. Also, do not drink tea scalding hot; see item 30 in this section (Do not drink scalding hot tea) for drink temperature. Some people worry about mycotoxins in tea. A Chinese study tested 158 samples of dark tea and detected aflatoxins in two. Based on the amount of tea people drink, the ingested amount was below internationally accepted limits. Another study tested 352 tea samples for 16 mycotoxins; only the average level of ochratoxin A in dark tea exceeded the limit. Based on tea consumption in China, neither study calculated a dietary risk. Store tea somewhere dry, and do not drink tea that has become damp and moldy. Green tea extract capsules are different: swallowing a large dose of highly concentrated catechins at once can damage the liver. Brewed tea does not have this problem. This item therefore refers only to brewed tea; do not substitute extract supplements for it.

entries.title: Drink three to four cups of coffee a day, with no more than 400 mg of caffeine in total, and without added sugar or milk foam topping
entries.cost: Brewing it yourself costs one or two yuan a day. Making a cup takes a few minutes and hardly any time overall. If you buy large cups, pay attention to how many milligrams of caffeine you drink in a day.
entries.summary: People who drank three to four cups of coffee a day had about a 17% lower probability of dying during the same period than people who did not drink coffee. In another study, people who drank their coffee mainly in the morning had about a 12% lower risk; no difference was apparent for people who drank it throughout the day. Caffeine content varies greatly from cup to cup, so keep the daily total at no more than 400 mg.
entries.benefit: An umbrella review brought together 201 meta-analyses. The original studies underlying these analyses only observed and recorded participants; they did not assign them to groups. For all-cause mortality, the review cited one of the dose-response meta-analyses. Compared with people who did not drink coffee, those who drank 3–4 cups a day had a 17% lower risk of death (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.79–0.88; this is the confidence interval). At 7 cups a day, the reduction narrowed to 10% (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.85–0.96); no increase in risk was observed. A study using the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) followed 40,725 adults, half of them for at least 9.8 years. It, too, only observed and recorded people; it did not assign them to groups. The researchers divided coffee drinkers into two categories. Morning-type drinkers consumed most of their coffee between 4:00 and 11:59 and drank almost none in the afternoon or evening. They made up 36%. Compared with people who did not drink coffee, their risk of death from any cause was 12% lower (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.81–0.96). After further adjustment for insufficient sleep and sleep difficulties, it was 16% lower (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.95). Their risk of death from cardiovascular disease was 19% lower (hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.70–0.94), or 31% lower after adjustment for sleep (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.55–0.87). All-day drinkers consumed coffee in the morning, afternoon and evening. They made up 16%. No difference was apparent in their risk of death from any cause (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.90–1.10). No difference in cancer mortality was apparent for either group. There is official guidance for the daily caffeine limit. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and Health Canada both set the limit for healthy adults at 400 mg per day. That is the total from all sources, including tea, cola and energy drinks. EFSA also says to spread intake across the day, with no more than 200 mg at one time. The amount in a cup of coffee varies greatly. EFSA’s table gives about 90 mg for a 200 mL cup of filter coffee. Health Canada’s table gives an average of 135 mg for an 8-ounce (237 mL) cup of brewed coffee. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) gives 113–247 mg for a 12-ounce (about 355 mL) cup of brewed coffee. The FDA therefore equates 400 mg to about 2 to 3 cups of 12-ounce coffee, while the review equates it to about 4 cups.
entries.sources: Poole R, Kennedy OJ, Roderick P, et al. (2017). Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes. BMJ, 359, j5024. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.j5024>, including the correction BMJ (2018), 360, k194. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.k194> (the confidence interval for all-cause mortality in the abstract was changed from 0.83–0.88 to 0.79–0.88); Wang X, Ma H, Sun Q, et al. (2025). Coffee drinking timing and mortality in US adults. European Heart Journal, 46(8), 749-759. <https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae871>; Yang R, Lei Q, Liu Z, et al. (2024). Relationship between timing of coffee and tea consumption with mortality (total, cardiovascular disease and diabetes) in people with diabetes: the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2003–2014. BMC Medicine, 22, 526. <https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-024-03736-x>; EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (2015). Scientific Opinion on the safety of caffeine. EFSA Journal, 13(5), 4102. <https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4102>; EFSA’s caffeine information page (table of amounts per serving) <https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/topic/caffeine>; FDA. Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine Is Too Much? <https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much>; Health Canada. Caffeine in foods. <https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/food-nutrition/food-safety/food-additives/caffeine-foods.html>; added sugar: Liu D, Li ZH, Shen D, et al. (2022). Association of Sugar-Sweetened, Artificially Sweetened, and Unsweetened Coffee Consumption With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality. Annals of Internal Medicine, 175(7), 909-917. <https://doi.org/10.7326/M21-2977>; Treskes RW, Clausen J, Marott JL, et al. (2023). Use of sugar in coffee and tea and long-term risk of mortality in older adult Danish men. PLOS ONE, 18(10), e0292882. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0292882>; atrial fibrillation: Wong CX, Cheung CC, Montenegro G, et al. (2026). Caffeinated Coffee Consumption or Abstinence to Reduce Atrial Fibrillation. JAMA, 335(4), 317-325. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.21056>; Joglar JA, Chung MK, Armbruster AL, et al. (2024). 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation, 149(1). <https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193>
entries.notes: The point of debate is that the review’s authors explicitly say most of the evidence comes from studies that only followed and recorded people. Reliable randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether the relationship is causal. The suggestion that morning coffee is better comes from just one US study, so it is not in the title. Its authors explicitly say the results cannot be interpreted as causal; people who drink coffee in the morning may simply have healthier lifestyles overall. In another US study involving only people with diabetes, those who drank coffee from dawn to morning had a 25% higher risk of death, while those who drank it from morning to noon had a 20% lower risk—the opposite pattern. None of these studies compared whether 12:00 or 14:00 is more suitable. Section 3, item 4 (Avoid caffeine after 2 p.m.) concerns sleep: count backward from your own bedtime. It does not conflict with this item. The 400 mg limit is a safety ceiling, not a beneficial dose. Decaffeinated coffee has similar benefits, though slightly smaller ones, so there is no need to drink extra coffee to reach a target amount. Pregnant women should have no more than 200 mg a day according to EFSA, or 300 mg according to Health Canada. This item does not apply to women at high risk of fractures. It also does not apply to people with anxiety or insomnia; that is this book’s judgment, as the review offers no conclusions for these two groups. People with atrial fibrillation do not all need to stop drinking coffee. In one trial, people who drank about 1 cup a day after electrical cardioversion for persistent atrial fibrillation had fewer recurrences than those who stopped drinking coffee (47% versus 64%). The 2023 US atrial fibrillation guideline likewise does not recommend giving up coffee to prevent episodes, but people whose symptoms are triggered by it should cut back. There is no evidence for other arrhythmias; follow your doctor’s advice. For mortality, added sugar was not observed to cancel out the benefits. Syrups and drinks with milk foam toppings have not been studied, however, and contain a lot of sugar, so the recommendation remains to leave them out.

entries.title: Eat 5 servings (about 400 g) of fruit and vegetables every day
entries.cost: A few to a dozen or so yuan a day. Washing and cutting them takes some time each day. The difficulty is buying and eating enough every day.
entries.summary: Eating an extra 200 g of fruit and vegetables a day was associated with about a 10% lower probability of dying during the same period. People who ate 5 servings a day had about a 13% lower risk than those who ate only 2. In the US study, eating more than that was not associated with a further reduction.
entries.benefit: Combining several follow-up studies (which only observed and recorded people, without assigning them to groups), each additional 200 g of fruit and vegetables eaten per day was associated with about a 10% lower risk of death (RR 0.90). This benefit continued up to 800 g a day. An analysis combining two large US follow-up studies with 26 other studies found that people who ate 5 servings a day had about a 13% lower risk of death than those who ate only 2 servings (HR 0.87). The best combination was 2 servings of fruit and 3 of vegetables; eating more was not associated with a further reduction.
entries.sources: Aune D et al. (2017). Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. International Journal of Epidemiology. <https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw319>; Wang DD et al. (2021). Fruit and Vegetable Intake and Mortality: Results From 2 Prospective Cohort Studies of US Men and Women and a Meta-Analysis of 26 Cohort Studies. Circulation. <https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.120.048996>
entries.notes: The two studies disagree about the optimal amount: in the US study, risk stopped falling beyond 5 servings. Bear in mind that these studies only followed and recorded people, and confounding is substantial: people who eat more vegetables differ from others in income, education and exercise. So the ‘about 10% lower risk’ figure is already an upper limit.

entries.title: Eat Less Ultra-Processed Food (Potato Chips, Instant Noodles, Pastries, Convenience Foods)
entries.cost: Costs no money; it is simply a matter of switching what you buy. Cooking for yourself or taking time to pick foods that are minimally processed will take up some time every day. The difficult part lies in fighting the inertia of "convenience is fine" over the long haul.
entries.summary: People with the highest consumption of ultra-processed food have about a 20% higher probability of dying during the same period than those with the lowest consumption, and a 50% higher probability of cardiovascular mortality. However, this type of evidence has been rated as having low certainty, so the numbers should be taken with a grain of salt.
entries.benefit: An umbrella review synthesized multiple pooled studies; the primary studies underlying these pooled analyses all only recorded data without grouping participants. Results: People with higher consumption of ultra-processed food had an approximately 21% higher risk of death than those with lower consumption (RR 1.21), and about a 50% higher cardiovascular disease mortality (RR 1.50). The evidence grades for these two outcomes were "highly suggestive" and "convincing", respectively. However, evaluated using the standard grading system for evidence (GRADE), the certainty was low or very low.
entries.sources: Lane MM et al. (2024). Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-077310>
entries.notes: The controversies lie in three areas. This classification system (NOVA) classifies foods with vastly different nutritional profiles into a single category. It overlaps heavily with sugar-sweetened beverages and processed meats (Entries 7 and 18), making it unclear which specific factor is having an effect. Evaluated using the standard grading system for evidence (GRADE), the grade is also low. Therefore, after accomplishing those two entries, it is uncertain how much additional benefit this entry can deliver. The counter-evidence is simply the low rating given by the umbrella review itself; currently, there are no primary studies that have reached the opposite conclusion. Thus, achieve Entries 7 and 18 first (do not drink sugar-sweetened beverages, eat less processed meat), and then consider this entry.

entries.title: Do Not Burn Coal or Wood for Cooking or Heating; Switch to Electricity or Gas
entries.cost: For rural households, replacing stoves plus fuel expenses costs a few hundred to over a thousand yuan per year. It is a one-time change and does not take up time over the long term. Urban residents basically already use electricity or gas.
entries.summary: People who burn coal or wood for cooking have about a 10% higher probability of dying during the same period; those who burn coal or wood for heating are about 14% higher. People who have already switched to electricity or gas have a 13%–33% lower probability of death than those who still burn coal or wood.
entries.benefit: A prospective cohort study on chronic disease in China followed 271,000 adults without cardiovascular disease, recording data only without grouping. People who used solid fuels like coal and wood for cooking had an approximately 11% higher risk of death than those using electricity or gas (HR 1.11). Those using solid fuels for heating were about 14% higher (HR 1.14). Compared to those who continued burning solid fuels, people who had already switched from solid fuels to clean fuels had an approximately 13% lower risk for cooking (HR 0.87) and about 33% lower for heating (HR 0.67). Outdoor PM2.5 is another calculation. Pooling 104 cohort studies together, for every 10 µg/m³ increase in long-term inhaled concentration, the risk of death from natural causes was about 8% higher (RR 1.08). Natural causes mean non-accidental disease deaths.
entries.sources: Yu K et al. (2018). Association of Solid Fuel Use With Risk of Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality in Rural China. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.2151>; Chen J, Hoek G (2020). Long-term exposure to PM and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Environment International. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.105974>
entries.notes: Such studies are only observational records. Households that switched fuels are often more affluent, so the figure "risk reduced to 0.67 times" is confounded by the effect of family socioeconomic status. As for outdoor PM2.5, what an individual can do is limited, coming down to nothing more than moving away, wearing masks, or using air purifiers. There are no studies on air purifiers with mortality as the endpoint, so this section provides no figures for them.

entries.title: Let Hot Things Sit for a Bit Before Drinking; Do Not Drink Scalding Hot Tea, Soup, or Coffee
entries.cost: Costs no money; just wait an extra two to three minutes each time. The difficult part lies in holding back when you are craving it.
entries.summary: In a study conducted in an area with a high incidence of esophageal cancer in Iran, drinking very hot tea was associated with 8 times the probability of developing esophageal cancer compared to drinking warm tea. Even if it was just "hot", it was 2 times. Drinking it less than two minutes after pouring carried 5 times the risk of waiting more than four minutes before drinking.
entries.benefit: In a high-incidence area for esophageal cancer in northern Iran, 300 patients were compared with 571 individuals without the disease. All of the following comparisons are with people who drank warm tea. People who drank "hot" tea had about 2.07 times the odds of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.28–3.35, confidence interval). Those drinking "very hot" tea were about 8.16 times (3.93–16.9). People who drank it within less than 2 minutes of pouring were about 5.41 times higher than those who waited 4 minutes or more before drinking (2.63–11.1).
entries.sources: Islami F, Pourshams A, Nasrollahzadeh D, et al. (2009). Tea drinking habits and oesophageal cancer in a high risk area in northern Iran: population based case-control study. BMJ, 338, b929. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.b929>；Loomis D, Guyton KZ, Grosse Y, et al. (2016). Carcinogenicity of drinking coffee, mate, and very hot beverages. Lancet Oncology, 17(7), 877-878. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(16)30239-X>；Yu C, Tang H, Guo Y, et al. (2018). Hot tea consumption and its interactions with alcohol and tobacco use on the risk for esophageal cancer: a population-based cohort study. Annals of Internal Medicine, 168(7), 489-497. <https://doi.org/10.7326/M17-2000>
entries.notes: The International Agency for Research on Cancer classified hot beverages above 65°C as Group 2A, meaning probably carcinogenic. The same evaluation concluded that coffee itself is not carcinogenic. A domestic study followed 456,000 people for a median of 9.2 years. People who drank scalding hot tea and also consumed more than 15 grams of alcohol per day had the highest risk of esophageal cancer. They were about 5 times as likely as those who rarely drank tea and consumed less than 15 grams of alcohol per day (HR 5.00, 3.64–6.88). For those who smoked and also drank scalding tea daily, the hazard ratio was 2.03 (1.55–2.67). The study authors concluded that the risk of esophageal cancer is even higher when scalding tea is combined with excessive alcohol consumption or smoking.

entries.title: Go Outside to Get Sunlight During the Day; Do Not Stay Out of the Light All Day Long
entries.cost: Costs no money. Ten-odd minutes a day, which can easily be covered by your daily commute and lunch breaks.
entries.summary: In a Swedish study, women who intentionally avoided the sun had a life expectancy 0.6 to 2.1 years shorter than those with the most sun exposure. Non-smokers who avoided the sun had a lifespan comparable to smokers with the most sun exposure.
entries.benefit: A Swedish study followed 29,500 women for 20 years. Compared with the group that had the most sun exposure, those who actively avoided sun exposure had a life expectancy that was 0.6 to 2.1 years shorter. The authors wrote: "non-smokers who avoided sun exposure had a life expectancy similar to smokers in the highest sun exposure group".
entries.sources: Lindqvist PG, Epstein E, Nielsen K, et al. (2016). Avoidance of sun exposure as a risk factor for major causes of death: a competing risk analysis of the Melanoma in Southern Sweden cohort. Journal of Internal Medicine, 280(4), 375-387. <https://doi.org/10.1111/joim.12496>
entries.notes: The controversy lies in: Sweden is located at a high latitude with little sunshine, so the conclusion cannot be directly transferred to China. Furthermore, people who avoid the sun may inherently have poorer health and dislike going outdoors, which is a speculation by the authors. The paper's authors also noted that women who frequently get sun exposure face a higher risk of skin cancer. Therefore, do not expose yourself to the point of sunburn, and you should still protect yourself under strong midday sunlight.

entries.title: Keep BMI Controlled Between 20–25; Lose Weight if Overweight
entries.cost: Costs no money. Diet plus exercise will take up time every day. This is the item requiring the most willpower in this entire section: it takes long-term commitment to watch your mouth and move your legs, and maintaining the weight loss afterward is even harder than losing it.
entries.summary: The probability of dying is lowest in the BMI 20–25 range. At a BMI of 27.5–30, it is about 20% higher; at 30–35, about 45% higher; at 35–40, it nearly doubles. For East Asians with a BMI above 25, for every 5-unit increase, the risk is about 40% higher.
entries.benefit: Pooling individual participant data from 239 prospective cohort studies (recording data only, without grouping). This analysis retained only three categories of participants: never-smokers, those without chronic disease at enrollment, and those who survived more than 5 years after enrollment. Results: The risk of death was lowest at a BMI of 20–25. A BMI of 25–27.5 was about 7% higher (HR 1.07). 27.5–30 was about 20% higher (HR 1.20). 30–35 was about 45% higher (HR 1.45). 35–40 was about 94% higher (HR 1.94). 40–60 was 2.76 times (HR 2.76). For people with a BMI over 25, for every 5 kg/m² increase, the risk for East Asian populations was about 39% higher (HR 1.39).
entries.sources: Global BMI Mortality Collaboration (2016). Body-mass index and all-cause mortality: individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 239 prospective studies in four continents. Lancet. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30175-1>; Flegal KM et al. (2013). Association of all-cause mortality with overweight and obesity using standard body mass index categories: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.113905> (opposing view)
entries.notes: Controversy. One side argues that "being a bit heavier actually helps you live longer". Upon pooling, they found: overweight individuals had an approximately 6% lower risk of death, and mildly obese individuals were about 5% lower. The disagreement between the two sides mainly lies in whether to exclude three categories of data: smokers, people with pre-existing disease, and data from the first few years after enrollment. The reason to exclude them is that people with severe illness will lose weight first. After the analysis pooling 239 studies excluded these three categories, the risk associated with being overweight reappeared. In addition, note that there are no randomized controlled trials demonstrating that weight loss itself reduces all-cause mortality. The benefits above were derived from cross-sectional comparisons between people of differing body sizes, and do not mean that shedding the weight will necessarily bring about a reduction of that magnitude. People trying to lose weight do not need to obsess over meal timing; neither breakfast nor 16:8 intermittent fasting offers extra benefits, see Section 6, Entry 26 (Do Not Rely on Eating Breakfast or 16:8 to Help You Control Weight).

entries.title: Eat Chili Peppers More Than Four Times a Week
entries.cost: Costs no money and takes up no time.
entries.summary: In an Italian study, people who ate chili peppers more than four times a week had an approximately 23% lower probability of dying during the same period than those who rarely ate them, and cardiovascular mortality was about one-third lower.
entries.benefit: An Italian study of 22,800 participants, half of whom were followed for a full 8.2 years, with a total of 1,236 deaths. People who ate chili peppers more than 4 times a week had an approximately 23% lower risk of death than those who rarely ate them (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.66–0.90, confidence interval). Cardiovascular mortality was about 34% lower (0.66, 0.50–0.86).
entries.sources: Bonaccio M, Di Castelnuovo A, Costanzo S, et al. (2019). Chili Pepper Consumption and Mortality in Italian Adults. Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 74(25), 3139-3149. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2019.09.068>
entries.notes: The controversy lies in: This was an observational cohort study conducted within the context of a Mediterranean diet; people who eat spicy food may have an overall diet closer to local traditional eating patterns. Note also that for people with gastroesophageal reflux, hemorrhoids, or irritable bowel syndrome, eating spicy food may aggravate symptoms, so there is no need to force it. This is based on the author's experience; no dedicated studies were found.

entries.title: Drink One to Two Servings of Milk or Yogurt Daily
entries.cost: A few yuan a day; takes up no time.
entries.summary: People who consume two or more servings of milk or yogurt daily have about a 17% lower probability of dying during the same period than non-consumers.
entries.benefit: The PURE prospective cohort study covered 21 countries and 136,000 individuals, followed for an average of 9.1 years, with a total of 6,796 deaths. People who consumed two or more servings of dairy products daily had an approximately 17% lower risk of death than non-consumers (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.96, confidence interval), trend P=0.0052.
entries.sources: Dehghan M, Mente A, Rangarajan S, et al. (2018). Association of dairy intake with cardiovascular disease and mortality in 21 countries from five continents (PURE): a prospective cohort study. Lancet, 392(10161), 2288-2297. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31812-9>
entries.notes: The controversy lies in: PURE included a large number of low- and middle-income countries, where being able to drink milk daily itself indicates good family financial circumstances, making this confounding layer hard to eliminate completely. In addition, people with lactose intolerance can switch to yogurt or low-lactose milk; there is no need to force yourself to drink cow's milk.

entries.title: No Need to Quit Eggs; Up to One a Day Is Fine
entries.cost: Costs no money and takes up no time.
entries.summary: Eating half a whole egg more per day is associated with about a 7% higher probability of dying during the same period. Swapping this half an egg for egg whites, fish, poultry, or nuts is instead associated with a lower risk of death. However, another batch of studies found that up to one egg per day showed no association with cardiovascular disease, so there is no need to quit eggs.
entries.benefit: A US cohort study of 521,000 participants recorded a total of 129,000 deaths. Eating half a whole egg more per day was associated with an approximately 7% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 1.06–1.08, this is the confidence interval). Replacing this half a whole egg with an equivalent amount of egg whites, poultry, fish, dairy products, or nuts and legumes was associated with a lower risk of death, and the risks of cardiovascular, cancer, and respiratory mortality were all lower as well. Counter-evidence: Three large US studies totaling 216,000 individuals followed participants for up to 32 years. People who ate at least one egg a day had no difference in cardiovascular disease risk compared to those who ate less than one per month (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82–1.05). In the same paper, pooling 33 cohorts and 1.72 million people showed that eating one more egg per day also brought no change in cardiovascular disease risk (RR 0.98, 0.93–1.03). The study authors concluded that up to one egg per day is not associated with cardiovascular disease.
entries.sources: Zhuang P, Wu F, Mao L, et al. (2021). Egg and cholesterol consumption and mortality from cardiovascular and different causes in the United States: A population-based cohort study. PLoS Medicine, 18(2), e1003508. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003508>；Drouin-Chartier JP, Chen S, Li Y, et al. (2020). Egg consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease: three large prospective US cohort studies, systematic review, and updated meta-analysis. BMJ, 368, m513. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.m513>；U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, U.S. Department of Agriculture (2015). 2015–2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, Chapter 1：「The Key Recommendation from the 2010 Dietary Guidelines to limit consumption of dietary cholesterol to 300 mg per day is not included in the 2015 edition, but this change does not suggest that dietary cholesterol is no longer important to consider」「individuals should eat as little dietary cholesterol as possible while consuming a healthy eating pattern」. <https://www.dietaryguidelines.gov/sites/default/files/2019-05/2015-2020_Dietary_Guidelines.pdf>
entries.notes: There is significant controversy: there are also long-term prospective studies tracking large populations, as well as meta-analyses of multiple studies, that did not find one egg a day to be associated with cardiovascular disease. The 2015 edition of the US Dietary Guidelines removed the upper limit of 300 mg of cholesterol per day. However, it also stated that this does not mean cholesterol is unimportant, and that intake should be as low as possible while eating a healthy diet. One egg a day currently appears to have no association with cardiovascular disease. The "up to one a day" in the title is based on this finding; amounts higher than this have not been directly tested by studies.

entries.title: Take Baths if Conditions Permit; Do Not Rely Only on Showers
entries.cost: A bit more spent on water and electricity. Half an hour each time.
entries.summary: In a Japanese study, people who took baths almost daily had about a 28% lower risk of cardiovascular events and about a 46% lower risk of cerebral hemorrhage compared to those who took baths less than twice a week.
entries.benefit: A Japanese study of 30,000 individuals aged 40 to 59 followed participants for 19 years, recording 2,097 cardiovascular events. People who took baths almost every day had an approximately 28% lower risk of cardiovascular events compared to those who bathed no more than twice a week (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.62–0.84, this is the confidence interval). Coronary heart disease was about 35% lower (0.65, 0.45–0.94). Stroke was about 26% lower (0.74, 0.62–0.87). Cerebral hemorrhage was about 46% lower (0.54, 0.40–0.73).
entries.sources: Ukai T, Iso H, Yamagishi K, et al. (2020). Habitual tub bathing and risks of incident coronary heart disease and stroke. Heart, 106(10), 732-737. <https://doi.org/10.1136/heartjnl-2019-315752>; Consumer Affairs Agency. Be careful of accidents among the elderly during the New Year holidays (page contains no publication date; figures cited from Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare 2024 Vital Statistics): "The number of deaths due to 'drowning and submersion while in or falling into a bathtub' reached 7,776 in Reiwa 6 (2024)" "Factors cited include rapid blood pressure fluctuations caused by temperature differences between warm rooms and cold changing rooms or bathrooms, as well as impaired consciousness due to elevated body temperature from prolonged soaking in bathtubs filled with hot water." <https://www.caa.go.jp/policies/policy/consumer_safety/caution/caution_084/>
entries.notes: The controversy lies in: These findings were obtained in a Japanese population and bathtub culture; most households in China do not have the conditions to take baths every day. Additionally, the water should not be too hot, nor should you soak for too long. For the elderly and people with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular diseases, excessively hot water and soaking for too long are actually dangerous. In Japan in 2024, 7,776 people drowned in bathtubs. Japan's Consumer Affairs Agency stated that common causes include large temperature differences between rooms and bathrooms in winter, and soaking in hot water for too long. Do not take a bath, visit hot springs, or take a sauna after drinking alcohol, see Section 22, Entry 11 (Do Not Soak in Hot Springs After Drinking Alcohol).

entries.title: Keep Naps Within Half an Hour, Do Not Exceed One Hour; If You Cannot Get Through the Day Without Sleeping One to Two Hours, Get Checked for Underlying Causes
entries.cost: Costs no money. Just set an alarm before sleeping; requires virtually no willpower.
entries.summary: For people whose naps do not exceed one hour, the risk of death and chronic disease did not increase, and their minds were clearer. For those sleeping over an hour, the risk of coronary heart disease was about 30% higher, and diabetes and obesity were about 20% higher. So set an alarm to wake yourself up in half an hour. If you must sleep one to two hours every day just to get through the day, that is a signal to get your health checked.
entries.benefit: An umbrella review synthesized 16 meta-analyses and 244 health outcomes. An umbrella review simply pools existing pooled studies once again. The conclusion was: for people napping less than 60 minutes, neither all-cause mortality nor chronic disease risk increased, and cognitive improvements were the most pronounced (SMD 0.69, 95% CI 0.37–1.00, this is the confidence interval). Short naps of 20 to 30 minutes provided the greatest improvement in athletic performance (SMD 0.99, 0.67–1.31). For people napping more than 60 minutes, the risk of coronary heart disease was about 30% higher, and the risks of diabetes and obesity were about 20% higher. Another study had 1,338 older adults over age 56 wear actigraphy watches to objectively measure naps rather than relying on self-reported questionnaires. Followed for up to 19 years, 926 participants died during the period. For every additional 1 hour of napping, the risk of death was about 13% higher (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04–1.23). For each additional nap taken per day, it was about 7% higher (HR 1.07, 1.02–1.13). People who napped in the morning had an approximately 30% higher risk than those who napped in the early afternoon (HR 1.30, 1.03–1.64).
entries.sources: Du P, Li J, Hua Z, et al. (2026). Multiple Health Outcomes of Daytime Napping: A Comprehensive Umbrella Review. Public Health Reviews. <https://doi.org/10.3389/phrs.2026.1609013>; Gao C, Cai R, Zheng X, et al. (2026). Objectively Measured Daytime Napping Patterns and All-Cause Mortality in Older Adults. JAMA Network Open. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.7938>; Dashti HS et al. (2021). Genetic determinants of daytime napping and effects on cardiometabolic health. Nature Communications. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20585-3>
entries.notes: The evidence is contested. The first two studies above only observed people; they did not assign them to groups. People who nap for a long time are already more likely to have sleep apnea, anemia, hypothyroidism, depression, or another chronic illness. So it is unclear how much of the finding that people who sleep longer die more often is caused by napping itself. Genetic causal inference (Mendelian randomization, involving 453,000 people plus 541,000 people) supports only one finding: more frequent napping raises blood pressure and waist circumference slightly. It found no causal effect of napping on coronary heart disease or diabetes. So do not treat “nap less” as a way to reduce mortality. The advice to “investigate the cause” is the author's recommendation and is grade C: if daytime sleepiness makes a long nap necessary, first investigate your nighttime sleep. Snoring and gasping during sleep warrant a check for sleep apnea; also get a complete blood count and thyroid tests. For how a short nap can restore alertness, see Section 3, Item 11 (sleep for 10 minutes when you feel sleepy in the afternoon). For how long to sleep at night, see Item 13 of this section (sleep 7 hours each night). For how to investigate and treat snoring and gasping during sleep, see Section 3, Item 27 (sleep apnea).

entries.title: After staying up late, catch up on sleep the next night; do not save it for the weekend
entries.cost: It costs nothing. You would already want to sleep for the extra hour or two.
entries.summary: People who slept less and did not catch up the next night had about a 15% higher risk of death than people with regular sleep schedules; those who lost a lot of sleep and did not catch up had about a 42% higher risk. No increase in risk was detectable among those who caught up. So if you stayed up late, go to bed earlier the next night.
entries.benefit: In the UK Biobank, 85,618 people with an average age of 61.8 wore wrist devices that recorded their sleep day by day; the median follow-up was 8 years. The researchers first used each person's own sleep need to identify “short-sleep nights,” defined as sleeping more than 2.5 hours less than they needed. The first night after that period of reduced sleep counted as the “recovery night”; sleeping more than they needed on that night counted as catching up. This produced five patterns. Compared with people who had regular sleep schedules, those who slept less and did not catch up had about a 15% higher risk of death from any cause (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01–1.31; this is the confidence interval). Those who accumulated more than 3.5 hours of lost sleep and did not catch up had about a 42% higher risk (HR 1.42, 1.24–1.63). Neither of the two groups that caught up showed a significant association; the group that caught up after reduced sleep had an HR of 1.12 (0.98–1.28). Among people who normally slept for short periods, those who slept less and did not catch up had about a 19% higher risk (1.19, 1.01–1.40), and those with severe sleep loss who did not catch up had about a 38% higher risk (1.38, 1.17–1.63). The result was also replicated in a separate US health survey of 4,586 people.
entries.sources: Li X, Zhang M, Li Z, et al. (2026). Acute sleep rebound following sleep restriction is associated with reduced mortality risk. Nature Communications. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72461-1>
entries.notes: This was an observational study; people were not assigned to groups. Those who could not catch up may already have been busier or in worse health, and those differences cannot be fully accounted for. “No detectable increase in risk in the two groups that caught up” means only that the study did not detect a difference. Their point estimates were still above 1, and catching up does not mean there is no harm. So repay lost sleep as soon as possible, but do not use this as a reason to stay up late whenever you like. In this study, catching up meant sleeping a little longer on the first night after sleeping less; it did not include saving up lost sleep for one weekend recovery.
