Making “stay up late on workdays, catch up on weekends” a weekly routine is a different matter, called social jet lag, which is itself associated with cardiovascular disease. See Item 13 of this section (sleep about 7 hours each night and keep a regular schedule). For the advice to keep a fixed wake-up time on weekends too, see Section 3, Item 2 (keep a fixed wake-up time, including weekends). It does not conflict with this item: this item tells you to go to bed earlier that night, not to sleep until noon the next day.

entries.title: The longer you work night shifts, the higher your cardiovascular risk; transfer to another role early if you can
entries.cost: Transferring to another role or changing jobs may mean earning less and losing your night-shift allowance. Job hunting takes time, and making the decision is hard. If you factor this in when choosing a job, the cost is zero.
entries.summary: People who work night shifts have about 13% more cardiovascular disease and about 27% more cardiovascular deaths than people who do not. The longer they do it, the greater the risk: each additional 5 years of night-shift work is associated with about 7% more cardiovascular disease. So count this cost in years, and transfer to another role early if you can.
entries.benefit: A combined analysis of 23 observational follow-up studies, in which people were not assigned to groups, found that night-shift workers had about a 13% higher risk of cardiovascular events (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.10–1.16; this is the confidence interval). Cardiovascular mortality was about 27% higher (RR 1.27, 1.18–1.36). By duration, each additional 5 years of night-shift work was associated with about a 7% higher incidence of cardiovascular disease (RR 1.07, 1.04–1.09) and about 5% higher cardiovascular mortality (RR 1.05, 1.03–1.06). By condition, coronary heart disease incidence was about 22% higher (1.22, 1.16–1.28), coronary heart disease mortality about 22% higher (1.22, 1.10–1.36), ischemic heart disease mortality about 39% higher (1.39, 1.06–1.84), and stroke mortality about 49% higher (1.49, 1.04–2.12). The finding for stroke incidence was not statistically significant (1.06, 0.95–1.18).
entries.sources: Xi J, Ma W, Tao Y, et al. (2025). Association between night shift work and cardiovascular disease: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1668848>; Esposito G, Bravi F, Santucci C, et al. (2025). Night shift work and breast cancer risk in healthcare workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Occupational Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1093/occmed/kqaf040>; Shen QM, Li ZY, Tan YT, et al. (2026). Night shift work and risk of total and site-specific cancer: results from a prospective cohort study among Chinese men. Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health. <https://doi.org/10.5271/sjweh.4290>; Czeisler CA, Johnson MP, Duffy JF, et al. (1990). Exposure to bright light and darkness to treat physiologic maladaptation to night work. New England Journal of Medicine, 322(18), 1253-1259. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199005033221801>; Eastman CI, Stewart KT, Mahoney MP, Liu L, Fogg LF (1994). Dark goggles and bright light improve circadian rhythm adaptation to night-shift work. Sleep, 17(6), 535-543: “Both bright light and goggles were significant factors for producing circadian rhythm phase shifts. The combination of bright light plus goggles was the most effective” “Goggles were necessary for producing phase delays”. <https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/17.6.535>; Crowley SJ, Lee C, Tseng CY, Fogg LF, Eastman CI (2003). Combinations of bright light, scheduled dark, sunglasses, and melatonin to facilitate circadian entrainment to night shift work. Journal of Biological Rhythms, 18(6), 513-523: “With bright light during the night shift, almost all of the earlier participants achieved complete re-entrainment, and the phase delay shift was so large that darker sunglasses and melatonin could not increase its magnitude”. <https://doi.org/10.1177/0748730403258422>
entries.notes: These were all observational studies; people were not assigned to groups. Night-shift workers already differ from other people in smoking, weight, and income, and adjustments cannot fully account for these differences. The evidence that night shifts cause cancer is much weaker than commonly claimed. In an analysis combining 12 studies and 12,132 breast cancer cases, the risk among people who had worked night shifts was only about 5% higher, and the confidence interval crossed 1 (RR 1.05, 0.96–1.14). The group who had worked night shifts for at least 20 years had about a 25% higher risk (1.25, 1.01–1.55). But after the authors performed an influence analysis, this finding was no longer significant. After adjustment for possible publication bias, it was close to 1; in the authors' words, the association was “far from established.” In another study that followed Chinese men for 16.1 years and recorded 8,202 cancer cases, night-shift work was not associated with cancer overall or with most common cancers. Only pancreatic cancer was about 59% higher in the group with 11 to 20 cumulative years of night-shift work (HR 1.59, 1.09–2.31). So this item weighs the cardiovascular risk, not the cancer risk. This book does not argue that everyone should leave night-shift work. It lays out the cost by years worked so you can weigh it yourself. If you already work night shifts, start with what you can change: for quitting smoking, see Item 1 of this section (quit smoking; the earlier, the better); for blood pressure and blood lipids, see Item 12 of this section (if you have high blood pressure or high blood lipids, take medication regularly as prescribed); for catching up on sleep after a night shift, see Item 38 of this section (after staying up late, catch up on sleep the next night). There are two other measures you can try: confine eating to daytime, and use bright light together with strict daytime light blocking to shift your body clock. The latter really did shift the body clock in experiments. After six consecutive night shifts under ordinary indoor lighting, the body clock did not budge; with 7,000 to 12,000 lux of bright light and near-total darkness during the day, it shifted completely within four days. **The light at night needs to be bright enough, daytime sleep needs strict light blocking, and you should wear sunglasses on the way home from work to block morning light; the researchers recommend doing all three together.** In a simulated night-shift experiment with 50 people, bright light at night and sunglasses after work each helped, and the combination worked best. In people who did not wear sunglasses, the body clock shifted only earlier, not later; the authors thought daylight on the journey home was preventing a later shift. In another experiment with 67 people, almost all those whose body clocks had initially been on the early side shifted completely when they had bright light at night; darker sunglasses did not shift them any further. Among those with indoor lighting only, darker sunglasses helped more. For both measures, the outcomes studied went only as far as metabolic markers and sleep; no trial has tested whether following them reduces cardiovascular risk. If you return to a daytime routine on days off, your body clock will shift back again. Doses, original figures, and the remaining sources, along with how the body tells time, are in [docs/Body Clock and Night Shifts](../docs/生物钟和夜班.md).

entries.title: Buy prepackaged cooking oil with an SC license number, not loose, freshly pressed peanut oil from a small workshop
entries.cost: Buy it somewhere else; the price is about the same. Just check the package for a food production license number beginning with SC. The hard part is persuading older family members who are used to buying freshly pressed oil.
entries.summary: Peanuts that become damp and moldy can develop aflatoxins, known carcinogens that mainly harm the liver. After Guangzhou brought small workshops under regulation, abnormal liver function among residents who regularly consumed freshly pressed oil fell by about 35%. In Guangxi, pregnant women who consumed freshly pressed peanut oil had about a 90% higher risk of having a baby with low birth weight and about an 80% higher risk of preterm birth.
entries.benefit: The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies aflatoxins as Group 1 carcinogens (known to cause cancer in humans), particularly liver cancer. A study in Guangzhou measured aflatoxin B1 in peanut oil freshly pressed by small workshops from 2010 to 2022. The median was 1.29 μg/kg, with the middle half of samples ranging from 0.12 to 6.58 μg/kg. After local regulations governing small workshops were introduced, the toxin level in the oil immediately fell by 2.865 μg/kg and then declined by another 2.593 μg/kg each year. The proportion of residents in the area who regularly consumed freshly pressed oil and had abnormal liver function subsequently fell (PR 0.650, 95% CI 0.469–0.902, the confidence interval), by about 35%. In a Guangxi study that followed 1,611 pregnant women, 81.7% consumed freshly pressed peanut oil. Those who consumed it had about a 90% higher risk of having a baby with low birth weight (aOR 1.9, 1.1–3.2) and about an 80% higher risk of preterm birth (aOR 1.8, 1.1–3.0).
entries.sources: Lei J, Li Y, Wang Y, et al. (2024). The impact of small food workshops management regulations on aflatoxin B1 in home-made peanut oil and the liver function of high-consumption area residents: an interrupted time series study in Guangzhou, China. Frontiers in Public Health, 12. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1484414>; Zhong Y, Lu H, Jiang Y, et al. (2024). Effect of homemade peanut oil consumption during pregnancy on low birth weight and preterm birth outcomes: a cohort study in Southwestern China. Global Health Action, 17. <https://doi.org/10.1080/16549716.2024.2336312>; IARC (2012). Chemical Agents and Related Occupations. IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Vol 100F. <https://publications.iarc.fr/123>; China's National Health and Family Planning Commission and China Food and Drug Administration (2017). National Food Safety Standard: Maximum Levels of Mycotoxins in Foods (GB 2761-2017)
entries.notes: Both studies only tracked and recorded outcomes; neither had a control group. The Guangzhou study measured liver function test results, not liver cancer or deaths. The median toxin level in home-pressed oil was actually below the Chinese national standard limit of 20 μg/kg for peanut oil. The risk comes from eating it over many years and from individual batches with high levels. The national standard limit applies to all peanut oil, but prepackaged oil must pass production licensing and pre-release factory inspection. Small workshops are regulated under each Chinese province's rules and are sampled for inspection far less often. For what to do with moldy peanuts, corn, and nuts stored at home, see item 46 in this section (throw out the entire package if it has gone moldy). The main beneficiaries of this item are you and the family members who eat with you.

entries.title: Use vegetable oil instead of lard and butter for cooking; you do not need to rotate among oils for health, and do not count on flaxseed oil to protect your heart
entries.cost: No extra expense. Vegetable oil is already the main cooking fat in most households. The hard part is changing your taste for stir-frying with lard and mixing it into rice.
entries.summary: Eating less saturated fat, such as lard and butter, and replacing it with vegetable oil reduces events such as heart disease and stroke by about 17%, but no change in the overall risk of death was found. Eating more of the main components of soybean and corn oils showed neither benefit nor harm. Eating more flaxseed oil did not show a reduction in heart disease risk either.
entries.benefit: Cochrane pooled 15 randomized trials involving 56,675 people, each lasting at least two years. Eating less saturated fat reduced cardiovascular events overall by about 17% (RR 0.83, 0.70–0.98). All-cause mortality was virtually unchanged (RR 0.96, 0.90–1.03), as was cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.95, 0.80–1.12). No difference in effect was found between replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat (the main components of soybean and corn oils) and replacing it with carbohydrates. There were too few data on replacing it with monounsaturated fat (the main components of rapeseed and olive oils) to draw a conclusion. Another Cochrane review pooled 19 randomized trials involving 6,461 people. For eating more omega-6 (linoleic acid), the RR was 1.00 (0.88–1.12) for all-cause mortality and 0.97 (0.81–1.15) for cardiovascular events, showing neither benefit nor harm. A third review pooled 86 randomized trials involving 162,796 people. Eating more plant-derived omega-3 (the main components of flaxseed and perilla oils) had an RR of 1.01 (0.84–1.20) for all-cause mortality and 1.00 (0.82–1.22) for coronary heart disease events, indicating essentially no effect.
entries.sources: Hooper L, Martin N, Jimoh OF, et al. (2020). Reduction in saturated fat for cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (5), CD011737. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD011737.pub3>; Hooper L, Al-Khudairy L, Abdelhamid AS, et al. (2018). Omega-6 fats for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (11), CD011094. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD011094.pub4>; Abdelhamid AS, Brown TJ, Brainard JS, et al. (2020). Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (3), CD003177. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD003177.pub5>; Chinese Nutrition Society (2022). Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Residents (2022). People's Medical Publishing House
entries.notes: Controversy: Some argue that the high omega-6 content of soybean and corn oils promotes inflammation, so people should eat less of them and switch oils. The randomized trials in the omega-6 review above found no harm; the authors rated the quality of the evidence as low. The magnitude of benefit is rated moderate based on the 17% reduction in cardiovascular events; all-cause mortality did not change. Whichever oil you use, limit the amount. The Chinese dietary guidelines recommend 25 to 30 grams of cooking oil per person per day.

entries.title: Turn on the range hood when stir-frying or pan-frying, and keep it running from the moment you turn on the heat until you finish cooking
entries.cost: If your home already has a range hood, the only extra cost is a little electricity. If it does not, buying and installing one costs several hundred to over a thousand yuan. The hard part is remembering to turn it on every time you cook and not switching it off because of the noise.
entries.summary: Among Chinese women who do not smoke, those who never or rarely use a range hood when stir-frying have about twice the risk of lung cancer as those who use one regularly. Women who have lived in homes with poorly ventilated kitchens also have about 50% higher risk; the difference is most pronounced in households that burn coal.
entries.benefit: A pooled analysis of 10 case-control studies included only Chinese women who did not smoke. Case-control studies compare people with lung cancer against people without it and ask them retrospectively about their past habits. Women exposed to cooking oil fumes had about 1.74 times the odds of lung cancer (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.57–1.94, confidence interval). In four of the studies, women exposed to oil fumes who did not use a range hood had about 2.11 times the odds (1.54–2.89). A study in Taiwan compared 1,302 women who did not smoke and had lung cancer with 1,302 women without the disease. It looked only at women who had cooked for more than ten years. Compared with women who used a range hood in less than one-third of those years, women who used one in more than two-thirds of them had about half the risk (odds ratio 0.49, 0.32–0.76). A prospective study in Shanghai followed 71,000 women who did not smoke from 1996 to 2009 and identified 429 lung cancer cases. Women who reported having lived in homes with poorly ventilated kitchens had about 49% higher lung cancer risk (HR 1.49, 1.15–1.95). For those who had burned coal in poorly ventilated kitchens for more than 20 years, the risk was about 2.03 times as high (HR 2.03, 1.35–3.05). Looking only at whether they had ever burned coal showed no difference (HR 1.03, 0.84–1.26). No difference was found by the type of oil used for stir-frying either.
entries.sources: Xue Y, Jiang Y, Jin S, Li Y (2016). Association between cooking oil fume exposure and lung cancer among Chinese nonsmoking women: a meta-analysis. OncoTargets and Therapy, 9, 2987-2992. <https://doi.org/10.2147/OTT.S100949>; Chen TY, Fang YH, Chen HL, et al. (2020). Impact of cooking oil fume exposure and fume extractor use on lung cancer risk in non-smoking Han Chinese women. Scientific Reports, 10, 6774. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-63656-7>; Kim C, Gao YT, Xiang YB, et al. (2015). Home kitchen ventilation, cooking fuels, and lung cancer risk in a prospective cohort of never smoking women in Shanghai, China. International Journal of Cancer, 136(3), 632-638. <https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.29020>
entries.notes: Controversy: The figures supporting range hood use come mainly from case-control studies. After a diagnosis, patients recalling the past may underreport how often they used a range hood, so the figures may be too high. In the prospective Shanghai study, the increased risk was concentrated mainly in households that burned coal and had poor ventilation. That study provides no separate figure for how much difference range hood use makes in households that burn only gas. The evidence is therefore rated B, while the benefit is rated large based on the roughly twofold difference in risk. For avoiding coal and firewood when cooking, see item 29 in this section (do not burn coal or firewood for cooking or heating). The main beneficiaries of this item are the people who usually cook at home.

entries.title: If hot flashes and night sweats around menopause affect your life, see a gynecologist to assess hormone therapy; do not just endure them or buy medication yourself, and do not use hormones to prevent heart disease
entries.cost: Visit a gynecologist or menopause clinic once. The doctor will ask about your medical history, check whether you have any conditions that make hormone therapy unsuitable, and prescribe it if appropriate. Once you start, you will need follow-up appointments as your doctor directs. The hard part is letting go of the fear that any exposure to hormones causes cancer, while also not buying them yourself because you heard they can slow aging.
entries.summary: For hot flashes and night sweats around menopause, hormone therapy reduces the number of hot flashes by about 75% compared with placebo. The trade-off is a small increase in breast cancer, blood clots, and stroke: about eight additional cases of each per 10,000 women per year. All-cause mortality was not higher among those who started between ages 50 and 59. Hormone therapy cannot be used to prevent heart disease or dementia.
entries.benefit: Cochrane pooled 24 randomized trials involving 3,329 people that compared oral hormones with placebo. Women taking hormones had about 75% fewer hot flashes per week than those taking placebo (95% CI 64.3–82.3, confidence interval). The severity of hot flashes also fell markedly (OR 0.13, 0.07–0.23). Hot flashes fell by about 57.7% among women taking placebo too, so any treatment claimed to relieve hot flashes must be compared with placebo to establish whether it works. For risks, consider the U.S. WHI randomized trial. It enrolled 16,608 women aged 50 to 79 who had a uterus, used estrogen plus progestin, and were followed for an average of 5.2 years. Coronary heart disease was about 29% higher (HR 1.29, 1.02–1.63). Invasive breast cancer was about 26% higher (HR 1.26, 1.00–1.59). Stroke was about 41% higher (HR 1.41, 1.07–1.85). Pulmonary embolism was about 2.13 times as likely (HR 2.13, 1.39–3.25). In absolute terms, per 10,000 women per year, there were 7 additional cases of coronary heart disease, 8 additional strokes, 8 additional pulmonary embolisms, and 8 additional cases of invasive breast cancer. At the same time, there were 6 fewer cases of colorectal cancer and 5 fewer hip fractures. Among women who had had a hysterectomy and used estrogen alone, breast cancer was instead about 21% lower over 13 years of cumulative follow-up (HR 0.79, 0.65–0.97). Across both trials, all-cause mortality did not change over 18 years of follow-up (HR 0.99, 0.94–1.03). By age at treatment initiation, the group aged 50 to 59 had about 31% lower all-cause mortality during the years they took the medication (HR 0.69, 0.51–0.94). The figures were 1.04 (0.87–1.25) for ages 60 to 69 and 1.13 (0.94–1.36) for ages 70 to 79; neither was statistically significant. At 18 years of follow-up, the figure for the 50-to-59 group was 0.89 (0.79–1.01), which was no longer statistically significant either. Looking only at women aged 50 to 59, a 2017 Cochrane review found that the only clear increase was in blood clots with combined estrogen and progestin, with an absolute risk below 1 in 500. Among women over 65 using combined estrogen and progestin, dementia cases rose from 9 per 1,000 to between 11 and 30 per 1,000 over four years. In 2022, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommended against using hormones to prevent chronic disease (grade D recommendation), concluding that there was no net benefit.
entries.sources: MacLennan AH, Broadbent JL, Lester S, Moore V (2004). Oral oestrogen and combined oestrogen/progestogen therapy versus placebo for hot flushes. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (4), CD002978. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002978.pub2>; Writing Group for the Women's Health Initiative Investigators, Rossouw JE, Anderson GL, Prentice RL, et al. (2002). Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results from the Women's Health Initiative randomized controlled trial. JAMA, 288(3), 321-333. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.288.3.321>; Manson JE, Chlebowski RT, Stefanick ML, et al. (2013). Menopausal hormone therapy and health outcomes during the intervention and extended poststopping phases of the Women's Health Initiative randomized trials. JAMA, 310(13), 1353-1368. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2013.278040>; Manson JE, Aragaki AK, Rossouw JE, et al. (2017). Menopausal hormone therapy and long-term all-cause and cause-specific mortality: the Women's Health Initiative randomized trials. JAMA, 318(10), 927-938. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2017.11217>; Marjoribanks J, Farquhar C, Roberts H, et al. (2017). Long-term hormone therapy for perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (1), CD004143. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD004143.pub5>; US Preventive Services Task Force, Mangione CM, Barry MJ, et al. (2022). Hormone therapy for the primary prevention of chronic conditions in postmenopausal persons: US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement. JAMA, 328(17), 1740-1746. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.18625>
entries.notes: Controversy: Women in the WHI had an average age of 63 and used a single fixed oral regimen. Today, most women start therapy in their 50s, shortly after menopause, to manage symptoms, which is not completely identical to the trial population. The lower mortality observed in the 50–59 age group came from subgroup analyses by age, and this difference was no longer statistically significant by year 18 of follow-up; therefore, it cannot be claimed that hormones extend lifespan. Cochrane also explicitly stated that the trial sample size was insufficient to clearly determine the risks for women within 10 years of menopause. The following groups are generally not suitable candidates: those with a history of breast cancer, a history of blood clots, high cardiovascular risk, or severe obesity, subject to a doctor's specific evaluation. In individuals with an intact uterus, estrogen alone increases the risk of endometrial cancer, so it must be combined with a progestogen. Only those who have had a hysterectomy can use estrogen alone. Hormones can also reduce fractures, but this is generally considered only when other anti-osteoporosis medications are unsuitable. For osteoporosis, first see Section 1, Item 39 (bone mineral density testing) and Section 1, Item 40 (initiating medication once osteoporosis is diagnosed). The magnitude of benefit is classified as large based on a ~75% reduction in hot flushes; the clinical endpoint is symptom relief, not all-cause mortality. The primary beneficiary of this item is yourself, but it also includes your mother and spouse.

entries.title: If you already wanted to get a dog, count daily dog walking toward your walking volume; do not get a dog specifically for longevity
entries.cost: Owning a dog is an ongoing financial expense: dog food, vaccines, deworming, veterinary care, and licensing all require out-of-pocket spending, and you must care for the dog until it dies of old age. You must carve out time every day to walk the dog, and you need to find someone to look after it when traveling for business or pleasure. The difficulty lies in daily persistence; once you get one, you cannot just stop whenever you want. In China, there are no official statistics on how much it costs to raise a dog, so no figures are listed here.
entries.summary: Dog owners have, on average, about a one-quarter lower probability of dying during the same follow-up period, with an even greater reduction among those with a history of coronary heart disease. However, after adjusting for other confounding differences, large studies in the UK and Norway showed no difference, and cat ownership showed no association either. Therefore, do not get a dog specifically for longevity; if you already wanted to get one, treat daily dog walking as part of your walking routine.
entries.benefit: Pooling 10 follow-up cohort studies together, covering about 3.84 million people with an average follow-up of 10.1 years: dog owners had about a 24% lower risk of death (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.86, which is the credible interval). Cardiovascular mortality was about 31% lower (RR 0.69, 0.67–0.71). Among individuals with prior coronary heart disease, having a dog in the household was associated with about a 65% lower risk (RR 0.35, 0.17–0.69). The authors explicitly stated that this pooled analysis did not control for other confounding factors. A nationwide Swedish registry study of about 3.43 million people controlled for factors such as income and marital status. Across all participants combined, dog ownership was associated with about a 20% lower risk of death (HR 0.80, 0.79–0.82). For individuals living alone, owning a dog was associated with about a 33% lower risk of death (HR 0.67, 0.65–0.69). For those living with others, the risk was about 11% lower (HR 0.89, 0.87–0.91). Among Swedish patients following a myocardial infarction, living alone with a dog was associated with about a 33% lower risk of death (HR 0.67, 0.61–0.75), and living with a partner or child was associated with about a 15% lower risk (HR 0.85, 0.80–0.90). Following an ischemic stroke, the risk was lower by about 27% (HR 0.73, 0.66–0.80) and 12% (HR 0.88, 0.83–0.93), respectively. Counterevidence: Six rounds of the Health Survey for England totaling 59,352 people were followed for an average of 11.5 years. After full adjustment, dog ownership had no association with all-cause mortality (HR 1.03, 0.98–1.09), nor with cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.07, 0.96–1.18). A Norwegian study with a median follow-up of 18.5 years showed nearly identical mortality risks among dog owners (HR 1.00, 0.91–1.09). Dog owners there also did not have higher physical activity levels than non-owners. In the Swedish Twin Registry, where lifestyle habits could be queried for 34,202 individuals, the association between dog ownership and lower cardiovascular disease or mortality risks could not be replicated. An Australian study of 15,735 people followed for 4 years showed that dog owners had about a 23% lower risk of death (OR 0.77, 0.59–0.99), part of which could be explained by higher physical activity levels. Owning cats, birds, or fish showed no association with mortality. A 2013 American Heart Association scientific statement noted that pet ownership, particularly dog ownership, "may be reasonable" for reducing cardiovascular risk—this is the weakest tier of recommendation. The same statement explicitly advised against adopting, rescuing, or purchasing a pet primarily to achieve cardiovascular risk reduction.

entries.notes: Controversy. The above are all observational cohort records without randomized controlled allocation; therefore, one cannot conclude that one should "get a dog for longevity." People who are capable of owning a dog may inherently be healthier and more physically active, while people who are sick or disabled may inherently be less likely to keep a dog; these differences cannot be completely adjusted away. The 24% figure in the meta-analysis did not control for any factors, and in the several studies where lifestyle habits could be investigated, the differences vanished. In another Swedish study, dog owners were actually slightly more likely to start taking antihypertensive and lipid-lowering drugs, so even if the mortality risk is genuinely lower, it is not achieved through lowering blood pressure or blood lipids. There is only one actionable takeaway: if you already own a dog or already intended to get one, count daily dog walking toward your walking volume; to see whether it is sufficient, refer to Section 2, Item 11 (reaching 7,000–8,000 steps daily). For matters regarding leashing, vaccination, and liability for dog bites, see Section 8, Item 30 (dogs must be leashed). For how older adults in the household should hold the leash to prevent falls while dog walking, see Section 17, Item 10 (dog walking for seniors). The magnitude of benefit is mechanically categorized as large based on the 24% meta-analysis figure, but this number did not adjust for other factors. The primary beneficiary of this item is yourself.

entries.title: If diagnosed with prediabetes (elevated blood glucose, not yet reaching diabetes), rely on eating less, losing weight, and being more active to delay diabetes, and recheck blood glucose every six months
entries.cost: Costs no money; eating less can even save a bit. Do at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity activity such as brisk walking, which averages out to twenty-some minutes per day. Eat 400 to 500 kcal less per day than before. The difficulty lies in ongoing persistence; after weight is lost, it must still be maintained. Draw blood for a recheck every six months; a fasting blood glucose test costs a dozen or so yuan.
entries.summary: For individuals with elevated blood glucose who have not yet developed diabetes, eating less, moving more, and losing a little weight can reduce the risk of developing diabetes by 30% to 60%. In the Da Qing trial in China followed for 30 years, people who did this had about a one-quarter lower probability of dying and lived about one and a half years longer on average. However, similar trials in the United States and Finland did not detect a difference in mortality.
entries.benefit: The Da Qing Study was a randomized trial conducted in Daqing, Heilongjiang, with assignment by clinic. It assigned 577 adults with impaired glucose tolerance (a form of prediabetes) to a control group or one of three intervention groups: diet alone, exercise alone, or both. The intervention lasted 6 years. Over those 6 years, the cumulative proportion who developed diabetes was 67.7% in the control group, 43.8% in the diet group, 41.1% in the exercise group, and 46.0% in the diet-plus-exercise group. After adjusting for differences in body mass index and fasting blood glucose, the risk of developing diabetes was about 31%, 46%, and 42% lower in the three intervention groups, respectively. The reductions were similar for people below and above a body mass index of 25. At 23 years of follow-up, cardiovascular mortality in the intervention groups was about 41% lower (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.36–0.96, the range of plausible values). All-cause mortality was about 29% lower (HR 0.71, 0.51–0.99). The risk of developing diabetes was about 45% lower (HR 0.55, 0.40–0.76). At 30 years of follow-up, the intervention delayed the onset of diabetes by 3.96 years (based on the median). Cardiovascular events were about 26% lower (HR 0.74, 0.59–0.92). Severe small-vessel complications affecting the retina, kidneys, or nerves were about 35% lower (HR 0.65, 0.45–0.95). Cardiovascular mortality was about 33% lower (HR 0.67, 0.48–0.94). All-cause mortality was about 26% lower (HR 0.74, 0.61–0.89). Participants lived an average of 1.44 years longer (0.20–2.68). The US DPP trial randomly assigned 3,234 people with elevated blood glucose. The lifestyle group's goals were to lose at least 7% of body weight and be active for at least 150 minutes a week. After an average follow-up of 2.8 years, the lifestyle group's risk of developing diabetes was 58% lower than the placebo group's (95% CI 48%–66%). The group taking metformin had a 31% lower risk (17%–43%), less of a reduction than with lifestyle changes. At an average follow-up of 15 years, the lifestyle group's risk was still 27% lower (HR 0.73, 0.65–0.83), but the gap narrowed year by year. At a median follow-up of 21 years, all-cause mortality did not differ between the lifestyle and placebo groups (HR 1.02, 0.81–1.28). Cardiovascular mortality did not differ either (HR 1.18, 0.77–1.81). The Finnish DPS trial randomly assigned 522 overweight people with impaired glucose tolerance. The cumulative proportion who developed diabetes over 4 years was 11% in the intervention group and 23% in the control group. During the trial, the risk was 58% lower. After one-on-one counseling ended, follow-up continued; at a median of 7 years, the risk was still 43% lower. At an average follow-up of 10.6 years, there was no clear difference in all-cause mortality (HR 0.57, 0.21–1.58), or in cardiovascular disease (HR 1.04, 0.72–1.51). The Healthy China Action sets these thresholds: fasting blood glucose of 6.1 to 7.0 mmol/L (excluding 7.0) counts as prediabetes. So does blood glucose of 7.8 to 11.1 mmol/L (excluding 11.1) two hours after drinking a glucose solution. It recommends that people who are overweight or obese bring their body mass index down to or close to 24, or lose at least 7% of their body weight. Reduce total daily dietary energy intake by at least 400 to 500 kilocalories, and get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity each week. Have fasting blood glucose or blood glucose two hours after a meal checked every six months.

entries.notes: Disputed. All three trials found that fewer people developed diabetes and that its onset was delayed. But only the Da Qing trial found a reduction in deaths. Da Qing had just 577 participants, and its authors also said the number was small because the trial had originally been designed to examine diabetes. After the US DPP trial ended, everyone was invited to attend a modified lifestyle program, including the placebo group. The authors of the Finnish trial stated that the number of participants might have been too small to detect modest differences. Delaying diabetes is therefore established, but whether it extends life remains unsettled. Participants in the US and Finnish trials had an average body mass index above 30. In Da Qing, the average was only 25.7. The trial advised weight loss only for people with a body mass index over 25, and participants did not lose much weight. The authors believe the main effects came from changing what people ate and moving more. So people who are not overweight should also change what they eat and move more. Start by giving up sugary drinks; see item 7 of this section (Do not drink sugar-sweetened beverages). To judge whether you are active enough, see item 11 of this section (Walk 7,000–8,000 steps a day). For a weight target, see item 32 of this section (Keep your BMI between 20 and 25). For how to find out whether you have prediabetes, see item 8 of section 1 (Have your fasting blood glucose checked once). Metformin can also reduce the risk of developing diabetes, but it is less effective than lifestyle changes; a doctor should decide whether you should take it. The benefit is rated large based on the approximately 26% lower all-cause mortality in Da Qing, but the US and Finnish trials did not replicate that result. The main beneficiary of this item is you.

entries.title: If peanuts, corn, nuts, rice, or flour at home have gone moldy, throw away the whole package; do not pick out the moldy pieces and eat the rest. Spit out a nut immediately if it tastes bitter when you chew it
entries.cost: Throwing away a package of peanuts or nuts, or a bag of rice or flour, costs a few to a few dozen yuan. Store grains and nuts in a dry, ventilated, cool place, buy small packages, and keep fewer supplies on hand. The hard part is being willing to throw food away, especially when persuading older family members.
entries.summary: Moldy peanuts and corn can contain aflatoxins, which can cause liver cancer. In a Shanghai study, people whose urine tested positive for this toxin had about 3.4 times the risk of liver cancer of those whose urine tested negative. People who carried the hepatitis B virus and tested positive for the toxin had about 59.4 times the risk of people with neither. Stir-frying, boiling, and deep-frying do little to remove the toxin.
entries.benefit: The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies aflatoxins as Group 1 carcinogens (known to cause cancer in humans); the cancer they cause is liver cancer. They are most common in peanuts and corn, and ordinary cooking methods such as stir-frying, boiling, and deep-frying do little to destroy them. A Shanghai study followed 18,244 middle-aged men starting in 1986, collecting one urine sample from each man when he entered the study. Over about 70,000 person-years of follow-up, researchers identified 55 cases of liver cancer. They compared 50 of those cases with 267 people in the same cohort who had not developed the disease. People whose urine tested positive for aflatoxins had about 3.4 times the risk of liver cancer (RR 3.4, 95% CI 1.1–10.0, the range of plausible values). Those who tested positive for hepatitis B surface antigen had about 7.3 times the risk (2.2–24.4). Those with both had about 59.4 times the risk (16.6–212.0), compared with people with neither. In an earlier analysis of the same cohort, after adjusting for hepatitis B, smoking, drinking, and education level, those who tested positive for the toxin had about 3.8 times the risk (1.2–12.2). Qidong, Jiangsu, used to have a high incidence of liver cancer. Starting in the 1980s, the local staple food changed from corn to rice. The median level of a toxin biomarker in residents' blood fell from 19.3 pg/mg in 1989 to undetectable levels (below 0.5) in 2009. Among residents under 35, the liver cancer mortality rate fell by more than half across cohorts born from the 1960s through the 1980s. All these cohorts were born before hepatitis B vaccination of newborns became widespread. The authors estimated that about 65% of the decline in liver cancer deaths could be attributed to reduced toxin intake, with 83% of that reduction occurring among people infected with hepatitis B. According to global estimates, the same amount of ingested toxin has about 30 times the cancer-causing effect in hepatitis B carriers as in people who do not carry the virus. Each year in China, a number of liver cancer cases can be attributed to this toxin. About 5,300 to 14,400 of these cases occur in hepatitis B carriers, and about 1,990 to 4,430 in people who do not carry the virus.

entries.notes: The figures in the benefit section measure the relationship between how much toxin people ingest and liver cancer. No study has directly measured how much throwing away moldy food at home reduces liver cancer. The Shanghai study tested urine only once, when participants enrolled. Intake estimated from dietary questionnaires showed no association with liver cancer, indicating that questionnaires do not estimate intake accurately enough and laboratory testing is needed. By 2009, toxin biomarkers were no longer detectable among Qidong residents. The amounts most households ingest today are probably far lower than they were then, but this is a judgment; there are no nationwide figures. So the benefit was judged moderate rather than mechanically classified as large based on the 3.4-fold figure. Why throw away the whole package? The Guangdong Provincial Health Commission advises throwing away the entire bag if nuts or peanuts smell off when opened, to avoid scattering mold spores when the contents are shaken out. Food with a moldy smell must be discarded. The US Department of Agriculture’s food safety guidance says to discard moldy peanut butter, legumes, and nuts, as well as cooked rice and noodles and bread. Only firm vegetables with low water content, such as cabbage and carrots, can be eaten after cutting away at least 2.5 centimeters around the moldy spot. The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs warns that moldy peanuts taste bitter and unusual; if you accidentally eat one, spit it out immediately and rinse your mouth. The added risk is clearest for hepatitis B carriers. If you have never been tested for hepatitis B, see Section 1, Item 14 (get the hepatitis B two-pairs-and-a-half panel). For buying oil, see Item 40 of this section (do not buy loose, freshly pressed peanut oil from small workshops). This item concerns grains and nuts stored at home. Acute poisoning from soaked wood ear mushrooms or fermented rice and flour products involves a different toxin; see Section 1, Item 48 (do not make fermented rice and flour products at home). Nuts without mold are still worth eating; see Item 22 of this section (eat a small handful of nuts every day). The main beneficiaries of this item are you and the family members who eat with you.

entries.title: Do not eat raw freshwater fish and shrimp dishes, including raw fish slices, raw fish porridge, and drunken shrimp; if you have eaten them often, go to a hospital for a liver fluke test, and if you test positive, take praziquantel as prescribed
entries.cost: Avoiding raw fish costs nothing. The hard part is changing a taste you have had for years and turning it down at group meals. If you have eaten it often, go to a hospital for a stool test for parasite eggs. The cost varies by location. If you test positive, take praziquantel at the dose prescribed by your doctor, usually for 1 to 2 days.
entries.summary: Eating freshwater fish or shrimp raw can infect you with liver flukes. This parasite is known to cause cancer. Infected people are about four to five times as likely to develop bile duct cancer as uninfected people. Vinegar, alcohol, and mustard cannot kill it effectively. If you are infected, two days of medication cures more than 90% of cases.
entries.benefit: Clonorchis sinensis is commonly called the liver fluke. At a meeting in 2009, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization, determined that long-term infection with it causes cancer in humans. It causes bile duct cancer and was classified as Group 1. The 1994 assessment had classified it only as Group 2A (probably carcinogenic). Combining published studies, the risk of bile duct cancer among people infected with liver flukes is about 4.8 times as high. The original paper reports a relative risk of 4.8 (95% CI 2.8–8.4, the confidence interval). This figure also includes another liver fluke found in Southeast Asia. In the same paper, the figures were 2.6-fold for hepatitis B and 1.8-fold for hepatitis C; liver flukes had the strongest association. Another paper pooled 36 studies. In case-control studies, the figure for bile duct cancer was about 4.37-fold (OR 4.37, 2.84–6.72). In follow-up studies, it was about 10.43-fold (RR 10.43, 2.90–37.47). The figure for cholangitis and cholecystitis was about 7.80-fold (RR 7.80). For gallstones, it was about 2.42-fold (RR 2.42). For hepatocellular carcinoma, it was about 4.69-fold (OR 4.69). No significant association was found for cirrhosis. The heavier the infection, the more common these diseases were. A nationwide survey in 2014–2015 found an infection rate of 0.47%, or about 6 million people. The four provinces with infection rates above 1% were Guangdong, Guangxi, Heilongjiang, and Jilin. Estimates based on surveillance data from 2016–2021 put the nationwide rate in 2020 at about 0.67%, or about 9.46 million people. The estimated rates were about 8.92% in Guangxi and 2.99% in Guangdong. In 2024, China’s National Disease Control and Prevention Administration and 14 other departments issued a prevention and control plan. The plan uses the average infection rates at surveillance sites from 2018–2022 as its baseline: 8.75% in Guangxi, 4.38% in Jilin, 3.16% in Heilongjiang, and 2.95% in Guangdong. In 2026, the China National Center for Food Safety Risk Assessment warned that seasonings such as alcohol, vinegar, and mustard cannot effectively kill liver flukes. Freezing requires a continuous period of at least 7 days below −20°C. Heating requires the center of the food to reach above 70°C and stay there for more than 10 minutes. The International Agency for Research on Cancer also states that cured and smoked freshwater fish can transmit the infection. For treatment, a 2022 review covered 26 trials involving 3,340 people. The World Health Organization’s recommended praziquantel regimen is 25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per dose, 3 times a day for 2 days. The predicted cure rate for Clonorchis sinensis infection is 98.5% (85.4%–99.9%).
