entries.notes: All the risk figures above come from case-control studies and follow-up records, without randomized control groups. No study has directly compared whether testing followed by treatment reduces bile duct cancer. Bile duct cancer is uncommon to begin with, so although the relative risks are high, the extra risk for any one person is small. The evidence grade is therefore B. The approximately 4.8-fold figure compares infected and uninfected people; it does not show how much disease this action can prevent. The benefit was therefore judged moderate, using the same approach as Item 46 of this section (throw away the whole package if it is moldy). The Guangdong Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention says liver flukes can live in the human body for 20 to 30 years. Mild infections often have no symptoms, so people who often eat raw fish should not wait until they feel unwell to get tested. Examining stool for parasite eggs is the way to confirm an infection; ultrasound, CT, and blood tests can only provide supporting information. A doctor must set the praziquantel dose according to body weight and the severity of the infection. The National Institute of Parasitic Diseases states that, in places where cysticercosis occurs, medical history should be checked before a high dose is given. If you resume eating raw fish after being cured, you can become infected again. Keep knives and cutting boards used for raw fish separate from those used for cooked food. Sea fish sashimi commonly carries other parasites, such as Anisakis. Hong Kong’s Centre for Food Safety advises buying it from licensed shops and says older adults, children, and pregnant women should not eat raw fish. Infection in children can affect their growth. Hepatitis B and C can also damage the liver and cause cancer; see Section 1, Item 14 (get the hepatitis B two-pairs-and-a-half panel) and Section 1, Item 45 (get a one-time hepatitis C antibody test). The main beneficiaries of this item are you and the family members who eat with you.

chapters.title: Do Not Waste Your Mental Energy
chapters.intro:
This section counts only mental energy and time. It looks at four things: how much attention you can use each day, how fast you react, how often you make mistakes, and how long it takes you to get back on track after an interruption. Most figures were measured directly, either in experiments or in records from following a group of people over time (cohort studies). These figures are not converted into years of life or mortality rates. Most items in this section have an evidence grade of B. That is normal for this field and does not mean the advice is unfounded. Item 19 concerns what to expect when dealing with police officers, doctors, and counter clerks. It cites regulations rather than experiments, so its grade is C. Item 15 (treat pessimistic thoughts as symptoms) and Item 22 (treat the thought that “other people expect me to be perfect” as a symptom) cite figures on mortality and suicide risk. Their measures differ from those of the other items in this section, so they are not compared together.

The items in this section are grouped by topic below, with item numbers in parentheses.

**Attention at work**: Turn off nonessential notifications (Item 1), handle messages in batches each day (Item 5), block interruptions that last just a few seconds (Item 6), do one thing at a time (Item 7), use earplugs in an open-plan office (Item 12), and do not keep increasing your weekly work hours indiscriminately (Item 13).

**Sleep and staying up late**: Keep a fixed wake-up time (Item 2), get 7 to 8 hours of sleep each night (Item 3), avoid caffeine after 2 p.m. (Item 4), avoid screens for an hour before bed (Item 8), go to sleep when it is time (Item 9), do not make major decisions late at night (Item 10), take a 10-minute nap if you are sleepy in the afternoon (Item 11), try cognitive behavioral therapy first for long-term insomnia (Item 26), and get checked for sleep apnea if you snore, stop breathing during sleep, and feel sleepy during the day (Item 27).

**Thoughts in your head**: Switch to a hands-on task when you keep going over something in your mind (Item 14), treat pessimistic thoughts as symptoms (Item 15), halve your estimate when you think you have embarrassed yourself (Item 21), and treat the thought that “other people expect me to be perfect” as a symptom (Item 22).

**Anger and low mood**: Leave the situation first when you are angry (Item 17), take a few initial steps when your mood is low (Item 18), do not try to vent anger by hitting a punching bag (Item 23), and write down what is on your mind for several days in a row (Item 24).

**People and social media**: Learn to refuse requests you do not want to take on (Item 16), regard police officers and doctors as people doing their jobs according to rules (Item 19), and set limits on apps where you scroll through updates from people your age (Item 20).

**Physical pain**: Take a pain reliever such as ibuprofen for menstrual cramps (Item 25).

entries.title: Turn off nonessential notifications, and keep your phone out of sight while you work
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Changing the settings takes a few minutes and requires almost no willpower.
entries.summary: When your phone makes a sound, your performance on an attention task drops even if you do not look at or touch it. The drop is about as large as if you actually answered a call or sent a text. There is another situation: your phone is sitting on the desk and you resist looking at it, yet your available mental capacity still shrinks. The more dependent you are on your phone, the greater the drop.
entries.benefit: Simply receiving a notification, without looking at or touching it, makes performance on an attention task markedly worse. The decline is comparable to actually making or answering a call or sending a text. This was a laboratory experiment with university students. Two other experiments showed that even when people successfully resisted looking at their phones, having their own phones nearby reduced their available mental capacity. Those most dependent on their phones had the largest decline.
entries.sources: Stothart, Mitchum & Yehnert (2015). The attentional cost of receiving a cell phone notification. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance. <https://doi.org/10.1037/xhp0000100>；Ward, Duke, Gneezy & Bos (2017). Brain Drain: The Mere Presence of One's Own Smartphone Reduces Available Cognitive Capacity. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research. <https://doi.org/10.1086/691462>
entries.notes: These were all single tasks performed in a laboratory. No one has measured what happens when this accumulates day after day. In jobs that genuinely require you to be reachable at any time, you can leave notifications on for just a few contacts.

entries.title: Keep a fixed wake-up time, including on weekends
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Sleeping in less on weekends takes a little willpower.
entries.summary: The one-fifth of people with the most irregular schedules had body clocks about 2.5 hours later than the one-fifth with the most regular schedules. That is like living with jet lag all the time. Students with more regular schedules also had better grades.
entries.benefit: A study tracked 61 university students for 30 days. The body clocks (circadian rhythms) of the one-fifth with the most irregular schedules ran about 2.5 hours later than those of the one-fifth with the most regular schedules. Specifically, melatonin secretion began at 00:08 versus 21:32. The period when they felt sleepiest and most wanted to sleep was also about 1.8 hours later. More regular schedules were associated with better academic performance (correlation coefficient r = 0.37).
entries.sources: Phillips et al. (2017). Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Scientific Reports. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-03171-4>
entries.notes: There is only this one study, with a small number of participants and no randomized control groups. Using a model, the researchers estimated that the difference in body clocks came mainly from differences in daily light exposure. They suggested trying light to adjust the body clock, but did not test this in an experiment. So, beyond keeping a fixed wake-up time, the advice to go outdoors more during the day for light exposure is an inference from their estimates. For how to catch up after occasionally staying up late, see Section 2, Item 38 (catch up on sleep the following night after staying up late): go to bed earlier that night, rather than sleeping until noon the next day.

entries.title: Get 7 to 8 hours of sleep each night; do not assume 6 hours is enough
entries.cost: It costs nothing. You need to set aside an extra 1 to 2 hours for sleep each day. Going to bed earlier takes a little willpower.
entries.summary: Sleeping only 6 hours a night for two weeks straight brings mental performance down to a level equivalent to staying awake for two days and nights. The trouble is that you do not notice it. Self-rated sleepiness rises for the first few days and then stops rising; people sleeping 6 hours rate themselves just as sleepy as people sleeping 4 hours. So the feeling that “6 hours of sleep is enough for me” is unreliable.
entries.benefit: In a study, 48 healthy adults aged 21 to 38 slept only 6 hours a night for 14 consecutive days. Their mental performance declined cumulatively to a level equivalent to going without sleep for 2 consecutive nights. Yet their self-rated sleepiness rose only during the first few days and barely increased after that. The 6-hour and 4-hour groups did not differ in self-rated sleepiness. This was a randomized controlled trial (RCT) that randomly assigned participants to groups. Separately, for short periods without sleep (acute sleep deprivation, no more than 48 hours), the effect size was g = -0.776 for lapses of simple attention and g = -0.125 for reasoning accuracy. These figures come from combining 70 studies.
entries.sources: Van Dongen, Maislin, Mullington & Dinges (2003). The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness. Sleep. <https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/26.2.117>；Lim & Dinges (2010). A meta-analysis of the impact of short-term sleep deprivation on cognitive variables. Psychological Bulletin. <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018883>
entries.notes: The most important point is that “I do not feel sleepy” is not evidence that you have slept enough. People who regularly sleep 6 hours have merely become used to it in how they feel; their performance has not caught up. The part that combines multiple studies concerns going without sleep for an entire night. Only one randomized controlled trial supports the findings on long-term sleep restriction. The relationship between sleep duration and mortality risk is assessed separately; see Section 2, Item 13 (sleep about 7 hours each night): measured by mortality rate, the 7-hour category has the lowest risk.

entries.title: Avoid caffeine after 2 p.m.
entries.cost: It costs nothing. People used to drinking coffee in the afternoon need a little willpower to refrain.
entries.summary: Taking 400 mg of caffeine 6 hours before bed—roughly three or four cups of coffee—cuts more than 1 hour off that night’s sleep as measured by instruments. Yet self-recorded sleep diaries show no difference at all. A 250 mL cup of coffee (107 mg) needs to be finished more than 8.8 hours before bedtime to avoid affecting sleep. If you go to bed at eleven, 2 p.m. is the cutoff.
entries.benefit: Taking a tablet containing 400 mg of caffeine 6 hours before bedtime resulted in 1.1 to 1.2 hours less total sleep time measured by instruments compared to taking a placebo tablet. Assuming a 250 mL cup of coffee contains 107 mg, 400 mg is roughly equivalent to three or four cups of coffee. The placebo tablet looked identical but contained no caffeine. However, the participants' self-reported sleep diaries did not report any difference; they did not perceive it themselves. Combining multiple studies (meta-analysis): caffeine reduced total sleep time by an average of 45 minutes. The proportion of time spent in bed actually asleep (sleep efficiency) dropped by 7%. A 250 mL cup of coffee (107 mg) must be finished more than 8.8 hours before bed so as not to affect sleep.
entries.sources: Drake, Roehrs, Shambroom & Roth (2013). Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.3170>；Gardiner et al. (2023). The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2023.101764>
entries.notes: The Drake study was conducted by only one laboratory, and the 400 mg used was on the larger side, equivalent to drinking an entire day's upper limit at once; for the upper limit, see Section 2, Item 26 (three to four cups of coffee). For people who metabolize caffeine slowly, the cutoff time needs to be even earlier. What you get back by drinking less caffeine is sleep duration, which stacks with Item 3 (getting a full 7 to 8 hours of sleep each night).

entries.title: Switch email and messaging to fixed batch processing a few times a day
entries.cost: Free. It takes a little time to explain clearly to colleagues how often you reply. Resisting the urge to check email at any time requires a bit of willpower.
entries.summary: The same cohort of people was compared across two weeks. During the week when email was restricted to checking only 3 times a day, daily stress was significantly lower, while the number of emails sent and received remained the same. When unrestricted, people checked an average of 15.5 times per day.
entries.benefit: 124 adults were compared before and after within the same cohort over two weeks (within-subject control). During the week restricted to checking email 3 times a day, daily stress was significantly lower than during the unrestricted week (effect size Cohen's d = 0.37). There was no difference in the number of emails received and replied to between the two weeks. Initially without restrictions, people checked email an average of 15.5 times per day.
entries.sources: Kushlev & Dunn (2015). Checking email less frequently reduces stress. Computers in Human Behavior. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2014.11.005>
entries.notes: There is only one study, the effect is small-to-medium, and what was measured was stress, not work output. Instant messaging has not been directly studied by anyone; here it is merely inferred by extension.

entries.title: When doing work that requires continuous thinking, block out interruptions even if they last only a few seconds
entries.cost: Free. Close the door, put on headphones, or hang a "Do Not Disturb" sign.
entries.summary: An interruption averaging just 2.8 seconds doubles the error rate of the subsequent operation. A 4.4-second interruption triples it. Field tracking also found that it took an average of 25 minutes to return to the interrupted task, with two other tasks interleaved in between. Interrupted workers worked faster, but stress, frustration, and perceived effort were all higher.
entries.benefit: An interruption averaging 2.8 seconds doubles the error rate in sequential tasks performed step-by-step. A 4.4-second interruption triples it. This was conducted in a laboratory. Another study was a field observation of 24 office white-collar workers (information workers). They switched work topics an average of once every 11 minutes. 57% of work topics were interrupted. Returning to the interrupted task on the same day took an average of 25 minutes and 26 seconds. An average of 2.26 other tasks were interleaved in between. There was also an experiment with 48 people: interrupted workers worked faster, but reported higher levels of stress, frustration, time pressure, and effort.
entries.sources: Altmann, Trafton & Hambrick (2014). Momentary interruptions can derail the train of thought. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0030986>；Mark, Gonzalez & Harris (2005). No task left behind? Examining the nature of fragmented work. CHI 2005. <https://doi.org/10.1145/1054972.1055017>；Mark, Gudith & Klocke (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress. CHI 2008. <https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072>
entries.notes: That field study divided interruptions into two categories: one where others come looking for you, and one where you click open something yourself. Closing the door only blocks the former. The latter needs to be used in conjunction with Item 1 (turn off non-essential notifications) and Item 5 (batch-process messages).

entries.title: Do only one thing at a time; do not reply to messages while in meetings
entries.cost: Free. Resisting the urge to reply to messages during meetings requires a bit of willpower.
entries.summary: Whenever tasks switch, reactions become slower and errors are more likely. People who frequently use multiple media simultaneously did not develop the ability to multitask; on the contrary, they performed worse on task-switching tests.
entries.benefit: After task switching, reactions are significantly slower and errors occur more easily. This part comes from a review of multiple studies. Another laboratory study had college students as participants. People who frequently used several media simultaneously (heavy media multitaskers) were more easily distracted by irrelevant stimuli and irrelevant memories. They actually performed worse on task-switching tests.
entries.sources: Monsell (2003). Task switching. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(03)00028-7>；Ophir, Nass & Wagner (2009). Cognitive control in media multitaskers. PNAS. <https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0903620106>
entries.notes: How much extra cost switching back and forth incurs varies greatly depending on the work being done, so no unified figure is provided here. The Ophir study was a cross-sectional comparison at a single time point, making it impossible to distinguish whether "multitasking impairs attention" or "people with poor attention are more prone to multitasking."

entries.title: Avoid illuminated screens one hour before bedtime; if reading, stick to paper books or e-ink screens with screen lights turned off
entries.cost: Free. Putting down your phone an hour before bed requires willpower to fight inertia over the long term.
entries.summary: Reading an illuminated screen before bed delayed falling asleep by about 10 minutes compared to reading a paper book. Melatonin was suppressed by 55%. The next day's biological clock was pushed back by more than 1.5 hours, morning sleepiness was higher, and it took longer to wake up fully.
entries.benefit: In a laboratory, the same participants rotated through two conditions (crossover trial). One condition was reading an e-book on an iPad at maximum brightness before bed for about 4 hours, for 5 consecutive nights. The other was reading a paper book in a similarly dimly lit room. Reading an illuminated e-book before bed took about 10 minutes longer to fall asleep compared to reading a paper book (25.7 minutes vs. 15.8 minutes). Evening melatonin was suppressed by 55%. The biological clock (circadian rhythm) the following day was delayed by more than 1.5 hours, with melatonin onset occurring at 22:31 vs. 21:01. Participants were sleepier the next morning and took longer to become fully alert.
entries.sources: Chang, Aeschbach, Duffy & Czeisler (2015). Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness. PNAS. <https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1418490112>
entries.notes: The sample size was small, conducted under strictly controlled laboratory conditions. Under routine phone brightness and usage durations, the effect might not be this large. How effective phone night modes are was not tested in this study. E-ink screens were not tested either. E-ink screens with screen lights turned off rely on reflecting room light just like paper books, so they are grouped with paper books, which is deduced from this study. E-ink screens with screen lights turned on also emit light, and there is no data on them.

entries.title: Go to sleep on time; do not stay up late for gaming, short-form videos, or pornography
entries.cost: Free. The difficulty lies in resisting the "just one more episode" inertia over the long term. Keeping your phone out of the bedroom takes the least effort.
entries.summary: In 2025, Chinese people slept an average of 6.97 hours at night, falling asleep at 0:10 on average. Among children and adolescents, those who use phones or tablets before bed have more than twice the odds of inadequate sleep and 2.7 times the odds of daytime sleepiness. The numbers are similar even if devices are merely placed in the bedroom without being used. Therefore, the least troublesome method is to keep phones out of the bedroom.
entries.benefit: In 2025, night sleep among residents of our country averaged 6.97 hours, with an average sleep onset time of 0:10 (Chinese Sleep Research Society). People using portable devices before bed had approximately 2.17 times the likelihood of inadequate sleep (OR 2.17). Poor sleep quality was about 1.46 times as likely (OR 1.46). Daytime sleepiness was about 2.72 times as likely (OR 2.72). Even when devices were merely placed in the bedroom without being used, the numbers were similar, roughly 1.79, 1.53, and 2.27 times (OR 1.79/1.53/2.27). This part is aggregated from 20 cross-sectional surveys encompassing 125,198 children and adolescents. Another cross-sectional survey involved 844 adults aged 18 to 94. Among them, those who continued using mobile phones after lights out fell asleep more slowly, had a lower proportion of time in bed actually asleep, and experienced more fatigue during the day.
entries.sources: Carter et al. (2016). Association Between Portable Screen-Based Media Device Access or Use and Sleep Outcomes. JAMA Pediatrics. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2016.2341>; Exelmans & Van den Bulck (2016). Bedtime mobile phone use and sleep in adults. Social Science & Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2015.11.037>; Chinese Sleep Research Society (2026). White Paper on Sleep Health Research in China 2026 (Health News report reprinted by Fujian Provincial Health Commission). <https://wjw.fujian.gov.cn/jggk/csxx/xcc/mtbd/202603/t20260323_7114382.htm>; Grubbs JB et al. (2018). Pornography Problems Due to Moral Incongruence: An Integrative Model with a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Archives of Sexual Behavior. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-018-1248-x> (one of the disputing parties in the notes); Prause N, Pfaus J (2015). Viewing Sexual Stimuli Associated with Greater Sexual Responsiveness, Not Erectile Dysfunction. Sexual Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1002/sm2.58> (the second disputing party in the notes)
entries.notes: Disputed. For the costs of staying up late itself, see Item 3 of this section (getting a full 7 to 8 hours of sleep each night). Regarding what impact pornography has on the energy and cognitive faculties of ordinary people, there is currently no reliable evidence clarifying whether it is causal. An analysis pooling multiple studies concluded that so-called "pornography problems" stem more from a mismatch between a person's moral beliefs and their own behavior, rather than the content itself. Another study pooled data from 280 men. The finding was that viewing duration had no relationship with erectile function during sexual activity with a partner. Here, we address only its encroachment on sleep time. Regarding the two figures of 6.97 hours and 0:10, no press release was found on the official website of the Chinese Sleep Research Society (checked in September 2026). The Health News report reprinted by the Fujian Provincial Health Commission is taken as the reference here.

entries.title: Do not make major decisions or send critical messages late at night
entries.cost: Free. Just postpone matters until after waking up.
entries.summary: When well-rested, people can quickly learn to avoid high-risk options. After two consecutive nights without sleep, they repeatedly choose high-risk options instead, an effect that becomes more pronounced with age. How much impact losing a few hours of sleep has has not been directly tested, but important decisions should still be postponed until after waking up.
entries.benefit: 34 healthy individuals performed the Iowa Gambling Task after 49.5 hours without sleep. This is an experiment measuring risk decision-making. When well-rested, they quickly learned to avoid high-risk options. After sleep deprivation, they chose high-risk options more frequently instead. Older individuals were more heavily affected. This was a single experiment; only this one study exists.
entries.sources: Killgore, Balkin & Wesensten (2006). Impaired decision making following 49 h of sleep deprivation. Journal of Sleep Research. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2006.00487.x>
entries.notes: The study investigated the extreme scenario of going without sleep for two consecutive nights. How ordinary people fare when staying up until 2 a.m. has not been directly tested. The half about "not sending messages" is authorial experience (Grade C); sending them the next day will still be in time.

entries.title: If sleepy in the afternoon, sleep for 10 minutes, not half an hour
entries.cost: Free. Spend 10 minutes and find a place where you can lie down or rest your head on a desk.
entries.summary: When sleep was insufficient the previous night, a 10-minute nap refreshes you on the spot, with part of the benefits lasting for two and a half hours. Sleeping for 5 minutes is essentially useless. Sleeping for 20 minutes takes 35 minutes before effects appear. After sleeping for 30 minutes, there is an initial period of grogginess upon waking, during which performance is even worse than not sleeping at all.
entries.benefit: Following insufficient sleep the previous night, a 10-minute nap immediately improves sleepiness, fatigue, vigor, and cognitive performance, with some benefits maintained past 155 minutes. Sleeping for 5 minutes offers almost no benefit. The benefits of a 20-minute nap do not appear until after 35 minutes. After a 30-minute nap, there is initial sleep inertia: performance right after waking is actually worse, improving only later.
entries.sources: Brooks & Lack (2006). A brief afternoon nap following nocturnal sleep restriction: Which nap duration is most recuperative? Sleep. <https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/29.6.831>
entries.notes: There is only one laboratory study, and the participants were all healthy young people. If you cannot fall asleep, do not force it. Whether lying down with your eyes closed for 10 minutes is useful is not supported by research. Midday naps exceeding one hour, conversely, are linked to higher mortality and coronary heart disease risk; see Section 2, Item 37 (keep afternoon naps within half an hour).

entries.title: When working in an open-plan office, use earplugs or find a quiet room for tasks requiring memory
entries.cost: A few tens of yuan for earplugs. Booking a quiet meeting room takes a little time.
entries.summary: When background noise increases from 39 dB to 51 dB, recalled words decrease, people feel more tired, and motivation to work drops. Watching nature scenery videos with sound during breaks restores energy better than continuing to listen to office noise.
entries.benefit: Students were asked to work in a simulated open-plan office. When background noise rose from 39 decibels to 51 decibels (dB, LAeq), they remembered fewer words, rated themselves as more fatigued, and were less willing to work. Watching nature videos with audio during breaks restored energy ratings better than listening only to river sounds or office noise.
entries.sources: Jahncke, Hygge, Halin, Green & Dimberg (2011). Open-plan office noise: Cognitive performance and restoration. Journal of Environmental Psychology. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2011.07.002>
entries.notes: There is only one laboratory study. The most disruptive element in noise is intelligible speech. White-noise headphones help with this, but headphones were not tested in this study.

entries.title: Do not blindly ramp up weekly working hours: past around 49 hours, each extra hour worked yields less and less additional output
entries.cost: You might earn less overtime pay. You may also need to spend effort negotiating with superiors.
entries.summary: Records from British munitions factories during World War I show that under 49 hours per week, output was directly proportional to hours worked. Beyond 49 hours, each additional hour worked yielded less and less output. Working 70 hours a week produced almost the same output as working 56 hours; those extra 14 hours were worked in vain.
entries.benefit: Output records of British munitions factory workers during World War I: under 49 hours per week, output was directly proportional to work hours. Beyond 49 hours, the rate of output growth began to slow. It reached a maximum at approximately 63 hours. Output at 70 hours showed almost no difference compared to 56 hours, meaning the extra 14 hours worked amounted to working for nothing.
entries.sources: Pencavel (2015). The Productivity of Working Hours. The Economic Journal. <https://doi.org/10.1111/ecoj.12166>
entries.notes: Data comes from factories a century ago, the work was manual labor, and the workers were predominantly female. This threshold may not necessarily be the same when transplanted to intellectual work; the author also noted that other occupations could be higher or lower. What is reliable is the direction: past a certain point, working more yields almost no extra output. The specific number 49 is not reliable.

entries.title: When you catch yourself repeatedly dwelling on the same frustrating matter, switch to a hands-on activity
entries.cost: Free. The hard part is noticing first that you are repeatedly dwelling on it (this is called rumination); noticing itself requires practice.
entries.summary: Repeatedly dwelling on the same frustrating matter worsens depression, anchors negative thoughts more firmly, makes people less able to solve problems, and makes taking real action harder. It also exhausts the people around you who are willing to listen. When you notice yourself circling in place, go do some hands-on work.
entries.benefit: Reviews of multiple studies state that repeatedly dwelling on the same frustrating matter (rumination) exacerbates depression. It also reinforces negative thinking and impairs problem-solving abilities. It hinders taking concrete action and depletes the people around you willing to listen. It is associated with anxiety, binge eating, alcohol abuse, and self-harm.
entries.sources: Nolen-Hoeksema, Wisco & Lyubomirsky (2008). Rethinking Rumination. Perspectives on Psychological Science. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-6924.2008.00088.x>
entries.notes: The review provided only direction, without figures. "Switching to another task" is the author's own practice. What the literature can support is only a single sentence: diverting attention is better than continuing to circle in place. As for what task to switch to, no one has compared options.

entries.title: Treat thoughts like "things will definitely get worse" as symptoms, not as facts
entries.cost: Free. The difficulty lies in viewing such thoughts as symptoms rather than facts.
entries.summary: In a twin study tracking participants for 20 years, for each notch higher in pessimism, the probability of dying during the same period was about 13% higher, and the probability of dying from cardiovascular disease was about 20% higher. Conversely, high optimism scores did not bring corresponding benefits. Therefore, what needs to be managed is pessimism, not "insufficient positive energy."
entries.benefit: In 2,978 Australian twins aged 50 and older tracked for an average of 20 years, 1,068 died during the period. For each 1 standard deviation increase on the pessimism scale, the risk of dying during the same period was about 13% higher (hazard ratio 1.134). The confidence interval for this figure is 95% CI 1.065–1.207, P=8.85×10⁻⁵. Cardiovascular death was about 20% higher (1.196, 1.045–1.368, P=0.0093). It was unrelated to cancer mortality. Optimism scores also showed no significant association with mortality.
entries.sources: Whitfield JB, Zhu G, Landers JG, Martin NG (2020). Pessimism is associated with greater all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, but optimism is not protective. Scientific Reports, 10, 12609. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-69388-y>
entries.notes: Disputed. This is observational only, without grouping. Some might say "illness actually preceded pessimism," which the author countered by noting that if that were the case, cancer mortality should also have been associated. However, unmeasured confounding factors may still exist. Optimism had no protective effect, so there is no need to force yourself to "think positively." What needs to be done is to avoid treating pessimistic expectations as accurate forecasts of the future.

entries.title: Cut back on draining relationships, and learn to decline requests you do not wish to accept
entries.cost: Free. In the short term there will be social friction, and you may lose some relationships. Speaking up to refuse requires considerable willpower.
entries.summary: In a survey of widowed women aged 60 to 89, the association between distressing interactions and well-being was stronger and more consistent than that of pleasant interactions. Therefore, subtract first, then add.
entries.benefit: A survey of 120 widowed women aged 60 to 89: the association between distressing interactions and psychological well-being was more consistent and stronger than that of pleasant interactions. According to this result, the loss caused by one draining person outweighs the benefit brought by one supportive person.
entries.sources: Rook (1984). The negative side of social interaction: Impact on psychological well-being. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. <https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.46.5.1097>
entries.notes: The surveyed population was specific, and it was a one-time questionnaire, making it impossible to determine precedence. What was measured was well-being, not energy. Placing it in this section is the author's inference. There is no objective standard for which relationships count as "draining"; you can only judge for yourself.

entries.title: Leave the scene first when angry; treat the other person as weather rather than as an enemy
entries.cost: Free. In the moment, you need to resist talking back, turn and walk away, and decide whether to address it later. This requires a bit of practice.
entries.summary: Looking at what just happened from another perspective, or putting yourself in the other person's shoes for a moment, can both bring emotions down, with the latter being more effective. Merely not showing emotions also has a slight effect. But forcibly suppressing inner feelings or forcing yourself not to think about it is useless. People who punished an offender ended up ruminating on the matter longer afterward, whereas people who did not retaliate moved on faster.
entries.benefit: Combining 306 experimental comparisons in a meta-analysis, reframing what happened (cognitive reappraisal) had an effect on emotion of d = 0.36. Taking the other person's perspective had an effect of d = 0.45. Distraction had an effect of d = 0.27. Suppressing the outward expression of emotion (not showing it) worked, d = 0.32. Forcibly suppressing feelings did not work (d = -0.04), and forcibly trying not to think about the incident did not work either (d = -0.12). These figures combine measures of subjective feelings, outward expression, and bodily responses; the abstract does not report them separately. Three other experiments found that people who punished an offender spent longer afterward repeatedly thinking about that person, while those who did not punish them moved on faster. People overestimated in advance how satisfying revenge would feel.
entries.sources: Webb TL, Miles E, Sheeran P (2012). Dealing with feeling: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation. Psychological Bulletin. <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0027600>；Carlsmith KM, Wilson TD, Gilbert DT (2008). The paradoxical consequences of revenge. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012165>
entries.notes: The studies combined in the first part measured emotional intensity, not energy. The effects were small to moderate. The revenge part rests on just one set of experiments, hence the B rating. The “empty boat” is a parable from “Mountain Trees” in the Zhuangzi: when an empty boat hits yours, you do not get angry; when someone is aboard, you do, even though the collision is the same. This is an analogy, not evidence. If you have suffered a real loss, use the legal routes in Sections 8 and 9. They cost much less than losing your temper on the spot.

entries.title: When you feel low, start with the most cost-effective steps: get moving, get more light, sleep on schedule, talk to someone, and call 12356
entries.cost: Free, or nearly so. Take a brisk walk, jog, or do strength training a few times a week. Go outside for sunlight during the day. Set a regular sleep schedule. When you feel you cannot see a way forward, make a phone call.
entries.summary: Brisk walking, jogging, yoga, and strength training can all reduce depression; higher intensity works better. See Section 22, Item 6 (walk or run when your mood is low) for details. Light therapy has a strong effect on seasonal depression and also works for depression that is not seasonal. Online self-help courses in cognitive behavioral therapy work; when symptoms are more severe, it is better to have someone guide you through them. If you feel you cannot see a way forward, call 12356 first.
entries.benefit: A network meta-analysis combined 218 randomized controlled trials involving 14,170 people. The control participants were also doing other activities. Compared with them, walking or jogging had an effect on depression of g = -0.62 (95% credible interval -0.80 to -0.45). The effect was -0.55 for yoga and -0.49 for strength training. Higher intensity produced better results. Combining multiple studies of light therapy gave an effect size of 0.84 (0.60 to 1.08) for seasonal depression and 0.53 (0.18 to 0.89) for nonseasonal depression. Another analysis combined individual patient data from the studies. It examined internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (online self-help courses). Both guided and unguided versions worked better than the control condition. For moderate to severe symptoms (PHQ-9 greater than 9), the guided version worked better. 12356 is China's national mental health assistance hotline, available for at least 18 hours each day.
entries.sources: Noetel M et al. (2024). Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-075847>; Golden RN et al. (2005). The efficacy of light therapy in the treatment of mood disorders: a review and meta-analysis of the evidence. American Journal of Psychiatry. <https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.162.4.656>; Karyotaki E et al. (2021). Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Depression: A Systematic Review and Individual Patient Data Network Meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2020.4364>; National Health Commission of China (2024). Notice on the Use of “12356” as the Nationwide Unified Telephone Number for the Mental Health Assistance Hotline (National Health Commission Medical Administration Letter [2024] No. 259). <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202412/content_6994470.htm>
entries.notes: These are all supplementary measures for mild to moderate depression. Anyone with moderate to severe depression or suicidal thoughts should seek medical care; call 12356 first (see Section 1, Item 25). Most exercise trials had small numbers of participants, and unlike a drug trial, they could not conceal who was exercising. The light therapy studies only go up to 2003 and also had small numbers of participants. Those studies used dedicated light therapy lamps, not sunlight. The suggestion to go outside for sunlight during the day is an extrapolation from light therapy. “Sleep on schedule” and “talk to someone” come from the author's experience; no separate references are listed for them. Do not treat “get moving” as a demand placed on someone with depression. Walking for ten minutes counts.

entries.title: See police officers, doctors, and clerks as people working under rules, rather than as roles: documents and deadlines move things forward, not emotion
entries.cost: Free. What changes is your expectation and the order in which you act. At first, you will have to resist the urge to “keep explaining until the other person agrees.”
entries.summary: Police officers, doctors, and clerks are people working under the rules of their jobs. They are subject to paperwork, deadlines, and oversight. Regulations specify how many days a matter should take and what document must be provided if it cannot be handled. So get a receipt, note the deadline, and appeal through the prescribed channels. Do not expect to talk someone into agreeing with your reasoning.
entries.benefit: Change how you deal with institutions: replace “pleading, getting angry, and repeatedly recounting how you were wronged” with “getting documents, noting deadlines, and appealing through the prescribed channels.” What you save is time spent communicating repeatedly and dwelling on the matter. This is a one-time shift in outlook, not a daily time saving. What you can verify are the deadlines themselves, all of which are written in the rules. For a public security administrative case, the investigation deadline is no more than 30 days from the date it is accepted; for a major or complex case, it may be extended by 30 days with approval from the public security authority at the next higher level. When a decision is made not to file a criminal case following a complaint, the notice of that decision must be delivered within 3 days. The complainant may apply for reconsideration within 7 days, and the public security authority must decide within 30 days. If dissatisfied, the complainant may apply to the authority at the next higher level for review within another 7 days.
entries.sources: Ministry of Public Security of China (2020). Provisions on the Procedures for Handling Criminal Cases by Public Security Authorities (as amended by Ministry of Public Security Order No. 159, Articles 171, 178, and 179). <http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2020/content_5549884.htm>; Ministry of Public Security of China (2013, amended 2019). Provisions on the Procedures for Handling Administrative Cases by Public Security Authorities (Ministry of Public Security Orders Nos. 125 and 149). <http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2013/content_2321117.htm>
entries.notes: Reason for the C rating: there is no source to cite for the claim that “many people see the person behind the counter as a role rather than as someone doing a job.” Only the rules half can be cited: deadlines, documents, and channels for redress are all stated explicitly. Every number cited in this item comes from the two Ministry of Public Security regulations cited in Section 8, Item 39 (what happens after you report a matter to the police). Following the process cannot fix “the other person's bad attitude,” nor does it guarantee a successful outcome. It changes only your expectations and your first action. The same applies to bank clerks and government service counters: their actions leave records, require review, and carry accountability for mistakes. So keep transaction slips, ask for receipts, and complain through the prescribed channels instead of guessing whether someone is going to cheat you. Legitimate priorities are stated openly: for example, emergency departments prioritize patients by the severity of their condition, not by arrival order (Section 24, Item 7, emergency pre-examination and triage). If you want to thank a doctor who saved you, send a thank-you letter or leave a patient satisfaction review; see Section 24, Item 11. If you want to “give them something so they will pay extra attention,” doing so with someone handling a case or enforcing the law constitutes the crime of bribery under Chinese law, with an explicitly prescribed heavier penalty; see Section 8, Item 40. If you encounter obvious unequal treatment, that is a matter for complaint and oversight, not an unwritten rule to imitate.

entries.title: Stop treating “how other people are doing” as required daily reading: limit or turn off apps where you scroll through updates from people your age
entries.cost: Free. Setting an app limit or deactivating an account takes just a few minutes. The hard part is not reopening it afterward; resisting the habit takes ongoing effort.
entries.summary: People who habitually compare themselves online with people who seem to be doing better tend to feel worse and have lower self-esteem. People who deactivated Facebook for four weeks had a small increase in well-being, but also knew less about current events. People who limited each of three social platforms to 10 minutes a day had less loneliness and depression after three weeks.
entries.benefit: A meta-analysis combined multiple studies: 54 independent samples, 94 effect sizes, and N = 36,583, using a three-level random-effects model. The average correlation between online upward social comparison and psychological maladjustment was r = 0.330 (95% CI 0.289–0.370, a credible range). Looking at specific outcomes separately, the correlation was 0.438 for negative feelings about social evaluation, such as fear of being looked down on, and 0.382 for anxiety. It was 0.306 for depression, 0.268 for lower well-being, and 0.263 for lower self-esteem. Age, cultural background, and year of data collection did not affect the strength of this association. Longitudinal studies did not find a stronger association than surveys conducted at a single point in time. Another randomized controlled trial involved 2,743 American Facebook users. Of these, 61% were willing to accept less than $102 to deactivate Facebook. These people were randomly assigned either to deactivate it for four weeks or to a control group. Deactivation freed up 60 minutes a day for the average participant. The subjective well-being index rose by 0.09 standard deviations. The component figures were 0.12 for life satisfaction, 0.10 for anxiety, 0.09 for depression, and 0.08 for happiness. They remained statistically significant after adjustment for the chance findings that can arise from multiple comparisons. The authors offered a reference point: psychological interventions intended to make people more positive. Such interventions have an effect of about +0.34 standard deviations on subjective well-being and about -0.23 standard deviations on depression. So this effect was about 25% to 40% as large as that of conventional psychological interventions. The accompanying costs were a decline of 0.19 standard deviations in the current-events knowledge index and a decline of 0.16 standard deviations in political polarization. After the experiment ended, the deactivation group still used Facebook 12 minutes less per day than the control group (0.31 standard deviations, a 23% decrease). Another randomized controlled trial involved 143 undergraduates assigned to two groups. One group limited Facebook, Instagram, and Snapchat to 10 minutes per platform per day; the other used them as usual. After three weeks, loneliness and depression had clearly decreased in the limited-use group. Anxiety and fear of missing out had decreased from baseline in both groups.
entries.sources: Lei Y, Hu S, Sun Y, Zheng L (2026). "Looking up" linked to feeling down: a meta-analysis of online upward social comparison and psychological maladjustment. Frontiers in Psychology. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1825169>; Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2020). The Welfare Effects of Social Media. American Economic Review, 110(3), 629–676. <https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20190658>; Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2019). The Welfare Effects of Social Media. NBER Working Paper No. 25514 (the specific figures cited in this item were checked word for word against this version; the abstract of the published version does not include the figures). <https://www.nber.org/papers/w25514>; Hunt MG, Marx R, Lipson C, Young J (2018). No More FOMO: Limiting Social Media Decreases Loneliness and Depression. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 37(10), 751–768. <https://doi.org/10.1521/jscp.2018.37.10.751>
entries.notes: The “correlation” part only shows that two things occur together; it cannot establish which causes the other. The authors themselves say more longitudinal research is needed. The randomized part supports a causal conclusion, but its participants were Facebook users in the United States before the 2018 midterm elections. Applying it directly to Chinese platforms would be a stretch. Hunt's study had only 143 undergraduates, and it is just one study. The effect sizes are all small; do not expect turning off an app to solve emotional problems. The use to curb is checking “how other people are doing”; keeping in touch with family and friends, looking up information, and finding work are outside that category. If you really cannot stop yourself, start by turning off push notifications, “People You May Know,” and homepage recommendations. For the accounting of total screen time, see Section 4, Items 15 and 16 (a strict cap on short videos; avoiding scrolling news). For what to do first when your mood is low, see Item 18 of this section (get moving, get sunlight, sleep on schedule). For buying things to regain a sense of identity, see Section 6, Item 23. For spending more money to “move up a rung,” see Section 6, Item 24.

entries.title: When you think “everyone saw me embarrass myself,” cut that estimate in half
entries.cost: Free. Just ask yourself one more question when you feel anxious: did they really notice?
entries.summary: People who entered a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt thought nearly half the people there would recognize the person printed on it. In fact, fewer than a quarter did. They also overestimated recognition when wearing a T-shirt they considered flattering. After a group discussion, people thought their verbal mistakes stood out more to others than they actually did; after a conversation, they often underestimated how much the other person liked them. So when you think “everyone saw me embarrass myself,” the actual number is often half your estimate or less.
entries.benefit: Experiment one: participants put on a T-shirt with Barry Manilow's portrait and entered a room with other participants. The wearers estimated, on average, that 46% of observers could correctly identify the person on the shirt. The observers' actual correct-identification rate was 23%, making the estimate exactly twice the actual rate. Subtracting the actual rate from the estimate for each session gave an average overestimate of 23 percentage points (95% CI 9–38, a credible range). After excluding the two sessions with only two and three observers, the overestimate was 27 percentage points (11–43). Experiment two: participants instead wore T-shirts they chose themselves and considered positive. Their average estimate was 48%, while the observers' actual correct-identification rate was 8%, a sixfold difference. In a footnote, the authors said wearers' estimates were nearly the same in the two experiments (48% and 46%); the difference lay in the observers' correct-identification rates (8% and 23%). The authors suspected the main reason was that the questionnaire for observers in experiment two required more mental effort, not that people overestimate recognition of flattering clothes more. Experiment three: undergraduates were divided into groups of 3 to 7, discussed an assigned topic for 20 minutes, and then wrote a policy recommendation together. Immediately afterward, each person separately estimated how the others in the group would rank everyone, with a smaller rank number meaning a higher position. For “how often they said the wrong thing,” their estimated average rank for themselves was 2.30, while the rank others actually gave them was 2.96, a difference of −0.66 (p < .01). Thus, people thought their verbal mistakes were more noticeable to others. The same held for “things that might offend people” (2.35 versus 2.90, p < .01); the difference was smaller for “things others might criticize” (2.61 versus 2.82, p < .05). Another series of studies covered three settings: paired conversations between strangers, first-year college roommates, and an adult workshop. People systematically underestimated how much their conversation partners liked them and how much those partners enjoyed the conversation. The authors called this the “liking gap.” It appeared in conversations of different lengths and persisted for months among first-year roommates.
entries.sources: Gilovich T, Medvec VH, Savitsky K (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211–222. <https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.78.2.211>；Boothby EJ, Cooney G, Sandstrom GM, Clark MS (2018). The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think? Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742–1756. <https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797618783714>
entries.notes: Reason for the B rating: all of these were laboratory or campus studies with relatively few participants. The settings involved clothing, conversations with strangers or roommates, and student group discussions, with participants questioned immediately after the discussion. There is no direct evidence for extending the findings to “coworkers talking about you” or “whether anyone still remembers a mistake you made in a meeting several days later.” The numbers indicate only the direction and approximate size of the overestimate; they cannot be used as a fixed multiplier. Other people's views are not always unimportant, either. When you are actually being evaluated, such as in a job interview, thesis defense, performance assessment, or medical examination report, the evaluation is real; prepare for it as needed. What you should discount is the everyday feeling that “everyone is watching me.” The thing to address there is your own estimation bias.

entries.title: Treat “other people expect me to be perfect” as a symptom, not as a fact
entries.cost: Free. The hard part is treating this thought as something that needs attention, rather than as an accurate measure of what other people actually expect.
entries.summary: People who constantly feel that “those around me expect me to be perfect and will reject me if I fall short” are more likely to have suicidal thoughts. The association between “I expect myself to be perfect” and suicidal thoughts is much weaker, only about one-third as strong as the first association. Even after accounting for thoughts people already had, the first feeling was still associated with an increase in those thoughts later, although the increase was small.
entries.benefit: Pooling multiple studies (a meta-analysis): 45 studies, N = 11,747, with participants including undergraduates, medical students, community adults, and psychiatric patients, using a random-effects model. The following are weighted average correlations with suicidal ideation. Perfectionistic concerns: r = .28 (95% CI .24–.32, confidence interval; 42 studies, 7,936 people). Perfectionistic concerns are a combined category that includes socially prescribed perfectionism, concern over mistakes, doubts about actions, and discrepancies between actual performance and standards. Calculated separately, socially prescribed perfectionism also had r = .28 (.25–.32; 30 studies, 3,640 people). Perfectionistic strivings: r = .10 (.07–.13; 31 studies, 4,588 people); this is a combined category of self-oriented perfectionism and personal standards. Parental criticism: r = .20 (.11–.29). Now consider the relationship with suicide attempts. Perfectionistic concerns: r = .12 (.07–.17; 15 studies, 5,275 people). Socially prescribed perfectionism: r = .19 (.08–.29; 8 studies, 689 people). Now consider the studies that followed people over time. After accounting for suicidal ideation present at the start, socially prescribed perfectionism was still positively associated with suicidal ideation at a later follow-up, though the association was small. No association was apparent for either self-oriented or other-oriented perfectionism.
entries.sources: Smith MM, Sherry SB, Chen S, Saklofske DH, Mushquash C, Flett GL, Hewitt PL (2018). The perniciousness of perfectionism: A meta-analytic review of the perfectionism-suicide relationship. Journal of Personality, 86(3), 522–542. <https://doi.org/10.1111/jopy.12333>
entries.notes: Why the rating is B: Most included studies used one-time questionnaires, which cannot establish what came first. The correlation is moderate (r about .28) and roughly explains only a few percent to about one-tenth of the variation. The outcomes measured were suicidal ideation and suicide attempts, not deaths themselves, so the magnitude of the benefit is rated small under the category “surrogate endpoints only.” The authors themselves also say that the group of studies on perfectionistic concerns and suicide attempts appears to have publication bias. Publication bias means studies with less favorable results were not published. After estimated missing studies were added back in, the direction of the conclusion did not change. Having high standards is not itself a problem, and there is no need to lower your standards because of this. What matters is where the standards come from and whether failing to meet them makes you feel, “I am a complete failure as a person.” Like the pessimistic expectations in Item 15 (“treat thoughts such as ‘things will definitely get worse’ as symptoms”), this is something that can be addressed as a symptom. If you have suicidal thoughts, first call China’s 12356 hotline and move lethal means out of reach; see Section 1, Item 25. For what you can do when someone close to you expresses such thoughts, see Section 8, Item 15. For depression screening in children, see Section 30, Item 8.

entries.title: When you are angry, do not rely on punching a bag or going for a run to vent; first let your body slow down
entries.cost: Free. When anger flares, spend a few minutes doing something that slows your heart rate instead: breathe slowly, sit down, and be still for a while. The hard part is that, at that moment, what you most want to do is vent.
entries.summary: Punching a bag, cycling, or going for a run—ways of venting that make the body more aroused—do not, overall, reduce anger. Slow breathing, mindfulness, and meditation—ways of calming the body—can noticeably reduce anger and the urge to lash out physically.
entries.benefit: Pooling 154 studies (a meta-analysis), with 184 samples and 10,189 people in total: methods that calm the body, such as deep breathing, mindfulness, and meditation, reduced anger and aggression. The effect size was g = -0.63, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.43 (confidence interval). This result was consistent across people of different sexes, races, ages, and cultures. Methods that make the body more aroused, such as punching a bag, jogging, and cycling, were ineffective overall. Their effect size was g = -0.02, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.09. The authors concluded that venting anger and going for a run are not effective ways to calm down.
entries.sources: Kjærvik SL, Bushman BJ (2024). A meta-analytic review of anger management activities that increase or decrease arousal: What fuels or douses rage? Clinical Psychology Review. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2024.102414>
entries.notes: The outcomes measured were anger and aggression, not energy. Recording the benefit under time is the author’s classification: one less argument means one less mess to clean up afterward. For methods you can use on the spot, see Section 22, Item 8 (cyclic sighing), and Item 17 of this section (leave the scene first when angry). Running is not useless. Over the long term, it helps with low mood; see Section 22, Item 6 (go for a walk or run when you feel down). It is just unsuitable for calming anger on the spot. Do not drive, send messages, or make decisions while angry. If someone is hitting you, leave first and call the police. At that point, the issue to address is not your emotions; see Section 8, Item 43 (experiencing domestic violence).

entries.title: If something is weighing on your mind, you can write down your thoughts and feelings for several days in a row, but do not expect it to treat an illness
entries.cost: Free. A common approach in the studies was to write 3 to 4 times, for 15 to 20 minutes each time. Write about something that upsets you, including your deepest thoughts and feelings.
entries.summary: Writing about upsetting experiences has a slight benefit on average, but it is very small. The pooled findings are also inconsistent: two reviews found no clear effect. It costs almost nothing, so you can try it. If your emotional problems become severe, do not use it instead of seeing a doctor.
entries.benefit: One analysis pooled 146 randomized studies (a meta-analysis). Participants wrote or spoke about matters important to them. The average effect was positive and statistically significant, but very small: effect size r = .075. Another review included only randomized controlled trials; pooling 30 trials found no significant effect on either physical or mental health. Pooling 16 randomized trials involving people with cancer and cancer survivors found no significant effect on psychological health, physical health, or quality of life. For psychological health, g = 0.04, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.14 (confidence interval).
entries.sources: Frattaroli J (2006). Experimental disclosure and its moderators: a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin. <https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.6.823>；Mogk C, Otte S, Reinhold-Hurley B, Kröner-Herwig B (2006). Health effects of expressive writing on stressful or traumatic experiences - a meta-analysis. Psycho-Social Medicine. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2736499/>；Zachariae R, O'Toole MS (2015). The effect of expressive writing intervention on psychological and physical health outcomes in cancer patients--a systematic review and meta-analysis. Psycho-Oncology. <https://doi.org/10.1002/pon.3802>
entries.notes: The evidence is disputed. The supporting side is a review of 146 studies, which found a positive but very small effect. On the other side, two reviews that included only randomized controlled trials found no significant effect. The number and length of writing sessions in the cost section come from the earliest experimental design and are stated in the abstract of Mogk’s review. This is included because it costs almost nothing, takes little time, and can be done alone. You can use it when you do not want to talk to someone or have no one around to talk to. The outcome measured was not energy; recording the benefit under time is the author’s classification. If writing makes you feel worse and worse, stop and call China’s 12356 hotline instead; see Section 1, Item 25 (12356).

entries.title: For period pain, take a painkiller such as ibuprofen instead of toughing it out; if the pain disrupts work or school or three months of medication does not control it, see a gynecologist for an evaluation
entries.cost: A box of ibuprofen costs a little over 10 yuan; take it only on the days when you have pain. If you need to see a gynecologist, the appointment and an ultrasound will cost some money and half a day.
entries.summary: With medicines such as ibuprofen for period pain, the proportion of people whose pain improves substantially rises from less than one-fifth to about half. They work better than acetaminophen but cause slightly more side effects. If the pain disrupts work or school, you have deep pain during sex, or three months of medication still does not control it, see a gynecologist to check for endometriosis. In a study across ten countries, the average delay from the first symptoms of this condition to diagnosis was 6.7 years.
entries.benefit: A Cochrane systematic review pooled 80 randomized controlled trials involving 5,820 women with primary dysmenorrhea. Primary dysmenorrhea means period pain for which no other condition can be found. Compared with placebo, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) relieved pain more effectively (OR 4.37, 95% CI 3.76–5.09, confidence interval). In absolute terms, 18% of people taking placebo had moderate or greater relief, compared with 45% to 53% of those taking these medicines. The trade-off was somewhat more side effects (OR 1.29, 1.11–1.51). Side effects occurred in 10% of people taking placebo and 11% to 14% of those taking these medicines. The additional side effects were mainly gastrointestinal discomfort (OR 1.58) and nervous system reactions (OR 2.74). These medicines also relieved pain more effectively than acetaminophen (OR 1.89, 1.05–3.43), although that comparison included only 3 trials. No difference was established as to which of these medicines works best. The UK’s NICE guideline (updated in 2024) lists several situations in which endometriosis should be suspected. They include chronic pelvic pain, period pain that affects daily activities and quality of life, and deep pain during or after sex. They also include pain when passing stool during a period, blood in the urine or painful urination during a period, and infertility accompanied by these symptoms. Girls aged 17 or younger are included. The guideline recommends first trying acetaminophen or one of these medicines, for example for 3 months. If pain relief is inadequate, seek further investigation. Normal gynecological examination and ultrasound results do not rule out this condition. One study surveyed 1,418 women undergoing laparoscopy at 16 hospitals in 10 countries. The average time from the onset of symptoms to surgical diagnosis of endometriosis was 6.7 years, with most of the delay occurring during primary care. Women who received a diagnosis lost an average of 10.8 hours of work per week, mostly because they were at work but less productive. A Dutch online survey asked 32,748 women aged 15 to 45. Of them, 13.8% had taken time off because of menstruation, averaging 1.3 days a year. During menstruation, 80.7% were at work but less productive, equivalent to 8.9 days of work lost per year.
entries.sources: Marjoribanks J, Ayeleke RO, Farquhar C, Proctor M (2015). Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for dysmenorrhoea. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (7):CD001751. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD001751.pub3>；National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2017, updated 2024). Endometriosis: diagnosis and management (NG73), recommendations 1.3.1, 1.4.2, 1.4.3, 1.5.4. <https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng73/chapter/Recommendations>；Nnoaham KE, Hummelshoj L, Webster P, et al.; World Endometriosis Research Foundation Global Study of Women's Health consortium (2011). Impact of endometriosis on quality of life and work productivity: a multicenter study across ten countries. Fertility and Sterility, 96(2):366-373.e8. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2011.05.090>；Schoep ME, Adang EMM, Maas JWM, De Bie B, Aarts JWM, Nieboer TE (2019). Productivity loss due to menstruation-related symptoms: a nationwide cross-sectional survey among 32 748 women. BMJ Open, 9(6):e026186. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-026186>；Haleon (2026). Advil (ibuprofen capsule, liquid filled), OTC drug label: Warnings. DailyMed. <https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=1f01c10a-9434-91a4-2ee4-352315a6b610>
entries.notes: People over 60, people with a history of stomach bleeding, and people taking anticoagulants or steroids should ask a doctor before using these medicines. For details, see Section 34, Item 3 (painkillers such as ibuprofen). The US ibuprofen label states that it may cause a severe allergic reaction, more readily in people allergic to aspirin, and that symptoms include an asthma attack. People with asthma should also ask a doctor before use. If you might be pregnant, ask a doctor first; after 20 weeks of pregnancy, do not take it on your own. See Section 34, Item 5 (after 20 weeks of pregnancy). If you cannot take these medicines, you can use acetaminophen instead; for the daily maximum, see Section 34, Item 1 (acetaminophen). Take medicine for period pain only on the days when you have your period. The threshold in Section 34, Item 9 (do not take painkillers for more than 15 days a month) applies to headaches; the number of days medication is taken for period pain is far below it. The rating is A because the pain relief findings come from many randomized trials. The review authors rated the quality of evidence for most comparisons as low, mainly because the trial methods were poorly described; 59% of the trials were funded by pharmaceutical companies. Rating the benefit as “moderate” is a judgment: the review measured pain relief, not how many fewer days of leave people took. In the Dutch survey, losses due to menstruation amounted to about 10 days a year, or hours per week when spread across the year. The group with endometriosis had already gone for laparoscopy and does not mean that most people with period pain have this condition. You are the main beneficiary.

entries.title: For long-term insomnia (more than three nights a week for more than three months), start with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia; do not begin by taking sleeping pills long term
entries.cost: Treatment at a hospital sleep clinic, psychiatry department, or psychology department involves appointment and treatment fees. Online self-help courses are much cheaper. A course of treatment generally lasts 6 to 8 weeks, and you need to keep a sleep diary every day. One thing you can start doing yourself is stimulus control: go to bed only when sleepy, and get out of bed if you are lying there unable to sleep. Use the bed only for sleep and sex, get up at the same time every day, and do not nap during the day. The difficult part is sleep restriction: for the first few weeks, you have to shorten your time in bed, which will make you sleepier during the day.
entries.summary: After completing this treatment, people fall asleep about 19 minutes faster on average and spend about 26 fewer minutes awake during the night. The effect gradually weakens but is still present after 12 months. Online self-help courses work about as well as in-person treatment. Sleeping pills provide little help to people over 60: for every 6 people who take them, 1 has a side effect, while only 1 in 13 sleeps better.
entries.benefit: China’s National Health Commission’s 2020 diagnostic and treatment standards set out the key diagnostic features of insomnia disorder according to international classification. First, difficulty falling asleep, waking easily after falling asleep, or waking too early. Second, tiredness or sleepiness during the day that interferes with activities. Third, these problems occur at least 3 times a week and last at least 3 months. If they last less than 3 months, the condition is called short-term insomnia disorder. The standards designate cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia as first-line treatment. It has 5 components: sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy, relaxation training, and sleep hygiene. A course generally lasts 6 to 8 weeks. The standards say its short-term effects are comparable to medication and its long-term effects are better. They also state that sleeping pills generally should not be taken continuously for more than 4 weeks; if treatment continues, it should be evaluated once a month. The American College of Physicians’ 2016 guideline strongly recommends that all adults with chronic insomnia try this treatment first. If it does not work on its own, discuss with a doctor whether to add medication for a short period. One analysis pooled 20 randomized controlled trials with 1,162 people (a meta-analysis). After treatment, the time taken to fall asleep decreased by 19.03 minutes (95% CI 14.12–23.93, confidence interval). Time spent awake after falling asleep decreased by 26.00 minutes (15.48–36.52). The proportion of time in bed actually spent asleep (sleep efficiency) rose by 9.91% (8.09%–11.73%). Total sleep time increased by only 7.61 minutes, which was not statistically significant (−0.51 to 15.74). None of the studies reported adverse outcomes. Another analysis pooled 30 randomized controlled trials to see how long the effects lasted. Compared with people who did not receive treatment, the improvement in insomnia severity diminished over time: g = 0.64 at 3 months, 0.40 at 6 months, and 0.25 at 12 months. The effect gradually weakened, but the authors considered it clinically meaningful for a year. For online treatment, one analysis pooled 11 randomized controlled trials with 1,460 people. All sleep measures improved, with effect sizes g ranging from 0.21 to 1.09. The authors said this was comparable to in-person treatment; longer courses and more follow-up produced larger effects. In another online randomized trial with 1,711 people, the control group received only sleep hygiene information. People who received digital treatment had a large improvement in sleep-related quality of life and small improvements in physical functioning and psychological well-being during the day. Now consider sleeping pills. One analysis pooled 24 randomized controlled trials involving 2,417 people over 60 with insomnia. Every trial involved taking the pills for at least 5 consecutive nights. Compared with placebo, people taking the pills slept 25.2 minutes longer in total and woke 0.63 fewer times during the night. For every 13 people who took the pills, 1 had better sleep quality. For every 6 who took them, 1 had a side effect (NNH 6, 4.7 to 7.1). Side effects affecting memory and thinking were 4.78 times as likely as with placebo (OR 4.78, 1.47–15.47). Daytime fatigue was 3.82 times as likely (OR 3.82, 1.88–7.80).
