entries.summary: If a dealership says you must pay a separate “financial services fee” to get a loan, the rules prohibit the dealer from charging it. You can obtain insurance, financing, and registration elsewhere or arrange them yourself. The dealership cannot force you to use its services or charge extra beyond the displayed price. Before taking out a loan, have the lender state the annualized interest rate and all charges in writing, then compare offers.
entries.benefit: The Measures for the Administration of Automobile Sales require dealers to display in the dealership the prices of cars and parts and the charges for each service. They may not raise the sale price or collect additional fees beyond the displayed price. Dealers may not restrict you based on where your household registration is located or dictate which provider's parts, accessories, financing, insurance, roadside assistance, or after-sales services you use. Parts and services paid for by the manufacturer under the three guarantees or a recall are excepted. A dealer may not force you to buy insurance when it sells you a car or force you to have it arrange registration for you. For violations of these provisions, the commerce department at county level or above orders correction and may issue a warning or impose a fine of up to 30,000 yuan. In 2022, the former China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission required financial institutions making car loans to supervise the dealers they work with. Dealers must not charge fees in the name of a financial institution or on the grounds that they are providing you with financial services. They must also tell you the annualized loan interest rate and fee rates. They must not entice you with claims such as “no loan default penalty” or “no vehicle mortgage required” if those claims are untrue, and must not bundle products or services against your wishes. Financial institutions themselves may not charge fees as a condition of lending. The Regulations for the Implementation of the Consumer Rights and Interests Protection Law prohibit businesses from forcing you, directly or indirectly, to buy things or excluding or restricting your choice of another business (nationwide).
entries.sources: Ministry of Commerce (2017). Measures for the Administration of Automobile Sales (Ministry of Commerce Order No. 1 of 2017, Articles 10, 14, and 32; effective July 1, 2017). <http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2017/content_5230275.htm>; China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission (2022). Notice on Further Regulating Automobile Finance Business (Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission Regulatory Document [2022] No. 22, Items 5 and 11). <https://policy.mofcom.gov.cn/claw/clawContent.shtml?id=96380> (reposted in the Ministry of Commerce's policy and regulations database); State Council (2024). Regulations for the Implementation of the Consumer Rights and Interests Protection Law (State Council Order No. 778, Articles 11 and 50). <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202403/content_6940159.htm>
entries.notes: This charge is often renamed a “service fee,” “handling fee,” or “loan service package.” Under the rules, all such charges must be disclosed in advance, and nothing extra may be charged beyond the displayed price. If you have already paid, first ask the dealership to return the money. If it refuses, call China's 12378 hotline for loan-related complaints or China's 12315 consumer complaint hotline for other complaints. If the amount is small and you want to sue, see Section 8, Item 22 (deception in online purchases and secondhand transactions) for the small-claims procedure. There are no official figures for the usual amount of this fee; the benefit magnitude is rated medium based on judgment. Include car-loan handling fees when comparing annualized interest rates; see Item 7 of this section (convert borrowing costs to an annualized interest rate first) for the method. The beneficiary category is you and your family.

entries.title: If a guide on a group tour takes you to an unagreed shopping stop where you buy something, ask the travel agency for a return within 30 days of getting home and have it advance the refund
entries.cost: No monetary cost. Keep the contract and itinerary when you travel, and get an invoice and card-payment receipt for anything you buy. Do not open or use the goods. After returning, contact the travel agency and send the goods back. If you cannot reach an agreement, file a complaint; the process may take one or two months altogether.
entries.summary: It is illegal for a travel agency to take you to a shopping stop without your agreement or to lure you onto a shopping tour with an absurdly low tour price. Within 30 days of returning, you can require it to arrange a return and advance the refund. If you signed a supplementary agreement saying you would shop voluntarily, that counts as your consent and makes it difficult to obtain a return this way.
entries.benefit: Article 35 of China's Tourism Law has three paragraphs. The first says travel agencies must not organize tours at unreasonably low prices to lure tourists and then recoup the money through kickbacks from arranged shopping. The second says travel agencies must not designate specific places to shop. Tourists may go only if both sides agree, or if a tourist requests it and doing so does not disrupt anyone else's itinerary. Signing a supplementary agreement for “voluntary shopping” generally counts as mutual agreement. The third says that, if a travel agency violates either of the first two paragraphs, tourists have the right to require it to arrange returns within 30 days after the trip ends and to advance the refund. They can also demand refunds for optional activities that cost extra. This paragraph does not require you to prove first that the goods have a quality problem. Article 9 of the Tourism Law also gives tourists the right to refuse forced transactions. In 2025, China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism reported a case involving a Chengdu travel agency that took 15 tourists to Jiuzhaigou and collected only 6,015 yuan in total tour fees. The agency then paid the company that recruited the tourists 8,220 yuan to “buy the tour group,” and received 13,706 yuan in kickbacks from shops. The agency was fined and had unlawful gains confiscated, for a total of 80,000 yuan, and was ordered to suspend business for rectification for 30 days. In 2024, the Guangdong Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism published a complaint involving two tourists who joined a Hong Kong–Macao–Zhuhai tour costing 800 yuan per person. They bought more than 20,000 yuan worth of jewelry and pillows at a duty-free shop. The tourists complained to the district culture and tourism department. The parties settled, the travel agency helped mail the goods back, and the tourists received a full refund (nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2018 amendment). Tourism Law (Articles 9, 35, 92, and 93). <https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff8080816f135f46016f1d08f6da12f6>; Ministry of Culture and Tourism (2026). Measures for Handling Tourism Complaints (Ministry of Culture and Tourism Order No. 14, Articles 11, 14, and 23; effective March 15, 2026). <https://zwgk.mct.gov.cn/zfxxgkml/zcfg/bmgz/202602/t20260211_964700.html>; General Office of the Ministry of Culture and Tourism (2021). Notice on Further Optimizing the Public Service Hotline of the Culture and Tourism System. <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2021-11/19/content_5651873.htm>; Ministry of Culture and Tourism (2025). Typical Cases of Forced Consumption in the Tourism Market (third batch, Case 15). <https://www.mct.gov.cn/whzx/whyw/202509/t20250908_962084.htm>; Guangdong Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism (2024). Guangdong Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism Publishes Typical Tourism Complaint Cases from 2024 (Case 1). <https://whly.gd.gov.cn/service_newscgldt/content/post_4385141.html>
entries.notes: Go to the travel agency, not the shop. If the agency will not handle it, call China's 12345 hotline to complain; the former 12301 hotline has been discontinued. You must file the complaint within 90 days after the tourism contract's performance period ends. Mediation must be completed within 60 days after the complaint is accepted. Both sides must agree to mediation; if it fails, your only options are arbitration or a lawsuit. Under the rules, an ordinary first-instance court proceeding must be concluded within six months, though this can be extended, and you pay your own lawyer's fees. For small-claims proceedings, see Section 8, Item 22 (scammed in online shopping or a secondhand transaction). If you signed a supplementary agreement, then unless the tour fee was unreasonably low, your only basis for negotiating is that the quality did not match the price. If you bought from a shop abroad, pursuing your rights across borders on your own is difficult; you need to rely on the domestic travel agency. Older people are often lured by “zero-fee tours”; for retirement-related scams, see Section 17, Item 5 (investing for retirement). The beneficiaries are you and your family.

entries.title: Before buying a financial product recommended by a bank employee, find it in that bank's own app or on its official website; if you cannot find it, the employee may be selling it privately as an “off-book sale”
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Search for the product name in the bank's app or on its official website before buying; it takes a few minutes. The hard part is telling an account manager you know, “I'll check it myself first.”
entries.summary: When bank employees privately sell products that the bank neither issued nor authorized them to sell on its behalf, this is called a “feidan,” or off-book sale. Products a bank sells on behalf of another institution may be sold only at its own branches, on its official website, or in its app, and you should be able to find them through those channels. If you cannot find a product there, do not buy it yet. In some off-book sale cases, courts have ordered banks to bear half the loss. In a case involving a securities branch, the first-instance court awarded no compensation; the second-instance court changed the ruling and awarded partial compensation.
entries.benefit: The Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People's Court says that an off-book sale of a financial product occurs when an employee of a financial institution uses the convenience of their job to privately sell a third-party product that their institution neither issued nor authorized them to sell on its behalf. Rules issued by China's National Financial Regulatory Administration in 2025 say that banks may sell products from other institutions on their behalf only in designated sections of channels they operate themselves, such as their branches, official websites, and apps. Banks must let customers look up these products through the bank's own channels and state that they are sold on behalf of another institution, what type of product each is, and who issued it. Banks must not sell these products mixed in with deposits or their own products. The first page of promotional material for such a product must say: “This product is issued and managed by ×× institution (the partner institution). ×× Bank, as the sales agent, does not assume responsibility for the product's investment performance or payment obligations.” Banks must authorize which products each salesperson may sell and display that information at their branches. Sales at branches must be audio and video recorded. Banks and their employees must not “privately promote or sell unapproved products under the name of the institution to which they belong” (nationwide, effective October 1, 2025). In 2022, the Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People's Court reported a case. In 2013, a bank wealth manager told a customer that a certain product was one of the bank's bestsellers and that the bank was its custodian bank. The customer signed a Partnership Agreement with a fund company and transferred 1.2 million yuan to the company's account. The principal was never returned, and the fund company's actual controller went to prison. The court held that the employee had used the convenience of their position to sell the product during working hours at the workplace, making it an act performed in the course of employment. The customer was also at fault for pursuing high interest without considering other factors. The first-instance court assigned half the loss to the bank and half to the customer; the second-instance court upheld the ruling. In October 2026, the Supreme People's Court, the People's Bank of China, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the China Securities Regulatory Commission jointly published a typical case. The head of a securities branch privately sold a private equity fund that the branch had not authorized for sale, and a customer invested 1 million yuan. The customer sued in August 2023, but the first-instance court dismissed the claim. The second-instance court found that both the branch and the customer were at fault and changed the ruling, ordering the branch to pay about 577,000 yuan (exactly 576,716.97 yuan). The case number is from 2024 (nationwide; 2022 and 2026).
entries.sources: National Financial Regulatory Administration (2025). Measures for the Administration of Agency Sales Business of Commercial Banks (Financial Regulatory Rules [2025] No. 6, Articles 32, 33, 34, 39, 41, 43, and 54). <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202503/content_7015054.htm>; Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People's Court (2022-05-08). Case Close-Up | Who Pays for My Losses from an Off-Book Sale of a Financial Product? <https://bj3zy.bjcourt.gov.cn/article/detail/2022/05/id/6713358.shtml>; Supreme People's Court, People's Bank of China, National Financial Regulatory Administration, and China Securities Regulatory Commission (2026-10-12). Typical Cases on Protecting the Lawful Rights and Interests of Financial Consumers and Investors (Case 3, (2024) Wan 05 Min Zhong No. 1088). <https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/513941.html>; National People's Congress (2020). Article 1191 of the Civil Code. <https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff808081729d1efe01729d50b5c500bf>
entries.notes: Article 1191 of China's Civil Code provides that, when an employee causes harm to another person while performing work duties, the employer bears tort liability. So a bank saying “this was the employee's personal conduct” does not necessarily mean it has no duty to compensate you. The share of the loss each party bears depends on how much fault lies with the bank's side and with you. You will generally need to sue to recover your money. Under the rules, an ordinary first-instance court proceeding must be concluded within six months, though this can be extended, and you pay your own lawyer's fees. Complain to the bank first. If you cannot reach an agreement, call China's 12378 hotline; see Item 43 of this section (call 12378 if you think you were misled). Even when a bank genuinely sells a product on behalf of another institution, the bank is not responsible for paying out on it. For returns that seem absurdly high, see Item 6 of this section (walk away when you see high returns). To check whether the contract you have is for insurance or a deposit, see Item 42 of this section (check whether it is a deposit or insurance). If there is an older person in your family, set a rule requiring two people to confirm large expenses; see Section 17, Item 3 (set a two-person confirmation rule for large expenses). The beneficiaries are you and the older people in your family. This is not investment advice.

chapters.title: The Don't-Do List
chapters.intro:
This section covers things that “look cheap and effective.” Once you examine the original research, their benefits are close to zero, equal to zero, or, in some cases, negative.

The items in this section are grouped by topic below, with item numbers in parentheses.

**Health products and supplements**: multivitamins (Item 1), ordinary fish oil (Item 2), vitamin D supplements (Item 3), antioxidant supplements to prevent cancer (Item 4), chondroitin for knee osteoarthritis (Item 5), vitamin C to prevent colds (Item 6), spending a lot on health products (Item 10), taking probiotics long term (Item 11), buying detox or colon-cleansing products (Item 13), taking large amounts of calcium after a fracture (Item 30), and relying on melatonin to cure chronic insomnia (Item 34).

**Health screenings and minor findings**: whole-body PET-CT scans and tumor-marker packages (Item 7), general health-screening packages (Item 18), not taking medication for high uric acid if it has never caused pain (Item 19), not having gallstones removed if they have never caused pain (Item 20), not cutting out calcium to prevent kidney stones (Item 21), and not having arthroscopic cleaning for knee pain caused by degeneration (Item 33).

**Health claims**: relying on a fitness tracker to help you lose weight (Item 8), buying organic food (Item 9), taking cold showers to boost immunity (Item 12), not forcing yourself to drink water (Item 14), blue-light-blocking glasses (Item 16), treating blood donation as a health practice (Item 17), eating breakfast or practicing intermittent fasting to control weight (Item 26), relying on proper lifting technique to prevent lower back pain (Item 29), and asking for an IV infusion whenever you have a cold or fever (Item 35).

**Spending money on luck and mood**: paying for fortune-telling or horoscopes (Item 15), buying objects such as crystals or pixiu figurines (Item 22), buying things to improve your mood (Item 23), spending more to move up one tier (Item 24), and deciding not to save because you think you could die at any time (Item 32).

**Willpower and sex**: willpower is like a muscle (Item 25), masturbation harms your health (Item 27), and sexual orientation conversion (Item 28).

**Answers from AI**: relying on an AI chatbot to assess your own medical condition (Item 31).

entries.title: Do not take multivitamins to live longer or prevent cardiovascular disease
entries.cost: About 0.5 to 2 yuan a day, or 200 to 700 yuan a year. Taking one costs almost no time; it is just one pill. After taking it for a long time, you can easily become reliant on it and feel as though you have left something undone on a day you miss it.
entries.summary: Fourteen thousand male doctors took multivitamins for eleven years. Just as many had major heart and blood vessel problems or died as among those who did not take them. Combining nine trials with more than 50,000 participants also showed no discernible effect on deaths. Not buying them saves 200 to 700 yuan a year. This item does not apply to people confirmed to lack a particular nutrient or to pregnant women taking folic acid.
entries.benefit: The PHS II trial enrolled 14,641 male doctors and followed them for 11.2 years (the median: half were followed longer and half for less time). The proportion who had major heart or blood vessel problems was the same among those who took multivitamins and those who did not. The HR for major cardiovascular events was 1.01 (HR means hazard ratio; 1 means the two groups were the same). The 95% CI of 0.91–1.10 is the range of plausible values for that figure. Deaths were the same, too: the HR for all-cause mortality was 0.94 (0.88–1.02). The USPSTF, the US body that grades preventive measures, pooled nine randomized controlled trials with 51,550 participants in 2022 and found no association between multivitamins and overall mortality. It gave the evidence an I rating, meaning the evidence is insufficient to draw a clear conclusion. Multivitamins seem like a good deal because “get every nutrient in one pill” sounds sensible, and they cost only a few tenths of a yuan a day.
entries.sources: Sesso HD et al. (2012). Multivitamins in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14805>; US Preventive Services Task Force (2022). Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.8970>; Gaziano JM et al. (2012). Multivitamins in the Prevention of Cancer in Men. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14641> (the cancer result discussed in the notes)
entries.notes: Point of debate: the same group of male doctors was also studied for cancer. About 8% fewer of those taking multivitamins developed cancer (0.86–0.998, P=0.04, just barely meeting the threshold for a result considered unlikely to be due to chance). About 12% fewer died of cancer (0.77–1.01). That range crosses 1, so this could simply be chance. The benefit is small and has only been observed in male doctors. This item does not include people confirmed to lack a nutrient, pregnant women (who need folic acid), or people whose usual diets are very unbalanced; take supplements as your doctor advises.

entries.title: Do not take ordinary fish oil to prevent cardiovascular disease
entries.cost: About 1 to 3 yuan a day, or 400 to 1,000 yuan a year. Taking it costs almost no time.
entries.summary: Two large trials enrolled 26,000 people and 15,000 people with diabetes, respectively. Among those taking 1 gram of fish oil daily, just as many had major heart and blood vessel problems or died as among those who did not take it. “Eating fish is beneficial” does not mean “taking fish-oil capsules is beneficial.” Not buying them saves 400 to 1,000 yuan a year.
entries.benefit: The VITAL trial enrolled 25,871 people, who took 1 gram of fish oil daily, and followed them for 5.3 years (median). It found no discernible difference between the groups in major heart and blood vessel problems or deaths. The HR for major cardiovascular events was 0.92 (HR means hazard ratio; 1 means the two groups were the same). The 95% CI of 0.80–1.06 is the range of plausible values for that figure. It crosses 1, meaning no difference can be discerned. The HR for all-cause mortality was 1.02 (0.90–1.15). The ASCEND trial enrolled 15,480 people with diabetes, who also took 1 gram daily, and followed them for an average of 7.4 years. It likewise found no discernible difference. The RR for serious vascular events was 0.97 (0.87–1.08). The RR for all-cause mortality was 0.95 (0.86–1.05). Fish oil seems like a good deal because many people assume that “eating fish is beneficial” directly means “taking fish-oil capsules is beneficial.”
entries.sources: Manson JE et al. (2019). Marine n-3 Fatty Acids and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1811403>; ASCEND Study Collaborative Group (2018). Effects of n-3 Fatty Acid Supplements in Diabetes Mellitus. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1804989>; Bhatt DL et al. (2019). Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia. New England Journal of Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1812792> (the trial of high-purity prescription fish oil discussed in the notes)
entries.notes: Point of debate: one trial did find a benefit. The REDUCE-IT trial enrolled 8,179 people who already had cardiovascular disease or diabetes, were all taking statins, and still had elevated triglycerides (135–499 mg/dL). They took a prescription drug containing 4 g of pure EPA daily. The proportion who had an event was 17.2% versus 22.0%, a reduction in risk of about one-quarter (HR 0.75, 0.68–0.83). But that was a high-dose prescription drug for high-risk patients, which is not the same as ordinary people taking fish-oil supplements. This item also does not apply to eating fish itself.

entries.title: Do not give vitamin D supplements to people who are not deficient in vitamin D in the hope of helping them live longer
entries.cost: About 0.2 to 0.5 yuan a day, or 100 to 200 yuan a year. The money is not much; the real cost is believing you have already taken a preventive measure.
entries.summary: Among people who were not deficient in vitamin D to begin with, taking supplements for five years made no difference in the numbers who developed cancer or cardiovascular disease or who died. Adults who rarely go outdoors and get little sunlight can take 400 IU a day; do not exceed 2,000 IU a day. At high doses, bone density falls more and falls become more frequent. Fatigue alone does not mean you are deficient in vitamin D. If you have been tired for several weeks and cannot tell why, see a doctor.
entries.benefit: The VITAL trial enrolled 25,871 people, who took 2,000 IU daily and were followed for a median of 5.3 years. No differences were seen in cancer, cardiovascular problems, or mortality. For invasive cancer, the HR was 0.96 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means both sides are identical; 95% CI 0.88–1.06 is the credible range). For major cardiovascular events, the HR was 0.97 (0.85–1.12). For all-cause mortality, the HR was 0.99 (0.87–1.12). The D-Health trial enrolled 21,315 Australians aged 60 and older. They took 60,000 IU monthly and were followed for 5 years. This study also found no difference, with an HR for all-cause mortality of 1.04 (0.93–1.18). The mortality rates were 5.3% versus 5.1%. It appears cost-effective because some studies merely tracked and recorded data without any intervention, finding that people with low vitamin D levels had higher mortality, which was misinterpreted as "supplementing it will work." There is a separate set of recommendations for people who rarely go outdoors. The UK Department of Health recommends that adults who rarely go outside, live in care homes, or wear clothes that cover most of their skin when outdoors take a daily supplement of 10 micrograms of vitamin D throughout the year. The NHS specifies that 1 microgram equals 40 IU, so 10 micrograms is 400 IU. China's health industry standard recommends 10 micrograms daily for adults aged 18 to 64, and 15 micrograms for those aged 65 and older. The same standard sets the tolerable upper intake level at 50 micrograms (2,000 IU) per day, because excessive intake causes hypercalcemia. The NHS upper limit for adults is slightly more generous at 100 micrograms (4,000 IU). There are many causes of fatigue; those listed by the NHS include insufficient sleep, stress and depression, iron deficiency anemia, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, and sleep apnea. It recommends seeing a doctor if you have been tired for weeks without a clear explanation, or if the fatigue interferes with daily life. Supplementing higher doses does not yield better outcomes either. VITAL also evaluated fractures: those taking 2,000 IU daily were identical to those taking nothing (HR 0.98, 0.89–1.08). VITAL also examined depression among 18,353 participants aged 50 and older who did not have depression at the time. Those who supplemented had 12.9 cases of depression or recurrence per 1,000 person-years, compared to 13.3 cases among those who did not supplement, showing no difference (HR 0.97, 0.87–1.09). There was also no difference in mood scores. The authors explicitly stated that the findings do not support adults taking vitamin D supplements to prevent depression. A Canadian trial enrolled 311 healthy individuals aged 55 to 70 without osteoporosis. They were divided into three groups taking 400, 4,000, and 10,000 IU daily for 3 years. The higher the dose, the more bone mineral density dropped in the radial bone of the wrist; the three groups decreased by 1.2%, 2.4%, and 3.5%, respectively. No difference was observed in compressive bone strength. The authors concluded that this does not support high-dose vitamin D supplementation as beneficial for bone health. A Swiss trial enrolled 200 seniors aged 70 and older with a history of falls. They took 24,000 IU or 60,000 IU monthly for one year. Lower extremity function did not improve in the 60,000 IU group, and actually more people in that group fell over the course of the year (66.9% vs. 47.9%). An Australian trial enrolled 2,256 women aged 70 and older who took a single annual dose of 500,000 IU in autumn or winter. Their incidence of falls was about 15% higher (RR 1.15, 1.02–1.30), and fractures were about 26% higher (RR 1.26, 1.00–1.59).
entries.sources: Manson JE et al. (2019). Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1809944>; Neale RE et al. (2022). The D-Health Trial: a randomised controlled trial of the effect of vitamin D on mortality. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(21)00345-4>; NHS. (2016). Monthly High-Dose Vitamin D Treatment for the Prevention of Functional Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2015.7148>; Sanders KM et al. (2010). Annual high-dose oral vitamin D and falls and fractures in older women: a randomized controlled trial. The effect of vitamin D supplementation on depression: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Psychol Med. <https://doi.org/10.1017/s0033291724001697>
entries.notes: Controversies: Neither VITAL nor D-Health intentionally recruited individuals who were genuinely vitamin D deficient, so the conclusions only apply to "people who were not deficient to begin with." Those diagnosed with an actual deficiency, individuals with osteoporosis, and infants and young children should still supplement according to their doctor's instructions. Even severe deficiency does not necessarily require injections. The 2016 global consensus on rickets recommends oral administration because oral intake replenishes levels faster than intramuscular injection. A trial recruited 61 children with rickets. One group received a single injection of 600,000 IU, while the other group took 60,000 IU orally once a week for 10 consecutive weeks. After 12 weeks, there were no differences between the two groups in lab tests or radiographs. After finishing the dose prescribed by your doctor, get rechecked; if levels still fail to rise, have the doctor investigate whether there is an absorption issue. For people without sun exposure, supplementing 400 IU daily is to prevent deficiency. The health industry standard explicitly states that vitamin D deficiency causes rickets, osteomalacia, and osteoporosis. This does not indicate that it can prevent cancer or heart disease, nor does it indicate that it can treat fatigue. If a doctor has prescribed a different dose for you, take it as directed by the doctor. Opinions differ on whether supplementing helps those who already have depression. A 2023 meta-analysis pooling 41 trials observed a modest reduction in depression scores, but results across studies varied widely, and the authors rated the quality of evidence in the lowest tier. A 2024 meta-analysis broken down by duration found that in trials followed for more than a year, no effect was observed. If you have depression, see a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist first, and do not use vitamin D as a substitute for treatment. Evaluated here are all-cause mortality, cancer, cardiovascular disease, bones, falls, and depression; other conditions were not assessed. For infant supplementation, see Section 20, Item 16 (Feed 400 international units of vitamin D daily).

entries.title: Do not take antioxidant supplements (beta-carotene, vitamin E, vitamin A) to prevent cancer
entries.cost: About 0.5 to 2 yuan a day. For smokers, the real cost is that the risk of lung cancer climbs along with it.
entries.summary: Antioxidant supplements are not merely useless. Pooling 78 trials and nearly 300,000 people, those taking them actually had slightly higher mortality rates in the trials with more rigorous designs. In two large trials conducted specifically in smokers, beta-carotene increased the rate of developing lung cancer by 18% to 28%. Mortality was also 8% to 17% higher. Smokers and individuals who have been exposed to asbestos, in particular, should not take them.
entries.benefit: Cochrane pooled 78 randomized controlled trials and 296,707 people. For those taking antioxidant supplements, the RR for all-cause mortality was 1.02 (RR is the relative risk; 1 means both sides are identical; 95% CI 0.98–1.05 is the credible range). Looking only at the trials with more rigorous designs and lower risk of bias, the RR was 1.04 (1.01–1.07), which was slightly higher. Looking at beta-carotene alone, the RR was 1.05 (1.01–1.09); for vitamin E alone, the RR was 1.03 (1.00–1.05). The ATBC study enrolled 29,133 male smokers taking 20 mg daily; the incidence of lung cancer was 18% higher (3%–36%), and all-cause mortality was 8% higher (1%–16%). The CARET study enrolled 18,314 smokers or people exposed to asbestos. Their risk of developing lung cancer was about 28% higher (RR 1.28, 1.04–1.57). The risk of death was about 17% higher (all-cause mortality RR 1.17, 1.03–1.33). It appears cost-effective because in the reasoning chain of "antioxidants mean anti-aging, and anti-aging can prevent cancer," every single step sounds like common sense.
entries.sources: Bjelakovic G et al. (2012). Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD007176.pub2>；The Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group (1994). The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199404143301501>；Omenn GS et al. (1996). Effects of a combination of beta carotene and vitamin A on lung cancer and cardiovascular disease. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199605023341802>
entries.notes: The USPSTF, the official US agency responsible for grading preventive measures, assigned a Grade D to beta-carotene and vitamin E in 2022, which means recommending against their use. Smokers and individuals exposed to asbestos have already suffered harm because of them. Antioxidants naturally contained in vegetables and fruits do not count toward this; eat them as usual.

entries.title: Do not count on glucosamine / chondroitin to treat knee osteoarthritis
entries.cost: About 2 to 5 yuan a day, or 700 to 1,800 yuan a year.
entries.summary: Among people with knee osteoarthritis who took dummy pills for 24 weeks, 60% also reported that it was less painful. Those taking glucosamine or chondroitin were only 4 to 5 percentage points higher than this, a difference small enough that it could just be coincidence. Spending 700 to 1,800 yuan a year buys an outcome essentially identical to taking dummy pills.
entries.benefit: The GAIT trial enrolled 1,583 patients with knee osteoarthritis treated for 24 weeks. Among those taking a placebo (dummy pill), 60.1% also reported pain relief. Glucosamine was only 3.9 percentage points higher (P=0.30). Chondroitin was 5.3 percentage points higher (P=0.17). Taking both together was 6.5 percentage points higher (P=0.09). These differences are all too small to rule out mere coincidence. The real medication, celecoxib, used as an active control in the same trial, was 10.0 percentage points higher (P=0.008). It appears cost-effective because "replenishing the raw materials of cartilage" sounds like the exact targeted remedy, and taking dummy pills alone leads 60% of people to report that it works.
entries.sources: Clegg DO et al. (2006). Glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, and the two in combination for painful knee osteoarthritis. NEJM. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa052771>
entries.notes: Controversies: In the same trial, among the subgroup with severe pain at baseline, the response rate for taking both together was 79.2%, compared to 54.3% in the control group (P=0.002). However, the authors stated that this was dredged post-hoc from the data and can only serve as a clue, not a conclusion. Practices for knee osteoarthritis that truly have supporting evidence are weight loss and muscle strengthening; see Item 33 of this section (Arthroscopic debridement).

entries.title: Do not rely on vitamin C to prevent colds
entries.cost: An effervescent tablet costs about 1 to 2 yuan, or 300 to 700 yuan a year.
entries.summary: Taking vitamin C daily basically will not make you catch fewer colds, and starting to take it only after catching a cold shows hit-or-miss results. Taking it daily can shorten the duration of a cold by about 8%; calculate for yourself whether that is worth 300 to 500 yuan a year. Marathon runners and soldiers on subarctic operations are exceptions: among them, those who took it had about half as many colds.
entries.benefit: Cochrane pooled 29 controlled trials and 11,306 people. For ordinary people, taking vitamin C daily basically does not reduce the number of colds caught. The cold incidence RR was 0.97 (RR is the relative risk; 1 means both sides are identical). 95% CI 0.94–1.00 is the credible range. In those trials where supplementation started only after cold onset, the original text states "no consistent effect was observed": some trials showed efficacy, while others did not. In the same review, regular daily long-term intake shortened the duration of cold discomfort by about 8% (in adults, 95% CI 3%–12%) and by 14% in children (7%–21%). Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers marching in subarctic conditions are exceptions. Across 5 trials and 598 people, the number of people who caught a cold was reduced by about half. Incidence RR 0.48 (95% CI 0.35–0.64). It appears cost-effective because it is cheap, tastes sweet and tart, and the claim that "vitamin C prevents colds" has already circulated for half a century.
entries.sources: Hemilä H, Chalker E (2013). Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4>
entries.notes: Controversies: In the same review, daily intake indeed shortened the duration of cold discomfort. It was shortened by about 8% in adults (3%–12%) and 14% in children (7%–21%). This works out to being sick for about half a day less per cold episode. Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers marching in subarctic conditions are exceptions. Across 5 trials and 598 people, the number of people catching colds was reduced by about half (RR 0.48, 0.35–0.64). The vast majority of people do not belong to these two groups.

entries.title: Do not get "whole-body PET-CT" or "tumor marker panels" for yourself when asymptomatic
entries.cost: A whole-body PET-CT costs about 7,000 to 10,000 yuan per scan, plus exposure to ionizing radiation. A tumor marker panel costs several hundred yuan. The real costs lie downstream: discovering an "abnormality" that is actually a false alarm (known as a false positive), followed by re-examinations, tissue biopsies, and surgery—both the financial expense and the physical suffering occur in this phase.
entries.summary: When asymptomatic people get screened, what is detected most often is a false alarm. Over 80% of people who get a whole-body CT have at least one "abnormality" found, and nearly 40% are called back for follow-up testing, yet the vast majority are benign. For women screened with ovarian cancer markers, deaths from ovarian cancer did not decrease, and some underwent surgery in vain because of a false alarm.
entries.benefit: The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), the American body that grades preventive measures, gave ovarian cancer screening with CA-125 and ultrasound a D grade for women without symptoms, meaning it recommends against it. The basis was the PLCO trial. The proportion who died of ovarian cancer was 0.34% in the screening group and 0.29% in the usual care group. RR 1.18 (95% CI 0.82–1.71). Screening showed no benefit. Across the trials, 0.2%–3.25% underwent unnecessary surgery because of false positives, and up to 15% of those people had serious surgical complications. Another study gave 1,192 people without symptoms whole-body CT screening. At least one “abnormality” was found in 86%, and further examination was recommended for 37%. The original paper says that “most findings were described as benign.” It looks like good value because “check the whole body once, find problems early, treat them early” feels so intuitive
entries.sources: US Preventive Services Task Force (2018). Screening for Ovarian Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA (the same recommendation also has an official USPSTF page). <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2017.21926>, <https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/ovarian-cancer-screening>; Furtado CD et al. (2005). Whole-body CT screening: spectrum of findings and recommendations in 1192 patients. Radiology. <https://doi.org/10.1148/radiol.2372041741>
entries.notes: The part about tumor markers is backed by randomized controlled trials. The part about whole-body CT and PET-CT has only follow-up records of what happened to people who had them, with no comparison groups. That is a weaker level of evidence, equivalent to grade B. The screenings that do have evidence, such as those for colorectal cancer, cervical cancer, and breast cancer, and low-dose chest CT for people at high risk, are a different matter; see Section 1. PET-CT for someone who already has symptoms or has already been diagnosed with cancer is part of medical care, not screening, and is a separate matter

entries.title: Do not count on a fitness band or watch tracking your activity to help you lose weight
entries.cost: The device costs 200 to 2,000 yuan. You also have to devote attention to checking its data every day.
entries.summary: Among overweight people following the same diet and exercise plan, those wearing fitness bands lost 3.5 kilograms over two years, while those without them actually lost 5.9 kilograms. If you want to lose weight, a device is not an expense you have to incur.
entries.benefit: The IDEA trial enrolled 471 overweight or obese adults and followed them for 24 months. Everyone followed the same diet and exercise plan; the only difference was whether they wore a wearable device. The group wearing one lost 3.5 kilograms (95% CI 2.6–4.5, the confidence interval). The group without one lost 5.9 kilograms (5.0–6.8), actually more. The difference between groups was 2.4 kilograms (1.0–3.7, P=0.002). It looks like good value because “you can only manage what you measure” sounds reasonable, and buying the device is a one-time expense
entries.sources: Jakicic JM et al. (2016). Effect of Wearable Technology Combined With a Lifestyle Intervention on Long-term Weight Loss: The IDEA Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2016.12858>
entries.notes: This is just one trial, and it used devices worn on the arm from the early 2010s. It does not justify saying “all wearable devices are useless.” Exercise itself is effective; see Section 2. The conclusion is simply this: if you want to lose weight, a device is not an expense you have to incur

entries.title: Do not pay a premium for organic food to be “healthier”
entries.cost: Generally one to three times the price of comparable conventional food.
entries.summary: There is no strong evidence that organic food is more nutritious. Only three studies actually looked at people's health after they ate it, and none found a difference. Organic produce was indeed 30 percentage points less likely to have detectable pesticide residues, but detection does not mean the level exceeds the limit.
entries.benefit: A systematic review combined 17 studies involving people and 223 studies measuring food composition. It concluded that there is “a lack of strong evidence that organic foods are significantly more nutritious than conventional foods.” Only three of those studies looked at people's health after eating the foods (specifically allergies and symptomatic infections), and found no difference between the two. Organic produce was 30 percentage points less likely to have detectable pesticide residues, but detection does not mean the level exceeds the limit. It looks like good value because “no pesticides means safer, and safer means healthier” sounds like common sense at every step
entries.sources: Smith-Spangler C et al. (2012). Are organic foods safer or healthier than conventional alternatives?: a systematic review. Ann Intern Med. <https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-157-5-201209040-00007>
entries.notes: Very few studies directly examine people's health after they eat the food. So the conclusion is “there is no evidence that it is better,” not “it has been proved to have no benefit.” Environmental impact, animal welfare, and taste are outside the scope here. Eating more vegetables and fruit is itself beneficial, whether or not they are organic

entries.title: Do not spend a lot on health supplements, medicinal pastes, or tonics to “improve your health”
entries.cost: Prices range from a few hundred to more than ten thousand yuan. Once packaged as gifts, they often cost several times as much.
entries.summary: Common ingredients such as multivitamins, fish oil, and vitamin D have already been examined one by one in the first six entries of this section, with no benefit found. The sentence on the package, “Health foods are not medicines and cannot replace medicines in treating disease,” must be printed under rules set by the authority that regulates health foods. If you are buying this for your parents and bringing it to their door, there is nothing wrong with the gesture; you have simply chosen the wrong thing.
entries.benefit: What you get back is the money saved. The reasons are in the first six entries of this section. The most common ingredients in health supplements—multivitamins, fish oil, vitamin D, antioxidants, glucosamine, and vitamin C—have not shown the expected benefits in randomized controlled trials. The figures for each are in the benefit fields of those six entries. Regulations only define what a product may claim; they are not evidence that it is ineffective. China's State Administration for Market Regulation requires the front of a health food package to devote no less than 20% of its area to the statement: “Health foods are not medicines and cannot replace medicines in treating disease.” The same regulation also confines the purposes of health foods to “supplementing dietary nutrients, maintaining or improving the body's state of health, or reducing risk factors for the occurrence of disease.” It looks like good value because “it doesn't treat illness; it just improves your health” can be phrased so that it is never quite wrong, and no one can prove it false. And when you pay for it as a gift, you are acting on a personal relationship, not evidence
entries.sources: State Administration for Market Regulation of China (2019). State Administration for Market Regulation holds a special press conference on the Guidelines for Labeling Warning Statements on Health Foods and the Measures for the Administration of the Catalogues of Health Food Ingredients and Health Functions. <https://www.samr.gov.cn/tssps/sjdt/tpxw/art/2023/art_4b658b824b1b4b0ba57c09a56cc93aad.html>
entries.notes: The conclusion is “there is no supporting evidence,” not “it has been proved ineffective,” so this receives only a C grade. For products with clearly listed ingredients, check the corresponding research in the earlier entries. If someone has been found to have a nutrient deficiency or is being treated for an illness, follow their doctor's advice. Reject the product, not the gesture. If an older person bought it themselves and is already taking it, there is no need to go to their home and argue about it, provided they have not substituted it for their prescribed medicine and it has not caused problems. Arranging the vaccinations and screenings they need matters more. Spend the same money on the following instead; the book gives a source for each. Accompany an older person to get the annual flu vaccine; see Section 1, Entry 20. For the shingles vaccine after age 50, see Section 1, Entry 21. For the pneumococcal vaccine for people aged 65 and over, see Section 1, Entry 22. Buy a blood pressure monitor, keep an eye on whether they take their blood pressure medicine as prescribed, and help them bring their blood pressure to the target level; see Section 1, Entry 7. Make changes to the bathroom and stairs at home, and practice balance and leg strength with them; see Section 1, Entry 13. Accompany them for an age-appropriate cancer screening; see Section 1, Entries 17 to 19. For an older person already confined to bed long term, see Section 17, Entries 7 and 8, on pressure sore prevention and China's long-term care insurance. If you want to bring something when you visit, fruit, rice, flour, or food they like is more practical than medicinal pastes. There are two kinds of things you really should stop: eldercare investment schemes that require payment up front, and products that would replace medicines; see Section 17, Entry 5

entries.title: Do not take probiotics long term when you have no gut problems
entries.cost: About 2 to 5 yuan a day, or 700 to 1,800 yuan a year.
entries.summary: Taken together, 45 trials in healthy adults show that probiotics do not produce lasting changes in gut bacteria; after you stop, they return to how they were. Blood lipids do not improve either. There is separate evidence for specific situations such as diarrhea caused by antibiotics, which this entry does not cover.
entries.benefit: A review combined 45 trials in healthy adults and concluded that the findings “did not support probiotics causing lasting changes in the gut microbiota or improving blood lipids in healthy adults.” Gut bacteria do change, but only temporarily; after you stop taking probiotics, they return to how they were. It looks like good value because “gut health” is broad enough to fit almost anything, and a bottle a day seems cheap
entries.sources: Khalesi S et al. (2019). A review of probiotic supplementation in healthy adults: helpful or hype? Eur J Clin Nutr. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41430-018-0135-9>
entries.notes: The same review also reports some small improvements in healthy people, such as stools that are more formed and of a suitable consistency, and an increase in lactobacilli in women's vaginas. Diarrhea caused by antibiotics, and the use of a particular strain for a particular illness, each have their own evidence and are separate matters. This entry is only about healthy people taking probiotics every day as a supplement

entries.title: Do not force yourself to take cold showers to “boost your immune system”
entries.cost: It costs nothing. You have to endure 30 to 90 uncomfortable seconds every day, and sticking with it in winter takes willpower. People with cardiovascular disease also need to be careful: cold exposure poses a risk for them.
entries.summary: In a trial of 3,018 people, those who took cold showers called in sick 29% less often. But their total number of sick-leave days was the same as everyone else's, so this does not establish that they got sick less. A 2025 review of 11 trials found that markers of inflammation briefly rose after cold-water exposure, while immune markers did not change. Take cold showers if you like them; just do not treat them as a health investment.
entries.benefit: A randomized controlled trial in the Netherlands enrolled 3,018 people who, after a hot shower, rinsed with cold water for 30, 60, or 90 seconds. They called in sick 29% less often (IRR 0.71, the ratio of the numbers of instances). But the original paper explicitly states that there was “no significant between-group difference in sick-leave days”: the total number of days they were ill was the same in both groups. There were no meaningful differences in quality of life, work productivity, or anxiety either. A 2025 systematic review pooled 11 randomized trials involving 3,177 people. Markers of inflammation actually rose immediately after cold-water immersion and one hour later. Immune markers did not change. Stress decreased only at the 12-hour time point. The authors themselves said the evidence was “limited by the small number of RCTs and small samples,” meaning there were too few randomized trials of this kind and too few people in each. It looks like good value because it costs nothing, and the intuition that “if it is hard, it must work” feels so natural
entries.sources: Buijze GA et al. (2016). The Effect of Cold Showering on Health and Work: A Randomized Controlled Trial. PLOS ONE. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0161749>；Cain T et al. (2025). Effects of cold-water immersion on health and wellbeing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLOS ONE. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317615>
entries.notes: A point of debate: the number of times people called in sick really was 29% lower, and that difference does not look like chance. But their total number of days ill did not decrease, so we cannot say they actually got sick less. Athletes using cold water to aid recovery after training is a different question and is outside the scope here. No obvious harm from cold showers has been seen in healthy people; just do not treat them as a health investment

entries.title: Do not buy detox, colon-cleansing, enzyme, or alkaline-water products
entries.cost: A few hundred to a few thousand yuan. The kind of “detox” that relies on going hungry may also lower your blood sugar and leave you short of nutrients.
entries.summary: The detox industry is large, but there is very little clinical evidence to support it, and no one has conducted a proper trial of commercially sold detox diets. Researchers looked for a connection between dietary acidity or alkalinity, alkaline water, and cancer; they found only one eligible study, and it found no association.
entries.benefit: That review concluded that “despite the booming detox industry, there is very little clinical evidence to support these diets,” and that “there have been no randomized controlled trials of commercial detox diets.” Another systematic review specifically examined whether dietary acidity or alkalinity and alkaline water were associated with cancer: of 8,278 publications examined, only one qualified for inclusion, and it found no association. The authors wrote that “promoting alkaline diets and alkaline water to the public for cancer prevention or treatment is unjustified.” It looks like good value because the premises “there are toxins in the body that need to be removed” and “an acidic body causes cancer” sound rather like physiology
entries.sources: Klein AV, Kiat H (2015). Detox diets for toxin elimination and weight management: a critical review of the evidence. J Hum Nutr Diet. <https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.12286>；Fenton TR, Huang T (2016). Systematic review of the association between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer. BMJ Open. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438>
entries.notes: We can only say “there is no supporting evidence,” so this receives only a C grade. Removing the waste produced by the body's metabolism is already the job of the liver and kidneys. As long as those organs are not diseased, you do not need to do any extra “detox”

entries.title: Do not force yourself to drink water just to reach “eight glasses a day”
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Remembering to drink takes some time and effort, and you may get up to urinate more often at night.
entries.summary: Someone specifically traced the origin of “eight glasses of water a day” and found no studies supporting it. Food and other drinks already contain a great deal of water, so you do not need to drink that much water on top of them. This conclusion applies only to healthy adults living in a temperate climate who are usually sedentary. People working in the heat, exercising vigorously, or needing to drink more to treat or prevent an illness should make a point of drinking more.
entries.benefit: A literature review specifically investigated the “8×8” rule: eight glasses of water a day, eight ounces per glass. It concluded that “no scientific studies were found to support 8×8.” It also wrote that “surveys of food and fluid intake in thousands of adults strongly suggest that such large amounts are unnecessary,” because food and other beverages already supply a great deal of water. The author expressly limited this conclusion to “healthy adults in a temperate climate who are sedentary most of the time.” He also wrote that the treatment or prevention of some illnesses requires drinking as much as 8×8 or more, and that “strenuous labor and exercise, especially in hot climates,” of course require more drinking. The rule looks like good value because water costs nothing, eight is a neat number, and saying “drink more water” seems harmless in any situation
entries.sources: Valtin H (2002). "Drink at least eight glasses of water a day." Really? Is there scientific evidence for "8 x 8"? Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol. <https://doi.org/10.1152/ajpregu.00365.2002>
entries.notes: What this rejects is the number of glasses you “must” drink each day, not the idea that drinking more water is harmful. People working in high temperatures or exercising vigorously are exceptions and should drink proactively. People who have had kidney stones should drink more; see Section 16, Entry 8 (if you have had kidney stones, drink enough water). The following two common-sense reminders are not stated in the paper listed in the sources field: ordinarily, drink when you are thirsty and check the color of your urine; older people who do not feel thirsty as readily should drink proactively

entries.title: Do not pay for fortune-telling, tarot readings, or horoscopes to make decisions
entries.cost: It costs nothing. The hard part is giving up a shortcut for making decisions; from then on, you have to think for yourself.
entries.summary: In a classic classroom experiment, the “personal personality analysis” students received was actually identical for everyone, yet they generally thought it was very accurate. That is why fortune-telling seems accurate. Astrologers picked the right answer about as often as a random guess would. The cost can be more than a few dozen yuan: in Xi County, Henan, a fortune-telling fraud ring collected “incense money” and sold “offering packages” costing up to 3,888 yuan; its ringleader was sentenced to eleven years in prison.
entries.benefit: In a classic classroom experiment, the “personal analysis” students received after taking a personality test was actually the same for everyone, yet they generally thought it was very accurate. The author's conclusion was that “acceptance by the person or the analyst cannot prove that an interpretation is correct.” Of 39 students who rated the analysis for accuracy from 0 to 5, 34 gave it a 4 or 5. Calculated from the distribution in the table, the mean was about 4.26. This explains why fortune-telling always seems accurate; the phenomenon is called the Barnum effect. Astrology has also undergone a double-blind test, with the results published in Nature. Astrologers had to choose which of three personality-test results matched an astrological chart. They chose correctly in 40 out of 116 cases. Random guessing would have yielded 38.5 correct choices, while the astrologers had predicted in advance that they would get 58.5 right. An official case: the procuratorate in Xi County, Henan Province, reported an online fortune-telling fraud ring that first drew people in with free palm readings, then charged “incense money” and sold “offering packages” costing up to 3,888 yuan. There were more than 50 victims; more than 2 million yuan in illicit proceeds was recovered; and the ringleader was sentenced to eleven years in prison and fined 100,000 yuan
entries.sources: Forer BR (1949). The fallacy of personal validation: A classroom demonstration of gullibility. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 44(1):118-123 (Table 1 score distribution: one person gave 2 points, four gave 3, 18 gave 4, and 16 gave 5; N=39). <https://doi.org/10.1037/h0059240>; Carlson S (1985). A double-blind test of astrology. Nature 318:419-425 (Table 2: 116 first choices, 40 correct, random expectation 38.5, astrologers' prediction 58.5; “The data are consistent with chance, inconsistent with astrological hypothesis”). <https://doi.org/10.1038/318419a0>, full text on the second author's homepage <https://muller.lbl.gov/papers/Astrology-Carlson.pdf>; Supreme People's Procuratorate of China (2026). Xi County, Henan: Three years of sustained investigation dismantles a group of online fortune-telling fraud rings. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/zdgz/202607/t20260728_732935.shtml>
entries.notes: Each of these two papers reports just one study. Forer's original paper does not directly state the mean score; 4.26 is calculated from the distribution in its Table 1. This entry says only that “its predictions are inaccurate”; it does not judge any belief. Spending a few dozen yuan on it as entertainment is outside the scope here. Using it to decide whether to quit a job, get married, or invest is where it can cost you money.

entries.title: Do not buy blue-light-blocking glasses to “protect your eyesight,” and do not believe that “a few months in front of a screen will ruin your eyes”—but treat swollen, painful, red eyes as an emergency
entries.cost: It costs nothing, and you can save the extra few hundred to a few thousand yuan charged for the lenses.
entries.summary: Blue-light-blocking lenses show no apparent benefit; skipping them can save you an added charge of a few hundred to a few thousand yuan. Compared with ordinary lenses, they make no difference to eye fatigue or how clearly people can see, and no evidence was found that they protect the retina. Sore, dry eyes from looking at a screen can recover; screen viewing will not permanently damage your eyes. What really can damage eyes is welding arc light, lasers, and an acute glaucoma attack.
entries.benefit: The 2023 Cochrane systematic review included 17 randomized controlled trials, each with 5 to 156 participants and follow-up ranging from less than one day to five weeks. Because there were too little data, the people recruited differed substantially across trials, and follow-up periods were inconsistent, the authors did not pool the results into a single overall estimate. All the results below compare blue-light-filtering lenses with lenses that do not filter blue light. With less than one week of follow-up, self-reported eye strain "may not differ"; the certainty of the evidence is low. In one trial of 120 people, the groups differed by 9.76 units. The plausible range for this difference was a 95% CI of −33.95 to 53.47. Because the range spans both negative and positive values, no difference can be discerned. Critical flicker fusion frequency is an objective measure of eye fatigue; there "may be little or no difference" between groups, with low certainty. Best corrected visual acuity—the best vision achievable with glasses—"probably is not affected." The groups differed by 0.00 logMAR (95% CI −0.02 to 0.02). This result came from just one study with 156 people, and the certainty was moderate. Whether the lenses affect daytime alertness is unclear (2 trials, 42 people; very low certainty). The review also found no evidence supporting protection of the macula at the back of the eye. An American Academy of Ophthalmology public information page says the claim that "looking at screens for long periods permanently damages your eyes" is "not true"; prolonged viewing can simply make your eyes uncomfortable. China's national Classification and Catalogue of Occupational Diseases (2024 edition) lists photokeratitis caused by welding arc light and eye injuries caused by lasers as occupational diseases.
entries.sources: Singh S, Downie LE, Anderson AJ, Keller PR, White SJ, Ang M, Wolffsohn JS (2023). Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses for visual performance, sleep, and macular health in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 8, CD013244. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013244.pub2>; American Academy of Ophthalmology (2024). Computers, Digital Devices, and Eye Strain ("You may have heard that looking at a computer, smartphone, or other digital screen for long periods of time will permanently damage your eyes. Thankfully, this is not true."). <https://www.aao.org/eye-health/tips-prevention/computer-usage>; National Health Commission of China and three other departments (2024). Notice on Issuing the Classification and Catalogue of Occupational Diseases (National Health Occupational Health Document [2024] No. 39; item 2, photokeratitis, under "III. Occupational Eye Diseases"; item 6, laser-induced eye injuries [cornea, lens, retina], under "VI. Occupational Diseases Caused by Physical Factors"). <https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2025/issue_11886/202502/content_7007111.html>
entries.notes: Screen use causes eye strain and dry eyes, which can feel sore or dry and make vision blurry after prolonged viewing. Taking a break and blinking more can relieve these symptoms. They can improve; they do not mean you have "ruined your eyes by looking." That statement comes from an American Academy of Ophthalmology public information page, not the Cochrane review in the sources, so it is rated only C. Sources of intense light such as welding arcs, ultraviolet light, and lasers really can cause irreversible eye injury in a short time. Eye injury from welding arc light is called "photokeratitis" and is a legally recognized occupational disease in China. Protection requires safety goggles and a face shield, not blue-light-filtering lenses; see Section 19, Item 10 (protection from dust, noise, and chemical toxins). If you stay up all night looking at a screen, there is one exception to watch for beyond the screen itself. Painful, swollen, red eyes; rainbow-colored halos around lights; and headache, nausea, and vomiting are signs of an acute angle-closure glaucoma attack. It can damage the optic nerve within days. Go to an ophthalmology emergency department that same day; see Section 13, Item 6 (eye emergencies). Pupils dilating in the dark and the lens being pushed forward by keeping your head down for a long time are both triggers. People at higher risk are those over 50, those with farsightedness, and those with a shallow anterior chamber. Dry eyes caused by screen use can also become a chronic condition requiring medical care if they persist; they do not always go away after a night's sleep. If your eyes remain uncomfortable or your vision really is declining, see an ophthalmologist to find the cause. Do not assume that changing lenses is enough. For preventing myopia in children and adolescents, see Section 30, Items 4, 12, and 9 (two hours outdoors each day, cycloplegic refraction, and avoiding products that claim to "cure myopia").

entries.title: Do not treat blood donation as a health measure: no randomized trials support claims that it "detoxifies," lowers blood lipids, or prevents heart attacks, while donating too often really can cause iron deficiency
entries.cost: It costs nothing. One donation, including filling out forms, having blood drawn, and staying for observation and rest, takes about an hour. For several weeks afterward, your body continues replacing the iron it lost.
entries.summary: Claims that blood donation detoxifies the body, lowers blood lipids, or prevents heart attacks are unreliable. People who can keep donating are healthier to begin with. After accounting for that, the reduction in mortality associated with one additional donation per year shrank from nearly one-fifth to 7.5%. In a trial that actually assigned people to different groups for comparison, there was no discernible difference in the number of deaths. Conversely, donating too often really can leave you weak and sensitive to cold because of iron deficiency.
entries.benefit: The Finnish Kuopio study followed 2,862 men aged 42 to 60 for an average of nearly nine years. Of the 153 who had donated blood in the 24 months before the start of data collection, 1 (0.7%) had an acute heart attack. Among the 2,529 who had not donated, 316 (12.5%) did (P<0.0001 for the difference between the two proportions). After accounting for age and other coronary heart disease risk factors, the risk of heart attack was about 88% lower among those who had donated. The relative risk was 0.12 (95% CI 0.02–0.86, P=0.035). But this was only an observational follow-up study, with no randomized comparison groups. The Nordic SCANDAT database included 1,182,495 blood donors, followed for a total of 9,526,627 person-years, during which 15,401 died. When only characteristics such as age and sex were accounted for, one additional donation per year was associated with 18.6% lower mortality (95% CI 16.8%–20.4%). After also accounting for the fact that people must remain healthy to keep being allowed to donate, the reduction fell to 7.5% (5.7%–9.4%). The authors concluded that this "cannot be interpreted as conclusive evidence of a health benefit." The FeAST randomized controlled trial recruited 1,277 patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease and randomly divided them into two groups: one underwent regular blood removal every six months to reduce iron stores, while the other was the control group. The primary outcome was death from any cause: 125/636 (20%) versus 148/641 (23%). The HR was 0.85 (HR means hazard ratio; 1 means the two groups are alike), with a 95% CI of 0.67–1.08 and P=0.17. Combining deaths with nonfatal heart attacks and strokes gave 180 (28%) versus 205 (32%), HR 0.88 (0.72–1.07, P=0.20). Neither outcome showed a discernible difference. The INTERVAL randomized trial recruited 45,263 whole-blood donors. They were assigned to three donation intervals: 12, 10, or 8 weeks for men and 16, 14, or 12 weeks for women. Shorter intervals yielded substantially more blood over two years (the men's 8-week group donated 1.69 more units than the 12-week group, 95% CI 1.59–1.80). No differences were discernible between groups in quality of life, physical activity, or cognitive function. But donation-related discomfort was more common, including fatigue, shortness of breath, vertigo, dizziness, and restless legs (legs feeling so uncomfortable at night that it is hard to lie still). Mean hemoglobin and ferritin levels were also lower, and donations were deferred more often because hemoglobin was too low (P<0.0001 for each measure). Iron deficiency affects the body's heat production: 10 women with iron-deficiency anemia, 8 people whose iron stores were depleted but who were not yet anemic, and 12 control women spent 100 minutes immersed in 28 ℃ water. Rectal temperature was 36.0±0.2 ℃ in the anemic group versus 36.2±0.1 ℃ in the control group (P=0.001). Oxygen consumption was 5.28±0.26 versus 5.99±0.29 mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (P=0.04). Levels of the thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodothyronine were also lower (P<0.002). The claim looks plausible because blood donors are healthy people who have been screened repeatedly, while randomized trials have not confirmed the hypothesis that removing iron protects the heart.
