Notice on Further Improving Incentives and Rewards for Voluntary Blood Donors. <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202401/content_6924875.htm>
entries.notes: What should be rejected is "donating blood for your own health," not blood donation itself. The blood is for someone else, so under this book's beneficiary categories it falls in category ④ (strangers). What can benefit you personally is what the system provides. Article 14 of China's Blood Donation Law says that when voluntary unpaid donors themselves receive blood in a hospital, they are exempt from fees for its collection, storage, separation, and testing. Their spouses and direct relatives may be exempt from or pay reduced fees under provincial government rules. A January 2024 notice from China's National Health Commission says that 28 provinces had already made it possible for voluntary unpaid donors and their relatives to have the cost of blood used in hospitals within their province waived directly at discharge. People who receive the Voluntary Blood Donation Contribution Award may also, under local "three exemptions" policies, ride public transport free, enter government-funded and government-run parks free, and pay no standard outpatient consultation fee at public hospitals. If you donate, follow the legally required intervals. Article 9 of China's Blood Donation Law says that a donation is generally 200 milliliters and must not exceed 400 milliliters. There must be at least six months between donations. The recommended age range is 18 to 55 years. Do not shorten the interval to the legal minimum just to earn an honor or meet a group target. Women, people with lower body weight, and people with heavy menstrual bleeding already have tighter iron reserves. People who donate repeatedly can pay for a ferritin test. If you remain fatigued or sensitive to cold after donating, or your legs feel so uncomfortable when you lie down at night that you cannot resist moving them (called restless legs), do not guess that your "vital energy has been depleted." Get a complete blood count and a ferritin test. If you are found to be iron deficient, take iron as your doctor advises and lengthen the interval between donations. The human evidence in the section about feeling cold includes only 10 people; it helps explain why this might happen, not how many people experience it.

entries.title: Do not rely on general health checkup packages to prevent disease; get the few evidence-supported screenings appropriate for your age and sex
entries.cost: It costs nothing and saves the several hundred to several thousand yuan a year that a checkup package would cost. In exchange, you need to remember which tests to get and how often to get each one.
entries.summary: People who regularly get general health checks have the same mortality rate as those who do not, and the same rates of death from cardiovascular disease and cancer. The few evidence-supported screenings appropriate for your age and sex are enough. People aged 35 and over can have their blood pressure measured free once a year, and people aged 65 and over are entitled to a free health check once a year in China.
entries.benefit: The 2019 update of a Cochrane systematic review included 17 randomized controlled trials. For overall mortality, it pooled 11 of those trials, with 233,298 participants and 21,535 deaths. The general health check group and the control group had the same result: RR 1.00. RR means risk ratio; 1 means the two groups are alike. The 95% CI of 0.97–1.03 is the plausible range. For deaths from cardiovascular disease, 9 trials with 170,227 people and 6,237 deaths were pooled: RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.94–1.16). For deaths from cancer, 8 trials with 139,290 people and 3,663 deaths were pooled: RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.92–1.12). Neither of these outcomes showed a discernible difference. The authors concluded that "general health checks are unlikely to be beneficial." China's National Basic Public Health Services program provides one free blood pressure measurement each year to permanent residents aged 35 and over. It also provides one free annual health examination to people aged 65 and over. This free examination includes a physical examination, complete blood count, routine urine test, fasting blood glucose test, and electrocardiogram. Liver function testing covers aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and total bilirubin. Kidney function testing covers serum creatinine and blood urea. Blood lipid testing covers total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Finally, it includes an abdominal ultrasound of the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen (nationwide in China).
entries.sources: Krogsbøll LT, Jørgensen KJ, Gøtzsche PC (2019). General health checks in adults for reducing morbidity and mortality from disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 1, CD009009. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009009.pub3>; National Health and Family Planning Commission of China (2017). National Basic Public Health Service Standards (Third Edition) (health management services for older adults; health management services for patients with hypertension). <https://www.nhc.gov.cn/ewebeditor/uploadfile/2017/04/20170417104506514.pdf>
entries.notes: What needs to be rejected is "treating annual checkup packages as a disease prevention measure," not that all screening tests should be skipped. Additionally, an annual free blood pressure measurement for those aged 35 and older, and an annual free physical exam for those aged 65 and older, are already provided by the National Basic Public Health Services program, with no need to pay out of pocket. Screenings that have valid justifications should still be performed as recommended. For blood pressure, blood glucose, and hepatitis B, see Section 1, Items 7, 8, and 14. For breast, cervical, and colorectal screenings, see Section 1, Items 17, 18, and 19. For Helicobacter pylori and low-dose CT, see Section 1, Items 23 and 24. For bone density scans in women aged 65 and older, see Section 1, Item 39 (Bone Density Scans). If high-risk sexual behavior has occurred, get tested; see Section 1, Item 31. At what age to begin screening and at what intervals to screen are all detailed there. Attend checkups organized by your employer or paid for by others as scheduled; what should be discouraged is paying out of pocket for commercial packages or adding self-selected screening items. People who already have chronic diseases, symptomatic individuals, or tests ordered by doctors based on clinical conditions do not fall under this scope—that is diagnostic care, not screening. The most common unevidenced items in checkup packages are tumor markers and whole-body imaging; see Item 7 of this section (Whole-Body PET-CT and Tumor Marker Packages). If high uric acid is detected on a checkup without any prior pain, or if gallstones are found without prior pain, what should be done? See Item 19 (Asymptomatic High Uric Acid) and Item 20 (Asymptomatic Gallstones) of this section. Furthermore, the majority of trials included by Cochrane were conducted in high-income countries where access to medical care is already convenient; regions with strained healthcare resources should not directly extrapolate this conclusion without modification.

entries.title: Do not start taking uric acid-lowering medications simply because high uric acid is detected on a checkup if you have never experienced pain
entries.cost: Costs nothing, saves long-term medication costs and the expense of regular follow-up testing, and avoids unnecessary medication risks.
entries.summary: For individuals with elevated uric acid who have never had a gout flare and have not developed tophi, the American College of Rheumatology recommends not initiating uric acid-lowering medications for the time being. It takes 24 people taking medication consistently for 3 full years to prevent just one gout flare. Relying on it to protect the kidneys has also proven futile; among kidney disease patients taking the medication, renal function declined just as quickly as in those taking a placebo. Treat it only after a genuine flare has actually occurred.
entries.benefit: The 2020 gout guideline from the American College of Rheumatology addresses asymptomatic hyperuricemia. It refers to serum urate >6.8 mg/dL without any prior gout flares or subcutaneous tophi. The guideline conditionally recommends against initiating any urate-lowering therapy in these individuals. Medications include allopurinol, febuxostat, and probenecid. The certainty of evidence is rated as "high." A footnote below the table specifies that "based on attributable risk, 24 patients would need to be treated for 3 years to prevent a single gout flare." The CKD-FIX randomized controlled trial enrolled 363 individuals. They had stage 3 or 4 chronic kidney disease, no history of gout, but a risk of progression. One group received 100–300 mg of allopurinol daily, while the other received a placebo. The trial lasted 104 weeks. eGFR is an indicator reflecting kidney function, measured in mL/min/1.73 m². One group had an annual change of -3.33 (95% CI -4.11 to -2.55). The other group had an annual change of -3.23 (-3.98 to -2.47). The difference between the two groups was -0.10 (-1.18 to 0.97), P=0.85; kidney function declined at the same rate. Serious adverse events were 46% versus 44%. The PERL randomized controlled trial enrolled 530 individuals with type 1 diabetes and early-to-moderate diabetic kidney disease, who took allopurinol for 3 years, followed by a 2-month washout period to clear the drug effect. Allopurinol did lower serum urate from 6.1 to 3.9 mg/dL. However, after drug withdrawal, the difference in the kidney function metric GFR between the two groups was only 0.001 mL/min/1.73 m². The confidence interval for this difference was 95% CI -1.9 to 1.9, P=0.99. Urinary albumin excretion was actually 40% higher (0 to 80) in the group receiving allopurinol. It seems cost-effective only because the intuition that "if an indicator is out of range, one should take medicine to suppress it" is overly appealing
entries.sources: FitzGerald JD, Dalbeth N, Mikuls T, et al. (2020). 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout. Arthritis Care & Research, 72(6), 744-760 (Table 1 and its footnotes). <https://doi.org/10.1002/acr.24180>; Badve SV, Pascoe EM, Tiku A, et al. (2020). Effects of Allopurinol on the Progression of Chronic Kidney Disease. New England Journal of Medicine, 382(26), 2504-2513. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1915833>; Doria A, Galecki AT, Spino C, et al. (2020). Serum Urate Lowering with Allopurinol and Kidney Function in Type 1 Diabetes. New England Journal of Medicine, 382(26), 2493-2503. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1916624>
entries.notes: What needs to be rejected is "starting lifelong urate-lowering medication when no flare has ever occurred," not that high uric acid is completely inconsequential. The same guideline also lists exceptions. Initiation of therapy can be considered in the following situations. First, having stage 3 or higher chronic kidney disease concurrent with a first flare. Second, serum urate >9 mg/dL (approximately 535 µmol/L). Third, a history of urolithiasis (urinary tract stones). For individuals who have developed tophi, show radiographic evidence of joint damage attributable to gout, or experience 2 or more flares per year, the guideline strongly recommends medication; for those who have experienced more than one flare but fewer than 2 per year, it is conditionally recommended. For details, see Section 16, Item 9 (Take Long-Term Urate-Lowering Medication Once Gout Is Confirmed). Approximately 7.4% of Han Chinese carry a genotype called HLA-B*5801, compared to only 0.7% of White individuals. People carrying this allele who take allopurinol are far more prone to life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse reactions; the risk of hypersensitivity syndrome in Asians is three times that of White individuals. Since this is a medication that can be deferred in the first place, there is no need to take on this additional risk. Before genuinely starting the drug, get tested for this genotype first; see Section 16, Item 9 (Take Long-Term Urate-Lowering Medication Once Gout Is Confirmed). Those two kidney trials were conducted in patients with chronic kidney disease and type 1 diabetes; they cannot be directly generalized to mean that "high uric acid is completely harmless to the kidneys." What they reject is solely the specific practice of "taking medication to lower uric acid in order to protect the kidneys"

entries.title: Do not undergo prophylactic gallbladder removal simply because gallstones are detected on a checkup if you have never had pain
entries.cost: Costs nothing, and saves an operation under general anesthesia as well as a hospitalization. In exchange, your obligation is to remember which warning signs require going to the hospital immediately once they appear.
entries.summary: Among people with stones in the gallbladder who have never experienced pain, roughly 80% remain completely symptom-free over nearly nine years. If left alone, the annual rate of acute conditions such as cholecystitis and pancreatitis is about 1 to 3 per 1,000. Gallbladder removal is not risk-free either, with bile duct injury occurring in approximately 1.5% of individuals. Therefore, both European and UK guidelines recommend against surgery for asymptomatic cases for the time being.
entries.benefit: The Italian MICOL population screening study performed ultrasounds on 11,229 individuals aged 29 to 69. It detected gallstones in 856 people, of whom 580 were asymptomatic, followed for an average of 8.7 years. Among these 580 individuals, 453 (78.1%) remained asymptomatic throughout, 61 (10.5%) developed mild symptoms, and 66 (11.4%) developed severe symptoms. A total of 189 cholecystectomies were performed during the follow-up period, 41.3% of which were performed on individuals who had no symptoms. The authors concluded that "expectant management remains a valid approach for most patients," where expectant management means watchful waiting without surgery. A US HMO (a type of managed care organization) conducted follow-up tracking on 691 individuals diagnosed with gallstones, with an average follow-up of 78±61.6 months. Among them, 135 asymptomatic individuals were followed for 58±50.2 months (median 46.3 months); only 10% developed biliary symptoms, and 7% underwent surgery. Out of 50 total deaths in the entire cohort, only 2 were biliary-related, and both occurred in the symptomatic group. The authors concluded that "patients with silent gallstones do not require prophylactic cholecystectomy," where silent gallstones refer to stones that cause no distress and never flare up. Item 1.2.1 of UK NICE guideline CG188 states: "Reassure people with asymptomatic gallbladder stones found incidentally who have normal gallbladders and normal bile ducts that they do not need treatment unless they develop symptoms." The European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) 2016 gallstone guideline presents the risks on both sides together. Among asymptomatic individuals, approximately 0.7% to 2.5% develop symptoms each year. The annual incidence of acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, obstructive jaundice (bile duct blockage causing yellowing of the skin/eyes), or cholangitis is 0.1% to 0.3%. Only after the first episode of biliary colic do complications rise to 1% to 3% per year, meaning most people experience pain once before a major event occurs. On the surgical side, in the Swedish national registry of 51,041 cholecystectomies, 1.5% suffered bile duct injuries. About one-fifth of these (0.3%) involved partial or complete transection of the bile duct. One-year mortality among those with bile duct injury was 3.9%, compared to 1.1% in those without. The guideline also notes that 10% to 40% of patients continue to experience discomfort after surgery, or symptoms return after temporary relief. The guideline concludes that surgery in asymptomatic individuals, whether open or laparoscopic, does not prolong life, because the risks of operative mortality and complications outweigh the risks of expectant management. Dealing with it once symptoms appear also results in lower overall costs. A 1983 decision analysis provided specific figures: a 30-year-old male undergoing prophylactic cholecystectomy lost an average of 4 days of life compared to watchful waiting, and a 50-year-old lost 18 days. To date, no randomized controlled trial has compared cholecystectomy against no surgery. Prophylactic removal seems cost-effective only because of the intuitive belief that "it will hurt sooner or later, so it's better to remove it once and for all while young"

entries.notes: Controversy. The 2021 domestic expert consensus on biliary surgery in China included a subset of asymptomatic gallstones among surgical indications. An interpretive article in the same journal specified that one of the core controversies lies precisely here. The full consensus text requires a subscription, and this book was unable to verify the exact clinical scenarios it specified. Another opposing viewpoint concerns small stones: stones smaller than 5 mm are more strongly associated with pancreatitis. A Dutch modeling study suggested that prophylactic cholecystectomy in such individuals might either increase or decrease life expectancy, depending on how common and how fatal pancreatitis is. European guidelines also list exceptions: gallbladder wall calcification (porcelain gallbladder) and concurrent gallbladder polyps larger than 1 cm—both of these should be resected. When undergoing other major abdominal surgeries, incidental cholecystectomy may be considered. What this entry addresses is strictly one situation: stones located within the gallbladder that have never caused pain. **Stones in the common bile duct are a completely different matter**. Item 1.3.1 of the same guideline clearly states that for common bile duct stones, regardless of whether symptoms are present, bile duct clearance and cholecystectomy must be performed. If any of the following signs occur, go to the hospital on the same day—do not attempt to tough it out relying on this conclusion: persistent severe colic in the right upper quadrant or upper abdomen, fever with chills, yellowing of the whites of the eyes or skin, or darkening of urine color. When a doctor recommends surgery after reviewing imaging, ask clearly which specific rationale it is based on—for example, involvement of the bile ducts, concurrent polyps, or abnormalities in the gallbladder wall. Do not use this conclusion to argue with them. What it discourages is merely "undergoing surgery purely because stones were detected, in the absence of any indication." Both of the aforementioned studies were prospective cohort studies without randomized control groups. However, since the question they aim to answer is "what happens if left untreated" rather than "which treatment is superior," they are appropriate here. Furthermore, the duration of follow-up in these two studies was 4 to 9 years; with longer follow-up, the proportion developing symptoms would increase.

entries.title: Do not quit calcium to prevent kidney stones
entries.cost: Costs nothing. It also saves trouble: you do not have to watch out every day for which foods contain calcium.
entries.summary: People who have had calcium oxalate stones are often advised to eat less calcium, but the trial results point in the opposite direction. Among men with recurrent stones, those who consumed a normal amount of calcium while eating less animal protein and salt had half as many recurrences over five years as those on a low-calcium diet. UK guidelines also explicitly say not to restrict calcium.
entries.benefit: A five-year randomized controlled trial enrolled 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and elevated urinary calcium (called idiopathic hypercalciuria). They were randomly assigned to two groups. One group consumed a normal amount of calcium, 30 mmol a day. This group also ate less animal protein (52 g a day) and less salt (50 mmol of sodium chloride a day). The other group followed a traditional low-calcium diet, consuming 10 mmol a day. Over five years, 12/60 versus 23/60 had a recurrence. The unadjusted relative risk was 0.49 (95% CI 0.24–0.98, the confidence interval), P=0.04: the recurrence risk in the normal-calcium group was only half as high. During follow-up, urinary calcium fell by about 170 mg a day in both groups. But urinary oxalate excretion differed. It rose by an average of 5.4 mg a day in the low-calcium group and fell by an average of 7.2 mg a day in the normal-calcium group. Section 1.8.1 of the UK NICE guideline NG118 explicitly says not to restrict daily calcium intake. Adults should maintain an intake of 700 to 1,200 mg a day. Children and adolescents should consume 350 to 1,000 mg a day, depending on age. Cutting out calcium seems sensible because of the intuition that “stones are made of calcium, so eat less calcium”
entries.sources: Borghi L, Schianchi T, Meschi T, et al. (2002). Comparison of two diets for the prevention of recurrent stones in idiopathic hypercalciuria. New England Journal of Medicine, 346(2), 77-84. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa010369>; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2019). Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management. NICE guideline NG118, section 1.8.1. <https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng118/chapter/Recommendations>
entries.notes: Caveats: This trial included only men, all of whom had recurrent calcium oxalate stones and elevated urinary calcium, so its findings cannot be applied directly to every type of stone. The intervention group also changed three things at once: normal calcium intake, less animal protein, and less salt. Therefore, all the benefits cannot be attributed to “not cutting out calcium” alone. Less salt and animal protein may also have played a role. The point to reject is “deliberately cutting out foods that contain calcium,” not to say “you should take more calcium.” This concerns calcium in everyday meals; calcium supplements are a separate matter. If you have had stones, ask your treating doctor whether you should take supplements. For drinking more water, see Section 16, Item 8 (after kidney stones, drink enough water to reach 2.5–3 liters a day).

entries.title: Do not buy crystals, bead bracelets, pixiu figurines, or similar objects to “change your luck,” “attract wealth,” or “nourish your body”
entries.cost: Costs nothing. All you need to do is leave “changing your luck” and “nourishing your body” out of your reasons for buying them. The hard part is not following along when everyone else is wearing them and saying they work.
entries.summary: There is no verifiable evidence that wearing them can change your luck, attract wealth, or nourish your body. They seem accurate for the same reason fortune-telling does: the claims are vague enough that you fit them to yourself. When sellers claim an item can treat illness, that is false advertising; a livestream was investigated and penalized for doing so in 2026. Buying one as a decoration is fine.
entries.benefit: A classic classroom experiment showed that everyone received the same vague “personal analysis,” yet people generally thought it was very accurate. This phenomenon is called the Barnum effect. It helps explain where the experience of “things really did go more smoothly after I put it on” comes from. The author’s conclusion was that “acceptance by the person concerned does not prove that an interpretation is correct.” An official case: On June 4, 2026, China’s State Administration for Market Regulation published a set of typical cases from its “crack down on fakes and clear the source” campaign in the traditional crafts market. A jewelry store in Sihui, Guangdong, fabricated claims about the materials of its products during livestreams. It also falsely claimed the products could “prevent and treat rheumatism, improve immunity, improve sleep quality, and clear blood vessels,” among other effects. The store used scripted performances to mislead and deceive consumers. This violated Article 9, Paragraph 1 of China’s Anti-Unfair Competition Law (applicable nationwide).
entries.sources: Forer BR (1949). The fallacy of personal validation: A classroom demonstration of gullibility. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology. <https://doi.org/10.1037/h0059240>; State Administration for Market Regulation of China (2026). The State Administration for Market Regulation publishes a set of typical cases from its “crack down on fakes and clear the source” campaign in the traditional crafts market. <https://www.samr.gov.cn/xw/zj/art/2026/art_1529399cfe874b8780c4496eb0158020.html>
entries.notes: There is only one conclusion: the claimed effects cannot be verified, and no predictive ability can be measured. This does not pass judgment on any belief or custom, or on using such objects as gifts, keepsakes, or family heirlooms. Keep two things separate. There are explicit legal provisions governing the effects sellers claim, and you can file a complaint about those claims. Claims such as “changing your luck,” however, have neither research behind them nor a way to prove them false, so you have to keep them within your own budget. Before buying, treat the item as ordinary jewelry and ask yourself, “If it changes nothing, would I still buy it at this price?” For how to check materials and certificates, and why treating it as an investment is poor value, see Section 5, Items 33 and 34 (count bead bracelets and luxury watches as money spent; look for CMA reports on jewelry and gemstones). For spending money on fortune-telling, see Item 15 of this section (fortune-telling, tarot, and astrology).

entries.title: Do not expect buying things to improve your mood or sense of status
entries.cost: Costs nothing. The hard part is resisting the urge to place an order when you feel bad.
entries.summary: People who place greater importance on money and possessions report feeling less happy, but the association is weak and does not show which causes which. Other research has found that spending money on an experience makes people happier than buying things. So, if you are spending the same amount, putting it toward an experience such as an outing is more likely to make you happy than filling a shopping cart.
entries.benefit: A meta-analysis (which combines the results of many studies) included 259 independent samples and 753 effect sizes. The result: people who valued material things more highly reported lower well-being. On the most commonly used multidimensional scale, the correlation coefficient was r = -0.19 (adjusted ρ = -0.24). On scales measuring only the importance placed on money, the association was weaker, r = -0.08 to -0.11. Its strength varied by the outcome examined. It was strongest for risky health and consumption behaviors and negative self-appraisals, r = -0.28 to -0.44. It was weakest for life satisfaction and negative emotions, r = -0.13 to -0.15. The authors also conducted a mediation analysis (examining what might account for the association), which suggested that the negative association might arise because psychological needs were not being met. Another study: In two surveys of different populations, respondents in both said that money spent on a life experience made them happier than money spent on things. In a subsequent laboratory experiment, recalling the good feelings after spending money on an experience also produced more happiness than recalling a purchase (these results cannot be taken as nationally representative for China; both studies used samples from other countries).
entries.sources: Dittmar H, Bond R, Hurst M, Kasser T (2014). The relationship between materialism and personal well-being: A meta-analysis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 107(5), 879-924. <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037409>；Van Boven L, Gilovich T (2003). To do or to have? That is the question. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 85(6), 1193-1202. <https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.85.6.1193>
entries.notes: Caveats: Most of the included studies asked a group of people about both things at the same point in time and examined whether they varied together, so they cannot establish which came first. The authors themselves say in their conclusion that more experiments and long-term follow-up studies are needed to establish the direction. So this cannot be read as “buying things makes people unhappy”; it can only be read as “buying things is unlikely to make you happy.” The association is also weak: r = -0.19 explains only a few percent of the variation, and people differ greatly. Both studies used samples from other countries; there are no comparable data from Chinese populations to cite. This does not argue against spending money on things you like. It argues against using shopping to regulate your mood, because that makes placing an order your first response the next time you feel bad. For specific ways to save money, see Section 5. For approaches with actual evidence when you feel bad, see the second half of Section 22 and Section 29. For the extra budget spent to be “one rung above other people,” see Item 24 of this section (moving up one rung).

entries.title: Do not spend more on a different home, car, or social circle just to “move up one rung among the people around you”
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Before increasing your budget, just ask one more question: am I paying more for the thing itself, or for my position among these people? The hard part is not following along when everyone around you has traded up.
entries.summary: Among people with the same income, those whose neighbors earn more report lower happiness. This mainly occurs with neighbors who have the same education level as they do, and it is more pronounced for people who interact with their neighbors often. So the extra money spent to move somewhere everyone is better off than you buys a move down one rung for yourself. But when everyone’s income rises together, people still feel better off.
entries.benefit: The US National Survey of Families and Households (NSFH) interviewed the same people in two waves. The author matched these data to local average income. Local average income (at the PUMA level) was estimated from the 5% sample of the 1990 census. After accounting for respondents’ own income and a range of personal characteristics, the result was that the higher their neighbors’ income, the lower the happiness they reported. The effect was large, remained robust under a different method of calculation, and was highly statistically significant. In the author’s words, the decline in happiness associated with an “increase in neighbors’ income” was of the same order of magnitude as that associated with an equal “decrease in one’s own income.” When the analysis instead compared each person with themselves over time (adding individual fixed effects), the coefficient kept the same direction and was similar in size, although its significance fell to the 10% level. Restricting the comparison to within the same state and survey wave (adding state and survey-wave fixed effects) left the result largely unchanged. This suggests the finding was not caused by people who like moving to poorer places being happier to begin with, or by unmeasured factors at the state level. The effect was stronger among people who often interacted with their neighbors and was not significant among those who interacted only with friends outside their community. There was no difference between renters and homeowners, which does not support the explanation that “housing costs more in expensive places, leaving less money to spend.” Happiness declined only as the incomes of neighbors with the same education level rose; it barely responded to the incomes of neighbors with different education levels. The association was mainly transmitted through “satisfaction with one’s material situation,” rather than satisfaction with other areas such as family life. Finally, if respondents’ and their neighbors’ incomes rose by the same proportion, happiness still increased.
entries.sources: Luttmer EFP (2005). Neighbors as Negatives: Relative Earnings and Well-Being. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 120(3), 963–1002. <https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/120.3.963>; Luttmer EFP (2004). Neighbors as Negatives: Relative Earnings and Well-Being. NBER Working Paper No. 10667 (the wording and order of magnitude cited in this item were checked word for word against this version). <https://www.nber.org/papers/w10667>
entries.notes: There are several reasons for the B rating: the data come from questionnaires that repeatedly interviewed the same people; there is only one study; and the sample is from another country. The outcome is happiness reported by respondents themselves, not money. The author did use statistical methods to rule out several kinds of confounding, such as comparing the same person over time and making comparisons within the same state and survey wave, but this was ultimately not a randomized trial. There are also no comparable data from Chinese populations to cite. The benefit magnitude is rated “medium,” following the approach used in Item 23 of this section (do not expect buying things to improve your mood). The money saved could indeed reach the level of tens of thousands of yuan. But there are no figures showing how much happiness saving that money would bring, so it is not rated “large” on the basis of a five-figure yuan saving. This does not argue against paying for a larger home, a quieter neighborhood, or a shorter commute: those purchases are for the things themselves. The reason to stop is “my coworkers have all traded up; I cannot be worse off than they are.” For how to prioritize a place to live, see Section 4, Item 18 (put commute time near the top when choosing where to live). For shopping to regulate your mood, see Item 23 of this section (do not expect buying things to improve your mood). For constantly comparing yourself upward online, see Section 3, Item 20 (do not make “how other people are doing” daily required reading).

entries.title: Do not believe that “willpower is like a muscle: use it for a while and it runs out”
entries.cost: Costs nothing. All you need to change is one way of describing it.
entries.summary: The popular claim is that after doing one thing that demands self-control, you are more likely to give in on the next task, so you should conserve your willpower. Twenty-three laboratories and 2,141 people repeated the experiment using the same protocol, and the result was almost zero. Stop explaining your behavior by saying “I used up my willpower today,” and do not spend money on courses that promise to teach you how to save it up.
entries.benefit: A preregistered multilaboratory replication involved 23 laboratories and a total of 2,141 participants. Following the standardized protocol of Sripada and colleagues, they repeated the sequential-task paradigm: first perform a task that uses self-control, then a second task requiring self-control. The pooled result showed a very small ego-depletion effect, and the 95% confidence interval included 0 (d = 0.04, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.15). On that basis, the authors discussed whether the model of “self-control as a limited resource” remained tenable. Another replication with a preregistered protocol, involving 36 laboratories and 3,531 people, found an effect size of d = 0.06, likewise too small to count for much.
entries.sources: Hagger MS, Chatzisarantis NLD, Alberts H, et al. (2016). A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546–573. <https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691616652873>；Vohs et al. (2021). A Multisite Preregistered Paradigmatic Test of the Ego-Depletion Effect. Psychological Science. <https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797621989733>
entries.notes: The model to reject is that “self-control is a resource that can be used up,” not the idea that “people get tired.” Too little sleep or working for too long without a break can reduce performance; that is a separate issue, addressed by the items on sleep and working hours in Section 3. Approaches actually supported by randomized trials involve changing your environment and how you write your plans. See Section 4, Item 10 (move things you do not want to touch farther away) and Section 4, Item 1 (write down “at what time, where, and what to do when something happens”). Fixing what you wear and eat in advance is still worth doing because it costs almost nothing. What it saves is those few minutes and a few moments of indecision, not willpower; do not expect it to improve your judgment in the afternoon. The other items in this section count money; this one counts time and mental effort. No conversion is made between them.

entries.title: Do not expect eating breakfast or 16:8 intermittent fasting to help you control your weight; choose meal times you can stick with long term
entries.cost: Costs nothing. What you save is the daily mental effort of struggling with meal times.
entries.summary: A popular claim is that skipping breakfast makes people overeat at lunch and dinner, so they end up eating more overall. That was not what happened in the trials: people who skipped breakfast ate more than 200 fewer kilocalories a day and weighed slightly less. After a year, weight was no different with 16:8 eating than with simply eating less. People who regularly skipped breakfast had about 17% more cardiovascular disease, but this was only an association; there was no clear difference in death from all causes.
entries.benefit: First, consider the claim that “skipping breakfast makes people eat more later.” A meta-analysis combined 13 randomized trials. People assigned to eat breakfast consumed 259.79 kcal more per day than those assigned to skip it (95% CI 78.87–440.71, the confidence interval). They weighed 0.44 kg more (0.07–0.82). People who skipped breakfast did not make up for it at lunch and dinner. All these trials had short follow-up periods: an average of seven weeks for weight and two weeks for intake. Next, consider practices such as 16:8, in which people eat only within a fixed window of several hours. One study assigned 116 overweight adults to follow such a schedule for 12 weeks. The difference in weight between the group that ate only from noon to 8 p.m. and the group that regularly ate three meals a day was −0.26 kg (−1.30 to 0.78), which was not statistically significant. Another study, conducted in Guangzhou, followed 139 patients with obesity for 12 months. Time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction produced 1.8 kg more weight loss than calorie restriction alone (−4.0 to 0.4), also not statistically significant. Finally, consider whether regularly skipping breakfast is harmful. In pooled data covering 2.38 million people, those who skipped breakfast had about a 17% higher risk of cardiovascular disease (OR 1.17, 1.09–1.26) and about a 49% higher risk of cardiovascular death (OR 1.49, 1.20–1.84). But these were observational studies, which recorded what people did without assigning them to groups. In the original study that followed people for 17 to 23 years, the risk ratio for death from any cause was 1.19, with a confidence interval of 0.99 to 1.42. Because that interval crossed 1, it did not establish a difference.
entries.sources: Sievert K, Hussain SM, Page MJ, et al. (2019). Effect of breakfast on weight and energy intake: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l42>; Lowe DA, Wu N, Rohdin-Bibby L, et al. (2020). Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity. JAMA Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153>; Liu D, Huang Y, Huang C, et al. (2022). Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss. New England Journal of Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114833>; Zhang H, Zhang S, Liu Y, et al. (2025). The association between skipping breakfast and cardiovascular disease: a meta analysis. Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fcvm.2025.1565806>; Rong S, Snetselaar LG, Xu G, et al. (2019). Association of Skipping Breakfast With Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2019.01.065>; Fernandes-Alves D, Teixeira GP, Guimarães KC, Crispim CA (2026). Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials Comparing Time-Restricted Eating With and Without Caloric Restriction for Weight Loss. Nutrition Reviews. <https://doi.org/10.1093/nutrit/nuaf053>; Sun T, Zhang L, Lu Y, et al. (2024). Non-linear relationship between the first meal time of the day and gallstone incidence in American adults. Frontiers in Nutrition. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2024.1521707>; Liu T, Wang Y, Wang X, et al. (2023). Habitually Skipping Breakfast Is Associated with the Risk of Gastrointestinal Cancers: Evidence from the Kailuan Cohort Study. Journal of General Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-023-08094-7>; National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (2022). Symptoms & Causes of Peptic Ulcers (Stomach or Duodenal Ulcers) (“The most common causes of peptic ulcers are Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).”). <https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/peptic-ulcers-stomach-ulcers/symptoms-causes>
entries.notes: Controversial. That 17% figure for cardiovascular disease comes from an observational study that only recorded what people did; it did not assign them to groups. People who skip breakfast are already more likely to smoke, drink alcohol, be sedentary, and have lower incomes, and adjustments cannot fully account for these factors. So it is unclear how much of that 17% was caused by skipping breakfast itself. The figure for all-cause mortality already had a range that crossed 1. The 16:8 approach is also disputed. A review pooling 30 trials with 1,341 participants found that, when both groups ate the same amount, the time-restricted eating group lost an additional 1.46 kg (−2.65 to −0.26). The cost was an additional loss of 0.41 kg of lean body mass. But most of these trials were very short, and the longest, most rigorous one, a twelve-month trial, found no difference. Long periods without food are also relevant to the gallbladder. In a cross-sectional survey of 6,547 people, each hour later that someone ate their first meal of the day was associated with about 5% higher odds of having gallstones detected (OR 1.05, 1.02–1.08); those who delayed their first meal until between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. had about 49% higher odds than those who ate earlier (OR 1.49, 1.24–1.77). The proposed mechanism is that the longer bile remains in the gallbladder, the more likely stones are to form from it. But this survey measured everything at one point in time; people may also have changed their eating habits after developing gallbladder problems. China’s Kailuan cohort was followed for 5.6 years and recorded 369 cases of gastrointestinal cancer. People who skipped breakfast had 2.32 times the risk of colorectal cancer (1.34–4.01) and 5.43 times the risk of gallbladder and extrahepatic bile duct cancer (1.34–21.93). The confidence interval for the latter extends as high as 21.93, indicating that there were too few events; it can only be treated as a clue. Taken together, meal timing has very little effect on weight control, so do not spend your energy on it. As for whether regularly skipping breakfast altogether is good in the long run, all the current evidence is associative and cannot prove causation, but it consistently points toward harm. If you want to play it safe, eat breakfast as usual; just do not expect it to help you lose weight. An information page from the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases states that the most common causes of peptic ulcers are Helicobacter pylori infection and painkillers such as aspirin and ibuprofen. Fasting is absent even from its list of other, less common causes. For what you should get checked, see Section 1, Item 23 (get tested for Helicobacter pylori and, if positive, have it eradicated). For what to do if a routine examination finds gallstones but you have never had pain, see Item 20 of this section (if a routine examination finds gallstones but you have never had pain, do not have your gallbladder removed as a preventive measure). If you want to control your weight, the things with real evidence behind them are what and how much you eat; see Section 2, Item 27 (eat at least five servings of fruit and vegetables every day), Section 2, Item 28 (eat less ultra-processed food), and Section 2, Item 32 (keep your BMI between 20 and 25). This advice does not apply to people with diabetes, people taking blood sugar-lowering medication, or pregnant people: missing a meal may cause low blood sugar, so follow your doctor’s instructions. Extreme fasting and self-induced vomiting are a separate matter; see Section 28, Item 1 (do not use extreme dieting, fasting, or self-induced vomiting to control your weight).

entries.title: Do not believe that “masturbation harms your health” or that “abstaining from sex is the only way to get better”; what matters is whether it interferes with sleep, work, or relationships
entries.cost: Costs nothing. You save the money you would have spent on dubious “kidney-tonifying” remedies and “sexual abstinence” courses, as well as the anxiety of prolonged self-blame.
entries.summary: There is no evidence that masturbation harms your health. Men who ejaculate more often have about 20% less prostate cancer, although some research has found higher risk among people who ejaculated more frequently when they were young. A small number of people feel weak and flu-like after every ejaculation and take days to recover. This is a rare condition for which they can see a urologist or andrologist. Feeling “addicted to pornography” more often reflects a conflict between the behavior and one’s own moral beliefs.
entries.benefit: First, consider physical health. A US study followed 31,925 men through 2010. Each man reported how many times he ejaculated per month, and the researchers then grouped them by frequency. Compared with men who ejaculated 4 to 7 times per month, those who ejaculated at least 21 times per month had a prostate cancer HR of 0.81 (95% CI 0.72–0.92, about 19% lower). This was calculated using their frequency at ages 20 to 29. Using their frequency at ages 40 to 49, the HR was 0.78 (0.69–0.89, about 22% lower). Most of the reduction was in low-risk prostate cancer. A counterpoint comes from a UK case-control study comparing 431 patients diagnosed before age 60 with 409 controls. People who masturbated frequently in their twenties and thirties had higher risk, while those who did so frequently in their fifties had lower risk. Next, consider pornography. A systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that many people who feel “addicted” are responding more to a mismatch between their behavior and their beliefs than simply to how much pornography they view. A small number of people really do feel unwell after every ejaculation, but this is not evidence that ejaculation “harms the body.” It is a rare condition called post-orgasmic illness syndrome (POIS). People with it should see a doctor rather than rely on sexual abstinence. Among 45 patients in the Netherlands, 87% developed symptoms within 30 minutes of ejaculation, 80% felt fatigued and weak, and 78% felt as if they had the flu. At a French hospital, 37 patients took an average of 4.7 days to recover. The cause is unclear. In the Dutch study, 29 of the 33 people who had skin tests (88%) showed an allergic reaction to their own semen. A study of 24 patients in China, however, found no antibodies indicating an allergy to semen, while the patients had elevated anxiety and depression scores. A 2025 review found only 14 treatment studies, 12 of which were case reports. Among 211 sexual medicine experts worldwide, only 18% said that more than 30% of patients could improve (US / UK / Netherlands / France / China).
entries.sources: Rider JR, Wilson KM, Sinnott JA, et al. (2016). Ejaculation Frequency and Risk of Prostate Cancer: Updated Results with an Additional Decade of Follow-up. European Urology, 70(6), 974–982. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eururo.2016.03.027>；Dimitropoulou P, Lophatananon A, Easton D, et al. (2009). Sexual activity and prostate cancer risk in men diagnosed at a younger age. BJU International, 103(2), 178–185. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1464-410x.2008.08030.x>；Grubbs JB, Perry SL, Wilt JA, Reid RC. (2019). Pornography Problems Due to Moral Incongruence: An Integrative Model with a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Archives of Sexual Behavior, 48(2), 397–415. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-018-1248-x>；Waldinger MD, Meinardi MM, Zwinderman AH, Schweitzer DH. (2011). Postorgasmic Illness Syndrome (POIS) in 45 Dutch caucasian males: clinical characteristics and evidence for an immunogenic pathogenesis (Part 1). The Journal of Sexual Medicine, 8(4), 1164–1170. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1743-6109.2010.02166.x>；Chea M, Teng M, Chesnel C, et al. (2023). Postorgasmic illness syndrome: one or several entities? A retrospective cohort study. The Journal of Sexual Medicine, 20(12), 1407–1413. <https://doi.org/10.1093/jsxmed/qdad139>；Xi GP, Yang RX, Zhang J, et al. (2023). Clinical characteristics, allergic response to autologous semen, and desensitization in patients with postorgasmic illness syndrome. Sexual Medicine, 11(6), qfad068. <https://doi.org/10.1093/sexmed/qfad068>；Ponce S, Chapalamadugu M, Levine S, et al. (2025). Treatments for postorgasmic illness syndrome: a systematic review. The Journal of Sexual Medicine, 22(7), 1236–1243. <https://doi.org/10.1093/jsxmed/qdaf112>；Duran MB, Rubin RS, Reisman Y, Serefoglu EC, et al. (2025). Recognition and practice patterns of sexual medicine experts towards postorgasmic illness syndrome. International Journal of Impotence Research, 37(6), 454–457. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41443-023-00753-x>
entries.notes: Controversial. Both prostate cancer studies were observational: they recorded behavior rather than assigning people to comparison groups, and the frequencies were recalled by the participants themselves. The conclusion can therefore go only as far as “no evidence of harm has been found”; it cannot be turned into advice to ejaculate more often. The authors of the UK study also said that, for men in their fifties, illness may have come first and reduced the frequency of masturbation. The abstract of the pornography review gave no effect size, so only the direction of the finding is reported here. The benefit is rated small because the reduction was mainly in low-risk prostate cancer, not deaths. The studies on discomfort after ejaculation each included only a few dozen patients. The literature describes the condition as rare, but no one has measured how many people in the general population have it. If you feel weak and flu-like after nearly every ejaculation and take days to recover, see a urologist or andrologist and mention the name of the condition yourself. Signs that you should see a psychiatrist or a mental health professional are staying up late over this, missing work, damage to your relationship with your partner, and being unable to stop despite wanting to. For staying up late, see Section 3, Item 9 (do not stay up late for games, short videos, or pornography). If you are worried that viewing pornography has caused erectile problems, first get the cardiovascular checks described in Section 1, Item 28 (if you develop erectile problems, get your cardiovascular health checked first). For the legal consequences in China of posting pornographic material in group chats or selling access to it, see Section 9, Item 4 (what you watch privately is your own business). You are the beneficiary.

entries.title: Do not pay for “sexual orientation correction” or “gay conversion therapy,” and do not send family members to it
entries.cost: Costs nothing. You save the money that correction organizations, psychological clinics, and “gay conversion” services would otherwise take in. The difficult part is when family members insist on sending someone.
entries.summary: After reviewing the research, an American Psychological Association task force concluded that such interventions are unlikely to change sexual orientation and may cause harm. In a US survey, people who had undergone them had nearly 90% higher odds of ever having suicidal thoughts. In China, a psychiatric hospital forcibly admitted a man under the label of “sexual preference disorder.” A court found that this infringed his rights and ordered the hospital to pay 5,000 yuan in compensation.
entries.benefit: A 2009 American Psychological Association task force report stated that efforts to change sexual orientation are “unlikely to be successful and involve some risk of harm.” The report advised parents and children against considering coercive or residential conversion programs for minors. A nationally representative US survey interviewed 1,518 sexual minority adults. About 7% had undergone conversion efforts, and religious figures had provided the intervention in 80% of those cases. After accounting for factors including age and adverse childhood experiences, people who had undergone conversion efforts had an OR of 1.92 for ever having suicidal thoughts (95% CI 1.01–3.64, about 90% higher). The OR for having planned suicide was 1.75 (1.01–3.06). The OR for a suicide attempt resulting in no or minor injury was 1.88 (1.01–3.50). Another study interviewed 245 young people aged 21 to 25. Among those who had not undergone conversion efforts during adolescence, 22.0% had attempted suicide. Among those whose parents had themselves tried to change their child’s sexual orientation, the figure was 48.1%. Among those whose parents had also sent them to a therapist or religious figure, it was 62.8%. The World Health Organization’s International Classification of Diseases, ICD-10, explicitly states: “Sexual orientation by itself is not to be regarded as a disorder.” In 2017, a court in Yicheng District, Zhumadian, Henan Province, China, heard a case in which a psychiatric hospital had forcibly admitted a man under the label of “sexual preference disorder.” The court found that his “condition was ordinary, and he had neither engaged in nor posed a risk of suicide, harming others, destroying property, or similar conduct; he did not meet the criteria for compulsory treatment.” The court ordered the hospital to apologize publicly and pay 5,000 yuan in compensation for emotional distress (US / China).

entries.notes: Controversy. Sullins 2022 recalculated using the same dataset, subtracting suicidal ideation that was already present prior to conversion efforts. Calculated this way, conversion efforts and suicidal ideation were no longer positively correlated (OR 0.44, 0.20–0.94). The institution where Sullins works holds a position against homosexuality, and the original authors also wrote a response. Therefore, how much harm is caused remains controversial, but no opposing evidence was found regarding the point that "it cannot be changed." Rated B because the figures on harm all come from retrospective recall surveys. Legally, inpatient treatment follows the principle of voluntariness; involuntary hospitalization is permitted only when there is a severe mental disorder accompanied by danger of harming oneself or others. Psychological counseling personnel are not permitted to practice psychotherapy. Intentionally sending someone without a mental disorder to a hospital for treatment incurs liability for compensation. In 2014, a man was subjected to hypnosis and electric shock "treatment" for homosexuality at Chongqing Xinyu Piaoxiang Psychological Counseling Center and subsequently filed a lawsuit. The Beijing Haidian Court ordered the center to make a public apology and compensate for economic losses. According to reports, the judgment stated that homosexuality is not a mental illness, and the center's promise that it could be cured constituted false advertising. This case is covered only in reporting by The Paper, and the original text of the judgment could not be found on the court's official website. Those who suffer long-term mental distress over this matter can visit a psychiatry or clinical psychology department, with the goal of alleviating distress. For how families should respond after a child comes out, see Section 30, Item 15 (When a child says they are attracted to the same sex). The beneficiaries are yourself and your family members.

entries.title: Do not count on learning "correct lifting posture" or attending manual handling training to prevent lower back pain; what needs to be reduced is the weight lifted and the frequency of lifting, combined with exercising regularly in daily life
entries.cost: Costs nothing. There is no need to fuss over whether your back was bent when lifting things, nor to spend money on back-care courses and lumbar support belts. What needs to be done are two things: break heavy items down to move them in parts, use a cart, or find someone to lift together—which only takes a few extra minutes; and set aside time several times a week to exercise, which requires long-term persistence.
entries.summary: Workers who received manual handling posture training did not develop lower back pain any less often than those who did not. People who bent their backs more when lifting things were also not observed to be more prone to lower back pain. What is associated with lower back pain is lifting heavy weights and lifting frequently: lifting 10 kg more per lift or lifting 10 more times per day is associated with an approximately 10% higher risk. People who exercise regularly in daily life experience over 30% to over 40% fewer episodes of lower back pain.
entries.benefit: First, looking at training. The 2011 Cochrane systematic review pooled 9 randomized controlled trials with a total of 20,101 employees. Among them, the results of 7 trials with 19,317 participants showed that those who received manual handling training and those who received no intervention reported similar subsequent lower back pain (OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.68–2.02, with the confidence interval crossing 1). Compared with those who only watched a video, RR was 0.93 (0.69–1.25), also similar. The quality of evidence was moderate. The authors concluded that manual handling advice and training, whether paired with handling equipment or not, do not prevent lower back pain or back-pain-related disability. Next, looking at lumbar flexion (bending the back). A 2020 systematic review pooled studies on the degree of lumbar flexion when lifting objects, with low-quality evidence. In the only prospective cohort study, between those who subsequently developed lower back pain and those who did not, the maximum angle of lumbar flexion during lifting differed by only 1.5 degrees (−0.7 to 3.7), which was not statistically significant. Out of 11 studies, 9 found no difference between the two groups. Another 7 studies used an alternative measurement method, and people with lower back pain actually flexed their backs 6.0 degrees less (−11.2 to −0.9) when lifting. The authors concluded that there is no evidence that greater lumbar flexion causes lower back pain. Finally, looking at what should be done. A meta-analysis pooled 8 prospective cohort studies: for every 10 kg increase in the weight lifted per lift, the risk of lower back pain had an OR of 1.11 (1.05–1.18, about 11% higher). For every 10 additional lifts per day, the OR was 1.09 (1.03–1.15, about 9% higher). Another review pooled 21 randomized trials with 30,850 participants: exercise combined with education reduced the risk of lower back pain episodes with an RR of 0.55 (0.41–0.74, about 45% lower), with moderate quality of evidence. Exercise alone had an RR of 0.65 (0.50–0.86, about 35% lower), with low to very low quality of evidence. Education alone had an RR of 1.03 (0.83–1.27), and lumbar support belts had an RR of 1.01 (0.71–1.44), neither showing an effect. Official guidance from the UK Health and Safety Executive (HSE) also explicitly states that training alone cannot ensure manual handling safety. Good handling technique is also no substitute for providing handling aids, redesigning tasks, and modifying loads.

entries.notes: Controversy. Findings vary regarding lifting heavy weights and lifting frequently. A 2010 systematic review identified 9 high-quality studies; 4 observed an association, while 5 did not. The authors concluded that occupational lifting is unlikely to independently cause lower back pain. Therefore, "lifting heavy loads less" has only correlational evidence and cannot prove causality. The studies on bending the back were of low quality, and most only compared two groups of people cross-sectionally at the same point in time. The confidence interval in the training review was very wide, and it also noted that no randomized trials have investigated whether training can treat existing lower back pain. The HSE still teaches a set of techniques: keep loads close to the waist, maintain a stable footing, avoid twisting the back, and avoid jerking. When rising, keep the back, hips, and knees slightly bent, which is better than fully bending the back or fully squatting. There is no harm in doing so; just do not expect it alone to prevent lower back pain. Benefit rated moderate. By magnitude of reduction, exercise qualifies as substantial. However, the quality of evidence for exercise alone is low, exercise plus education has not been shown to reduce sick leave, and lower back pain is not fatal. For how to exercise, see Section 2, Item 16 (Do 30–60 minutes of strength training per week) and Section 2, Item 11 (Walk 7,000–8,000 steps per day). The beneficiary is yourself.

entries.title: Do not count on aggressively supplementing calcium or drinking bone broth after a fracture to make bones heal faster
entries.cost: Costs nothing, and saves money and effort spent on calcium tablets, vitamin D, and stewing broth every day. What needs to be done is simply supplementing if a deficiency is detected, and not taking extra supplements if you are not deficient.
entries.summary: None of the trials supplementing vitamin D after a fracture showed better bone healing. Studies supplementing calcium together with vitamin D are scarce, making it unclear whether it is beneficial. The calcium in a large bowl of bone broth is only a fraction of several tenths of the daily recommended intake. Those who already have a vitamin D deficiency or osteoporosis are a different matter.
entries.benefit: First, looking at vitamin D. A 2023 systematic review included 14 studies with 2,734 fracture patients. The authors concluded that supplementing vitamin D alone has minimal effect on bone healing, union rates, and functional recovery after rehabilitation. The few studies that showed benefits were generally of low quality. The authors explicitly stated that among randomized controlled trials alone, none showed a benefit from supplementation. One of the trials enrolled 100 patients with long bone fractures who had low vitamin D levels. Half received a single dose of 100,000 IU within two weeks after injury, and half received a placebo (dummy drug). In both groups, 2 patients experienced nonunion of the bone, totaling 4%. Another trial enrolled 102 patients aged 18 to 50 with femur or tibia fractures, divided into four groups receiving different doses or placebo. At 3 months and 12 months, no differences were seen in healing scores. Another trial enrolled 32 postmenopausal women with wrist fractures. Compared with those who did not supplement, the high-dose group receiving the equivalent of 1,800 IU daily actually had lower bone compressive stiffness. Next, looking at calcium. A 2014 systematic review noted that clinical studies examining how vitamin D insufficiency or vitamin D supplementation affects fracture healing are scarce, and conclusions remain unclear. The two studies it identified evaluated combined supplementation of calcium and vitamin D. What was observed was an increase in bone mineral density or callus (newly formed bone tissue) at the fracture site, without assessing the speed of healing. Finally, looking at bone broth. An assay in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, purchased three types of bone broth noodle dishes, with one serving of broth weighing 450 to 550 grams. The calcium per serving of broth averaged 14 to 39 mg, accounting for 1.4% to 3.9% of the daily recommended intake of 1,000 mg. The authors concluded that the calcium in one serving of broth is less than 5% of the daily recommended intake. China's recommended intake is 800 mg per day for ages 18 to 49, 1,000 mg for ages 50 and above, with a daily upper limit of 2,000 mg. The health industry standards that established these numbers also specify that long-term excessive calcium intake increases the risk of kidney stones. A US trial enrolled 36,282 postmenopausal women taking 1,000 mg of calcium plus 400 IU of vitamin D daily, followed for an average of 7 years. The risk of kidney stones was approximately 17% higher (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.02–1.34, confidence interval). Hip fractures were approximately 12% lower, but not statistically significant (HR 0.88, 0.72–1.08). It appears worthwhile because of the intuition that "bones are made of calcium, so eating more calcium will make them heal faster"

entries.notes: Disputed evidence: There are two small hints of a benefit. A Danish trial enrolled 30 older women with fractures of the upper arm near the shoulder who had osteoporosis or low bone mass. Those who took 800 IU of vitamin D plus 1 gram of calcium daily had higher bone density at the fracture site in week 6 (0.623 versus 0.570 g/cm²). But the trial measured only bone density, not whether the bone had healed, and it included too few people. When researchers analyzed the 102-person trial by subgroup after the fact, people given high-dose vitamin D had slightly better functional scores. The authors said further trials were needed to confirm this. People who are already deficient in vitamin D are a separate case. In a Dutch observational study, delayed healing occurred in 9.7% of those who remained deficient after supplementation, compared with 0.3% of those who were not deficient to begin with and 1.7% of those whose deficiency was corrected. This was only an observational study and cannot establish cause and effect. If testing shows a deficiency, follow your doctor's advice to bring your level back to normal. People already diagnosed with osteoporosis, or who break a bone after a minor fall, need osteoporosis medication; see Section 1, Item 40 (Osteoporosis medication). Calcium tablets cannot replace it. Long-term supplementation does not benefit people who are not deficient in vitamin D; see Item 3 of this section (Vitamin D supplements). The advice against taking large extra doses does not mean cutting back on calcium. Continue getting enough calcium from your meals; see Item 21 of this section (Cutting out calcium to prevent kidney stones). If you have just fallen and suspect a fracture, see Section 13, Item 41 (Suspected fracture). The benefit is rated medium based on the cost of a year's supply of calcium tablets and vitamin D. You are the beneficiary.

entries.title: Do not rely on an AI chatbot to judge medical conditions or legal issues yourself. Before seeking medical care, going to court, or spending a lot of money, find and check the original source for its claims
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Each check takes an extra few minutes to half an hour. Ask the AI to identify the legal provision, guideline, or paper it relies on, then open the original yourself and find the relevant passage. The habit to change is acting on its advice just because it sounds certain.
entries.summary: When given a complete case history, AI can identify the condition more than 90% of the time. But when ordinary people use it to ask about symptoms, fewer identify the condition than people who search online themselves, and they are no better at deciding whether to go to the emergency department. For legal questions, at least 58% of answers from general-purpose AI contain fabricated content, and it may also go along with false premises in your question.
entries.benefit: First, consider medical questions. In 2026, Nature Medicine published a preregistered randomized trial involving 1,298 ordinary people in the UK. Each person received two constructed case histories and had to decide what the condition was and whether to go to the emergency department or observe it at home. Some participants used AI chatbots for help: GPT-4o, Llama 3, or Command R+. The control group used their usual methods, mostly searching online or consulting the UK National Health Service (NHS) website. Given the complete case histories directly, the AI identified a relevant condition in 94.9% of cases and correctly determined where to seek care in 56.3%. Among ordinary people using the same AI, fewer than 34.5% identified a relevant condition and fewer than 44.2% correctly decided where to seek care. The control group was 1.76 times as likely to identify a relevant condition as the AI users (95% CI 1.45–2.13, confidence interval). It was 1.57 times as likely to identify a serious condition with warning signs (1.28–1.92). The two groups performed about the same in deciding where to seek care. The authors reviewed the chat transcripts and found two problems: users did not give a full account of their symptoms, and when the AI mentioned the correct condition, users did not accept it. Now consider legal questions. In 2024, a US research team asked publicly available models, including ChatGPT 4, about US federal court cases. ChatGPT 4 gave answers containing fabrications 58% of the time; the rate for Llama 2 was as high as 88%. A fabrication is content that does not match the legal facts; the paper calls it a “hallucination.” The models could not tell which of their own statements were fabricated. When users' questions contained false legal premises, the models often accepted them. In 2025, the same team also tested specialized legal AI tools used by lawyers. Despite claims that these tools would not fabricate content, 17% to 33% of their answers contained fabrications. AI seems like good value because it is available on demand, costs nothing, and speaks with the confidence of a doctor or lawyer
entries.sources: Bean AM, Payne RE, Parsons G, et al. (2026). Reliability of LLMs as medical assistants for the general public: a randomized preregistered study. Nature Medicine, 32(2), 609–615. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-025-04074-y>; Dahl M, Magesh V, Suzgun M, Ho DE (2024). Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models. Journal of Legal Analysis, 16(1), 64–93. <https://doi.org/10.1093/jla/laae003>; Magesh V, Surani F, Dahl M, Suzgun M, Manning CD, Ho DE (2025). Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools. Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, 22(2), 216–242. <https://doi.org/10.1111/jels.12413>; Kalai AT, Nachum O, Vempala SS, Zhang E (2025). Why Language Models Hallucinate. arXiv:2509.04664 (preprint, the paper mentioned in the notes). <https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04664>; Counterargument: Ayers JW, Poliak A, Dredze M, et al. (2023). Comparing Physician and Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Responses to Patient Questions Posted to a Public Social Media Forum. JAMA Internal Medicine, 183(6), 589. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2023.1838>
entries.notes: Disputed evidence. A 2023 study sampled 195 patient questions from a US forum and asked medical professionals to rate the answers without knowing their source. In 78.6% of ratings, ChatGPT's answer was judged better than the doctor's. But the study compared how well the answers were written; it did not examine whether the people asking the questions ultimately made the right decisions. The 2026 trial used models from 2024, and newer models may be stronger. But the same trial also found that an AI model's performance when tested on its own did not predict how well ordinary people would do using it. In a 2025 paper that had not undergone peer review, OpenAI researchers explained why AI fabricates information. Training and scoring methods reward “guessing an answer,” while saying “I don't know” earns no points, so it speaks with certainty even when it is unsure. To check an answer, ask it for the name and section number of the legal provision, or the title of the guideline or paper. Open the original on an official website and find the relevant passage yourself. If you cannot find it, treat the claim as though it had never been made. Do not put your own conclusion into the question. Ask, “What does the law say about this situation?” rather than “Am I guaranteed to win in this situation?” If someone suddenly has a drooping mouth, weakness on one side, or pressure-like chest pain, do not ask AI first; call China's emergency number, 120, directly. See Section 13, Item 3 (Drooping mouth and weakness in one arm) and Section 13, Item 7 (Pressure-like chest pain). If you cannot afford a lawyer for a court case, see Section 7, Item 3 (Applying for legal aid). The benefit is rated small because the evidence measures only intermediate outcomes such as whether people identified the condition, with no figures showing fewer deaths. You and your family are the beneficiaries.

entries.title: Do not give up saving because “people can die at any time, so spending all your money sooner is the way to be happy”: about nine in ten 30-year-olds will live to 60
entries.cost: Costs nothing. When the thought “I might be gone any day anyway” comes up, first consider your chance of living to 60. The hard part is that people around you say the same thing, and what you want to buy is right in front of you.
entries.summary: According to the World Health Organization's figures for China, about 92% of 30-year-olds will live to 60, and more than half will live to 80. Young people generally overestimate their chance of dying early. When they live according to that impression, they save about a quarter less than they should. Based on these figures, most people need to save for old age.
entries.benefit: First, consider how long people are likely to live. The World Health Organization's Global Health Observatory produced a 2023 life table for China. A life table uses death rates at each age in a given year to estimate how long a group of people will live. According to this table, the probability that a 30-year-old will live to 60 is 92.0% (89.2% for men, 94.9% for women). The probability of living to 65 is 87.4% (83.0% for men, 92.0% for women). The probability of living to 80 is 55.6% (45.8% for men, 66.1% for women). These three sets of figures were calculated by dividing the numbers of people still alive at the relevant ages in the table. People who reach 65 can expect to live another 17.5 years on average. Next, consider people's own estimates. A 2019 study in The Journal of Finance surveyed people about how long they expected to live. It found that younger people underestimated their chances of surviving, while older people overestimated theirs. An earlier working-paper version gave this example: a 28-year-old man's actual probability of surviving another five years was 99.4%, but he estimated it at 92.8%. The authors put people's own probability estimates into a standard model of how to save and spend over a lifetime. Compared with calculations based on actual death rates, younger people saved 26% less, while retirees spent their savings 27% more slowly. In the survey, the more inaccurate people's estimates of survival and death were, the more their saving behavior deviated, even after accounting for risk preferences, cognitive ability, and family circumstances. The authors suggest that one reason is that people give too much weight to rare, memorable ways of dying
