Electronic Signature Law (amended 2019, Articles 3, 13, 14, and 15). <https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff8080816f135f46016f2163e4261aa1>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2022). Anti-Telecommunications and Online Fraud Law (Articles 31 and 44). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202209/t20220902_575631.shtml>
entries.notes: You are the main person who benefits from this advice; A, who asks you for help, is probably a family member or friend. A chief prosecutor in Shanghai’s Pudong district wrote that B often knows they are taking out the loan but goes along out of concern for the relationship, and ultimately faces the bank’s demands for repayment. If you really want to help, first establish what role you have under the contract. If it is a loan contract, do not sign it. If you are willing to guarantee the loan, sign a guarantee contract as the guarantor; see Item 18 (Guaranteeing Someone Else’s Debt). If a loan has already been taken out in your name, first report it to the police, then call the lending bank at the number on its official website to explain the situation. Keep your chat and transfer records. To find out how many loans are in your name, see Item 9 (Checking Your Credit Report). When the bank asks questions before approving a loan, do not repeat what the intermediary coached you to say. You may be held responsible for false statements; see Section 9, Item 6 (Obtaining Loans with Falsified Application Materials). Facial recognition and electronic confirmation generally count as signatures too; see Item 17 (Read the Document Before Signing). Courts do not always order the named person to repay. In a 2021 case, the Guangzhou Internet Court ruled for a woman who had immediately reported her stolen identity card to the police and registered it as lost. The bank could not produce evidence that she herself had completed facial recognition. So if you lose your identity card, immediately report it to the police and register it as lost, and keep the receipt. Asking an institution for another method when it wants you to complete facial recognition is a separate matter; see Section 14, Item 9 (You Do Not Have to Agree to Facial Recognition). For a similar scheme involving the use of your name, see Item 28 (Serving as a Nominal Legal Representative). Do not lend out your phone or account; see Item 8 (Do Not Lend Someone Your Bank Card). The evidence is rated B because regulators provided descriptions of the scheme and cases, but no statistics on the number of people deceived or the sums involved.

entries.title: Fit good locks to doors and windows, install a motion-activated light outside, and actually lock up when you leave: these measures help prevent burglary; an alarm alone shows no clear benefit
entries.cost: Change the door lock to one that needs a key to lock it securely, add window locks, and install a motion-activated light outside the door. This generally costs tens to hundreds of yuan. Replacing the entire security door costs more than 1,000 yuan. The hard part is actually locking the doors and windows every time you go out, including remembering the windows when you have them open in summer.
entries.summary: British data show that homes with both door and window locks had about one-twelfth the chance of being entered and burgled compared with homes with none of these measures. Add an outdoor motion-activated light, and the chance fell to less than one-thirtieth. Installing only an alarm, with none of the other measures, showed no clear burglary-prevention benefit. This concerns burglary, not robbery while someone is at home.
entries.benefit: The Crime Survey for England and Wales asked 37,416 households which security measures they had between 2008 and 2012, then compared them with households that had been burgled. Homes with none of the measures made up only 4.9% of all households but 36.6% of households entered and burgled. The authors calculated a “protection factor”: how many times lower the chance of burglary was than for a home with none of the measures. Door locks plus window locks had a factor of 12.54, reducing the chance to about one-twelfth. Here, door locks means double locks or “deadlocks” whose bolts can be retracted only with a key. Door and window locks plus an outdoor motion-activated or timer-controlled light had a factor of 34.41. Adding an indoor timer-controlled light raised it to 49. Among single measures, an outdoor light had a factor of about 3 and a door lock about 2.8. Window locks alone showed no clear difference. Having five measures was no more effective than having the right three. With only an alarm and none of the other measures, the chance of burglary was actually higher than with no measures. Homes with a dummy alarm box also had a higher chance of an attempted break-in that did not succeed. Locks count only if they are actually locked. Burglaries involving a forced lock, a smashed window, or a removed door panel fell from 31 to 7 per 1,000 households between 1993 and 2006/07, a 77% drop. Burglaries in which doors or windows were unlocked and the burglar simply walked in stayed at 7 per 1,000 households, with no decline (England and Wales).
entries.sources: Tseloni A, Thompson R, Grove L, Tilley N, Farrell G (2017). The effectiveness of burglary security devices. Security Journal 30(2):646–664. <https://doi.org/10.1057/sj.2014.30>; Tilley N, Thompson R, Farrell G, Grove L, Tseloni A (2015). Do burglar alarms increase burglary risk? A counter-intuitive finding and possible explanations. Crime Prevention and Community Safety 17(1):1–19. <https://doi.org/10.1057/cpcs.2014.17>; Tseloni A, Farrell G, Thompson R, Evans E, Tilley N (2017). Domestic burglary drop and the security hypothesis. Crime Science 6:3. <https://doi.org/10.1186/s40163-017-0064-2>; State Administration for Market Regulation and Standardization Administration of China (2022). GB 17565-2022 General Technical Requirements for Burglar-Resistant Security Doors. <https://openstd.samr.gov.cn/bzgk/gb/newGbInfo?hcno=A75C1C66CB989D0A40BFA7A262C93290>; National People’s Congress (2020). Civil Code (Article 715). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202006/t20200602_463888.shtml>
entries.notes: Dispute: there are contrary data on alarms. Using data from 1992 to 1996, the same group of authors previously calculated that adding an alarm reduced the chance of burglary. The authors also said the counterintuitive later result should be treated cautiously; one possibility is that households installed alarms only after being burgled. All the figures are British and compare homes with and without the measures, without assigning households to comparison groups, so the evidence is rated B. These figures concern only burglary; there are no data here showing that door locks prevent a home robbery. If you encounter someone in your home, first move away and call the police; see Item 10 (Call the Police First and Do Not Fight When a Conflict Starts). If you have no way to retreat, see Item 11 (You May Fight Back Against an Attack You Cannot Escape). If you rent, agree with your landlord before changing the lock or adding window locks. Under the Civil Code, if a tenant makes additions or alterations without the landlord’s consent, the landlord can require the property to be restored or demand compensation. Burglar-resistant security doors are subject to the mandatory Chinese national standard GB 17565-2022, which took effect on January 1, 2024. You can check it when buying one. The main beneficiaries are you and your family.

chapters.title: Legal Lines Ordinary People Can Easily Cross
chapters.intro:
This section weighs two costs: your personal freedom and your money. Ordinary people often think the following actions are “no big deal,” but they can lead to detention or fines and, in serious cases, a criminal sentence. Each item gives the specific figures in the law and cases published through official channels. The Public Security Administration Punishments Law cited in this section is the 2025 revised version, effective January 1, 2026; its article numbers differ from those in the old law. The Criminal Law cited is a consolidated text, reposted by the Beijing Traffic Management Bureau of the Public Security Bureau, that states it was “revised in accordance with Criminal Law Amendment (XI).” The text identifies the relevant amendment where applicable.

The items in this section are grouped by topic below, with item numbers in parentheses.

**Posting and forwarding online**: Do not forward unverified news about disasters (Item 1), do not forward content insulting heroes and martyrs (Item 2), close foreign websites after viewing what is on them (Item 3), and do not post pornographic videos in group chats (Item 4).

**Receiving money for others, fraudulent loans, and insurance fraud**: Part-time work receiving money through your own card (Item 5), falsifying application materials to obtain a loan (Item 6), not withdrawing money with a bank card you find (Item 7), claiming discounts using your real identity (Item 8), not lending your identity card to others (Item 16), and fabricating an accident to obtain insurance compensation (Item 21).

**Small matters in daily life**: Do not throw things out of balcony windows (Item 9), do not buy replica guns online (Item 10), register drones under your real name first (Item 11), do not take a cut or organize gambling card games (Item 13), do not eat wild animals (Item 14), never use electricity to catch fish (Item 27), and do not light fires in forests or grasslands when visiting graves or having a picnic (Item 28).

**Conflicts and the police**: Do not detain someone to collect a debt (Item 15), cooperate when the police stop you (Item 17), understand the consequences before hitting someone (Item 19), and do not carry an expandable baton or stun gun for self-defense (Item 26).

**Sex, children, and the body**: Do not secretly photograph or film others (Item 12), do not have sexual relations with anyone under 14 (Item 18), register through the civil affairs authorities if you cannot raise a child (Item 20), do not sell your own organs (Item 22), and expect detention as the default consequence of paying for sex (Item 23).

**Copyright and derivative works**: Translating content into Chinese for redistribution and pirated ebooks (Item 24), and obtaining permission before writing and selling fan fiction (Item 25).

**Exams**: Do not arrange for someone else to take an exam for you or buy or sell answers (Item 29).

entries.title: Do not forward unverified disaster, epidemic, or police incident reports in group chats; do not alter images or use AI to fabricate images of the scene
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Before forwarding a message, check whether it is an official notice. If you are unsure, do not forward it, alter an image, or add “reportedly.” The hard part is resisting the urge to be the first to tell everyone.
entries.summary: If you know a report about a disaster, epidemic, or police incident is false but forward it anyway, you can face the same penalty as the person who invented it. It makes no difference that you did not make it up: detention for 5 to 10 days, plus a possible fine of up to 1,000 yuan. If it seriously disrupts public order, the sentence is up to 3 years; if it causes serious consequences, 3 to 7 years. Falsifying images with editing software or AI counts as inventing the report yourself.
entries.benefit: Anyone who deliberately spreads rumors or falsely reports a dangerous situation, epidemic, disaster, or police incident, disrupting public order, faces detention for 5 to 10 days. An additional fine of up to 1,000 yuan may be imposed. For less serious circumstances, the penalty is detention for up to 5 days or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Fabricating a false report of a dangerous situation, epidemic, disaster, or police incident and posting it online is punishable by a sentence of up to 3 years. Deliberately spreading it while knowing it is false carries the same penalty. The condition is that it seriously disrupts public order, the wording used in the law. If it causes serious consequences, the sentence is 3 to 7 years (China nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (revised 2025, Article 29). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2015). Criminal Law Amendment (IX) (Article 32, corresponding to the second paragraph of Article 291-1 of the Criminal Law). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180205_364562.shtml>; National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (revised in accordance with Criminal Law Amendment (XI), Article 291-1). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html> (reposted by the Beijing Traffic Management Bureau of the Public Security Bureau).
entries.notes: The police apply the same provision whether you knowingly forward a false report or make it up yourself. “I only forwarded it” does not exempt you from liability. Fabricated images of a scene made with editing software or AI likewise count as making it up yourself. In 2025, China’s Ministry of Public Security published several batches of typical cases involving online rumors about disasters and dangerous situations. The ministry’s website was inaccessible when this section was written, so no specific case is cited.

entries.title: Do not post or forward images, memes, or comments insulting heroes and martyrs, or joke about the Chinese national flag or anthem
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Do not comment on, alter, or forward content involving heroes and martyrs, the Chinese national flag, national emblem, or national anthem. The hard part is holding back from joining in when someone in a group chat makes a joke.
entries.summary: Joking about heroes and martyrs, the Chinese national flag, or the national anthem can bring detention for 5 to 10 days or a fine of 1,000 to 3,000 yuan in less serious cases. More serious cases bring detention for 10 to 15 days. If the conduct constitutes a crime, the sentence is up to 3 years. Someone posted two messages disparaging Yuan Longping in a villagers’ WeChat group of 499 people and was sentenced to 6 months of public surveillance: they were not imprisoned, but their movements were restricted.
entries.benefit: Infringing the names, likenesses, reputations, or honor of heroes and martyrs through insults, fabricated claims, or similar means, where this harms the public interest, carries the following penalty: detention for 5 to 10 days or a fine of 1,000 to 3,000 yuan. Desecrating or denying the deeds and spirit of heroes and martyrs, or producing and spreading statements, images, audio, or video glorifying wars of aggression, where this disrupts public order, carries the same penalty. For more serious circumstances, the penalty is detention for 10 to 15 days, with a possible additional fine of up to 5,000 yuan. When the circumstances are “serious,” the conduct constitutes a crime and carries a sentence of up to 3 years. Publicly insulting the Chinese national flag or national emblem, or changing the lyrics or music of the national anthem or singing it in a distorted and derogatory way, also carries a sentence of up to 3 years when the circumstances are serious. Official cases: Xiao posted two messages disparaging and insulting Yuan Longping in a villagers’ WeChat group of 499 people and was sentenced to 6 months of public surveillance. Public surveillance is a punishment that restricts a person’s movements without imprisoning them. Qiu used a Weibo account with more than 2.5 million followers to post two messages distorting the deeds of soldiers who defended China’s border. Qiu was sentenced to 8 months and ordered to apologize publicly in national media (China nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (revised in 2025, Article 35). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2018). Law on the Protection of Heroes and Martyrs (Articles 22 and 26). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/gyssshmhsh/201912/t20191202_440079.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law Amendment (XI) (Article 35, which became Article 299-1 of the Criminal Law). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/zdgz/202012/t20201227_503682.shtml>; National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment (XI), Articles 299 and 299-1). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People's Court (2022). Ten Typical Cases Concerning the Protection of the Rights and Interests of Heroes and Martyrs (Cases 2 and 3). <https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/382301.html>
entries.notes: This provision of the Public Security Administration Punishments Law was added only in the 2025 revision. Before then, cases of this kind could be pursued only under criminal law or through a civil public interest lawsuit brought by a procuratorate. In the courts’ view, a WeChat group with several hundred members counts as a public setting.

entries.title: When you finish viewing something on an overseas website, close it: do not take screenshots, forward it, bring it into a group chat, or join in the comments
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Close the page and leave it there. Do not archive it, forward it, or move it onto a platform in China. Do not use an account that can be linked to your identity to post political content on overseas platforms over a long period. Do not accept payment for writing or financial support from overseas institutions, organizations, or individuals. The hard part is resisting the urge to take a screenshot or share content that catches your attention.
entries.summary: These legal provisions punish passing material on, not viewing it. Forwarding it, bringing it into a group chat, and joining in the comments all count as dissemination when a case is investigated. If the conduct reaches the level of inciting subversion or secession, the sentence is up to 5 years; ringleaders receive more than 5 years. Books and audio or video materials promoting terrorism or extremism are an exception: knowingly keeping them in your possession can result in a sentence of up to 3 years if the circumstances are serious.
entries.benefit: Inciting others to subvert state power or overthrow the socialist system through rumors, defamation, or other means is punishable by up to 5 years’ imprisonment. Ringleaders (the term used in the law) and those whose crimes are grave receive more than 5 years; the maximum fixed-term prison sentence is 15 years. Inciting secession or undermining national unity carries the same prison terms. Committing either of these acts in collusion with overseas institutions, organizations, or individuals brings a heavier punishment. If an institution, organization, or individual inside or outside China provides money to fund others in carrying out these acts, the directly responsible persons face up to 5 years, or more than 5 years if the circumstances are serious. Stealing, spying on, buying, or illegally providing state secrets or intelligence for overseas institutions, organizations, or personnel is punishable by 5 to 10 years. For this offense, especially serious circumstances bring more than 10 years or life imprisonment; less serious circumstances bring up to 5 years. Crimes endangering national security also carry deprivation of political rights for 1 to 5 years. During that period, the person loses the right to vote and eligibility to hold public office. Confiscation of property may also be imposed, transferring personal property to the state. There are administrative provisions as well. No individual or organization may use the internet to engage in activities that endanger national security, honor, or interests. Nor may they incite subversion of state power or the overthrow of the socialist system, or incite secession or undermine national unity. Publishing or transmitting such information is punished under the relevant laws and administrative regulations (nationwide). There is another category of offense that does not require dissemination. Knowingly possessing material that promotes terrorism or extremism, when the possession is illegal and the circumstances are serious, is enough for a conviction. The material includes books, audio or video materials, and other items. The penalty is up to 3 years’ imprisonment, criminal detention (short-term confinement), or public surveillance (restrictions on movement without confinement). A fine must also be imposed or may be imposed on its own: the person may be fined along with another sentence or may receive only a fine. The basis is Article 120-6 of the Criminal Law, added by Criminal Law Amendment (IX).
entries.sources: National People’s Congress (1997). Criminal Law (Articles 45, 55, 56, 103, 105, 106, 107, 111, and 113; these articles have not been changed by amendments). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180206_364975.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2025). Cybersecurity Law (amended in 2025, effective January 1, 2026, Article 13, paragraph 2, and Article 71, item 1). <https://www.cac.gov.cn/2025-12/29/c_1768735112911946.htm>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2015). Criminal Law Amendment (IX) (adding Article 120-6). Full text republished by the National Public Complaints and Proposals Administration <https://www.gjxfj.gov.cn/gjxfj/fgwj/flfg/webinfo/2017/03/1601761496614423.htm>
entries.notes: The laws cited here punish inciting others, passing material on, and providing it to others; merely viewing it is not covered. Materials promoting terrorism or extremism are the exception expressly stated in the law: merely keeping them in your possession can be a crime (Article 120-6). Do not archive this kind of material. If you see it, stop there: do not take screenshots to save it, forward it, add comments, or get others to forward it with you. Forwarding it and joining in the comments both count as dissemination when a case is investigated; “I only forwarded it once” does not exempt you from liability. Committing the acts in collusion with overseas institutions, organizations, or individuals brings a heavier punishment. Be especially careful not to forward something when you are unsure whether it is true; see item 1 of this section (do not forward messages whose truth you do not know). For penalties relating to tools used to bypass internet restrictions, see item 11 of section 11. Passing this kind of content on brings no tangible benefit, while the cost may be imprisonment, deprivation of political rights, and confiscation of property. This book did not obtain judgments that could be checked through official channels, so it describes only the legal provisions and includes no cases.

entries.title: Keep pornographic videos you watch to yourself: do not post them in groups, sell “resources,” or create groups
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Do not forward the material, save it in group files, or become the owner or administrator of such a group.
entries.summary: Watching it yourself is not covered by the punishment provisions. Posting it in a group is online dissemination; the provision does not specify a minimum number of times it must be posted. The penalty is 10 to 15 days’ detention, with a possible additional fine of up to 5,000 yuan. Serious circumstances bring up to 2 years’ imprisonment. Selling “resources” to make money brings up to 3 years, and the most severe sentence is life imprisonment. If a group with 30 or more members is created to disseminate the material, its creator, administrators, and main contributors are all treated as having committed a crime.
entries.benefit: Disseminating obscene information online is punishable by 10 to 15 days’ detention, with a possible additional fine of up to 5,000 yuan. This provision does not specify a minimum number of times the information must be sent. By comparison, the provision in the same law that punishes sending messages to harass others expressly says “repeatedly sending.” For less serious circumstances, the penalty is detention of up to 5 days or a fine of 1,000 to 3,000 yuan. If the content involves minors, the punishment is heavier. Disseminating obscene materials when the circumstances are “serious” is punishable by up to 2 years’ imprisonment. Selling or disseminating them to make money is punishable by up to 3 years plus a fine. For this offense, serious circumstances bring 3 to 10 years; especially serious circumstances bring more than 10 years or life imprisonment. Creating a group used primarily to disseminate obscene electronic information is treated as a crime if it has 30 or more members. The same applies if it causes serious consequences. The group’s creator, its administrators, and those who are the main contributors of material are all convicted of the crime of disseminating obscene materials (nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (revised in 2025, Article 50, paragraph 1, item 5, and Article 80). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment (XI), Articles 363 and 364). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2010). Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Specific Application of Law in Handling Criminal Cases Involving the Production, Reproduction, Publication, Sale, and Dissemination of Obscene Electronic Information Using the Internet, Mobile Communication Terminals, and Audio Information Services (II) (Article 3). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/zdgz/201002/t20100204_25001.shtml>
entries.notes: Both laws punish “dissemination”; watching privately is not covered by their provisions. Posting material in a group is online dissemination. The provision does not specify a number of times, so even posting it once falls within the provision; this is an inference from the wording. The quantity required for circumstances to count as “serious” is set by judicial interpretation; this section has not verified the specific figure.

entries.title: If a “part-time job” asks you to use your own bank card to receive money, withdraw cash, or make transfers, refuse regardless of the fee offered
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Turn down jobs advertised as “several hundred yuan paid daily” or “bring your bank card to the bank.”
entries.summary: These part-time jobs pay a few hundred yuan but can leave you with a criminal record. One person took his ID card and one bank card to a designated place, helped transfer and withdraw money, and earned more than 500 yuan. The procuratorate did not prosecute him, but the police still detained him for 10 days and fined him 1,000 yuan. Another person gave a criminal group his own and other people’s bank cards and mobile phone SIM cards to receive money and withdraw cash. He was sentenced to 2 years and 3 months and fined 22,000 yuan.
entries.benefit: Knowingly helping to transfer, buy, or sell money or property obtained through crime, or helping to conceal it by other means, is punishable by up to 3 years’ imprisonment and a fine, or by a fine alone (the fine may accompany a prison sentence or be the only penalty). Official case: Wang brought his ID card and one bank card as instructed, went to a designated place, and helped transfer and withdraw money. He earned more than 500 yuan. The procuratorate did not prosecute him, but the police detained him for 10 days under the Anti-Telecommunications and Online Fraud Law and fined him 1,000 yuan. Man gave a criminal group his own and other people’s bank cards and mobile phone SIM cards to receive money, make transfers, and withdraw cash. He was sentenced to 2 years and 3 months and fined 22,000 yuan (nationwide). Converting the money to virtual currency and transferring it out is treated the same way. An and two others followed instructions from a telecommunications fraud group and used their own bank cards to receive money. On a trading platform, they used the money to buy virtual currency, then transferred it to an account designated by the group and took a commission based on the amount. Investigators confirmed that the money included more than 500,000 yuan stolen from victims through fraud. The three were each convicted of concealing or disguising criminal proceeds and sentenced to terms ranging from 2 years and 8 months to 3 years and 3 months. Each was fined between 30,000 and 40,000 yuan (Tongzhou, Beijing).
entries.sources: National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment (XI), Article 312). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2023). Typical Cases of Procuratorial Authorities Punishing Telecommunications and Online Fraud and Related Crimes in Accordance with Law (Case 9). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/xwfbh/wsfbt/202311/t20231130_635188.shtml>; Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2025). Typical Cases of Punishing Crimes Involving the Concealment or Disguise of Criminal Proceeds and Proceeds Derived from Crime in Accordance with Law (Cases 1 and 5). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/xwfbh/wsfbt/202508/t20250825_704514.shtml>
entries.notes: For the consequences of lending someone a bank card or helping someone “run transactions” through it, see item 8 of section 8 (lending someone a bank card). This item concerns withdrawing cash or making transfers yourself. Receiving money, converting it to virtual currency such as Tether, and transferring it out is the same kind of act. For why you may be unable to recover money lost when buying virtual currency yourself, see item 45 of section 5 (do not buy virtual currency). Saying “I didn’t know where the money came from” may not be accepted when a case is investigated. In commenting on Man’s case, the Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuratorate stated that courts consider what information you encountered, how the money was converted and transferred, and whether the transactions and accounts showed anomalies. They also consider your experience and your relationship with those upstream to assess whether you knew. The person in the case above who was not prosecuted was still detained for 10 days.

entries.title: If someone recruits you to “dress up” loan application documents and offers you a share of the loan, refuse every such offer
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Refuse outright. Do not lend anyone your ID card or credit report, sign a loan contract you have not read, or attend an in-person loan signing at a bank on someone else’s behalf.
entries.summary: Helping someone “dress up” application documents to get a loan in exchange for a share of the proceeds is treated as fraud. One group of 126 people presented unemployed people as “high-quality customers” and fraudulently obtained more than 30 million yuan in loans from over 80 bank branches. Those who appeared to sign received 30% of the loan as a fee. Of the 80 people sentenced so far, 76 received terms ranging from 1 year and 4 months to 6 years and 6 months. Whoever has the loan in their name owes the debt.
entries.benefit: Obtaining loans, acceptance of bills, letters of credit, guarantees, or similar products from a bank or other financial institution by deception is punishable by up to 3 years if it causes the institution significant losses. A fine must also be imposed or may be imposed on its own: the person may be fined along with a prison sentence or receive only a fine. Especially significant losses or other especially serious circumstances bring 3 to 7 years plus a fine. The threshold for police to open a criminal investigation is a direct economic loss of at least 500,000 yuan. Obtaining a loan by inventing a reason involving a project to bring in funds, or by using a false economic contract, false supporting documents, or false proof of property rights, when there was no intention to repay from the outset, constitutes loan fraud. For that offense, police open a case when the amount fraudulently obtained reaches 50,000 yuan. The penalty is up to 5 years plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan. A large amount or other serious circumstances bring 5 to 10 years; an especially large amount brings more than 10 years, up to life imprisonment. Forging, altering, buying, or selling official documents, identity documents, or seals of state organs is punishable by up to 3 years, or 3 to 10 years if the circumstances are serious. Official case: a group of 126 people across 16 provinces and cities presented unemployed people as “high-quality customers” and fraudulently obtained more than 30 million yuan in loans from over 80 bank branches. The “blank-credit-file” applicants who appeared as borrowers received a fee equal to 30% of the loan amount. The procuratorate prosecuted 105 of these applicants. Of the 80 people sentenced at first instance by 2026, 76 were convicted of loan fraud and sentenced to terms ranging from 1 year and 4 months to 6 years and 6 months, plus fines. Another 4 people withdrew cash for the group and received combined sentences for loan fraud and money laundering (the sentences for the two offenses were calculated together). These 4 received terms ranging from 2 years and 4 months to 7 years and 6 months (nationwide). The offense of obtaining loans by deception discussed in this item follows the text of Criminal Law Amendment (XI) effective from March 2021.
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law Amendment (XI) (Article 11, amending Article 175-1 of the Criminal Law). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202012/t20201227_503700.shtml>; National People’s Congress (1997). Criminal Law (Articles 88, 193, and 280). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180206_364975.shtml>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate and Ministry of Public Security (2022). Provisions on the Standards for Filing and Prosecuting Criminal Cases Under the Jurisdiction of Public Security Organs (II) (Articles 22 and 45). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/xwfbh/wsfbt/202204/t20220429_555906.shtml>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2026). Money Launderers Hidden Behind a Loan Fraud Assembly Line (Procuratorial Daily). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/zdgz/202604/t20260428_726494.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2012). Exit and Entry Administration Law (Article 12). <https://www.nia.gov.cn/n741440/n741547/c1013311/content.html> (National Immigration Administration); Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (amended in 2023). Civil Procedure Law (Article 266). <https://amr.guizhou.gov.cn/zwgk/xxgkml/jcxxgk/zcfg/fl/202401/t20240129_83645867.html> (republished by the Guizhou Provincial Administration for Market Regulation)
entries.notes: “I intended to repay it at the time” was not accepted in that case. The procuratorial authorities established that the people had no jobs or fixed assets and could not repay the loans, and that they had spent all the money they received. On that basis, the authorities concluded that they had never intended to repay. Withdrawing cash for the group may also bring a separate money laundering charge. Whoever has the loan in their name and signed the contract is the borrower. Even if the conduct is not a crime, the debt and the entry on the credit report are still theirs. Taking the money and fleeing overseas will not settle the matter either: after a criminal case has been opened, hiding does not stop prosecution no matter how many years pass. People who have been sentenced but have not finished serving their sentence, and people who are criminal suspects or defendants, are prohibited from leaving China. If a civil case remains unresolved, a court may bar you from leaving China; it may also restrict the departure of a person subject to enforcement who fails to fulfill their obligations. For withdrawing cash or making transfers for someone else, see item 5 of this section (a “part-time job” asks you to use your own card to receive money). For how to discover that someone has taken out a loan in your name without your knowledge, see item 9 of section 8.

entries.title: Do not withdraw money with a bank card you find; if you find a phone or wallet, contact the owner or hand it to the police instead of keeping it
entries.cost: It costs nothing and takes a few minutes. Call to find the owner, or take the item to a police station.
entries.summary: Keeping something you find for your own use and refusing to hand it over is punishable by up to 2 years if its value reaches the threshold for a “relatively large amount,” or 2 to 5 years if the amount is huge. Taking a bank card you found to an ATM and withdrawing money is more serious: it counts as using someone else’s bank card without authorization. A relatively large amount brings up to 5 years plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan. For this kind of withdrawal, the police open a case directly; the owner does not have to bring the case to court themselves.
entries.benefit: If you find something someone else has lost, you must return it to the owner, promptly notify them to collect it, or hand it over to the police or another relevant department. Keeping something another person left behind for your own use and refusing to hand it over constitutes the crime of misappropriation if its value reaches the threshold for a “relatively large amount.” The penalty is up to 2 years. A huge amount brings 2 to 5 years. Taking someone else’s credit card that you found and using it at an ATM is “using another person’s credit card without authorization.” Under a 2004 interpretation by the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, “credit card” in the Criminal Law means an electronic payment card issued by a bank or other financial institution. A card qualifies if it has all or some of these functions: making payments for purchases, obtaining credit, settling transfers, and depositing or withdrawing cash. Ordinary bank cards that can be used to deposit or withdraw cash are therefore included. If the conduct reaches the criminal threshold, it is treated as credit card fraud: a relatively large amount brings up to 5 years plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan. A huge amount or other serious circumstances bring 5 to 10 years plus a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 yuan (nationwide).
entries.sources: National People’s Congress (2020). Civil Code (Article 314). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202006/t20200602_463888.shtml>; National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment (XI), Articles 196 and 270). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2008). Reply on How to Classify the Act of Finding Another Person’s Credit Card and Using It at an Automated Teller Machine (ATM). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/flfg/sfjs/201208/t20120830_47871.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2004). Interpretation of the Provisions Concerning Credit Cards in the Criminal Law of the People’s Republic of China. <http://www.npc.gov.cn/zgrdw/npc/xinwen/lfgz/zxfl/2004-12/30/content_334756.htm>
entries.notes: The crime of misappropriation is handled only upon a complaint: the owner must bring a case to court themselves, and the police do not initiate one. Withdrawing money using a card you found is different. The owner does not need to bring a case; the police open one directly. The specific value that counts as a “relatively large amount” is set by judicial interpretation; this section has not verified it. After an item has been handed over to the relevant department, the owner must pay storage costs when collecting it (Civil Code, Article 317).

entries.title: Claim discounts using your real identity; do not buy virtual phone numbers to register accounts in bulk or repeatedly claim offers through a loophole
entries.cost: It costs nothing. Turn down jobs in groups devoted to exploiting promotions. If you discover a loophole on a platform, do not use it. The hard part is resisting the urge to treat discounts as income you can reproduce in bulk.
entries.summary: Using your real identity to claim a coupon once on a single account does not fall within the scope of administrative or criminal penalties. Registering fake users in bulk or placing orders yourself and taking orders yourself to fraudulently claim extra coupons is handled as fraud. Defrauding an amount reaching the threshold set by each province (3,000 to 10,000 yuan) is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 3 years; reaching 30,000 to 100,000 yuan is punishable by 3 to 10 years. One courier used virtual numbers costing 0.1 yuan each to churn coupons and cashed out over 90,000 yuan; 12 co-defendants in the case were sentenced.
entries.benefit: Whoever defrauds public or private property of a relatively large amount shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 3 years, and concurrently or solely fined (fined alongside imprisonment, or fined alone). If the amount is huge, or if there are other serious circumstances, the penalty is 3 to 10 years of fixed-term imprisonment, plus a fine. If the amount is extraordinarily huge, or if there are other especially serious circumstances, the penalty is 10 or more years of fixed-term imprisonment or life imprisonment, plus a fine or confiscation of property. For the three tiers—relatively large, huge, and extraordinarily huge—each province sets its local criteria within the following ranges: relatively large is 3,000 yuan to over 10,000 yuan; huge is 30,000 yuan to over 100,000 yuan; extraordinarily huge is over 500,000 yuan. Teaching methods to others or selling "tutorials" is penalized as the crime of imparting criminal methods with fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 5 years; if the circumstances are serious, 5 to 10 years; if the circumstances are especially serious, 10 or more years of fixed-term imprisonment or life imprisonment. Upstream and downstream parties buying and selling mobile phone numbers and verification codes are penalized for the crime of infringing on citizens' personal information with fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 3 years; if the circumstances are especially serious, 3 to 7 years. Using batch accounts, automatic network address switching systems, and verification-code-receiving platforms that batch-receive SMS verifications is itself explicitly prohibited by Article 14 of the Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law. Illegally buying, selling, leasing, or lending telephone SIM cards and Internet accounts, or assisting others through real-name verification, falls under Article 31. Those who violate Article 14 will have all illegal gains confiscated and be fined 1 to 10 times the amount of their earnings. If there are no illegal gains or the earnings are less than 50,000 yuan, they shall be fined not more than 500,000 yuan, and in serious circumstances, also detained for not more than 15 days. For violating Article 31, the fine is likewise 1 to 10 times the earnings; if there are no earnings or the earnings are less than 20,000 yuan, the fine is not more than 200,000 yuan, and in serious circumstances, also administrative detention for not more than 15 days. Those who participate in telecom and online fraud whose conduct does not yet constitute a crime shall be detained for 10 to 15 days, have their illegal gains confiscated, and be fined 1 to 10 times the earnings; if there are no earnings or the earnings are less than 10,000 yuan, the fine is not more than 100,000 yuan. Official Case 1: Delivery rider Liu bought virtual mobile phone numbers at 0.1 yuan each to register new user accounts on a certain platform. He claimed new-user coupons offering "15 off 29" to place orders, and then resold the goods to small shops to cash out. He also used virtual numbers to refer each other and collect referral rewards of 2 yuan to 20 yuan. He and courier Tan fraudulently obtained over 90,000 yuan and over 70,000 yuan respectively. The People's Procuratorate of Yangpu District, Shanghai, prosecuted 12 individuals for fraud; the court sentenced them to penalties ranging from 3 years and 6 months of fixed-term imprisonment down to 3 months of criminal detention. Official Case 2: Wang exploited the time gap between an online shop's refund process and the retrieval of virtual lucky-draw coins. He requested 1,156 refunds and withdrew 224 collectible figures, totaling an amount of over 249,000 yuan. He also liquidated them on second-hand platforms. The court sentenced him for fraud to 3 years of fixed-term imprisonment suspended for 4 years, along with a fine of 30,000 yuan. During trial, he returned the illicit gains and prepaid his fine, totaling 330,000 yuan. Official Case 3: A certain ride-hailing platform's new-user coupons and driver subsidies were fraudulently obtained through fake ride dispatches where individuals "hailed rides themselves and took their own orders," involving over 2 million yuan across 19 provinces and more than 70 cities. The People's Procuratorate of Longcheng District, Chaoyang, Liaoning, prosecuted 163 individuals, all of whom were convicted. Principal offenders Huang and Cai were punished for multiple crimes concurrently (calculating sentences for several offenses combined)—fraud, infringing on citizens' personal information, and imparting criminal methods—each receiving 3 years and 6 months of fixed-term imprisonment. For an additional 34 accessories whose circumstances were minor, the procuratorate decided not to prosecute and transferred them to public security organs for administrative penalties (Nationwide).
entries.sources: National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law (amended in accordance with Amendment (XI) to the Criminal Law, Articles 253-1, 266, 295). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html> (reprinted by Beijing Public Security Bureau Traffic Management Bureau); Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate (2011). Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Specific Application of Law in Handling Criminal Cases of Fraud (Fa Shi [2011] No. 7, Article 1). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/sfjs/201802/t20180201_363736.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2022). Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law (Articles 14, 31, 38, 42, 44). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202209/t20220902_575631.shtml>; National People's Congress (2020). Civil Code (Article 985). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202006/t20200602_463888.shtml>; Supreme People's Procuratorate (2021). Targeting Telecom and Online Fraud | Lawbreakers Target Loopholes in the E-Commerce Economy (Procuratorial Daily). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/zdgz/202106/t20210607_520557.shtml>; Supreme People's Procuratorate (2025). This Kind of "Wool Pulling" is Suspected of Fraud (Procuratorial Daily). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/zdgz/202508/t20250826_704625.shtml>; Supreme People's Procuratorate (2024). Longcheng District, Chaoyang, Liaoning: Handling a Series of Telecom and Online Fraud Cases (Legal Daily). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/zdgz/202401/t20240124_641099.shtml>; Kankan News (2026-08-25). Man Buys Over 870 Mobile Phone Numbers Online to "Pull Wool" on Automakers, Steals Over 400,000 in Electricity (Reporter Chen Minjia). <https://www.kankanews.com/detail/80290xAJDw6> (web archive <https://web.archive.org/web/20261005044233/https://www.kankanews.com/detail/80290xAJDw6>)
entries.notes: The dividing line is not "how much wool you pulled," but whether you fabricated falsehoods. Participating in promotions with your own real identity, claiming once per account, and using coupons on yourself is a legitimate discount given to you by the platform. Registering fake users, fabricating transactions, or concealing that you have already received a refund in order to claim extra benefits means inducing the other party to deliver property based on mistaken beliefs, which is deemed fraud. The amount only determines how long the sentence is. People have also exploited automakers' charging services like this. In August 2026, Kankan News reported that two individuals in Shanghai purchased large numbers of virtual phone numbers and alternately linked them as sub-accounts on a new-energy vehicle maker's app. Each account was unlinked after two charges using "charge first, pay later," leaving the electricity bills unpaid, and the charging quotas were resold to truck drivers. The Pudong New Area Procuratorate considered this fraud rather than theft and approved their arrest. This case only has media reports, without a verdict or official notification. When the amount is insufficient for criminal sentencing, there are still consequences: the platform can ban accounts, claw back discounts, and demand restitution under "unjust gains must be returned." Participating in telecom fraud below the criminal threshold also brings administrative detention and fines. "Someone led the group and paid me per order" does not change the legal nature of your own part. Teaching methods to others and reselling accounts and phone numbers constitute separate crimes, and multiple crimes will be tallied together. The beneficiary is yourself. For writing and selling scripts yourself, see Section 11, Item 3; for selling SIM cards and accounts, see Section 8, Item 8 (lending bank cards to others) and Section 16 of this chapter (not lending your ID card to others).

entries.title: Never throw anything out of balconies or windows, including cigarette butts, garbage bags, and wine bottles
entries.cost: Costs no money and takes no time. Carry cigarette butts, trash bags, and wine bottles to indoor trash bins instead of tossing them out of windows and balconies.
entries.summary: Throwing objects down from a building can result in administrative detention of up to 5 days or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan even if nobody is hit; if the circumstances are serious, detention is 10 to 15 days. If someone is hit, the charge escalates: someone who threw empty wine bottles and glass cups down onto a playground from the 21st floor after drinking, hitting a 13-year-old student and causing severe injury, was sentenced to 10 years. Another person threw 8 bricks down from the 32nd floor, killing 1 person, and the death penalty was ratified in 2024.
entries.benefit: Throwing objects from a building or other high places can result in administrative detention of up to 5 days or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan, as long as there is a danger of injuring people, damaging property, or endangering public safety. If the circumstances are serious, detention is 10 to 15 days, and an additional fine of up to 1,000 yuan may be imposed. If the circumstances are serious enough to constitute the crime of throwing objects from a height, it is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 1 year, and concurrently or solely fined (fined alongside imprisonment, or fined alone). Hitting and injuring or killing someone will be handled under more serious charges. Official Case: Li Chen threw empty wine bottles and glass cups down onto a playground from the 21st floor after drinking, hitting a 13-year-old student and causing Grade II severe injury. He was sentenced to 10 years for the crime of endangering public safety by dangerous means. Zhou threw 8 bricks from the 32nd floor into a crowd, killing 1 person; in 2024, the Supreme People's Court ratified the death penalty (Nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Article 43). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2020). Amendment (XI) to the Criminal Law (Article 33, i.e., Criminal Law Article 291-2). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/zdgz/202012/t20201227_503682.shtml>; National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law (amended in accordance with Amendment (XI) to the Criminal Law, Article 291-2). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People's Court (2024). Typical Cases on Punishing Crimes Endangering Public Safety in Accordance with Law (Case 1). <https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/429522.html>; Supreme People's Court (2025). Exclusive Interview with Vice President Li Yong of the Supreme People's Court: Ensuring Every Perpetrator of Throwing Objects from Heights Is Penalized. <https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/458381.html>
entries.notes: You can be administratively detained even if nobody is hit; the statutory provision only requires "there being danger." The Civil Code has a separate civil compensation provision for throwing objects from heights (Article 1254). The original text could not be opened when writing this section, so it was not cited.

entries.title: Do not purchase imitation guns, steel-ball guns, or airguns online; do not buy "toy guns" of unknown origin
entries.cost: Costs no money. If you want to shoot guns, go to a legitimate shooting range.
entries.summary: Steel-ball guns and airguns bought online are legally identified as firearms once their muzzle specific kinetic energy reaches 1.8 joules/square centimeter. Holding them without a permit is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 3 years; if the circumstances are serious, 3 to 7 years. A married couple sold "toy guns," and 18 out of 43 seized guns were appraised as firearms; they were spared prosecution only because knowledge on their part could not be proven.
entries.benefit: Possessing or privately concealing firearms without a license is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 3 years; if the circumstances are serious, 3 to 7 years. For non-standard firearms unable to fire standard ammunition, as long as the muzzle specific kinetic energy is greater than or equal to 1.8 joules/square centimeter, they are without exception classified as firearms. Muzzle specific kinetic energy refers to the energy carried per square centimeter when the projectile leaves the muzzle. Many steel-ball guns and airguns purchased online exceed this figure. Since 2018, the Supreme People's Court and Supreme People's Procuratorate have required comprehensive assessments before deciding whether to convict in cases involving airguns with relatively low specific kinetic energy. The assessment must examine appearance, material, price, intended use, whether the individual knowingly had knowledge, and so on. Official Case: Zhao and his wife sold "toy guns" at a public fair, and 43 were seized, 18 of which were determined through appraisal to meet firearm standards. Because there was insufficient evidence proving they knew these were firearms, the case was dropped without prosecution due to doubtful evidence (Nationwide).
entries.sources: National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law (amended in accordance with Amendment (XI) to the Criminal Law, Article 128). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate (2018). Official Reply on Issues Concerning Conviction and Sentencing in Criminal Cases Involving Guns Powered by Compressed Gas and Airgun Pellets (Fa Shi [2018] No. 8). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/xwfbh/wsfbt/201803/t20180328_372604.shtml>; Supreme People's Court (2018). Understanding and Application of the "Official Reply". <https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/88472.html>
entries.notes: The key to non-prosecution in that case was establishing that they "had no knowing awareness." For an adult intentionally going online to buy steel-ball guns or airguns, claiming afterwards that they did not know it was a gun will rarely hold up. For penalties regarding carrying crossbows and controlled knives on one's person, see Section 26 of this chapter (Do not buy expandable batons, stun guns, or daggers for self-defense).

entries.title: Register drones under your real name after purchase, do not fly near airports, military zones, or city controlled airspace, and do not crack altitude limits
entries.cost: Real-name registration is free and takes just a few minutes. Before each flight, check official channels to verify whether the airspace where you plan to fly is controlled airspace.
entries.summary: Flying without real-name registration is punishable by a fine of up to 200 yuan; if the circumstances are serious, 2,000 to 20,000 yuan. Flying in controlled airspace without approval is punishable by a fine of up to 500 yuan; if the circumstances are serious, the drone is confiscated, plus a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 yuan. If the circumstances are relatively serious, administrative detention of 5 to 10 days can also be imposed. One person paid to crack the altitude limit, flew to nearly 3,000 meters to film cloud layers, posted it online, and was detained for 5 days.
entries.benefit: Flying without completing real-name registration warrants an order to rectify and can result in a fine of up to 200 yuan; if the circumstances are serious, a fine of 2,000 to 20,000 yuan. Flying micro, light, or small unmanned aerial vehicles in controlled airspace without approval warrants an order to cease flight and can result in a fine of up to 500 yuan. For this category, if the circumstances are serious, the drone will be confiscated alongside a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 yuan. Violating airspace management regulations with relatively serious circumstances leads to 5 to 10 days of administrative detention. Official Case: Li paid to crack the altitude limit, flew a drone to nearly 3,000 meters to film clouds, published the footage, and was detained for 5 days. Zhang cracked altitude limits and no-fly zone restrictions for others over 20 times, earning over 15,000 yuan. He was convicted of the crime of providing programs or tools for intruding into or illegally controlling computer information systems, sentenced to 6 months of fixed-term imprisonment suspended for 1 year, and fined (Nationwide, effective January 2024).
entries.sources: State Council, Central Military Commission (2023). Interim Regulation on the Flight Management of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (State Council Decree No. 761, Articles 10, 19, 47, 51). <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/content/202306/content_6888799.htm>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Article 46). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; Hubei Provincial Public Security Department (2026). Ministry of Public Security Releases Eight Typical Cases of Combating Illegal and Criminal Drone "Black Flights" According to Law (reprinted from People's Public Security Daily). <http://gat.hubei.gov.cn/bmdt/gayw/202602/t20260205_5870949.shtml>
entries.notes: Micro and light drones flying in suitable flight airspace do not require approval. Micro refers to those with an empty aircraft weight of less than 0.25 kilograms. Suitable flight airspace means areas outside of controlled airspace, whereas the vicinities of airports, military installations, and government agencies mostly belong to controlled airspace. The Ministry of Public Security's original page could not be opened when this section was written, so the reprint page from the Hubei Provincial Public Security Department was cited instead.

entries.title: Do not surreptitiously photograph others; do not install cameras in rented housing, homestays, or hotel rooms
entries.cost: Costs no money and takes no time. Do not secretly photograph others, and do not install cameras in rented homes, homestays, or hotel rooms.
entries.summary: Secretly photographing, peeping on, or disseminating the privacy of others carries administrative detention of up to 5 days or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan; if the circumstances are relatively serious, detention is 5 to 10 days. Using specialized equipment for secret filming resulting in serious consequences is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 2 years. Two individuals installed equipment in rooms across three hotels for remote secret recording, receiving sentences of 1 year and 3 months, and 1 year, respectively. Rooms occupied by others may not be photographed without consent.
entries.benefit: Peeping, surreptitiously photographing, eavesdropping, or disseminating the privacy of others is punishable by administrative detention of up to 5 days, or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. If the circumstances are relatively serious, detention is 5 to 10 days, with an optional concurrent fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Illegally using specialized equipment for eavesdropping or secret photography resulting in serious consequences is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 2 years. Specialized equipment for eavesdropping or secret photography refers to equipment dedicated to secret listening and secret filming. Official Case: Yan Ping and Yan Jian bought secret filming equipment online, installed it in multiple rooms across three hotels for remote secret photography, and were sentenced to 1 year and 3 months, and 1 year, respectively. Article 1033 of the Civil Code provides an additional layer: unless otherwise provided by law or expressly consented to by the individual, no person shall "enter, photograph, or peep into another person's private space such as residence or hotel room," nor "photograph, peep into, eavesdrop on, or disclose another person's private activities" (Nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Article 50). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law (amended in accordance with Amendment (XI) to the Criminal Law, Article 284). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People's Court (2024). Typical Cases on Punishing Crimes of Illegally Producing, Selling, and Using Eavesdropping and Secret Photographing Equipment in Accordance with Law (Case 2). <https://www.court.gov.cn/shenpan/xiangqing/449581.html>; National People's Congress (2020). Civil Code (Articles 1032, 1033). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202006/t20200602_463888.shtml>
entries.notes: Once secretly photographed material is sold or disseminated, it is handled under other crimes such as producing or selling obscene materials for profit; within the same batch of cases, there were 10-year sentences. Installing surveillance in one's own home that only captures one's own family with everyone's knowledge is not prohibited by the provisions—this is inferred from the statutory text. If the lens captures rooms where renters or guests reside, or photographs others' private activities, it falls squarely within the prohibitions of the Civil Code.

entries.title: Mahjong and poker can be played, but do not take cuts, do not act as the banker, do not organize games to collect money, and do not engage in online gambling
entries.cost: Costs no money. Small-stakes recreational card games among relatives and friends are fine. Do not take cuts from games, do not act as the banker, and do not organize games to collect money. The hard part is resisting taking over when someone is organizing one.
entries.summary: Playing cards for small stakes among relatives and friends is not governed by the law. Providing conditions for gambling games for the purpose of making money, or participating in gambling involving relatively large amounts of gambling funds, warrants administrative detention of up to 5 days or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Assembling a crowd to gamble for profit or making a living off gambling is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 3 years; opening a casino is punishable by up to 5 years. What constitutes a "relatively large amount of gambling funds" is determined locally by each region; there is no unified national figure.
entries.benefit: Providing convenient conditions for gambling for the purpose of making money, or participating in gambling where the gambling funds are relatively large, warrants administrative detention of up to 5 days, or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. If the circumstances are serious, administrative detention is 10 to 15 days, with a concurrent fine of 1,000 to 5,000 yuan. Gathering people to gamble for profit, or making a living off gambling, is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 3 years plus a fine. Opening a casino is punishable by fixed-term imprisonment of not more than 5 years plus a fine; if the circumstances are serious, 5 to 10 years (Nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Article 82). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law (amended in accordance with Amendment (XI) to the Criminal Law, Article 303). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2020). Amendment (XI) to the Criminal Law (Article 36, raising the prison term for opening a casino to not more than five years, and five to ten years). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/zdgz/202012/t20201227_503682.shtml>
entries.notes: There is no nationwide figure for what counts as a “relatively large amount of gambling funds”; each locality sets its own threshold, so this item receives only a B rating. Taking a cut from a gambling operation or collecting bets on behalf of an online gambling platform is often treated as operating a casino when cases are handled. The original text of the relevant judicial interpretation was not verified for this section. No official case was found either.

entries.title: Do not eat wild animals, buy or sell protected animals, or keep them as pets; do not dig up or trade wild orchids, Chinese arborvitae, or yews either
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Buy only pets from lawful sources that were bred in captivity. If you see wild orchids in the mountains, do not dig them up. Buy potted orchids and yews only if they were cultivated at a flower market or nursery.
entries.summary: If you eat an animal under key state protection, it will be confiscated and you will be fined 2 to 20 times its value. Buying, selling, or transporting rare or endangered animals carries a sentence of up to 5 years, or 5 to 10 years in serious cases. Buying and selling captive-bred pets generally is not a crime if breeding techniques are mature and breeding has reached a substantial scale; this does not cover animals caught in the wild. Most wild orchids in the mountains are protected. One person who dug up 3 plants intending to sell them was sentenced to short-term detention.
entries.benefit: If you eat a wild animal under key state protection, or buy one to eat, it will be confiscated and you will be fined 2 to 20 times its value. Breeding wild animals under key state protection without a permit leads to confiscation and a fine of 1 to 10 times their value. Illegally purchasing, transporting, or selling rare or endangered wild animals under key state protection or products made from them carries a sentence of up to 5 years and a fine. Serious cases under this provision carry 5 to 10 years; especially serious cases carry more than 10 years. Hunting, purchasing, transporting, or selling other terrestrial wild animals for consumption carries up to 3 years in serious cases. Official case: A breeder surnamed Wang and two others sold more than 40 captive-bred Fischer’s lovebirds, a species under second-class state protection, for a total of less than 400 yuan. In 2021, the procuratorate decided not to prosecute. Since 2022, the Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuratorate have made clear that when captive-breeding techniques are mature, breeding has reached a substantial scale, and the animals are bought, sold, or transported as pets, the conduct generally is not treated as a crime (nationwide). Wild plants are covered by a separate criminal offense. Illegally cutting down or damaging plants under key state protection, or purchasing, transporting, processing, or selling those plants or products made from them, falls under that offense. The sentence is up to 3 years and a fine, or 3 to 7 years in serious cases. A 2023 interpretation by the Supreme People’s Court set the thresholds. One wild plant under first-class state protection, two under second-class protection, or plants worth at least 20,000 yuan are enough for a conviction. Five first-class plants, ten second-class plants, or plants worth at least 200,000 yuan constitute a serious case. A buyer is covered only if they know the plants were dug up illegally. In the 2021 list, Chinese arborvitae and every species in the yew genus are first-class protected. Every species in the orchid genus is second-class protected, including Cymbidium goeringii, Cymbidium faberi, and Cymbidium tortisepalum. Within that genus, only the rabbit-ear orchid is absent from the list; Cymbidium insigne and Cymbidium wenshanense are first-class protected. Digging up a plant to transplant it at home is also prosecuted as illegal cutting, although the transplanting purpose is considered at sentencing. Cultivated plants are excluded, except for ancient and notable trees. Official cases: In 2022, a person in Nanzhao, Henan, dug up 3 wild orchids on a hillside and posted a video intending to sell them. He received 6 months of short-term detention, suspended for 10 months, and a 3,000-yuan fine. In Suizhou, Hubei, a group dug up more than 30,000 wild Cymbidium goeringii and Cymbidium faberi plants over more than two years. In 2025, one member received a sentence of 1 year and 7 months, suspended for 2 years (nationwide).
