A Small Parrot Case, a Major Livelihood Case. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/zdgz/202302/t20230211_601023.shtml>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2020). The Two Supreme Judicial Bodies Issue a Reply Clarifying the Scope of Precious Trees or Other Plants Under Key State Protection and the Understanding and Application of Illegal Transplantation of Plants Under Key State Protection (includes the original text of Article 344 of the Criminal Law and the full reply, Judicial Interpretation [2020] No. 2). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/xwfbh/wsfbt/202003/t20200320_456927.shtml>; Supreme People’s Court (2023). Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Hearing Criminal Cases Involving Damage to Forest Resources (Judicial Interpretation [2023] No. 8, Article 2). <https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/408822.html>; National Forestry and Grassland Administration and Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs (2021). List of Wild Plants Under Key State Protection (2021 Announcement No. 15, attachment). <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2021-09/09/content_5636409.htm>; Procuratorial Daily (2023). Nanzhao, Henan: Promoting the Establishment of a Care Mechanism for Wild Plants Involved in Cases. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/dfjcdt/202307/t20230720_622083.shtml>; Procuratorial Daily (2025). Zengdu District, Suizhou, Hubei: Cracking Down on the Illegal Digging and Livestream Sale of Wild Orchids. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/zdgz/202505/t20250513_695459.shtml>
entries.notes: “Generally not treated as a crime” refers only to the category of animals bred in captivity and kept as pets. It does not apply to animals caught in the wild or of unknown origin. Check the official list to see which animals are under key state protection. Checking before buying is easier than explaining afterward if something goes wrong. The same principle applies to plants: the rule concerns those growing naturally in their native habitats. Orchids sold in livestreams as “freshly dug on site” or “plants brought down from the mountains” are wild. Chinese arborvitae root carvings, bead bracelets, and similar products are also covered by this offense if someone buys or sells them knowing they came from plants dug up illegally.

entries.title: When collecting a debt, do not detain or confine the debtor, or follow them home and refuse to leave
entries.cost: Costs nothing. If someone owes you money and will not repay it, sue in court. For how to write an IOU, see Section 8, Item 18 (IOUs). The hard part is refraining from using force or following the person home when they refuse to pay.
entries.summary: Even if the debt is real, you cannot detain or confine the debtor: the law expressly says doing so to collect a debt is still treated as unlawful detention. If the conduct does not warrant a criminal sentence, the penalty is 10 to 15 days of detention and a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. If it constitutes the crime of unlawful detention, the sentence is up to 3 years; causing serious injury carries 3 to 10 years, and causing death carries more than 10 years. Sue in court to collect a debt.
entries.benefit: Unlawfully restricting another person’s freedom of movement, entering their home without authorization, or unlawfully searching their person carries 10 to 15 days of detention and a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. In less serious cases, the penalty is 5 to 10 days of detention and a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Unlawful detention carries up to 3 years of imprisonment, short-term detention (brief confinement), public surveillance (restrictions on movement without confinement), or deprivation of political rights. Causing serious injury carries 3 to 10 years; causing death carries more than 10 years. Detaining or confining someone to collect a debt is punished under the same provisions, even when the debt is real (nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Article 47). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment XI, Article 238). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>
entries.notes: “He really does owe me money” is no defense here. The law expressly says detaining or confining someone to collect a debt is treated as unlawful detention. The China Courts website has several cases in which people confined someone to collect a lawful debt and received sentences ranging from 7 months to 1 year. The website was inaccessible when this section was written, so those cases are not cited.

entries.title: Do not lend anyone your ID card, use someone else’s, or use another person’s documents to register, open a card account, or buy tickets
entries.cost: Costs nothing. If someone asks to borrow it, just refuse. If you must provide a photocopy, write on the copy exactly what it may be used for.
entries.summary: Lending, renting out, or transferring your ID card to someone else brings a warning and a fine of up to 200 yuan. Using someone else’s ID card or one obtained by deception brings a fine of 200 to 1,000 yuan or up to 10 days of detention. Using a fake document or another person’s document for situations requiring real-name identification, such as buying a train ticket or staying at a hotel, carries short-term detention or public surveillance in serious cases.
entries.benefit: Renting out, lending, or transferring your own resident ID card to someone else brings a warning and a fine of up to 200 yuan. Using someone else’s ID card or an ID card obtained by deception brings a fine of 200 to 1,000 yuan or up to 10 days of detention. Buying, selling, or using a forged or altered ID card falls in the same penalty range. In some situations, national rules require proof of identity. Using a forged or altered document, or another person’s document without authorization, in those situations is a crime in serious cases. The documents include ID cards, passports, social security cards, and driver’s licenses. The sentence is short-term detention (brief confinement) or public surveillance (restrictions on movement without confinement), together with or instead of a fine: you may be fined alongside the criminal sentence, or receive only a fine (nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2011). Resident Identity Card Law (2011 amendment, Articles 16 and 17). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/203777/index.html> (reposted by the Beijing Municipal Public Security Traffic Management Bureau); National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment XI, Article 280-1). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; State Council (2002). Regulations on the Administration of Internet Access Service Business Premises (State Council Order No. 363, Article 23). <http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2002/content_61788.htm>
entries.notes: If you lend out your ID card, it may be used to register a company or obtain a bank card. For the consequences of those two situations, see Section 8, Items 28 and 8 (Do Not Be a Nominal Legal Representative; Do Not Lend Your Bank Card to Anyone). Using another person’s ID card to buy a train ticket or stay at a hotel falls under what the law calls an “activity for which proof of identity must be provided.” No official case was found for this item. Use your own ID card at an internet café too. Internet cafés must check and register ID cards, retain the registration details and internet-use records for at least 60 days, and make them available to the public security and cultural authorities at any time. Whatever is done on the computer during that period is recorded under the name of the person whose ID card was used.

entries.title: Cooperate when police stop or take you away; do not push, hit, or grab a body camera, and be especially restrained if you have been drinking
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Do not use force at the scene. Raise any objection afterward by filing a complaint, applying for administrative reconsideration, or suing in court. The hard part is controlling your temper during those few minutes after being stopped, especially if you have been drinking.
entries.summary: Obstructing law enforcement at the scene brings a warning or a fine of up to 500 yuan; serious cases bring 5 to 10 days of detention. Using force against a police officer is a separate level of offense: biting, slapping, kicking, punching, grappling and throwing, or throwing objects counts as a violent assault on a police officer if it causes at least a minor injury, and carries up to 3 years. Using a firearm or a controlled knife, or driving a vehicle into an officer, carries 3 to 7 years. Ordinary resistance such as swinging your arms or pulling free does not count.
entries.benefit: Obstructing a state agency employee in the lawful performance of official duties brings a warning or a fine of up to 500 yuan. Serious cases bring 5 to 10 days of detention and may also bring a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. The penalty is heavier if the person obstructed is a people’s police officer. Violently assaulting a people’s police officer who is lawfully carrying out their duties carries up to 3 years. Using a firearm or a controlled knife, driving a vehicle into an officer, or acting in another way that seriously endangers the officer’s personal safety carries 3 to 7 years. Biting, slapping, kicking, punching, grappling and throwing, or throwing objects counts as a “violent assault” only if it causes at least a minor injury. Ordinary resistance such as swinging one’s arms, pulling free, or kicking one’s legs does not count (nationwide).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Article 61). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law Amendment XI (Article 31, namely Article 277, paragraph 5, of the Criminal Law). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/zdgz/202012/t20201227_503682.shtml>; National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment XI, Article 277). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2025). Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Handling Criminal Cases of Assaulting Police Officers (Supreme People’s Procuratorate Interpretive Document [2025] No. 1, Articles 1, 8, and 12). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/xwfbh/wsfbt/202501/t20250116_679579.shtml>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2021). In the First Month After Assaulting a Police Officer Became a Separate Criminal Offense, Procuratorial Organs Approved the Arrest of 405 People. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/xwfbh/wsfbh/202105/t20210517_518308.shtml>
entries.notes: The Supreme People’s Procuratorate reported in 2021 that, in the first month after assaulting a police officer became a separate criminal offense, arrests of 405 people were approved. Of 42 cases in Jiangsu, 47.6% arose from drunken disturbances. In 12 of the 16 cases in Hubei, the conduct went no further than punching, kicking, or biting. Using force against auxiliary police officers is handled as the crime of obstructing official duties. No official case setting out an individual’s circumstances was found for this item.

entries.title: If the other person is under 14, you cannot have sex with her; “she agreed” is no defense
entries.cost: Costs nothing. If you are unsure of the other person’s age, do not have sex.
entries.summary: If the other person is under 14, whether she agrees or not, the case is treated as rape with a heavier penalty; the basic sentence is 3 to 10 years. If she is under 12, you are always deemed to have “reason to know” her age. If she is 12 to 14 and her development, behavior, or clothing suggests she may be a girl under 14, yet you have sex with her, you are deemed to have “known.” Courts apply a very strict standard to claims that you truly did not know.
entries.benefit: Having sexual relations with a girl under 14 is treated as rape and punished more severely, with a basic sentence of 3 to 10 years. The Supreme People’s Court’s position is as follows: if force, threats, or other coercive means are used, it is rape regardless of whether you knew she was under 14. If no coercive means are used and she is under 12, you are always deemed to have had “reason to know.” If she is 12 to 14 and her physical development, speech and behavior, clothing, or other features suggest she may be a girl under 14, yet you have sex with her, you are deemed to have “known.” The exception for “truly not knowing” is applied very strictly (nationwide).
entries.sources: National People’s Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended by Criminal Law Amendment XI, Article 236). <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html>; Supreme People’s Court (2015). Reply to the Question “Must a Person Know That a Girl Is Under Fourteen for Sexual Relations with Her to Constitute a Crime?” <https://www.court.gov.cn/hudong/xiangqing/13363.html>
entries.notes: When this section was written, neither the original text of the opinion on handling criminal cases of sexual assault against minors issued by the Supreme People’s Court, Supreme People’s Procuratorate, and two ministries, nor the page containing the Supreme People’s Court’s 2003 reply, could be opened. The standard for determining “knowledge” is therefore cited from a reply on the Supreme People’s Court’s official website. The term used in the law is “girl under 14.” This item does not distinguish whether the person who acts is male or female. For how parents can teach children to prevent sexual assault, see Section 30, Item 19 (Recognizing Private Parts of the Body).

entries.title: Before hitting someone, add up the costs: detention, compensation, and a criminal sentence
entries.cost: Costs no money or time. The hard part is those few seconds before you strike.
entries.summary: The cost of hitting someone once: 5 to 10 days of detention plus a fine of 500 to 1,000 yuan. Causing a minor injury makes it a criminal case, carrying up to 3 years; causing a serious injury carries 3 to 10 years. Compensation is extra: one person broke three of another person’s ribs and paid 113,000 yuan in a settlement before avoiding prosecution. Another broke someone’s radius bone, paid no compensation, and received a 10-month sentence.
entries.benefit: Hitting or intentionally injuring someone brings 5 to 10 days of detention and a fine of 500 to 1,000 yuan. Attacking in a group; attacking a person with a disability, a pregnant woman, an older person, or a child; repeatedly attacking someone; or attacking several people on one occasion brings 10 to 15 days of detention and a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. Causing a minor injury constitutes the crime of intentional injury, carrying up to 3 years of imprisonment, short-term detention (brief confinement), or public surveillance (restrictions on movement without confinement). Causing a serious injury carries 3 to 10 years. Civil compensation must also cover medical expenses, lost income (earnings lost because the person could not work), nursing costs, transportation costs, a hospital meal allowance, and nutrition expenses. If the person becomes disabled, disability compensation is payable as well. Disability compensation is calculated using the previous year’s per capita disposable income of urban residents in the location of the court hearing the case, multiplied by 20 years. For an injured person over 60, the number of years decreases by one for each additional year of age; for someone over 75, it is calculated using 5 years. In 2022, procuratorial organs nationwide received more than 70,000 minor injury cases, most arising from disputes involving marriages, families, or neighbors, or from chance incidents. Typical cases published by the Supreme People’s Procuratorate: A person surnamed Lu broke three of another person’s ribs (grade-two minor injury) and paid 113,000 yuan in a settlement, which led to a decision not to prosecute. A person surnamed Shi broke another person’s radius bone (grade-two minor injury), paid no compensation, and was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment (nationwide; the Public Security Administration Punishments Law takes effect on January 1, 2026).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Articles 9 and 51). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; National People’s Congress (1997). Criminal Law (Article 234). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180206_364975.shtml>; Supreme People’s Court (amended 2022). Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Hearing Personal Injury Compensation Cases (Judicial Interpretation [2022] No. 14, Articles 6–12 and 15). <https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/357071.html>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate and Ministry of Public Security (2023). Guiding Opinions on Properly Handling Minor Injury Cases in Accordance with the Law. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/xwfbh/wsfbt/202303/t20230302_604352.shtml>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2023). Typical Cases of Procuratorial Organs Properly Handling Minor Injury Cases in Accordance with the Law. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/xwfbh/dxal/202303/t20230302_605116.shtml>
entries.notes: For how to avoid conflict, why striking first puts you at a disadvantage, and the limits of lawful self-defense, see Section 8, Item 10 (Conflict and Lawful Self-Defense). For the costs of attacking someone to vent anger, see Section 8, Items 12 to 14. The public security authorities may mediate fights arising from private disputes when the circumstances are relatively minor. If you cause a minor injury, agreeing on compensation with the other person and actually paying it can lead to a lighter sentence or even no prosecution, but you must pay the full agreed amount. The degree of injury that counts as minor injury is determined by an assessment standard, which was not verified for this section. Lost income and nursing costs are calculated from actual income and the number of days affected; there is no uniform figure.

entries.title: If you cannot raise a child after birth, registration with the civil affairs department is the only lawful route: taking money to give the child to someone else may be prosecuted as child trafficking, while abandoning the child is the crime of abandonment
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Apply for adoption registration with a civil affairs department at county level or above. You must submit documents and wait for review and an adoption assessment, so the process takes some time.
entries.summary: If you cannot raise the child, there is a way forward, but only one lawful route: register the adoption with the civil affairs department. The adoptive relationship is established only on the date of registration. Privately giving a child to someone else, especially if you receive money, can turn “placing a child for adoption” into the crime of trafficking in children, which carries a minimum sentence of five years. Abandoning a child or refusing to support one, when the circumstances are serious, is the crime of abandonment, punishable by up to five years.
entries.benefit: Article 240 of China’s Criminal Law: “Whoever traffics in women or children shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of five to ten years and fined.” Where aggravating circumstances apply, the sentence is at least ten years’ imprisonment or life imprisonment, plus a fine or confiscation of property. “Where the circumstances are especially serious, the offender shall be sentenced to death and have their property confiscated.” Article 17 of the Opinions on Punishing Crimes of Trafficking in Women and Children in Accordance with the Law explains how to distinguish selling one’s biological child from an informal adoption placement. The deciding question is “whether the person acted for the purpose of making an illegal profit.” In other words, did they intend to make money from it? Three situations can be treated as selling one’s biological child and prosecuted as trafficking in women or children. The first is “using childbirth as a means of making an illegal profit and selling the child immediately after birth.” The second is “knowing that the other party has no intention of raising the child, or giving no consideration at all to whether the other party intends to raise the child, and ‘giving’ the child to that person in exchange for money.” The third is “‘giving’ the child to someone in exchange for a large sum of money that plainly does not qualify as ‘nutrition expenses’ or a ‘thank-you payment.’” Conversely, privately placing a child for adoption because of genuine financial hardship, without intending to make money and while accepting only a small amount for nutrition expenses or as a thank-you payment, is an informal adoption placement and is not prosecuted as trafficking. Now consider Article 261 of the Criminal Law: “Whoever has a duty to support an elderly, young, sick, or other person unable to live independently and refuses to provide that support, where the circumstances are serious, shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of up to five years, criminal detention, or public surveillance.” Article 1094 of China’s Civil Code provides that only three kinds of people or institutions may place a child for adoption: the guardians of an orphan, child welfare institutions, and biological parents who cannot raise their child because of special difficulties. Article 1105: “An adoption shall be registered with the civil affairs department of a people’s government at or above the county level. The adoptive relationship is established on the date of registration.”
entries.sources: National People’s Congress (1997). Criminal Law (Articles 240 and 261). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180206_364975.shtml>; Supreme People’s Court, Supreme People’s Procuratorate, Ministry of Public Security, and Ministry of Justice (2010). Opinions on Punishing Crimes of Trafficking in Women and Children in Accordance with the Law (Fa Fa [2010] No. 7, Article 17). Official website of the Supreme People’s Court <https://www.court.gov.cn/fabu/xiangqing/977.html>; National People’s Congress (2020). Civil Code (Articles 1094 and 1105). Full text of the adoption part republished by the Yancheng Municipal People’s Government <https://xxgk.yczf.gov.cn/xzf/ycmzj/fdzdgknr/fgwj_41995/202112/t20211203_1506640.shtml>
entries.notes: Whether to have a child is beyond the scope of this entry. Once the child is born, following this order makes things easier. First, give birth in a hospital; see Section 27 for prenatal checkups and hospital delivery. The Medical Certificate of Birth is a prerequisite for all the procedures that follow. Second, if you want to place the child for adoption, contact a civil affairs department at or above the county level directly. Do not go through a middleman. Once money changes hands, the legal nature of the arrangement may change. During the first year after childbirth, if you have “thoughts of harming yourself or the child,” treat it as an emergency. For the list of situations during pregnancy and after childbirth that require an immediate hospital visit, see Section 27, Item 7. The checkup 42 days after childbirth is also a screening for postpartum depression; see Section 27, Item 16. If you have suicidal thoughts, call China’s 12356 hotline; see Section 1, Item 25. This entry has no case example: official representative cases involving trafficking in one’s biological child were not checked individually in this round, so only the statutory provisions and the original text of the Opinions are cited.

entries.title: Do not stage an accident or exaggerate losses to claim insurance money: it is insurance fraud, and people who testify for you, repair your car, or assess your claim can be implicated too
entries.cost: It costs no money or time. Just do not do it.
entries.summary: Fabricating an accident or exaggerating losses to obtain an insurance payout is insurance fraud. If the amount is relatively large, the sentence is up to five years, plus a fine of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan. People who deliberately issue false documents by testifying, appraising, or assessing property for you are convicted as accomplices. A car repairer who agrees with you to falsify a claim is treated as a joint offender. In one case in Xuancheng, Anhui, eight people received sentences of two to four years and were each fined 10,000 yuan.
entries.benefit: Article 198 of China’s Criminal Law lists five situations. (1) A policyholder deliberately invents an insured subject: something supposedly insured that does not exist at all. (2) A policyholder, insured person, or beneficiary invents a false cause for an insured event that occurred, or exaggerates the extent of the loss. (3) Someone fabricates an insured event that never occurred. (4) A policyholder or insured person deliberately causes an insured event involving property loss. (5) A policyholder or beneficiary deliberately causes the insured person’s death, disability, or illness. Where the amount involved is relatively large, the penalty is fixed-term imprisonment of up to five years or criminal detention, plus a fine of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan. Where the amount is huge or there are other serious circumstances, the penalty is five to ten years, plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan. Where the amount is especially huge or there are other especially serious circumstances, the penalty is at least ten years, plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan or confiscation of property. The final paragraph of this article covers people who help: appraisers of insured events, witnesses, and property assessors. If they deliberately issue false supporting documents that enable someone else to commit insurance fraud, they are treated as accomplices and convicted along with the person making the fraudulent claim. Car repairers are not among those three categories, but a repairer who agrees with you to falsify a claim is treated as a joint offender. Article 25 of the Criminal Law: “A joint crime is an intentional crime committed jointly by two or more persons.” In a 2021 briefing, Beijing’s Changping District People’s Court said that motor vehicle insurance fraud cases it had concluded since 2019 were “predominantly joint crimes, with auto repair shops a key industry involved in the offenses.” Article 27 of China’s Insurance Law: If someone falsely claims that an insured event occurred when it did not, the insurer has the right to terminate the contract without refunding premiums. If someone uses forged or altered supporting materials, invents a false cause for an accident, or exaggerates the extent of a loss, the insurer need not pay the overstated portion. Payouts already made must be returned or compensated for. Case: In the case involving Zhang Mousong in Xuancheng, Anhui, Wang Mouxin and seven others were sentenced to between four and two years in prison for insurance fraud, and each was fined 10,000 yuan. The case also exposed a fraudulent lawsuit. The insurer assessed the loss at 20,000 yuan. A party forged a vehicle transfer agreement to establish standing to sue, and the court awarded more than 70,000 yuan. That civil judgment, which had already taken effect, was overturned on retrial on September 26, 2019. The Measures for Anti-Insurance Fraud Work require risk information to be checked at both ends: when policies are sold and when claims are paid (underwriting and claims handling). They also call for exploring the establishment of an industry anti-fraud information platform covering multiple types of insurance and an anti-fraud intelligence center. These platforms screen pooled data for suspected fraud, and leads are passed to industry associations, anti-fraud organizations, and insurers for verification. Suspected crimes must be reported promptly to the public security authorities. China’s National Financial Regulatory Administration and its local offices must establish and improve mechanisms linking administrative law enforcement with criminal justice. Those mechanisms involve the public security authorities, people’s procuratorates, and people’s courts (nationwide; issued July 31, 2024).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress. Criminal Law of the People’s Republic of China (consolidated text as amended by Criminal Law Amendment XI), Article 198. <https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff808181796a636a0179822a19640c92>; National People’s Congress (1997). Criminal Law (Article 25, unchanged by subsequent amendments). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180206_364975.shtml>; Beijing Changping District People’s Court (2021-11-23). Changping Court Briefing on Motor Vehicle Insurance Fraud Crimes (Beijing Courts website). <https://bjgy.bjcourt.gov.cn/article/detail/2021/11/id/6385519.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (amended 2015). Insurance Law of the People’s Republic of China, Article 27. <https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=2c909fdd678bf17901678bf7c4060811>; National Financial Regulatory Administration (2024). Notice on Issuing the Measures for Anti-Insurance Fraud Work. <https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2024/issue_11586/202409/content_6975080.html>; Anhui Provincial People’s Procuratorate, republishing Legal Daily (2020-01-13). Wife-Murder Insurance Fraud Exposes Another Case Within the Case. <http://www.ah.jcy.gov.cn/jczt/jjslhyqkjc/mtjj/202001/t20200113_2758841.shtml>
entries.notes: The following practices, which some people think are harmless, all fall within those five categories: asking a repair shop to “claim a little extra” after a minor accident; including old damage in the new claim; arranging a collision with a friend and then reporting it; or inventing an accident that never happened. For how to buy car insurance, see Section 5, Item 26 (buy enough third-party liability coverage). Deliberately causing a family member’s death after taking out insurance on them expressly requires punishment for multiple crimes under the law; see Section 8, Item 38 (insuring family members). China’s medical insurance operates under a different set of rules. Using a medical insurance card to buy health products and cash out the benefit is insurance fraud; see the notes to Section 5, Item 13.

entries.title: Do not sell your organs or help someone find a donor: a kidney seller gets just over 20,000 yuan, while the same kidney is resold for 200,000 yuan; the proceeds are confiscated and the fine is 10 to 20 times the transaction amount
entries.cost: It costs no money or time. Just do not do it.
entries.summary: A living person may donate an organ only to a spouse, a direct blood relative, or a collateral blood relative within three generations. Buying or selling organs is illegal. In one Beijing case, the person selling a kidney received just over 20,000 yuan, while the same kidney was sold to a patient for 180,000 to 220,000 yuan. The proceeds of the sale are confiscated, and an additional fine of 10 to 20 times the transaction amount is imposed. For the physical cost of having a kidney removed, see Section 1, Item 35 (the remaining kidney does the work of two).
entries.benefit: Article 5 of China’s Regulations on Human Organ Donation and Transplantation: “No organization or individual may buy or sell human organs in any form or engage in activities connected with the buying or selling of human organs.” Article 10: “No organization or individual may obtain a living organ from a citizen under the age of 18 for transplantation.” Article 11: “Recipients of living organs are limited to the living donor’s spouse, direct blood relatives, or collateral blood relatives within three generations.” Article 37 sets out the penalties for buying and selling human organs. Such transactions and related activities are investigated and dealt with by the health department of a local people’s government at or above the county level. First, the illegal proceeds are confiscated: all the money made from the transaction is taken away. Then a fine of 10 to 20 times the transaction amount is imposed. Medical personnel who participate have their licenses revoked and are permanently barred from providing medical and health services. If the conduct constitutes a crime, criminal responsibility is pursued according to law (nationwide; effective May 1, 2024, when the former Regulations on Human Organ Transplantation were repealed). Article 234-1 of the Criminal Law: “Whoever organizes others to sell human organs shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of up to five years and fined; where the circumstances are serious, the sentence shall be at least five years’ imprisonment, plus a fine or confiscation of property.” Three other situations are prosecuted and punished under Articles 234 and 232 of the Criminal Law. The first is removing someone’s organ without their consent. The second is removing an organ from a person under 18. The third is forcing or deceiving someone into donating an organ. These are treated as intentional injury or intentional homicide. Case one: In the final judgment issued by Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People’s Court on August 20, 2014, in the case of Zheng Wei and 14 others, 51 kidneys were involved, with more than 10.34 million yuan at stake. The people selling kidneys (donors) “received only 20,000 to 25,000 yuan in payment.” The prices paid by the patients waiting for kidneys (recipients) “used to be 180,000 or 190,000 yuan for one kidney, and later were 210,000 or 220,000 yuan.” The kidney removals took place in a small four-story building rented for 7,500 yuan a month. The group’s head nurse testified that it was “filthy and disorderly, without even resuscitation equipment.” Organizer Zheng Wei was sentenced to 12 years in prison for organizing the sale of human organs; the other 14 received sentences ranging from three and a half to nine years. Case two: the “teenager sells kidney to buy an Apple phone” case published by the Supreme People’s Procuratorate. Seventeen-year-old Wang had his right kidney removed in Chenzhou on the evening of April 28, 2011. The operation took place in a department contracted out to individuals inside a hospital that lacked transplant qualifications. On discharge on May 2, he received 22,000 yuan. The recipient paid the intermediary 150,000 yuan and US$10,000, and the principal offender made more than 56,000 yuan. After the operation, Wang had impaired kidney function; “his injuries constituted serious injury and a level-three disability.”

Regulations on Human Organ Donation and Transplantation (State Council Order No. 767, Articles 5, 8, 10, 11, 23, 28, 29, and 37). <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202312/content_6920196.htm>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress. Criminal Law of the People’s Republic of China (consolidated text as amended by Criminal Law Amendment XI), Article 234-1. <https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff808181796a636a0179822a19640c92>; Supreme People’s Procuratorate (2012-04-09). “Teenager Sells Kidney to Buy an Apple Phone” Case Brought to Court. <https://www.spp.gov.cn/gs/201204/t20120409_34342.shtml>; republished on the official website of the Langfang Intermediate People’s Court, Hebei Province (2014-09-02). Final Judgment in China’s Largest Kidney Trafficking Case: Organizer Profited Ten Million Yuan from 51 Kidney Removals. <https://lfzy.hebeicourt.gov.cn/article/detail/2014/09/id/1430881.shtml>
entries.notes: The person who benefits is you. On the surface, the deal looks like “getting 20,000 yuan in one go.” In reality, it is trading an organ for a phone. The expert assessment in the teenager’s kidney-sale case found serious injury and a level-three disability; a few months of rest will not make that go away. In that case, prosecutors found that five defendants had violated the second paragraph of Article 234 of the Criminal Law and charged them with intentional injury. One reason was that the medical personnel removed Wang’s right kidney without first checking whether the “donor” was a minor. If the same thing happened today, those who recruited people would be prosecuted for organizing the sale of human organs. Removing an organ from a person under 18 is still prosecuted and punished as intentional injury under Article 234. Black-market intermediaries perform operations in rented homes or borrowed premises. In the Beijing case, the kidney-removal site did not even have resuscitation equipment. Lawful living donation is performed at a hospital qualified to carry out transplants, after review by the hospital’s ethics committee. Before surgery, doctors must explain the risks and obtain signed informed consent; afterward, the hospital must also conduct follow-up care (Articles 23, 28, and 29 of the Regulations). Black-market intermediaries bypass all of this, making it hard to find someone to hold responsible if complications arise; that sentence is the author’s inference from the Regulations. If you truly want to donate to a relative, follow the route in Article 11. Under Article 8 of the Regulations, donation is voluntary and unpaid. Donation of organs after death is also unpaid and is outside the scope of this entry. For the physical cost of having one kidney removed, see Section 1, Item 35 (the remaining kidney does the work of two). If you are so short of money that you are considering selling an organ, first look at the safety-net options in Section 7 (unemployment insurance, temporary assistance, and minimum living allowances). For the traps of online loans and loans obtained with “dressed-up paperwork,” see Item 6 of this section.

entries.title: Do not pay for sex: the standard penalty is 10 to 15 days of detention, not just a fine
entries.cost: It costs no money or time. Just do not do it.
entries.summary: If caught, you do not simply pay a fine and leave. The standard penalty written into the law is 10 to 15 days of detention, with a possible additional fine of up to 5,000 yuan. Only when the circumstances are relatively minor is the penalty up to five days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Also, knowingly paying for sex when you have syphilis or gonorrhea is a crime punishable by up to five years.
entries.benefit: Article 78 of China’s Public Security Administration Punishments Law: A person who engages in prostitution or pays for sex shall be detained for 10 to 15 days and may also be fined up to 5,000 yuan. Where the circumstances are relatively minor, the penalty is detention for up to five days or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Soliciting customers for prostitution in a public place is punishable by detention for up to five days or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Article 79: A person who lures, harbors, or introduces another person into prostitution shall be detained for 10 to 15 days and may also be fined up to 5,000 yuan. Where the circumstances are relatively minor, the penalty is detention for up to five days or a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. Article 87: Personnel of hotels, food service businesses, cultural and entertainment businesses, taxi businesses, and similar establishments who tip off offenders while public security authorities investigate prostitution or the purchase of sex, or who otherwise provide conditions for those activities, shall be detained for 10 to 15 days. Article 360 of the Criminal Law addresses the crime of spreading a sexually transmitted disease: A person who engages in prostitution or pays for sex while knowing that they have syphilis, gonorrhea, or another serious sexually transmitted disease shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of up to five years, criminal detention, or public surveillance, and fined (nationwide; the Public Security Administration Punishments Law took effect on January 1, 2026).
entries.sources: Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Articles 78, 79, and 87). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml>; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress. Criminal Law of the People’s Republic of China (consolidated text as amended by Criminal Law Amendment XI), Article 360. <https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index.html> (republished by the Beijing Municipal Public Security Traffic Management Bureau); Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (2015). Criminal Law Amendment IX (Article 43, deleting the second paragraph of Article 360 of the Criminal Law). <https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180205_364562.shtml>
entries.notes: The detention here is administrative detention: you go to a detention center, rather than paying a fine and leaving. Introducing someone to a sex worker or providing a venue is punished as heavily as paying for sex yourself; that is what Article 79 covers. People working at hotels or KTV venues who tip off customers are likewise detained for 10 to 15 days under Article 87. Article 360 of the Criminal Law originally had a second paragraph on the “crime of paying for sex with a young girl,” which Criminal Law Amendment IX deleted in 2015. Such conduct is now punished more severely as rape; see Item 18 of this section (you cannot have sexual relations with someone under 14). Signs advertising “at-home health care” or “massage therapy” do not change the nature of the activity; it is judged by what actually happens. For the risks of sexually transmitted diseases and HIV, see Section 1, Item 30 (use a condom throughout sex) and Section 13, Item 38 (get post-exposure medication within 72 hours). For precautions concerning entertainment venues themselves, see Section 22.

entries.title: Translating comics into Chinese, reposting films and TV shows, sharing cloud-drive files, and distributing pirated ebooks infringe copyright even if you charge nothing; running ads or charging membership fees can lead to a prison sentence
entries.cost: It costs no money. You can read or watch what you bought or downloaded yourself, and translate it for your own amusement; just do not post it online for everyone to see. Do not run a resource site or sharing group with ads or membership fees, and do not sell cloud-drive links. The hard part is resisting the urge to repost things when “everyone else is sharing them.”
entries.summary: Translating someone else’s work and posting it without permission, or uploading their work to the internet, is copyright infringement even if you charge nothing. You may have to take it down and pay compensation. Once you run ads or charge membership fees, you are acting to make money. If you earn 30,000 yuan, distribute 500 works, or reach 1,000 members, that is enough for a criminal sentence, with a maximum of 10 years. The head of the Renren Yingshi subtitling group was sentenced to three years and six months.
entries.benefit:
First, civil liability. Among the rights granted to authors by copyright law is the right of translation, which is the right to convert a work from one language into another. There is also the right of dissemination via information networks, which is the right to make a work available on the Internet so the public can access it at any time and from anywhere. Translating another person's work without permission constitutes infringement. Uploading a work to the Internet without permission also constitutes infringement. Infringers must cease the infringement and compensate for damages. Only when using another person's already published work for personal study, research, or appreciation is permission not required and payment not needed. As for the amount of compensation, it is first calculated based on the right holder's actual losses or the money you made. Where both are difficult to calculate, the court determines it between 500 yuan and 5,000,000 yuan. For intentional infringement with serious circumstances, the court may award punitive damages of 1 to 5 times. The reasonable expenses incurred by the right holder to stop the infringement must also be compensated by you.

Next, criminal liability. The prerequisite under Article 217 of the Criminal Law is "for the purpose of making a profit." Putting another person's work on the Internet for the public to view without permission in order to make money constitutes the crime of copyright infringement once it reaches the threshold. The sentence is fixed-term imprisonment of up to 3 years, concurrently with a fine, or a fine alone. If the amount is huge or the circumstances are particularly serious, the sentence is 3 to 10 years of fixed-term imprisonment along with a fine. What counts as being for the purpose of making money: in addition to selling, running paid advertisements on webpages counts, and charging registration fees or other fees through a membership system also counts. The service fees, membership fees, and advertising fees collected all count as illegal gains. Reaching any one of the following thresholds is sufficient to constitute the crime:
- Illegal gains of 30,000 yuan or more.
- An illegal business volume of 50,000 yuan or more; in the YYeTs (Renren Yingshi) case, this was calculated as the total revenue from membership fees, advertising fees, and hard drive sales.
- Disseminating others' works on the Internet totaling 500 pieces (works) or more.
- Being downloaded 10,000 times or more, or clicked 100,000 times or more.
- Dissemination through a membership system with 1,000 or more registered members.
- If none of these individual thresholds are reached, but two items each reach more than half of their respective thresholds, it also counts.
Reaching 10 times these numbers moves into the 3 to 10 year sentencing tier. Fines are generally 1 to 10 times the illegal gains.

Official Case 1: Liang Yongping and others downloaded unauthorized movies and TV dramas from overseas websites, organized people to translate them and create subtitles, and then uploaded them. These videos were placed on the "YYeTs Subtitle Group" website and client app for people to watch online and download. There were 32,824 unauthorized audiovisual works on the site, and over 6.83 million members. From January 2018 to January 2021, they collected over 2.7 million yuan in membership fees and over 8.8 million yuan in advertising fees. By selling external hard drives loaded with copied movies and TV dramas, they earned another 1 million-plus yuan. The website displayed "donation" QR codes; donating unlocked membership privileges. Procuratorial authorities determined that this was simply collecting membership fees under a different name. On November 22, 2021, Liang Yongping was sentenced to 3 years and 6 months of imprisonment and fined 1.5 million yuan. The other 14 individuals were sentenced to terms ranging from 1 year and 6 months to 3 years, all with probation, and fined 40,000 to 350,000 yuan.

Official Case 2: A certain Ke used web crawler software to scrape the playback links of over 50,000 movies and TV dramas and put them on his own website and app for free viewing. He ran open-screen launch ads, charged by impressions, and earned over 350,000 yuan. In 2023, he was sentenced to 3 years of imprisonment with a 4-year probation and fined 400,000 yuan.

Official Case 3: A certain Huang rented servers at his home and set up a music download forum. He uploaded over 100,000 songs to 18 cloud drives and posted links on the forum. Members had to purchase forum currency through top-ups to obtain the links and extraction codes. Member top-ups totaled over 500,000 yuan. In 2023, he was sentenced to 3 years of imprisonment with a 4-year probation and fined 550,000 yuan (Nationwide; judicial interpretation effective from April 26, 2025).

Consulate-General of the People's Republic of China in Nagasaki Reminds Chinese Citizens in Japan to Abide by Copyright Laws. <http://nagasaki.china-consulate.gov.cn/chn/tzgg/201802/t20180208_4564322.htm>
entries.notes: The beneficiary is yourself. Buying it for yourself to watch and translating it for yourself to read are within the scope permitted by the statutory provisions. The dividing line lies in "putting it on the Internet for everyone to view." Subtitle groups and scanlation/localization groups that do not charge money do not reach the threshold for the crime of copyright infringement, because this crime requires the purpose of making a profit. However, civil infringement is still fully established; right holders can demand deletion and monetary compensation. In Japan, doing this without charging money can also be a crime. In February 2018, several Chinese citizens in Japan were arrested on suspicion of violating Japanese copyright law. The Consulate-General of the People's Republic of China in Nagasaki subsequently issued a reminder: translating, publishing, and disseminating works without authorization, even if not for profit, may violate the law. Once you display advertisements, open memberships, or exchange "donations" for membership privileges, you fall into the bracket of doing so to make money. In the YYeTs case, participants who only did translation and proofreading had a low degree of involvement, and the police obtained their testimony as witnesses. The Supreme People's Procuratorate explicitly noted in this case that those who initiated, divided money, and managed the platform must be strictly prosecuted. Hired accomplices may be treated leniently, and temporarily recruited individuals whose circumstances are minor may be exempted from criminal liability. The three old criminal judicial interpretations on intellectual property from 2004, 2007, and 2020 are abolished as of April 26, 2025. The 2011 three-department Opinions were not named for abolition; where inconsistent with the new interpretation, the new interpretation prevails. For instance, the click-count threshold was changed from 50,000 times to 100,000 times. For another risk regarding publishing fan fiction and derivative creations, see Item 25 of this section (Writing Fan Fiction). For printing others' artwork on merchandise for sale, see Section 12, Item 21 (Licensing Required for Graphic Designs). For what to do when running your own platform and receiving an infringement notice from a right holder, see Section 26, Item 9 (Receiving an Infringement Notice). For creating and selling crack patches and keygens, see Section 11, Item 20 (Crack Patches, Keygens).

entries.title: If publishing fan fiction or derivative creations or selling them for money, first obtain permission from the original work, or replace the borrowed character names and relationships with your own
entries.cost: Free. Before submitting for publication or selling for money, negotiate a license with the right holder of the original work first. If negotiations fail, replace the borrowed character names, personalities, and interpersonal relationships with your own. In the book title, subtitle, and promotional slogans, do not ride on the fame of the original work either.
entries.summary: Even if fan fiction only borrows character names, personalities, and relationships, publishing it can still be ruled as infringement. Jiang Nan's novel *There They Were* (*Ci Jian De Shao Nian*) borrowed over 60 characters from Louis Cha (Jin Yong). The second instance court ordered him to pay 1.68 million yuan in damages, plus 200,000 yuan in expenses. After a 9-year legal battle, it finally ended in a settlement, with him agreeing not to reprint it in its original form. As for how free fan fiction written just for fun is treated, the court stated that it requires specific case-by-case analysis.
entries.benefit: Jiang Nan's novel *There They Were* (*Ci Jian De Shao Nian*) used character names from Louis Cha's novels, such as Guo Jing, Huang Rong, Qiao Feng, and Linghu Chong. The book tells the story of these individuals on a university campus. When published in 2002, its subtitle was "The University Life of the Condor Heroes." By the time of the lawsuit, multiple editions of this book had been released, with over a million copies in circulation. In 2016, Louis Cha sued Jiang Nan and the publishers, seeking 5 million yuan in compensation. The first-instance court held that it did not constitute copyright infringement. The reasoning was: separated from the specific plots, character names, relationships, and personalities alone can hardly be considered protectable specific expressions. However, the first-instance court determined that Jiang Nan's borrowing of the original work's fame to attract readers constituted unfair competition. Based on 30% of the historical royalties of 5.6 million yuan, it ordered compensation of 1.68 million yuan, plus 200,000 yuan in attorney fees. The second instance was heard by the Guangzhou Intellectual Property Court, which reversed the decision to find copyright infringement. The second-instance court held that the plotlines of the two works were not substantially similar, meaning the plot was not plagiarized. However, the "ensemble character gallery" formed by combining over 60 characters—with their names, personalities, relationships, and backgrounds—was Louis Cha's own selection and arrangement. This belongs to the expression protected by copyright law; Jiang Nan infringed on the copyright of four of Louis Cha's novels. Intentionally tying the subtitle to *The Legend of the Condor Heroes* additionally constituted unfair competition. The second-instance court ordered Jiang Nan to cease unfair competition, publish a statement in newspapers to eliminate the adverse impact, and pay 1.68 million yuan in damages and 200,000 yuan in reasonable expenses. Two publishing and distribution companies bore joint and several liability for 330,000 yuan of that amount, meaning that portion had to be paid jointly. The second instance did not order an injunction to stop the infringement, but required that for any future reprints, 30% of the reprint royalty income must be paid to the right holder of the original work. Following the second instance, both parties applied for retrial to the Higher People's Court of Guangdong Province. On September 19, 2025, under the auspices of the Guangdong High Court, the parties reached a settlement. In the settlement, the parties agreed not to characterize the matter as "plagiarism." Jiang Nan acknowledged that when writing, he lacked copyright legal knowledge and failed to obtain Louis Cha's adaptation permission beforehand, causing harm to Louis Cha. Jiang Nan agreed not to reprint the book in its original form. In any future reprints, he will no longer use original character names and related content from Louis Cha's works. The parties confirmed that the subtitle constituted unfair competition. Jiang Nan had already paid the compensation awarded in the second instance. Once the mediation agreement was signed and received, the original first- and second-instance judgments ceased to have legal effect. The defendant in another case was Zhang Muye, the author of *Ghost Blows Out the Light* (*Gui Chui Deng*), pen name Tianxia Bachang. In 2006, he transferred all property rights in the copyright of this novel series to Shanghai Xuanting Entertainment Information Technology Co., Ltd. Later, he authorized the publication of a new book, *The Mojin Xiaowei*, which used the character names, character relationships, and tomb-robbing rules from *Ghost Blows Out the Light*. The cover of the new book used the movie poster of *Mojin: The Lost Legend*, a film adapted from *Ghost Blows Out the Light*. Xuanting Company sued, demanding 20 million yuan in compensation. The Shanghai Pudong Court held that the new book had its own independent plot and did not constitute copyright infringement. However, the cover misled readers into believing the book was related to the original work of *Mojin: The Lost Legend*, constituting false advertising. The court ordered two publishing and distribution companies to pay 900,000 yuan, with the publishing house bearing joint and several liability for 600,000 yuan of that, which was upheld in the second instance. Statutorily, the right of adaptation is the right to modify a work and create an original new work. Using a work by means of adaptation, translation, annotation, etc. without the permission of the copyright owner entails civil liabilities such as ceasing the infringement and compensating for losses (Nationwide).

(reprinted from *Legal System and News*, first issue of July 2023). <https://www.gipc.gov.cn/front/content.action?id=7b7cb9a7b2cc45f286199fd427fc6b1f>; Higher People's Court of Guangdong Province (2025). The "Louis Cha v. Jiang Nan" Copyright and Unfair Competition Dispute Case Reached Settlement in Guangdong. <https://www.gdcourts.gov.cn/xwzx/fayuanxinmeiti/content/post_1843458.html>; National Copyright Administration (2020). Top Ten Copyright Typical Cases of Shanghai in 2019 Released (released by Shanghai Copyright Bureau, Case 6: "Ghost Blows Out the Light" Copyright Infringement and Unfair Competition Dispute Case). <https://www.ncac.gov.cn/xxfb/ywxx/202004/t20200430_47269.html>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2020). Copyright Law (2020 Amendment, Article 3; Article 10, Paragraph 1, Item 14; Article 52, Item 6; Article 54). <http://www.npc.gov.cn/npc/c2/c30834/202011/t20201119_308796.html>
entries.notes: The beneficiary is yourself. Rated Grade B because the legal boundaries of fan fiction have no final consensus yet. This case had different conclusions in its two instances and ultimately concluded with a mediation agreement, leaving neither judgment in effect. In an interview, the presiding judge of the Guangdong High Court stated that the settlement agreement binds only the parties to this case. Whether fan fiction constitutes infringement "requires concrete analysis based on specific circumstances, and cannot be generalized." The judge provided a three-step evaluation order: First, see whether what the two works share is an abstract idea or a specific expression. Next, see whether those expressions were original to the author of the original work. Finally, see whether it falls under non-infringing situations such as fair use. Therefore, merely borrowing a genre or a world setting carries a different risk compared to borrowing character names, personalities, and relationships as an entire system. For fan fiction posted online for free, this book found no official cases with court rulings. Nor is there an exception in copyright law stating that "it does not count as infringement if you don't charge money." Process costs must be factored in: this case took 9 years from filing in July 2016 to the settlement in September 2025. It went through first instance, second instance, and retrial review, and Louis Cha himself passed away during the second instance. Even after an original author sells their copyright, writing a sequel themselves can still get them sued by the buyer, which was the case for Tianxia Bachang. In copyright litigation, reasonable expenses incurred by the winning party to stop the infringement can be included in compensation; the 200,000 yuan awarded in the first instance of this case was attorney fees. For the risks of scanlating, re-uploading, and sharing others' works, see Item 24 of this section (Scanlating Comics, Re-uploading Movies and TV Shows).

entries.title: Do not buy expandable batons, stun guns, daggers, or pepper spray to carry on your person for self-defense; keeping them in your car also counts as carrying
entries.cost: Free. Leave items you have already bought at home; do not carry them outside, and do not put them in your car. If you actually encounter an incident, back away and call the police first; strike back only if you cannot escape.
entries.summary: If controlled knives such as daggers and switchblades are discovered while carrying them outside, you may be detained for up to 5 days. Carrying them into stations, shopping malls, or buses carries 5 to 10 days of detention. Police batons may only be possessed by police officers; if held by individuals, they are confiscated, and you may also be detained. Pulling them out and using them in a real encounter also easily puts you at a disadvantage: someone was punched once with bare hands, stabbed the person with a knife hidden in advance, and was sentenced to 4 years for excessive defense.
entries.benefit: First, consider Article 38 of the Public Security Administration Punishment Law. Illegally carrying controlled instruments prescribed by the state, such as crossbows and daggers, results in administrative detention of up to 5 days, and may concurrently carry a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. If the circumstances are relatively minor, a warning or a fine of up to 500 yuan is imposed. Carrying them into public places or public transportation results in detention of 5 to 10 days, and may concurrently carry a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Article 130 of the Criminal Law is even more severe: whoever illegally carries controlled knives into public places or public transportation, endangering public safety where the circumstances are serious, shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of up to 3 years. Which knives count as controlled knives: the identification standards issued by the Ministry of Public Security in 2007 list five categories. The first category is daggers: having a handle, guard, and fuller, with a point angle of less than 60 degrees. The second category is triangular scrapers. The third category is spring-loaded knives with self-locking mechanisms, commonly known as switchblades. The fourth category is knives with a point angle of less than 60 degrees and a blade length exceeding 150 millimeters. The fifth category is knives with a point angle greater than 60 degrees and a blade length exceeding 220 millimeters. Unsharpened martial arts and craft gift knives with rounded tips do not count. Police batons are police equipment. The People's Police Law stipulates that police equipment may only be held and used by police officers. If held by others, it is confiscated, and administrative detention of up to 15 days or a warning is imposed, and a fine of up to 5 times the illegal gains may concurrently be imposed. The railway prohibited items catalog lists police batons, tear gas devices, stun devices, and defense devices as controlled instruments. These items are neither allowed as carry-on nor allowed as checked luggage when taking trains. The road passenger transport prohibited items catalog similarly lists tear gas devices and stun devices as controlled instruments; carrying them on long-distance buses is also prohibited. As to whether stun devices can be possessed normally, the Shanghai Municipal People's Procuratorate published a case in 2013. Four individuals hawked stun devices to drivers at street intersections and were sentenced to terms ranging from 1 year and 3 months to 6 months of fixed-term imprisonment for the crime of illegally trading police equipment. The procuratorate cited two Ministry of Public Security notices. According to these two notices, "this type of stun device is a state-controlled instrument and also a type of police weapon/equipment." The procuratorate also explicitly wrote that such stun devices "are contraband items domestically, and individuals are prohibited from producing, selling, or possessing them." The prosecutor additionally stated that self-defense items such as high-concentration sprays belong to police equipment, and ordinary citizens cannot purchase them either. Keeping them in a car will be checked just the same: someone drove through an inspection checkpoint with controlled knives in the car, was caught by police officers, and was administratively detained. As for the legal reckoning if actually used, look at the Guiding Opinions on Justifiable Defense. It lists "whether a deadly weapon was used or prepared for use" as one of the circumstances distinguishing defense from mutual brawling. Official case: A certain Yang argued with someone, and the other party threatened to find people to retaliate; Yang went home and concealed two knives on his person. The other party returned and punched Yang in the face with bare hands; Yang stabbed the other party in the chest and abdomen with the knife, resulting in the other party's death. The court found that his actions had defensive nature, but because the other party only struck with bare hands while Yang stabbed vital areas, it constituted excessive defense. He was sentenced to 4 years of fixed-term imprisonment for the crime of intentional injury (Nationwide; Public Security Administration Punishment Law effective from January 1, 2026).

entries.notes: You are the beneficiary. Carrying a knife does not automatically rule out justifiable defense. In Guiding Case No. 45, a student named Chen was beaten by a group of nine people. He pulled out a fruit knife he was carrying and fought back, and his actions were still found to be justifiable defense. The procuratorate stated that the deciding factor was whether he intended to engage in a mutual fight, not whether he carried a tool. The risks lie in two places. First, if the item itself is illegal, you can be penalized for possessing it when checked, whether or not you have used it. Second, with a knife close at hand, you may stab someone in response to even a punch or a shove. If the injury is serious or worse, your actions may become excessive defense. This book did not find the original text of a nationwide ban on stun devices or pepper spray. It found the names of the Ministry of Public Security's two notices only in a case published by the Shanghai Municipal People's Procuratorate. That procuratorate's case supports the conclusion that individuals may not possess stun devices. As for pepper spray, this book found only a prosecutor's statement that “high-concentration sprays” cannot be purchased; it did not find a uniform determination of whether the lower-concentration self-defense sprays sold on the market are covered. Neither can be carried on trains or long-distance coaches. This book also did not find the original text of a uniform nationwide determination of whether the telescopic batons sold online count as police batons. If something actually happens, first see Section 8, Item 10 (call the police first when a conflict starts; do not use force). If there is no way to retreat, see Section 8, Item 11 (you may fight back against an attack you cannot escape). If someone corners you outdoors and demands money, see Section 13, Item 36 (a stranger demands money in a remote area).

entries.title: When catching or angling for fish, do not set nets during closed fishing seasons or in closed fishing areas; never use electricity, poison, explosives, or prohibited fishing gear
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Before going into the water, check the closed fishing areas, closed seasons, and no-angling areas published by the local agriculture and rural affairs department. Do not buy equipment such as electric fishing devices or take it to the water's edge. If you want to angle, go to waters where angling is permitted, or to a fishing venue or fishpond. The hard part is resisting the urge to follow others when you see how many fish they catch with electricity.
entries.summary: Using electricity, poison, or explosives to fish in a closed fishing area or during a closed fishing season meets the threshold for the crime of illegally catching aquatic products, with a maximum sentence of three years. Only where the catch is small and the harm clearly minor might prosecution be waived. Electric fishing also carries a fine, generally up to 200,000 yuan, and you can be fined for entering the water with electric fishing equipment. One person caught fish with electricity along the Yangtze River, sold them for 9,000 yuan, and was sentenced to one year.
entries.benefit: Article 340 of the Criminal Law: Where the circumstances are serious, catching aquatic products in a closed fishing area, during a closed fishing season, or with prohibited tools or methods is punishable by up to three years' fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention, public surveillance, or a fine. A 2022 judicial interpretation by the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate specifies what counts as “serious circumstances”; any one of the following is enough. Illegally catching at least 500 kilograms of aquatic products in inland waters, or products worth at least 10,000 yuan. Catching at least 50 kilograms in an aquatic germplasm resources protection area, or products worth at least 1,000 yuan. Fishing with methods such as electricity, poison, or explosives in a closed fishing area. Fishing with these methods during a closed fishing season. The same article also leaves room for an exception: depending on the quantity and value caught and the tools used, prosecution may be waived or criminal punishment exempted if the harm is found to be clearly minor. Then there is the Fisheries Law, revised in 2025 and effective May 1, 2026. It prohibits fishing in violation of closed-area and closed-season rules, as well as angling in violation of the rules. It prohibits fishing with explosives, poison, or electricity, and bringing such devices into fishery waters. Fishing with prohibited gear or nets whose mesh is smaller than the minimum size is likewise prohibited. The penalties are as follows: for fishing with electricity, poison, or explosives, the gear, catch, and unlawful proceeds are confiscated, and the fine is up to 200,000 yuan. In serious cases, the fine is 200,000 to 2 million yuan. Merely bringing electric fishing equipment into fishery waters results in confiscation of the equipment and may bring a fine of up to 100,000 yuan. Fishing in violation of closed-area or closed-season rules, or using prohibited gear, carries a fine of up to 200,000 yuan. Angling in violation of the rules in a closed fishing area or during a closed fishing season results in confiscation of the catch, unlawful proceeds, and fishing gear, and may bring a fine of up to 50,000 yuan. There is an additional layer for the Yangtze River: the Yangtze River Protection Law completely prohibits commercial fishing for wild fishery resources in key waters, including the main stream, important tributaries, and large lakes connected to the river. The Yangtze's ten-year fishing ban began on January 1, 2021. Fishing in waters covered by the ban results in confiscation of the catch, unlawful proceeds, fishing vessels, and gear, plus a fine of 10,000 to 50,000 yuan. Fishing with electricity, poison, or explosives carries a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 yuan. Official case: Li Xugen knew the Jiangdu side channel in the Yangzhou section of the Yangtze was a closed fishing area, yet used an inverter to fish with electricity from a speedboat. From January 2018 to April 2019, he did this more than 60 times, caught more than 900 jin of wild fish, sold them, and made 9,000 yuan. He turned himself in, returned the unlawful proceeds, and released the first batch of fish fry, but was still sentenced to one year's fixed-term imprisonment for illegally catching aquatic products. Under a settlement agreement, he also had to apologize publicly in provincial-level media and release fish fry worth 25,000 yuan and 22,500 yuan in two batches. In another guiding case from the Supreme People's Court, eight people fished with silk nets and homemade electric nets in the closed fishing area of East Dongting Lake 30 to 40 times. Their sentences ranged from three months' criminal detention, suspended, to one year and one month of fixed-term imprisonment. All 100,000 yuan of unlawful profits was recovered (nationwide; the Fisheries Law takes effect May 1, 2026).

entries.notes: You are the beneficiary. The Fisheries Law states that occasional angling by an individual for recreation does not count as a fishing operation and does not require a fishing permit. But if you angle in violation of the rules in a closed fishing area or during a closed fishing season, your gear can still be confiscated and you can be fined. There is no uniform nationwide number governing whether you may angle in waters covered by the Yangtze fishing ban, or how many rods and hooks one person may use. The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs' 2024 opinions require local authorities to set their own rules and designate no-angling areas. Angling is prohibited throughout the core zones of protected areas and important habitats for aquatic organisms. Even where angling is allowed in Yangtze waters covered by the fishing ban, nationwide restrictions apply: you may not use fish finders or underwater cameras, use toxic bait or groundbait, or sell fish you catch. Fishing methods such as “explosive hooks” and “string hooks” are specifically targeted for enforcement. If your catch is clearly excessive or you take it to sell, you may be investigated for illegal fishing. So before you go, check the local agriculture and rural affairs department's website or posted notices. The criminal thresholds above apply only to inland waters; the sea has a separate set of standards. Knowingly buying or selling illegally caught fish is handled as the crime of concealing or disguising criminal proceeds. Penalties are heavier for catching aquatic animals under key national protection; see Item 14 of this section (do not eat wild animals or trade in protected animals).

entries.title: Do not light fires in forests or grasslands when visiting graves, burning off vegetation, or cooking outdoors; call 12119 or 119 in China if you see a wildfire
entries.cost: Costs nothing. When visiting graves, bring flowers, clear weeds, or plant flowers instead; do not burn paper offerings, incense, candles, or firecrackers on the mountain. Do not set fire to weeds or crop straw in the fields. Bring food that needs no open flame for outdoor meals, and take cigarette butts back down the mountain. The hard part is that older family members may feel a grave visit does not count unless paper offerings are burned.
entries.summary: Lighting a fire in a fire prevention zone during a fire prevention period carries a fine of 300 to 5,000 yuan even if nothing catches fire. Burning two hectares of forested land meets the threshold for opening a criminal case for negligently causing a fire, punishable by three to seven years; where the circumstances are relatively minor, the sentence is under three years. One person burned paper offerings at a grave and started a fire that spread over 39 hectares. He received a one-year sentence suspended for two years and also had to replant 32 hectares of forest.
entries.benefit: The Regulations on Forest and Grassland Fire Prevention and Suppression took effect on January 1, 2026; the former Forest Fire Prevention Regulations and Grassland Fire Prevention Regulations were repealed at the same time. Article 27: During fire prevention periods, outdoor use of fire is prohibited in fire prevention zones, and no one may discard ignition sources in those zones. In hot, dry, or windy weather, local governments may order a complete ban on outdoor use of fire. Article 54: Anyone who uses fire outdoors in a fire prevention zone during a fire prevention period without approval will be ordered to stop. Individuals are fined 300 to 5,000 yuan; organizations are fined 20,000 to 100,000 yuan. Article 34: Anyone who discovers a forest or grassland fire must report it immediately. China's Ministry of Emergency Management states that the nationwide forest fire emergency number is 12119. If a fire starts and meets the threshold for opening a criminal case, it becomes a criminal matter. Article 115, paragraph 2, of the Criminal Law covers negligently causing a fire: a fire caused through negligence is punishable by three to seven years, or, where the circumstances are relatively minor, under three years or criminal detention. One threshold for opening a case relates directly to wildfires. A case must be opened if at least two hectares of forested land burn, or at least four hectares of sparsely forested land, shrubland, land with young forests not yet established, or nursery land burn. One death, three serious injuries, direct losses of 500,000 yuan, or the destruction of ten households' homes also each meets the threshold. In a Xinhua article reposted by the National Forestry and Grassland Administration, experts said human activities such as ritual offerings and agricultural burning account for more than 90% of fire causes. In historical data, ritual burning ranks first. Official case one: In February 2021, Xie Moujun burned paper offerings at a grave in the Qilian Mountains National Nature Reserve, igniting weeds and shrubs. The fire spread over 39.2156 hectares, most of it natural shrubland. After the fire started, he called to report it, helped fight it, and voluntarily turned himself in, which counted as surrender. He had also already replanted 9,420 Qinghai spruce trees elsewhere. Even so, he was sentenced to one year's fixed-term imprisonment for negligently causing a fire, suspended for two years. The court also ordered him to reforest 32.05 hectares in three stages; if he could not complete the work, he would have to pay the assessed amount. Official case two: In May 2022, Wang Mouqian took part in a folk activity and used a lighter to ignite materials for a ritual “weisang” offering. He covered the fire with stones and left without checking that it was out. The remaining fire ignited dry grass and burned 121.69 mu, causing losses of about 469,000 yuan (exact amount: 468,578 yuan). He was sentenced to nine months' fixed-term imprisonment, suspended for one year and six months. He had to replant according to the restoration plan; if he could not finish, he would be liable for 986,700 yuan in restoration costs (nationwide; the regulations took effect January 1, 2026).
