Supplementary rinsing within three hours is still useful. For scald prevention while bathing infants, see Section 20, Item 17 (run cold water first before blending in hot water).

entries.title: If a sudden whole-body rash occurs along with shortness of breath or dizziness, treat as anaphylactic shock, call 120 immediately, and explain clearly
entries.cost: Free of charge. For individuals with known severe allergies, self-purchasing an epinephrine auto-injector costs money, and it is a prescription medication.
entries.summary: If a sudden whole-body rash occurs accompanied by shortness of breath or dizziness, handle it as anaphylactic shock. Call 120 immediately and say directly "suspected anaphylactic shock" so that emergency responders bring epinephrine. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are slow to take effect and cannot replace epinephrine. Anyone who has experienced a severe allergic reaction should ask a doctor whether an auto-injector pen can be prescribed; inject into the anterolateral thigh, which can be done even through non-thick clothing.
entries.benefit: Epinephrine is the drug of choice (first-line drug) for Grade 2 and higher anaphylactic shock, and guidelines list it as a strong recommendation. Antihistamines and corticosteroids act slowly and cannot take its place. The International Red Cross 2025 First Aid Guidelines state that epinephrine auto-injectors can be administered through clothing, provided the clothing is not thick. Where prescribed by a physician and permitted by local laws, bystanders may assist in administering it when the patient cannot self-administer.
entries.sources: China Association for Pharmaceutical Education et al. (2022). Clinical practice guideline for the emergency management of anaphylaxis (2020 edition). Frontiers in Pharmacology: "Epinephrine is the first-line medicine in GRADE II to IV anaphylaxis", "Intramuscular epinephrine should be injected in the mid-anterolateral thigh", with an intramuscular injection upper limit of 0.5 mg for adults and 0.3 mg for those under 14 years old; if there is no response, it can be repeated every 5–15 minutes; "If an epinephrine pre-filled injector/auto-injector is available, they should follow the instructions written on the packaging or insert". <https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2022.845689>; Muraro A, et al. (2022). EAACI guidelines: Anaphylaxis (2021 update). Allergy. <https://doi.org/10.1111/all.15032>; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, p. 376: "The epinephrine auto-injection may be administered through the person's clothing if the clothes are not thick". <https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20International%20First%20Aid,%20Resuscitation%20and%20Education%20Guidelines%202025.pdf>
entries.notes: This anaphylaxis guideline (EAACI) itself explicitly states that in this field, "most evidence remains at a very low level." It is classified as a strong recommendation because the benefits far outweigh the risks, not because of large clinical trials. Epinephrine is a prescription medication; if you do not have it on hand, what you can do is call 120 and state "suspected anaphylactic shock" so that the emergency responders bring the medication. For those who have experienced severe anaphylaxis once, ask a doctor whether they can prescribe a pre-filled epinephrine syringe or an auto-injector, learn how to inject into the mid-anterolateral thigh (the front-outer side), which can also be administered through pants that are not thick.
entries.gradeNote: (Strongly recommended by guidelines, but the underlying level of evidence is low)

entries.title: If someone collapses with convulsions, clear the surroundings, place them on their side, time it with a watch, and do not put anything into their mouth; the same applies when a child has convulsions during a fever
entries.cost: Free.
entries.summary: Move hard objects away from their surroundings, place them on their side with their mouth facing downward, and look at a watch to time it. Do not hold them down, and do not put anything into their mouth, which will only injure teeth and the jaw. If it does not stop after more than 5 minutes, if it is a first-time episode, or if they cannot be awakened after the convulsions end, call an ambulance. Do the same when a child convulses with a high fever; do not remove their clothes, and do not sponge them with cold water to cool them down.
entries.benefit: Avoids damage to teeth and the jaw caused by prying the mouth open or inserting hard objects. Avoids fractures caused by forcefully holding the person down. Not stopping after more than 5 minutes is a red line where an ambulance must be called. Convulsions in children during a fever are called febrile seizures. The UK's National Health Service (NHS) states that they are most commonly seen in children aged 6 months to 6 years. They usually convulse for 2 to 3 minutes, rarely exceeding 10 minutes, and generally do not harm the child or leave long-term complications. The NHS lists several situations requiring a call to emergency services: a first-time seizure, a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, difficulty breathing, or seizing on only one side of the body. Also, being sleepier than usual for more than 1 hour after the seizure stops, as well as seizing more than once within 24 hours. The American Academy of Pediatrics' 2011 guideline states that for a simple febrile seizure in children aged 6 to 60 months, there is generally no need for an electroencephalogram, blood tests, or brain imaging. Doctors mainly look for the cause of the fever. The UK's National Health Service (NHS) also cautions not to try to cool the child down by undressing them or sponging them with cold water.
entries.sources: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Seizure First Aid: "Don't hold the person down or stop their movements", "Don't put anything in their mouth. This can hurt their teeth or jaw", "Don't offer water or food until they are fully alert", "Time the seizure to track if it lasts more than 5 minutes. If it does, seek immediate medical attention or call 911". <https://www.cdc.gov/epilepsy/first-aid-for-seizures/index.html>; NHS. Febrile seizures: "it's unlikely to harm your child or cause long-term effects", "Febrile seizures usually last for 2 to 3 minutes. It's rare for them to last more than 10 minutes", "They usually affect children between 6 months and 6 years old", "has a seizure for the first time", "has a seizure that lasts more than 5 minutes", "is more sleepy than usual for more than 1 hour after the seizure stops", "protect their head with your hands or something soft", "do not move your child or try to hold them in place", "do not try to lower your child's temperature by undressing them or sponging them with cold water", "Do not take your child to A&E if they are still having a seizure or are unconscious, call 999 instead", "your child will need to be checked in hospital after having a febrile seizure for the first time". <https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/febrile-seizures/>; Subcommittee on Febrile Seizures, American Academy of Pediatrics (2011). Neurodiagnostic evaluation of the child with a simple febrile seizure. Pediatrics, 127(2), 389-394: "In general, a simple febrile seizure does not usually require further evaluation, specifically electroencephalography, blood studies, or neuroimaging". <https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2010-3318>
entries.notes: The same page also lists several other situations where an ambulance should be called immediately. For example, if another seizure occurs shortly after one ends, if the person cannot be awakened or has difficulty breathing after the seizure, if they were injured during the seizure, if it occurred in water, or if this is the first seizure. After the seizure stops, place them on their side with the mouth facing downward, and only offer water once the person is fully alert. For households with epilepsy patients, this set of actions is the most useful. When a child has febrile seizures, the NHS also states not to move the child around and not to hold them down; you can protect the head with your hands or something soft. If the child is still seizing or cannot be awakened, do not carry them to the hospital yourself—call 120 directly. For a first-time febrile seizure, go to the hospital for an evaluation after the seizure stops. Performing the same actions on a stranger carries a lower chance of personal benefit returning to you. However, you bear no civil liability for harm caused during voluntary rescue efforts (Article 184 of the Civil Code; see item 2 of this section, Do not rush to help someone up).

entries.title: If a person with diabetes suddenly trembles, breaks into a cold sweat, or slurs their speech, administer 15 grams of sugar first, and recheck after 15 minutes
entries.cost: Free. Carry a few sugar cubes or a small juice box with you.
entries.summary: First consume 15 grams of sugar; sugar cubes or a small juice box will do. Recheck after 15 minutes; if it is still low, repeat the process. Blood glucose below 3.0 mmol/L is medically significant hypoglycemia; once it reaches the point where assistance from others is needed to manage it, it can be fatal. Do not feed a single bite to someone who is unconscious, as it will be aspirated into the trachea; call 120 directly.
entries.benefit: Blood glucose below 3.0 mmol/L is clinically significant hypoglycemia. Experiencing altered consciousness or motor function requiring assistance from others for treatment constitutes severe hypoglycemia, which can be fatal.
entries.sources: American Diabetes Association (2025). Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025: Chapter 6 Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia. Diabetes Care: Classification "Level 1: Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L)", "Level 2: Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)", "Level 3: A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level"; Treatment "For most individuals, 15 g carbohydrates should be ingested", "Fifteen minutes after initial treatment, repeat the treatment if hypoglycemia persists". <https://doi.org/10.2337/dc25-S006>
entries.notes: Do not feed anything to an unconscious person, as it will be aspirated into the airway; call 120 directly. The same standard also recommends that individuals taking insulin and those prone to hypoglycemia should keep glucagon on hand. The original text states: "All individuals treated with insulin or who are at high risk of hypoglycemia...should be prescribed glucagon". Nasal sprays and pre-filled syringes are easier to use than medications that require reconstitution on the spot. These practices are by default intended for yourself or family members with diabetes, and carrying sugar with you is also for them.

entries.title: If someone suffers an electric shock, disconnect the power first, then use a dry wooden stick or similar object to push the power source away; do not pull them directly with your hands
entries.cost: Free.
entries.summary: Cut the power first, or use a dry wooden stick or similar object to push the power source away before touching the person. Pulling them directly with your hands will turn one victim into two. If there is no normal breathing after separating from the power source, perform compressions immediately according to item 1 (press firmly on the chest); do not hesitate to touch them just because it is an electrical injury. For downed high-voltage lines or near transformer equipment, do not handle it yourself; retreat far away and wait for the power department to disconnect the electricity.
entries.benefit: Prevents the rescuer from also being electrocuted, turning one victim into two. If the person has no normal breathing after separating from the power source, perform CPR according to item 1 of this section (press firmly on the chest). The US CDC's first-aid steps are: Look first, do not touch; the person may still be in contact with electricity. Cut the power first if possible; if it cannot be cut, use non-conductive objects such as cardboard, plastic, or wood to push the power source away. Once separated from the power source, if breathing or pulse has stopped, perform CPR immediately. A narrative review noted that individuals who suffer cardiac arrest following electrocution and are resuscitated often have a favorable prognosis.
entries.sources: US CDC. What to Do to Protect Yourself From Electrical Hazards (First aid section). <https://www.cdc.gov/natural-disasters/response/what-to-do-protect-yourself-from-electrical-hazards.html>; Spies C, Trohman RG (2006). Narrative review: Electrocution and life-threatening electrical injuries. Annals of Internal Medicine 145(7):531-537. <https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-145-7-200610030-00011>
entries.notes: "Disconnect the power before touching the person" is a purely self-preserving rule: if you pull them directly with your hands, the second person to collapse will be you. For downed high-voltage wires or areas near transformer equipment, do not handle it yourself; back away and wait for the power department to cut the power. For cardiac arrest caused by electric shock, simply perform compressions and defibrillation according to routine procedures; do not hesitate to step in just because it is an "electrical injury."

entries.title: If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, or if everyone in a room develops a headache and nausea at the same time, go outside first before making a phone call
entries.cost: Free.
entries.summary: If the alarm sounds, or if a room full of people develops headaches, nausea, and dizziness at the same time, take everyone outside first before calling. Do not stay inside to look for the cause, and do not go back to close the valves. The symptoms resemble a cold; "improving once going outside" is the strongest indicator. In 2018, China reported 11,523 deaths from carbon monoxide poisoning, with the highest numbers in winter, and about 70% occurring at home during the three winter months.
entries.benefit: The Chinese CDC's cause-of-death surveillance system reported 11,523 deaths from carbon monoxide poisoning in 2018. The highest numbers occurred in January (2,845 cases), February (2,321 cases), and December (2,010 cases). During these three winter months, deaths occurring at home accounted for 66% to 73%. These are figures reported within the surveillance system, not extrapolated from the national population. In the United States, more than 400 people die each year from unintentional carbon monoxide poisoning unrelated to fires. Over 100,000 visit emergency departments, and over 14,000 are hospitalized. The US CDC notes that symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning are often described as "flu-like." The NHS clearly states that symptoms worsen while remaining in the affected room, and improve upon leaving or going outdoors.
entries.sources: You J, Liu J, Zhou M (2020). Number of Deaths due to Carbon Monoxide Poisoning by Month and by Place of Death — China, 2018. China CDC Weekly 2(2):32: "In 2018, there were 11,523 deaths caused by carbon monoxide poisoning reported in China". <https://doi.org/10.46234/ccdcw2020.008>; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: "More than 400 Americans die from unintentional CO poisoning not linked to fires", "More than 100,000 visit an emergency department", "More than 14,000 are hospitalized", common symptoms "headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion", "CO symptoms are often described as \"flu-like.\"". <https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html>; US Consumer Product Safety Commission. Carbon Monoxide Information Center: "If you suspect CO poisoning, get outside to fresh air immediately, and then call 911". <https://www.cpsc.gov/Safety-Education/Safety-Education-Centers/Carbon-Monoxide-Information-Center>; NHS. Carbon monoxide poisoning: "They may get worse when you spend time in an affected room or building and get better when you leave or go outside". <https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/carbon-monoxide-poisoning/>
entries.notes: Symptoms resemble a cold or flu. Feeling better upon going outside is the strongest indicator. Take it seriously when an entire roomful of people feels unwell at the same time; the author deduced this from the premise that "people in the same room are breathing the same air." Do not stay in the room trying to find the cause, do not go back to shut off valves, and get outside before making a call. See Section 1, Item 3 for how to install an alarm.

entries.title: Do not induce vomiting if detergents, pesticides, or medications are accidentally ingested; bring the bottle and seek medical attention immediately; if splashed into eyes or onto skin, flush with copious running water for at least 15 minutes
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Store detergents, disinfectants, pesticides, and medications up high out of children's reach, or in locked cabinets. Never decant them into beverage bottles.
entries.summary: Do not induce vomiting if detergents, pesticides, or medications are accidentally swallowed, as vomiting can injure the throat and may also cause choking. If strong acid or alkali detergents are accidentally ingested, China CDC advises drinking an appropriate amount of milk or egg white first, and heading to the hospital immediately with the bottle in hand. If splashed onto skin or into eyes, flush with copious amounts of water for at least 15 minutes; for eyes, hold the eyelids open while flushing and do not rub. Mixing disinfectants with toilet bowl cleaners produces chlorine gas.
entries.benefit: The National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control of the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention divides handling protocols into four types. For ingestion by mouth (digestive tract ingestion): immediately drink an appropriate amount of milk or egg whites, and "remember, do not induce vomiting." Seek medical attention as soon as possible, while bringing along the packaging or instructions, "so that physicians can quickly determine the ingredients and formulate a treatment plan." Inhalation (respiratory tract inhalation): immediately move to a well-ventilated area, loosen the collar, and keep breathing unobstructed. If severe coughing, shortness of breath, or breathing difficulty occurs, seek medical attention immediately. Skin contact: immediately flush the contact site with copious running water for at least 15 minutes, taking care not to let the runoff splash into eyes or onto other intact skin. Eye contact: immediately flush the eyes with copious amounts of water or normal saline for at least 15 minutes. Hold the eyelids open during flushing so the water stream makes full contact with the eyeballs and the inside of the eyelids; "do not rub the eyes." Go to an ophthalmology department immediately after flushing. Identify high-risk products by acidity and alkalinity (pH). Those with pH < 3 are toilet bowl cleaners, descalers, floor cleaners, and stainless steel brighteners. Some heavy-duty pipe drain openers also contain dilute sulfuric acid. Those with pH > 11 are pipe drain openers, heavy-duty kitchen degreasers, dishwasher powder, oxygen bleach powder (sodium percarbonate), and scouring powder. There is also a combination that causes immediate disaster: using disinfectant together with toilet bowl cleaner containing hydrochloric acid produces chlorine gas. Chlorine gas irritates the respiratory tract, causing severe coughing and shortness of breath, and can even be life-threatening. Refraining from inducing vomiting applies not only to cleaning agents. The NHS poisoning page lists medicines, household cleaning products, certain plants and mushrooms, and pesticides as common causes of poisoning, explicitly stating that if you think someone has swallowed something harmful, do not try to make them sick, as "they could choke and stop breathing," and do not give them anything to eat or drink. If the patient vomits, put some vomit in a container to show the doctor. The International Red Cross 2025 first aid guidelines explicitly state that a person who has swallowed a poisonous substance should not be encouraged to vomit, as this "may damage their throat." Hand over bottles, packaging, and labels to emergency personnel.
entries.sources: National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2025). Summer Vacation Safety Tips: Beware of Strong Acid and Strong Alkali Detergents. <https://niohp.chinacdc.cn/kpdw/202507/t20250722_308659.htm>; NHS. Poisoning: "do not try to make someone sick if you think they've swallowed something harmful – they could choke and stop breathing", "do not give the person anything to eat or drink", "if the person vomits, try putting some vomit in a container to give to healthcare professionals"; common causes listed include "medicines", "household cleaning products", "certain plants and mushrooms", "pesticides". <https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/poisoning/>; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 346–347: "The person should NOT be encouraged to vomit as this may damage their throat", "First aid providers should not give any diluents such as milk, water or activated charcoal to a person who has swallowed a poisonous substance unless they are instructed to do so by the poison control centre or equivalent poison expert". <https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20International%20First%20Aid,%20Resuscitation%20and%20Education%20Guidelines%202025.pdf>
entries.notes: Rated B because official public science communications only explain how to handle and identify these situations, without figures on "how many incidents can be prevented by following along." On whether to drink milk, the two sides give differing statements. China CDC states that those who accidentally ingest strong acid or strong alkali detergents should first drink an appropriate amount of milk or egg whites. The International Red Cross states that unless instructed by poison control experts, do not give diluents like milk or water, and the NHS also says not to give food or drink. For substances other than detergents, such as medications and pesticides, do not feed anything on your own. If you are unsure what was accidentally swallowed, bring the bottle and instructions along with any vomit to the hospital. Prevention is far cheaper than emergency rescue: store items by category, do not mix them with food or beverages, tighten caps after use, discard empty bottles, and never pour them into mineral water bottles. Wear rubber gloves and protective goggles during use, open windows for ventilation, and do not mix different types. For carbon monoxide, see Item 19; for burns and scalds, see Item 14. For chemical splashes like acids and alkalis onto the body, how to strip clothes, and how long to flush, see Item 21 (Chemical Splashes on the Body). If a child swallows a button battery or magnetic beads, see Item 45 (Children Swallowing Button Batteries).

entries.title: If chemicals such as acids or alkalis splash onto the body, immediately strip off contaminated clothing, flush with copious running water, pry eyelids open to flush eyes, and flush for the full duration before leaving
entries.cost: Costs nothing. Check the locations of emergency eyewash stations and safety showers on your very first day on the job; do not wait until an accident happens to start searching.
entries.summary: Step 1: Immediately take off contaminated clothing, shoes, and socks; areas trapped by clothing sustain the most severe injuries. Step 2: Flush with copious amounts of running room-temperature water—do not use hot water—for at least 15 minutes for both skin and eyes. For open skin wounds, the Hunan Provincial Department of Emergency Management recommends 20 to 30 minutes; follow the longer duration. Step 3: Hold eyelids open to flush eyes, and proceed directly to an ophthalmology department after flushing.
entries.benefit: Three on-site steps. Step 1: Immediately strip off contaminated clothing, shoes, and socks: toxic substances will continue to be absorbed through the skin, and areas where clothing holds the chemical sustain the most severe injury. Step 2: Flush with copious running water. The baseline duration given by the National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control of the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention is "at least 15 minutes" each for skin and eyes. The protocol given by the Hunan Provincial Department of Emergency Management is flushing the wound surface for 20 to 30 minutes, and "longer for strong chemicals." Take the longer duration between the two protocols. Step 3: For the eyes, "hold the eyelids open to ensure the water stream makes full contact with the eyeballs and the inside of the eyelids," "do not rub the eyes," and go to an ophthalmology department immediately after flushing. Use room-temperature or lukewarm water; hot water is strictly prohibited. Do not apply ointment, Mercurochrome, or anything else to fresh wound surfaces, and do not wrap them in dirty cloth; applying substances impairs a physician's ability to evaluate burn depth. Legally, "chemical skin burns" and "chemical eye burns" are both listed in the statutory occupational disease catalog; incidents occurring during work follow occupational disease and work-related injury procedures. When an acute occupational disease hazard accident occurs, the employing unit "shall promptly organize rescue, conduct health examinations and medical observation, with the required expenses borne by the employing unit" (nationwide).
entries.sources: National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2025). Summer Vacation Safety Tips: Beware of Strong Acid and Strong Alkali Detergents. <https://niohp.chinacdc.cn/kpdw/202507/t20250722_308659.htm>; Hunan Provincial Department of Emergency Management (2015). Emergency Handling and Treatment of Common Chemical Poisoning Accidents. <http://yjt.hunan.gov.cn/yjt/tszt/aqzs/201509/t20150919_3113778.html>; National Health Commission and other four ministries (2024). Classification and Catalog of Occupational Diseases (Effective August 1, 2025). <https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202412/content_6992843.htm>; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2018). Law on the Prevention and Control of Occupational Diseases (Article 37). <https://www.beijing.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengcefagui/qtwj/201711/t20171104_779851.html> (reposted by the People's Government of Beijing Municipality)
entries.notes: Rated B because there is no unified national standard figure for how long to flush. One official document states 15 minutes, while another states 20 to 30 minutes. When going to the hospital, bring along the chemical's name, packaging, or its Safety Data Sheet (SDS); doctors rely on it to determine treatment plans. Do not grab another acid or alkali off the shelf to try to "neutralize" it: mixing the two releases heat, and there is no way to control how much is poured. The "neutralizing solution" mentioned in that Hunan document refers to dedicated rinsing fluids prepared by the facility in advance, not mixing things together on the fly at the scene. Dry powders such as lime powder and cement powder should be brushed off before flushing with water. Some local emergency pages state on this basis that concentrated sulfuric acid should also be wiped dry first; because protocols vary across sources on this point, this book does not include it. For household cleaners and accidental ingestion, see Item 20. For pre-job protection and health checks, see Section 19, Items 9 and 10 (Review Hazard Disclosures Before Starting Work, Employers Must Provide Protective Equipment).

entries.title: If experiencing dizziness, nausea, lack of sweating, or altered consciousness in high heat, move immediately to a cool, shaded area, remove clothing, splash water to cool down, do not give water to unconscious individuals, and call 120
entries.cost: Costs nothing.
entries.summary: Hot, red skin, slurred speech, and confusion indicate heat stroke. Body temperature can rise above 41°C within 10 to 15 minutes, and severe cases have an extremely high fatality rate. Move immediately to a cool, ventilated area, remove clothing, cool down with cool water and wet towels, and simultaneously call 120. Do not give a single sip of water to anyone who is not fully conscious.
entries.benefit: US National Weather Service: Heat stroke is a "serious medical emergency." Its manifestations include a body temperature exceeding 103°F (39.4°C), confusion, slurred speech, and hot, red skin. Management consists of calling emergency medical services immediately, moving to a cool place, cooling down with cool water and damp cloths, and "do not give liquids." Heat exhaustion manifests as heavy sweating, weakness, cold and clammy skin, and a fast, weak pulse; management involves moving to a cool place, loosening clothing, and sipping water. Seek medical care if vomiting occurs, symptoms worsen, or there is no relief after 1 hour. Yunnan Provincial Disease Control and Prevention Bureau tips: transfer immediately to a cool, ventilated area, use cold wet towels to cool down, replenish salt-containing beverages for conscious individuals, and immediately dial emergency telephone numbers for severe symptoms. It also states that severe heat stroke has an "extremely high fatality rate." Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention tips: cool down first, transport later, and reduce body temperature within the "golden half hour" after the patient loses consciousness. Where conditions permit, young and middle-aged adults without underlying conditions can use cold-water immersion to cool down rapidly; elderly individuals and those with underlying conditions can spray water onto the skin to cool via evaporation. The Wilderness Medical Society's 2024 updated heat illness guidelines state that cold-water immersion is the most important method for treating severe heat illness and cools the fastest. If ice water is unavailable, use the coolest water at hand; if immersion is not possible, spray water combined with fanning, which cools at roughly half the rate of immersion. The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) states that when heat stroke occurs, body temperature can rise to 106°F (about 41°C) or higher within 10 to 15 minutes. Its listed symptoms include "hot, dry skin or profuse sweating." The China CDC's 2014 edition heat stroke guidelines list manifestations of heat stroke including "red, hot, dry skin without sweat," with management instructions demanding "do not give the patient water to drink," and rolling the patient onto their side if they vomit to keep the airway open.
entries.sources: US National Weather Service. Heat Related Illnesses. <https://www.weather.gov/safety/heat-illness> ; Yunnan Provincial Disease Control and Prevention Bureau (2026). If These Symptoms Appear, You Might Have Heat Stroke. <https://ynsjkj.yn.gov.cn/html/2026/jikongkepu_0719/2606.html> ; Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. High-Temperature Weather, China CDC Reminds You to Guard Against Heat Stroke: "Where conditions permit, the cold-water immersion method can be used for rapid cooling in young and middle-aged adults without underlying diseases. Elderly patients and those with underlying diseases may spray water onto the skin to cool via evaporation. Cooling should follow the principle of 'cool down first, transport later'". <https://www.chinacdc.cn/jkkp/ggws/hjyssj/202409/t20240906_296985.html> ; National Health Commission (2010). Key Points of Knowledge on Prevention of High-Temperature Heat Stroke. <https://www.nhc.gov.cn/wjw/jbyfykz/201007/1edb19b7dd4e4bdf8da5ea45f4a64e23.shtml> ; Eifling KP et al. (2024). Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Heat Illness: 2024 Update. Wilderness & Environmental Medicine 35(1_suppl):112S-127S. <https://doi.org/10.1177/10806032241227924> (The full-text site blocks automated scraping; specific recommendations were verified against the update summary on the official Wilderness Medical Society website: "cold water immersion … is the most important method of treating severe heat illness", "If CWI is unavailable, evaporative cooling is the recommended second-line treatment. … generally half as fast as CWI" <https://wms.org/magazine/magazine/1540/Heat-Illness-CPG/default.aspx>); Lipman GS et al. (2019). Same guidelines, 2019 edition. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2018.10.004>; US CDC/NIOSH. Heat-related Illnesses: "When heat stroke occurs, the body temperature can rise to 106°F or higher within 10 to 15 minutes", "Hot, dry skin or profuse sweating". <https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/heat-stress/about/illnesses.html>; National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2014). Guidelines for Public Prevention and Emergency Treatment of High-Temperature Heat Stroke (2014 Edition). <https://niohp.chinacdc.cn/sndt/201405/t20140530_97623.htm>
entries.notes: Do not wait to "give it some time to pass"; during heat stroke, body temperature can surge to over 41°C within ten-odd minutes. Heat stroke may present without sweating, or it may present with profuse sweating; NIOSH lists both, so do not dismiss it just because the person is still sweating. Do not pour water into an unconscious person's mouth; if they vomit, roll them onto their side. On where to apply ice packs, the two sources differ. China CDC recommends applying them to the neck, armpits, and groin, whereas the Wilderness Medical Society states that studies fail to show a cooling effect from applying them to these specific spots. The Wilderness Medical Society's recommendation is that if ice packs are the only option available, cover the entire body; if there are not enough ice packs, place them on the cheeks, palms, and soles of the feet instead. Both sources agree that cold-water immersion should be used whenever conditions permit.

entries.title: As long as a heatstroke victim is conscious, have them sip cool light salt water or sports drinks frequently in small amounts; do not chug, and do not drink alcohol or high-sugar beverages
entries.cost: Free. A bottle of sports drink costs a few yuan.
entries.summary: Only give fluids if the person is conscious; have them sip cool light salt water or sports drinks frequently in small amounts, 500 to 1,000 mL per hour. Do not drink alcohol or high-sugar beverages, as they cause the body to lose more water. Cool down first before rehydrating; if the person is unresponsive or slurring their words, do not feed them a single sip.
entries.benefit: The Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention issued the Guidelines for Public Prevention and Emergency Management of High-Temperature Heatstroke (2014 Edition). It states: "Drink at least 2–4 cups of cool water (500–1000 mL) every hour; water temperature should not be excessively high, and drinking should be in small amounts frequently." It also states: "Do not consume beverages containing alcohol or large amounts of sugar. These drinks cause the loss of more body fluids. At the same time, avoid drinking excessively cold frozen beverages." For heat stroke, it explicitly states: "Do not give the patient water to drink." US NIOSH: for heat exhaustion, "Encourage frequent sips of cool water"; for heat cramps, replenish with a sports beverage containing carbohydrates and electrolytes every 15 to 20 minutes, "Do not use salt tablets."
entries.sources: National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2014). Guidelines for Public Prevention and Emergency Management of High-Temperature Heatstroke (2014 Edition). <https://niohp.chinacdc.cn/sndt/201405/t20140530_97623.htm> ; US CDC/NIOSH. Heat-Related Illnesses. <https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/heat-stress/about/illnesses.html>
entries.notes: The 2014 edition of the China CDC guidelines notes that heavy sweating depletes salt and minerals which must be replaced, and sports drinks can help replenish them, which is why the water should contain a little salt. Drinking in small amounts frequently is also a requirement from this guideline. "Do not drink iced beverages" also comes from this guideline, based on concerns about stomach cramps without quantitative evidence. Do not misread this as "cannot use cool fluids." Item 22 (Stripping clothes and splashing water to cool down when dizzy and nauseous in high heat) describes several cooling methods. These are cool water wiping, cold-water immersion, and applying ice packs to the head, armpits, and groin. These are applied to the body, not poured into the mouth. Cooling down always takes priority over rehydration. If the person is unconscious or slurring their words, do not feed them a single sip.

entries.title: During a fire, crawl low, feel the door before opening, do not open if hot, use stairs instead of elevators, and never turn back once out
entries.cost: Installing 1 to 2 standalone smoke detectors at home costs several tens of yuan. Check the two exit routes in the stairwell in advance.
entries.summary: Drop to the floor and crawl toward the exit beneath the smoke. Feel the doorknob and door panel before opening; if it is hot or smoke is seeping through the cracks, do not open it—take your secondary escape route. Even if opening, do so slowly, and shut it immediately if dense smoke surges in. Take the stairs instead of elevators, and once outside, never turn back to retrieve belongings. If clothes catch fire, stop, drop, and roll, protecting your face with your hands.
entries.benefit: US FEMA original escape text: "Get low and crawl under the smoke to your exit." Before opening a door, feel the doorknob and door: "If either is hot, or if smoke is coming around the door, leave the door closed and use your second way out." Open doors slowly, and shut them immediately if there is heavy smoke. If clothes catch fire, "Stop, drop, and roll," covering your face with your hands. If you cannot get out, close the door, seal cracks and vents with cloth or tape, and call to report your location. The Ministry of Emergency Management's fire self-rescue advice aligns: do not take elevators when escaping; when the fire is not large, try to run downstairs; cover your mouth and nose with a damp towel or mask, and evacuate crawling or crouching.
entries.sources: US FEMA Ready.gov. Home Fires. <https://www.ready.gov/home-fires>; Ministry of Emergency Management (2019). Fire Self-Rescue Methods in Public Places: "Do not take elevators when escaping; when the fire is not large, try to run down to lower floors as much as possible" "A damp towel or mask can be used to cover the nose, evacuating by crawling or bending over". <https://www.mem.gov.cn/kp/shaq/201904/t20190401_366015.shtml>; Guizhou Provincial Fire and Rescue Brigade (2020). Fire Safety Knowledge丨Three Key Points for Escape: "Folding a damp towel 3 times (stacked into 8 layers) yields a relatively high smoke removal rate, but when smoke and toxic gas concentrations are excessively high, filtering efficacy can no longer be guaranteed. Furthermore, an overly wet towel will lead to breathing difficulties". <https://gz.119.gov.cn/xfkp/xfcs/202010/t20201026_71437855.html>
entries.notes: Do not take elevators; if power cuts out, you will be trapped inside. Do not turn back to grab valuables. Do not run upstairs unless you have confirmed the rooftop access door is unlocked. Do not jump out of the building. Fold a damp towel 3 times into 8 layers; do not use too much water, as an overly wet towel will actually make it impossible to breathe. When smoke and toxic gases are too thick, even a towel cannot block them. For wildfires and outdoor fires, see Section 9, Item 28 (Do not light fires in forested areas or grasslands during picnics).

entries.title: When seeing someone drowning, call for help and dial 110/120 first, extend a pole or throw floatable objects, and do not enter the water yourself
entries.cost: Free. The hard part is resisting the impulse to jump in.
entries.summary: Call for help and dial 110/120 first; extend a pole or throw flotation aids from the shore, and do not enter the water yourself. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally after being brought ashore, perform CPR immediately. Trained individuals should combine chest compressions with rescue breaths. If you do not know how, cannot, or are unwilling to deliver rescue breaths, provide continuous chest compressions and follow the emergency dispatcher's guidance.
entries.benefit: WHO: Globally, approximately 300,000 people drown each year, with 92% occurring in low- and middle-income countries. Drowning is the 4th leading cause of death for children aged 1 to 4, and the 3rd leading cause for children aged 5 to 14. Interventions recommended by WHO include "training bystanders in safe rescue and resuscitation," such as first learning rescue methods that do not involve entering the water. Shout loudly for help and call 110/120 first, then pass a long pole or rope from shore, or throw buoyant objects like lifebuoys or empty buckets. The International Red Cross 2025 First Aid Guidelines state clearly that rescuers should try to avoid entering the water: reach with something rigid (such as a pole or tree branch) from land or a boat, or throw a rope or buoyant object. Rescuers should not touch an actively drowning person because of the risk of being pulled into the water. Those already performing in-water rescues must understand water conditions and carry flotation devices. Once the person is pulled out, if they are unresponsive and breathing abnormally, perform CPR immediately. The American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics 2024 Drowning Resuscitation Guidelines emphasize that drowning cardiac arrest is typically caused by severe hypoxia. Trained rescuers should deliver rescue breaths together with chest compressions. If unable, incapable, or unwilling to provide rescue breaths, perform continuous chest compressions until rescue personnel arrive. Put the emergency call on speakerphone and follow the dispatcher's guidance.
entries.sources: WHO. Drowning Fact Sheet. <https://www.who.int/zh/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/drowning>; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 214–215: "An attempted rescue by first aid providers should be made without entering the water, either from land or a boat, by reaching with something rigid (e.g. a pole or tree branch), or by throwing a rope or buoyant object. Providers should not touch an actively drowning person because of the risk of being pulled into the water". <https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20International%20First%20Aid,%20Resuscitation%20and%20Education%20Guidelines%202025.pdf>; American Heart Association / American Academy of Pediatrics (2024). Highlights of the 2024 Focused Update on Resuscitation Following Drowning, pp. 3–4. <https://www.heart.org/-/media/CPR-Files/CPR-Guidelines-Files/Highlights/2024_Drowning/Hghlghts_2024GLFU_Drowning_240927.pdf>
entries.notes: Rated C because "not entering the water" is merely a procedural recommendation in the International Red Cross guidelines without controlled studies or statistics. Do not form a human chain holding hands to enter the water; this is an inference drawn by the author from "do not enter the water." Without training, do not attempt to drag someone out; touching someone who is actively struggling carries the risk of being pulled under. "Do not enter the water" is likewise a self-interest rule: if the rescuer drowns, it makes no difference who the person in the water was. The person needing rescue will most often be one's own child; how to prevent this is covered in Section 1, Item 12 (Keep children in sight when near water). If someone falls into an ice hole, likewise do not run onto the ice to pull them; for ice safety prevention, see Section 1, Item 41 (Measure thickness before stepping onto outdoor ice).

entries.title: If someone is choking and unable to speak, stand behind them (if age 1 or older) to perform 5 back blows plus 5 abdominal thrusts; start CPR if they collapse
entries.cost: Free. Watch the motion once: place a fist just above the navel, grasp it with the other hand, and give quick inward and upward thrusts.
entries.summary: First ask, "Are you choking? Can you speak?" Let anyone who can still cough or make sounds keep coughing on their own. If someone age 1 or older cannot speak, stand behind them and alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts; switch to chest thrusts for pregnant women or individuals with obesity. Repeat until the foreign object comes out or the person collapses; if they collapse, perform CPR and have someone call emergency services simultaneously. Do not reach into the mouth to fish out objects you cannot see.
entries.benefit: US National Library of Medicine original text: First ask, "Are you choking? Can you speak?" "DO NOT perform first aid if the person is coughing forcefully and able to speak," as coughing itself can often clear the foreign object. If they cannot speak, repeatedly give "5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is dislodged or the person becomes unconscious." "If the person becomes unconscious, start CPR" while having someone call emergency numbers. Switch to chest thrusts for pregnant or obese individuals. The International Red Cross 2025 First Aid Guidelines specify not to perform blind finger sweeps in the mouth, as this may push the object deeper; only remove solid objects with fingers if they are visible.
entries.sources: US National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Choking – adult or child over 1 year. <https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000047.htm>; Fuzhou Municipal Health Commission (2026). The Heimlich Maneuver Has Been Updated: "Toddlers, children over 1 year old, and adults: changed from the old version of abdominal thrusts alone to a cycle of '5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts'" "First aid training across the Red Cross Society of China system has always been taught using the '5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts' cycle approach". <https://www.fuzhou.gov.cn/zgfzzt/swjw/fzwj/jkkp/202601/t20260108_5268351.htm>; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, p. 238: "First aid providers should not use a blind finger sweep in people with a foreign-body airway obstruction as this may push the object further down the person's airway". <https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20International%20First%20Aid,%20Resuscitation%20and%20Education%20Guidelines%202025.pdf>
entries.notes: Do not stick fingers into the mouth to blindly retrieve unseen objects; doing so can push them deeper. Do not slap the back of someone who is still able to cough. The beneficiaries are mainly family members eating together. Domestic teaching methods also follow this set of protocols. The Fujian Red Cross Emergency Rescue Training Center noted that the Red Cross Society of China system has consistently taught this approach: cycling between 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts for children over 1 year old and adults. Many older online tutorials only teach abdominal thrusts, which reflects the outdated edition. For infants under 1 year old, do not compress the abdomen—switch to chest compressions, as detailed in Item 43 of this section (Choking in infants).

entries.title: If lost or vehicle breaks down in Gobi, desert, or uninhabited wilderness, stay put or by the car, report coordinates first, seek shade/warmth, conserve water, and do not wander off
entries.cost: Inform others of your route, destination, return date, and vehicle model/license plate before entering uninhabited wilderness. At least 4 liters of water per person per day. Satellite communicators or BeiDou short-message devices cost over 1,000 yuan to buy or several hundred yuan to rent once. The difficult part is sticking to "staying in place and not wandering off."
entries.summary: Stay in place or beside your vehicle; the car is your largest source of shade. The priority sequence is: send coordinates first when you have cell service, then call → seek shade and retain warmth → conserve water → do not wander off → signal for help using mirrors, smoke, or three fires. Tell others your route, destination, return date, vehicle model, and license plate before heading in.
entries.benefit: The US National Park Service Mojave National Preserve page has three direct quotes: "Carry at least 1 gallon (approx. 3.8 liters) of water per person per day, 2 gallons per person per day for hikers and cyclists." "Let someone know your route, destination, expected return date, and the make, model, and license plate of your vehicle." And "Cellular phone service is spotty at best." Death Valley original text: "Do not hike in the valley floor or at lower elevations during hot weather," wilderness areas have "almost no cellular phone service," and carrying a satellite phone is recommended. Mojave Desert Driving Safety original text: "In an emergency, staying with your vehicle is the single most important thing you can do." The page also adds that while uncommon, people have died from exposure to extreme heat or cold while attempting to walk back to the highway. Priorities break down into five steps: Step one is reporting safety status and coordinates—send your location first when you have service, then call. Step two is seeking shade and insulation—the vehicle provides the largest shelter. Step three is conserving water. Step four is not wandering off. Step five is signaling. Chongqing Emergency Management Bureau safety tip: three fires arranged in a triangle is an internationally recognized distress signal. If nearby, shout "three short, three long, then three short blasts," repeating after a 1-minute interval. In sunny conditions, use reflective surfaces like mirrors or can lids. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism reminds self-driving tourists to exercise caution before traveling to uninhabited areas, travel in multi-vehicle convoys whenever possible, and rent satellite phones when necessary.
entries.sources: US National Park Service. Mojave National Preserve Safety. <https://www.nps.gov/moja/planyourvisit/safety.htm> ; US National Park Service. Death Valley Safety. <https://www.nps.gov/deva/planyourvisit/safety.htm> ; US National Park Service. Desert Driving Safety. <https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/desertdrivingsafety.htm> ; Chongqing Municipal Emergency Management Bureau (2024). Emergency Science Popularization >> Distress Signals You Need to Know in the Wilderness (Infographic): "Lighting three fires is an internationally recognized distress signal, arranging the fire pits in a triangle" "Three short, three long, then three short; repeat after an interval of 1 minute". <https://yjj.cq.gov.cn/yjkp/scshaq/202409/t20240918_13639172.html> ; Ministry of Culture and Tourism (2018). Ministry of Culture and Tourism Reminds Tourists to Choose Outdoor Adventure Tourism with Caution: "Proceed with caution to uninhabited and sparsely populated areas" "Travel in multi-vehicle convoys as much as possible, prepare walkie-talkies in advance, and rent satellite phones when necessary". <https://www.mct.gov.cn/zxbs/cxts/201811/t20181127_836244.htm>
entries.notes: Grade C is assigned because these are official safety tips rather than study data. Water intake requirements, trip reporting, signal coverage, staying with the vehicle, and distress signals are all direct official statements. The popular "groups of three blasts" lacked an official primary source, so the officially recommended three fires and three short-three long-three short signals are used here. Do not hike to find a route at midday. Do not drink urine. Do not withhold drinking merely to ration water.

entries.title: Shivering, slurred speech, and stumbling indicate hypothermia; replace wet clothing, bundle up, warm the core first, and drink hot sweet beverages without alcohol
entries.cost: An aluminum foil emergency space blanket costs a few yuan, plus an extra set of dry spare clothes. Learning to recognize the warning signs is free.
entries.summary: A drop in body temperature below 35°C is hypothermia; the person will shiver, slur their speech, stumble when walking, and suffer impaired thinking. Replace wet clothes, wrap them in an emergency blanket or dry garments, and warm the torso first rather than hands and feet. Provide warm, sweet drinks; do not give alcohol, as alcohol suppresses shivering. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, perform CPR in accordance with Item 1 of this section (Press firmly on the center of the chest).
entries.benefit: US National Weather Service original text: A body temperature below 95°F (35°C) is hypothermia; "seek medical attention immediately if you feel cold and sluggish or are unable to think clearly." Treatment involves: "Seek medical attention immediately. Move the victim inside to a warm room. Warm the center of the body first," and offer warm beverages. "Alcohol will reduce shivering," so do not drink it. "If the victim is unconscious, perform CPR"; on determining whether compressions are needed, see Item 1 of this section (Not breathing normally). For frostbite, rewarm using warm water or body heat, and "do not use hot water or radiant heat like a fireplace." The Wilderness Medical Society 2019 hypothermia guidelines represent the clinical practice standard in this field.
entries.sources: US National Weather Service. During Extreme Cold. <https://www.weather.gov/safety/cold-during> ; Dow J et al. (2019). Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update. Wilderness & Environmental Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2019.10.002>
entries.notes: Do not rub hands or feet. Do not take a hot bath. Do not drag or pull forcefully when moving the person, as the hearts of those with severe hypothermia are prone to sudden arrest. Do not assume improvement just because they have "stopped shivering"; cessation of shivering (shivering stopping) indicates worsening. The full text of the Wilderness Medical Society guideline requires a subscription; only the abstract was verified this time.

entries.title: If bitten by a snake, sit down and do not move, remove rings and watches, and get to a hospital as soon as possible for antivenom; do not cut, do not suck, and do not tie off tightly
entries.cost: Costs no money. Know in advance which nearby hospital has antivenom. The hard part is resisting the urge to handle the wound yourself.
entries.summary: Sit down and do not move. Immobilize the bitten limb and first remove rings and watches to prevent constriction when swelling occurs. Transport to a hospital with antivenom as soon as possible; antivenom is the most effective means to prevent or reverse most toxic effects. Do not cut open, do not suck with the mouth, do not apply ice, do not rub, do not bind with rope, and do not walk around. If you can safely take a photo of the snake, take one, but do not try to catch it.
entries.benefit: The original WHO text has three key points. One is to "immediately and completely immobilize the bitten body part and transport quickly to the nearest medical facility for care." Another is to "avoid using tourniquets, and avoid cutting the wound." A third is to "treat with appropriate antivenom targeted to the local snake species." "High-quality antivenom is the most effective treatment to prevent or reverse most of the venomous effects of snakebites." Globally, approximately 81,000 to 138,000 people die each year from snakebites, and the number of amputations and permanent disabilities is roughly three times the number of deaths. China's 2024 snakebite treatment guideline estimates that there are 250,000 to 280,000 cases of venomous snakebites nationwide each year. Most of those bitten are people aged 50 and older. Hospitals in 11 provinces across the Yangtze River Basin and southern China admitted 40,817 snakebite patients between 2017 and 2021. During hospitalization, 23 people died (0.06%). The International Red Cross 2025 first aid guidelines explicitly state: the bitten individual should move as little as possible; if bitten on a leg, do not walk. Remove jewelry, watches, and tight clothing to prevent swelling from constricting blood flow. Do not use tourniquets, do not suck, do not apply cold compresses, do not rub, and do not cut open with a knife; these practices are ineffective and may cause further harm. If you can safely take a photo of the snake, do so; do not try to catch or kill it
entries.sources: WHO. Animal bites fact sheet. <https://www.who.int/zh/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/animal-bites> ; WHO (2023). Snakebite envenoming fact sheet. <https://www.who.int/zh/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming> ; Lai R et al. (2024). The Chinese guideline for management of snakebites. World Journal of Emergency Medicine 15(5):333-355: "An estimated 250,000–280,000 cases of venomous snakebites occur in China each year, affecting mainly patients aged ≥50 years". <https://doi.org/10.5847/wjem.j.1920-8642.2024.076> ; Yan S et al. (2026). Clinical epidemiology of snakebite envenoming in hospitals 11 provinces of Yangtze River Basin and southern regions of China. PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases: "withdrawal (4346, 10.65%), and death (23, 0.06%)". <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0013247> ; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 339–341: "Remove jewellery, watches or tight clothing to prevent blood flow being restricted if there is swelling" "The following actions are not effective and may even cause further harm: applying a tourniquet, sucking out the venom, applying a cold compress, rubbing the bite, cutting the wound with a knife to increase bleeding" "Do not try to catch or kill the snake. Consider taking a photo". <https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20International%20First%20Aid,%20Resuscitation%20and%20Education%20Guidelines%202025.pdf>
entries.notes: If you can take a photo of the snake, take one; do not try to catch it. Do not run, do not suck with the mouth, do not apply ice, and do not bind with rope. There are no official nationwide statistics for snakebite deaths in China. The inpatient mortality rate across those 11 provinces appears low, but more than 10% of patients discharged themselves against medical advice before completing treatment; what happened to them afterward is not included in the statistics.

entries.title: During an earthquake, first check what kind of building you are in: shelter in place in buildings meeting seismic design standards; get outside if you are in a collapsible old building and the door is only a few steps away
entries.cost: Costs no money. Take a look in advance at how many steps it takes to exit your home, which path to take, and which table is sturdy.
entries.summary: First, assess what kind of building you are in. In buildings constructed according to seismic codes, where exiting requires going down stairs or crossing a lobby, shelter in place: protect your head and neck, crawl under a sturdy table, and hold on tight to the table legs. In single-story houses, old brick buildings, or self-built houses lacking seismic design, if the door is only a few steps away, get outside. Under no circumstances should you jump from buildings, take elevators, or descend stairs while the ground is shaking.
entries.benefit: The rule of thumb in the China Earthquake Administration's popular science video *When an Earthquake Hits, Should You Shelter or Run?* is "shelter nearby during the shaking, evacuate rapidly after the shaking stops," explicitly qualified as "referring here to being inside buildings that meet seismic design requirements." The rationale is that such buildings have "a relatively low probability of complete structural collapse." The original text states that "falling architectural components and decorative items" "are in fact the greatest threat to life safety." Meanwhile, "running around blindly without protective measures during shaking" "on the contrary makes it easy to be struck and injured by falling ceilings, pendant lights (ceiling fans), and other objects." The procedure for sheltering is to "protect the head and neck with hands or other soft objects" "and firmly grip the table legs"; if there is no table, "rapidly crouch down tightly against a load-bearing wall" "and stay clear of exterior walls, windows, and balconies." "If outdoors," one "should evacuate immediately to an open space to take shelter." Looking at it from the opposite perspective, the 1988 Armenian earthquake involved widespread collapse of Soviet-era precast concrete panel buildings. The case-control study from that event noted that "leaving the building after the first shock was a protective behavior." People who stayed indoors were 4.40 times as likely to be injured compared to those who ran outside (odds ratio 4.40), 95% CI 2.24–8.71 (confidence interval). The likelihood of being injured inside a building was 12.20 times that of being outdoors (3.62–63.79). In buildings with 5 or more stories, it was 3.65 times that of lower buildings (2.12–6.33). Popular science materials on earthquakes from the Ministry of Emergency Management state: "People living in old brick-and-mortar buildings should more actively seek opportunities to evacuate rapidly." For those living in single-story houses, "if you happen to be next to a door or window, and there are no other hazardous buildings outside the window, you can flee immediately to open ground in the middle of the yard." During an earthquake, "never use elevators"; for those living on the first or second floor, "do not choose to jump from the building to escape either"; in high-rise buildings, "be mindful not to go downstairs." Once outdoors, steer clear of buildings with glass curtain walls, overpasses, utility poles, streetlights, and billboards
entries.sources: China Earthquake Administration (produced by Anhui Earthquake Agency). When an Earthquake Hits, Should You Shelter or Run? (popular science video, subtitle transcription). <https://www.cea.gov.cn/cea/dzpd/dzcs/5537260/index.html> ; Armenian HK, Noji EK, Oganesian AP (1992). A case-control study of injuries arising from the earthquake in Armenia, 1988. Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 70(2), 251-257. <https://europepmc.org/article/MED/1600585> ; US FEMA Ready.gov. Earthquakes. <https://www.ready.gov/earthquakes> ; Mahue-Giangreco M, Mack W, Seligson H, Bourque LB (2001). Risk factors associated with moderate and serious injuries attributable to the 1994 Northridge Earthquake. Annals of Epidemiology, 11(5), 347-357. <https://doi.org/10.1016/s1047-2797(01)00220-4> ; Ministry of Emergency Management (2019). Earthquake self-rescue manual, life-saving in critical moments! <https://www.mem.gov.cn/kp/zrzh/201904/t20190401_366172.shtml> ; Ministry of Emergency Management (2019). Common knowledge for earthquake hazard avoidance, self-rescue, and mutual rescue: "Never jump from buildings in panic" "Avoid tall buildings or structures: multistory buildings, especially buildings with glass curtain walls; pedestrian bridges, overpasses" "Avoid hazardous, towering, or suspended objects: transformers, utility poles, streetlights, billboards, cranes, etc." <https://www.mem.gov.cn/kp/zrzh/201902/t20190226_366163.shtml> ; Ministry of Emergency Management (2019). How to respond to an earthquake in different venues: "If in a high-rise, be mindful not to go downstairs". <https://www.mem.gov.cn/kp/zrzh/201903/t20190328_366164.shtml>
entries.notes: Controversial; the two opposing conclusions apply to two different types of buildings. The China Earthquake Administration itself sets the prerequisite for "sheltering" as being "inside buildings that meet seismic design requirements." It also calls for "adapting to local conditions" and "differing from person to person," taking into account together whether the building is earthquake-resistant, where you are located, and whether you are physically able to run. In Armenia, entire buildings collapsed; there was nowhere to shelter, so getting outside was advantageous. US FEMA gives advice for domestic housing as "drop, cover your head and neck, and hold on; do not run outside," where injuries mainly stem from falling objects and falls while moving during shaking. The Northridge study also suggested that reaching out to catch falling objects or steadying objects that "appear stable" exacerbated injuries. Therefore, merely asking "to run or not to run" is useless; one must judge "will this building collapse, and can you reach an open area within seconds?" In buildings meeting seismic design standards, where descending stairs or crossing a lobby is required, shelter in place. Identifying these as buildings constructed according to code after 2001 is a rough demarcation provided by the author; the official original text only states "meeting seismic design requirements." For single-story houses, older brick buildings, and self-built houses lacking seismic design, if the door is only a few steps away, get outside. The Armenia study only compared injured versus uninjured among survivors, did not factor in fatalities, and did not clarify whether the confounding effect of floor level was controlled for. Those who were able to run outside may have already lived on lower floors, so the figures should be taken with a grain of salt. Under no circumstances should you jump from buildings, take elevators, or descend stairs while shaking is ongoing. Once outdoors, stay far away from tall buildings, overpasses, utility poles, glass curtain walls, and billboards.

entries.title: When encountering bears, wild boars, or packs of stray dogs, do not run; turn sideways and back away slowly
entries.cost: Costs no money. Bring a trekking pole when entering mountains; walk in groups and make noise so animals know you are coming ahead of time. The hard part is standing your ground without running.
entries.summary: Do not run when encountering a bear; it can run uphill and downhill like a racehorse. Do not climb trees either; both black bears and brown bears can climb. Stand your ground, speak to it continuously in a low-pitched voice, and once it stops moving, turn sideways and slowly back away. If a brown bear charges, lie flat on the ground and play dead with hands clasped behind your neck; if a black bear charges, flee into a car or a building, and fight back if you cannot escape. For dog scratches and bites, flush and get vaccinated according to Item 13.
entries.benefit: The original US National Park Service text regarding bears contains six key statements. One is "Do not run, bears can run as fast as a racehorse both uphill and downhill." One is "Remain calm, most bears do not want to attack you; they usually just want to be left alone." One is "Continue to talk to the bear in low tones." One is "When the bear is stationary, move away slowly sideways; this allows you to keep an eye on the bear and avoid tripping." One is "Make yourself look as large as possible." And another is "Do not climb a tree; both grizzlies and black bears can climb trees." When attacked by a brown bear, "play dead, lie flat on your stomach with hands clasped behind your neck and spread your legs." When attacked by a black bear, "do not play dead, escape to a secure place such as a car or building; if escape is not possible, fight back using any available object." For dog bites, handle according to Item 13
entries.sources: US National Park Service. Staying Safe Around Bears. <https://www.nps.gov/subjects/bears/safety.htm> ; General Office of the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration, General Office of the National Health Commission (2023). Specifications for Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis and Management (2023 Edition). <https://www.ndcpa.gov.cn/jbkzzx/c100014/common/content/content_1706569159854649344.html>
entries.notes: Grade B corresponds only to bears. For wild boars and stray dogs, "do not run, retreat slowly, find high ground or obstacles to shield yourself" is empirical advice, rated as Grade C; official guidance from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration and local forestry departments was not identified this time. Do not use food to lure them, do not approach for photos, and do not bring dogs into mountains known to have wild boars. Bears in China are mostly black bears and brown bears; whether to play dead or not should be distinguished according to these two types.

entries.title: If caught in a thunderstorm in the wilderness, get inside a hard-topped vehicle or building; avoid ridges, isolated trees, bodies of water, and metal
entries.cost: Costs no money. The trade-off is having your itinerary interrupted for more than half an hour. The hard part is being willing to turn back while thunder is still distant.
entries.summary: There is no safe place outdoors within the vicinity of a thunderstorm. Get inside a hard-topped vehicle or a building; convertibles, motorcycles, tents, pavilions, staying under trees, or sheltering beneath overhangs do not count. Avoid open terrain, mountain ridges, hilltops, isolated large trees, bodies of water, and metal railings; if a group cannot leave, spread out. Evacuate upon hearing thunder; it is only safe once 30 minutes have passed after the last clap of thunder.
entries.benefit: There is no safe place outdoors within the vicinity of a thunderstorm. It is safe only after 30 minutes have passed since the last thunderclap. The US National Weather Service explicitly states: run into a substantial building or a hard-topped vehicle. Tents provide no protection against lightning strikes, and picnic shelters open on all sides are not safe either. Cave entrances and small rock overhangs are also dangerous, as electrical arcs can jump across the gap. Sheltering under a tree is the second leading cause of lightning casualties. If you hear thunder, you are likely already within striking distance of lightning: "When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors"
entries.sources: US National Weather Service. Outdoor Lightning Safety: "There is no safe place outside when thunderstorms are in the area" "Avoid open fields, the top of a hill or a ridge top. Stay away from tall, isolated trees or other tall objects" "Stay away from water, wet items, such as ropes, and metal objects, such as fences and poles"; when truly unable to leave: "If you are in a group, spread out to avoid the current traveling between group members"; resuming activities: "Wait 30 minutes until after the last rumble of thunder"; "Remember, a tent offers NO protection from lighting" "Do NOT seek shelter under the beach picnic shelters" "Cave entrances are dangerous during thunderstorms. Small overhangs can allow arcs to cross the gap". <https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-outdoors> ; US National Weather Service. Lightning Safety: "If you hear thunder, you are likely within striking distance of the storm" "When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors". <https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-safety> ; US National Weather Service. Lightning Myths: "Run to a substantial building or hard topped vehicle" "Being underneath a tree is the second leading cause of lightning casualties". <https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-myths>
entries.notes: Tents, pavilions, areas under trees, and rock overhangs do not count as shelters. Hard-topped vehicles do. Convertibles and motorcycles do not count; this is deduced by the author from the "hard-topped" criterion. Begin evacuating as soon as you hear thunder; do not wait until rain starts falling.

entries.title: When ascending to high altitude, climb slowly based on sleeping altitude (how high you sleep that night); descend if symptoms worsen, do not tough it out
entries.cost: Spend an extra one to two days acclimatizing. Prophylactic medications are prescription drugs, and you need to consult a doctor before departure. The hard part is being willing to set aside these days when your itinerary is tight.
entries.summary: What counts is how high you sleep, not how high you reached during the day; sleeping above 2,450 meters carries a risk of altitude illness. Once above 3,000 meters, increase your sleeping altitude by only 500 meters per night, and add an extra acclimatization day for every 1,000-meter gain. If you have a headache or nausea, do not sleep any higher; if symptoms worsen after rest, descend. If you are staggering when walking or gasping for breath even while resting, descending and supplemental oxygen work much better than taking medication.
entries.benefit: Sleeping above 2,450 meters carries a risk of altitude illness. High-altitude cerebral edema and pulmonary edema (fluid buildup in the brain and lungs) can be fatal if you do not descend to lower elevations in time. The U.S. CDC Yellow Book provides three rules to prevent severe illness: recognize early symptoms and be willing to admit them; when symptoms are present, no matter how minor, do not ascend to sleep at a higher altitude; if symptoms continue to worsen despite rest or treatment at the same elevation, descend. Acute mountain sickness usually improves rapidly upon descending 300 meters or more. In remote areas, initiate descent immediately for suspected high-altitude cerebral edema, using dexamethasone and oxygen together if available. In most cases, one must descend immediately for high-altitude pulmonary edema; both descent and supplemental oxygen are far more effective than taking medication.
entries.sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yellow Book · High-Altitude Travel & Altitude Illness: "Any unacclimatized traveler proceeding to a sleeping altitude of ≥2,450 m (≥8,000 ft)—and sometimes lower—is at risk for altitude illness"; ascent rate "500 m (1,650 ft) per night in sleeping altitude once above 3,000 m (9,800 ft)", add one acclimatization day for every 1,000 m gained; acetazolamide prophylaxis "125 mg twice a day; 250 mg twice a day if >100 kg body weight"; "If symptoms become worse despite rest or treatment at the same elevation" must descend; "Never ascend to sleep at a higher altitude when experiencing symptoms of altitude illness, no matter how minor the symptoms seem" "AMS improves rapidly with a descent of 300 m (1,000 ft) or more" "In remote areas, initiate descent for anyone suspected of having HACE" "Descent and oxygen are much more effective treatments than medication". <https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/high-altitude-travel-and-altitude-illness.html>; Wilderness Medical Society (2024). Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Acute Altitude Illness: 2024 Update. Wilderness & Environmental Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2023.05.013>
entries.notes: What counts is "how high you sleep," not how high you reached during the day. If symptoms appear, do not sleep at a higher altitude; if they worsen after rest, head down. Staggering while walking, changes in consciousness, or gasping for breath even while resting may indicate cerebral edema or pulmonary edema; in the wild, descend immediately. Taking medication cannot compare to descent and oxygen.

entries.title: If bitten by a tick, pull it out steadily with fine-tipped tweezers against the skin; do not apply oil or use fire
entries.cost: A pair of fine-tipped tweezers.
entries.summary: Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick's head close to the skin and pull it straight out steadily. Do not apply oil, do not use fire, and do not twist or jerk it; doing so can agitate it into squeezing pathogen-bearing fluids into the skin, and easily leaves the mouthparts behind in the flesh. Note the date after removal. If you develop a fever, rash, or fatigue in the following weeks, proactively tell your doctor that you were bitten by a tick.
entries.benefit: Applying oil, using fire, or twisting and pulling can agitate the tick, squeezing pathogen-bearing fluids into the skin. Doing so can also easily leave the part of its mouth lodged in the flesh (mouthparts) behind. In China, ticks transmit a disease called severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS). In 2024, 6,602 cases and 306 deaths were reported nationwide, both the highest levels since the disease was discovered. From 2010 to 2024, the average case fatality rate was 4.79%, increasing with age, reaching 9.15% among those aged 85 and above.
entries.sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. After a Tick Bite: "Grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible using clean fine-tipped tweezers" "Pull tick away from the skin with steady, even pressure" "Do not use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish, or other substances to try and make the tick detach from the skin. This may agitate the tick and force infected fluid from the tick into the skin". <https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html>; Ren Q et al. (2026). Epidemiological characteristics of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) in China, 2010–2024: a fifteen-year national surveillance analysis. BMC Infectious Diseases 26:1497: "The number of reported cases (6,602 cases) and deaths (306 cases) in 2024 were both the highest levels since the discovery of this disease" "The average CFR was 4.79%, and the CFR increased with age, reaching 9.15% among those aged 85 years and above". <https://doi.org/10.1186/s12879-026-14066-z>
entries.notes: Record the date after removing it. If you develop fever, rash, or fatigue in the following weeks, proactively mention that you were bitten by a tick when seeking medical care. If the doctor doesn't ask and you don't mention it, it can easily be treated as a common cold.

entries.title: Always boil water in the wild before drinking; a rolling boil for one minute is enough, and there is no need to boil longer due to elevation at common travel altitudes
entries.cost: The added weight of carrying a stove set and fuel.
entries.summary: All microorganisms capable of causing disease through drinking water die within seconds at boiling temperature. Boiling for an additional minute is merely a safety margin to account for misjudging the boiling point; at common travel altitudes, there is no need to boil longer due to high altitude. If you cannot boil water, use a filter or disinfectant tablets; each of these two methods leaves certain pathogens uncovered, so boil water if you can. Crystal-clear stream water may still harbor parasites.
entries.benefit: All microorganisms capable of causing illness from drinking water are killed (inactivated) within seconds at the temperature of boiling water. That "water does not boil adequately at high altitudes" is a common misconception. The same page notes that the other two methods each have shortcomings: most portable filters do not reliably remove viruses; chlorine and iodine barely kill parasites like Cryptosporidium at practical concentrations.
