Those engaged in driving, machinery operation, and high-altitude work should use them with caution. A US driving simulator trial enrolled 40 drivers with seasonal allergic rhinitis, aged 25 to 44. Each participant switched treatments at one-week intervals and drove for 1 hour under each condition: diphenhydramine 50 mg, fexofenadine 60 mg, alcohol to a blood alcohol concentration of approximately 0.1%, and placebo. Fexofenadine is a non-drowsy antiallergic medication. The ability to track the speed of a lead vehicle was worst after taking diphenhydramine, and noticeably better after drinking alcohol or taking fexofenadine. The ability to maintain lane position deteriorated after both alcohol and diphenhydramine. When a lead vehicle suddenly blocked the lane, reaction time was slowest after drinking alcohol, averaging 2.21 seconds, compared with 1.95 seconds after fexofenadine. Driving performance after fexofenadine was similar to that after placebo. The authors concluded that diphenhydramine's impairment on driving is even greater than that of alcohol. Drivers' self-reported degree of sleepiness did not reflect how well they drove; therefore, you cannot rely on "whether you feel sleepy" to determine whether you are fit to drive.
entries.sources: State Food and Drug Administration (2010). Adverse Drug Reaction Information Bulletin (Issue 32) Focusing on the Safety Issues of Chinese-Western Compound Preparation Vitamin C Yinqiao Tablets. <https://www.nmpa.gov.cn/xxgk/yjjsh/ypblfytb/20100919162601498.html>; National Medical Products Administration (2020). Top Ten Public Medication Tips for 2020 | (3) Use Cold Medicines with Caution: Safety and Rational Use Are Key. <https://www.nmpa.gov.cn/xxgk/kpzhsh/kpzhshyp/20201111095256170.html>; Weiler JM, Bloomfield JR, Woodworth GG, et al. (2000). Effects of fexofenadine, diphenhydramine, and alcohol on driving performance. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial in the Iowa driving simulator. Annals of Internal Medicine, 132(5):354-363. <https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-132-5-200003070-00004>; Road Traffic Safety Law of the People's Republic of China (2021 Amendment), Article 22, Paragraph 2. <https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff8081817ab231eb017abd617ef70519>
entries.notes: Drugs singled out by the drug administration—such as Fenmameimin (paracetamol, pseudoephedrine, dextromethorphan, and chlorpheniramine), compound paracetamol and amantadine, and Angahuangmin (paracetamol, caffeine, artificial cow-bezoar, and chlorpheniramine)—all contain chlorpheniramine; check the ingredient list before buying. What the Road Traffic Safety Law explicitly prohibits is driving after taking state-controlled psychotropic substances or narcotic drugs. Common cold medications and allergy medications are not included there; driving prohibitions are written in package inserts and drug administration advisories. If you must take them and also need to drive, ask a doctor or pharmacist to switch to a non-drowsy medicine. Many of these cold medicines also contain acetaminophen—see Section 34, Item 1 (Acetaminophen). For other risks of drowsy driving, see Section 1, Item 9 (Pull Over and Rest When Drowsy). The evidence is rated B because there is only one 40-person simulator trial and no real-world road crash numbers. The benefit is rated "Small": the endpoint is driving performance in a simulator, not crashes and fatalities. Besides yourself, beneficiaries include family members in the car and others on the road.

entries.title: If you take medications like lipid-lowering drugs or antihypertensives long-term, check first whether the package insert mentions grapefruit; if it does, do not eat grapefruit or pomelos, and do not drink grapefruit juice
entries.cost: Free. When you receive a medication intended for long-term use, flip through the package insert under "Drug Interactions" and "Precautions." If grapefruit is mentioned, do not eat grapefruit, pomelo, sour orange, or lime, nor drink their juice while taking the medication. If you love grapefruit, you can ask your doctor if you can switch to a drug that is not affected.
entries.summary: Grapefruit can elevate blood levels of certain medications to several times their normal level; even though the dose taken has not changed, it is equivalent to an overdose. A single grapefruit or a glass of grapefruit juice can have this effect, and some effect persists even if you take the medicine a day later. Severe cases can cause muscle damage, kidney damage, or potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Pomelos also have this effect; regular sweet oranges do not.
entries.benefit: A 2013 review by Canadian pharmacologists stated that more than 85 drugs are known or anticipated to interact with grapefruit. Among them, 43 can cause serious adverse reactions. Serious reactions include torsades de pointes, an arrhythmia that can lead to sudden death. Others include rhabdomyolysis (massive muscle destruction that harms the kidneys), myelosuppression, respiratory depression, gastrointestinal bleeding, and kidney damage. Furanocoumarins in grapefruit permanently inactivate an enzyme in the small intestine that metabolizes drugs (CYP3A4). When less drug is broken down in the gut, more enters the blood. A single whole grapefruit or 200 ml of juice is enough to raise drug concentrations in the blood to a clinically significant level. When the antihypertensive drug felodipine is taken with one serving of grapefruit, the drug level in the blood averages 3 times that when taken with plain water. Drinking the same 250 ml serving of juice ranges from 0-fold to 8-fold across different individuals. When the lipid-lowering drug simvastatin is taken with 200 ml of juice daily for 3 consecutive days, the total drug exposure in the blood (AUC) is 330% of that with plain water. For atorvastatin taken with juice, it is 180% to 250%. Pravastatin, rosuvastatin, and fluvastatin are not affected. Drinking 200 ml of juice within 4 hours before taking medication produces the greatest effect. Half the effect remains after 10 hours, and one-quarter remains after 24 hours. The review noted that Seville oranges (frequently used to make marmalade), limes, and pomelos have the same effect. Sweet oranges such as navel oranges and Valencia oranges do not contain furanocoumarins and do not have this effect. Public educational materials from the US FDA specifically singled out simvastatin, atorvastatin, and nifedipine. It states that when drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice, excessive amounts of lipid-lowering drugs remain in the body, increasing the risk of liver and muscle damage and potentially leading to kidney failure.
entries.sources: Bailey DG, Dresser G, Arnold JMO (2013). Grapefruit–medication interactions: forbidden fruit or avoidable consequences? CMAJ, 185(4):309-316. <https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.120951>；U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2021). Grapefruit Juice and Some Drugs Don't Mix. <https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/grapefruit-juice-and-some-drugs-dont-mix>
entries.notes: Not all medications are affected, and differences exist even within the same drug class. Commonly used drugs listed in that review include the lipid-lowering drugs simvastatin, lovastatin, and atorvastatin, and the antihypertensive drugs felodipine and nifedipine. Others include amiodarone, ticagrelor, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, domperidone, quetiapine, oxycodone, and others. Clopidogrel is the opposite: when combined with grapefruit, it will not work. If it is not mentioned in the package insert or you are uncertain, consult the prescribing physician or a pharmacist. The review noted that individuals over age 45 purchase the most grapefruit and take the most medications. When older adults take felodipine and consume grapefruit, their heart rate does not accelerate to compensate when blood pressure drops. The rating is set at B because the figures come from pharmacokinetic trials observing blood drug concentrations, whereas severe outcomes exist only as case reports. The benefit is rated as "small": the endpoint is blood drug concentration, and the studies cannot provide the number of adverse incidents that can be averted.
